Session IDs in URLs The Django sessions framework is entirely, and solely, cookie-based. It does not fall back to putting session IDs in URLs as a last resort, as PHP does. This is an intentional design decision. Not only does that behavior make URLs ugly, it makes your site vulnerable to session-ID theft via the “Referer” header. 3.4 Working with forms About this document This document provides an introduction to the basics of web forms and how they are handled in Django. For a more detailed look at specific areas of the forms API, see The Forms API, Form fields, and Form and field validation. Unless you’re planning to build websites and applications that do nothing but publish content, and don’t accept input from your visitors, you’re going to need to understand and use forms. Django provides a range of tools and libraries to help you build forms to accept input from site visitors, and then process and respond to the input. 3.4.1 HTML forms In HTML, a form is a collection of elements inside ... that allow a visitor to do things like enter text, select options, manipulate objects or controls, and so on, and then send that information back to the server. Some of these form interface elements - text input or checkboxes - are built into HTML itself. Others are much more complex; an interface that pops up a date picker or allows you to move a slider or manipulate controls will typically use JavaScript and CSS as well as HTML form elements to achieve these effects.

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



As well as its elements, a form must specify two things:

• where: the URL to which the data corresponding to the user’s input should be returned

• how: the HTTP method the data should be returned by

As an example, the login form for the Django admin contains several elements: one of type="text" for the username, one of type="password" for the password, and one of type="submit" for the “Log in” button. It also contains some hidden text fields that the user doesn’t see, which Django uses to determine what to do next.

It also tells the browser that the form data should be sent to the URL specified in the ’s action attribute-/admin/- and that it should be sent using the HTTP mechanism specified by the method attribute -post.

When the element is triggered, the data is returned to /admin/.



GET and POST



GET and POST are the only HTTP methods to use when dealing with forms.

Django’s login form is returned using the POST method, in which the browser bundles up the form data, encodes it for transmission, sends it to the server, and then receives back its response.

GET, by contrast, bundles the submitted data into a string, and uses this to compose a URL. The URL contains the address where the data must be sent, as well as the data keys and values. You can see this in action if you do a search in the Django documentation, which will produce a URL of the form https://docs. djangoproject.com/search/?q=forms&release=1.

GET and POST are typically used for different purposes.

Any request that could be used to change the state of the system - for example, a request that makes changes in the database - should use POST. GET should be used only for requests that do not affect the state of the system.

GET would also be unsuitable for a password form, because the password would appear in the URL, and thus, also in browser history and server logs, all in plain text. Neither would it be suitable for large quantities of data, or for binary data, such as an image. A web application that uses GET requests for admin forms is a security risk: it can be easy for an attacker to mimic a form’s request to gain access to sensitive parts of the system. POST, coupled with other protections like Django’s CSRF protection offers more control over access.

On the other hand, GET is suitable for things like a web search form, because the URLs that represent a GET request can easily be bookmarked, shared, or resubmitted.



Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



3.4.2 Django’s role in forms



Handling forms is a complex business. Consider Django’s admin, where numerous items of data of several different types may need to be prepared for display in a form, rendered as HTML, edited using a convenient interface, returned to the server, validated and cleaned up, and then saved or passed on for further processing.

Django’s form functionality can simplify and automate vast portions of this work, and can also do it more securely than most programmers would be able to do in code they wrote themselves.

Django handles three distinct parts of the work involved in forms:

• preparing and restructuring data to make it ready for rendering

• creating HTML forms for the data

• receiving and processing submitted forms and data from the client

It is possible to write code that does all of this manually, but Django can take care of it all for you.



3.4.3 Forms in Django



We’ve described HTML forms briefly, but an HTML is just one part of the machinery required.

In the context of a web application, ‘form’ might refer to that HTML , or to the Django Form that produces it, or to the structured data returned when it is submitted, or to the end-to-end working collection of these parts.



The Django Form class



At the heart of this system of components is Django’s Form class. In much the same way that a Django model

describes the logical structure of an object, its behavior, and the way its parts are represented to us, a Form class describes a form and determines how it works and appears.

In a similar way that a model class’s fields map to database fields, a form class’s fields map to HTML form

elements. (A ModelForm maps a model class’s fields to HTML form elements via a Form; this is what the Django admin is based upon.)

A form’s fields are themselves classes; they manage form data and perform validation when a form is sub-

mitted. A DateField and a FileField handle very different kinds of data and have to do different things with it.

A form field is represented to a user in the browser as an HTML “widget” - a piece of user interface machinery.

Each field type has an appropriate default Widget class, but these can be overridden as required.

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



Instantiating, processing, and rendering forms



When rendering an object in Django, we generally:

1. get hold of it in the view (fetch it from the database, for example)

2. pass it to the template context

3. expand it to HTML markup using template variables

Rendering a form in a template involves nearly the same work as rendering any other kind of object, but there are some key differences.

In the case of a model instance that contained no data, it would rarely if ever be useful to do anything with it in a template. On the other hand, it makes perfect sense to render an unpopulated form - that’s what we do when we want the user to populate it.

So when we handle a model instance in a view, we typically retrieve it from the database. When we’re dealing with a form we typically instantiate it in the view.

When we instantiate a form, we can opt to leave it empty or prepopulate it, for example with:

• data from a saved model instance (as in the case of admin forms for editing)

• data that we have collated from other sources

• data received from a previous HTML form submission

The last of these cases is the most interesting, because it’s what makes it possible for users not just to read a website, but to send information back to it too.



3.4.4 Building a form



The work that needs to be done



Suppose you want to create a simple form on your website, in order to obtain the user’s name. You’d need something like this in your template:

<form action ="/your-name/" method="post">

<label for="your_name">Your name: label>

<input id="your_name" type="text" name="your_name" value="{{ current_name }}"> <input type="submit" value="OK">

form>



This tells the browser to return the form data to the URL /your-name/, using the POST method. It will display a text field, labeled “Your name:”, and a button marked “OK”. If the template context contains a current_name variable, that will be used to pre-fill the your_name field.

You’ll need a view that renders the template containing the HTML form, and that can supply the current_name field as appropriate.

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



When the form is submitted, the POST request which is sent to the server will contain the form data.

Now you’ll also need a view corresponding to that /your-name/ URL which will find the appropriate key/value pairs in the request, and then process them.

This is a very simple form. In practice, a form might contain dozens or hundreds of fields, many of which might need to be prepopulated, and we might expect the user to work through the edit-submit cycle several times before concluding the operation.

We might require some validation to occur in the browser, even before the form is submitted; we might want to use much more complex fields, that allow the user to do things like pick dates from a calendar and so on.

At this point it’s much easier to get Django to do most of this work for us.



Building a form in Django



The Form class



We already know what we want our HTML form to look like. Our starting point for it in Django is this:



Listing 10: forms.py

from django import forms



class NameForm(forms.Form):

your_name = forms.CharField(label="Your name", max_length=100)



This defines a Form class with a single field (your_name). We’ve applied a human-friendly label to the field,

which will appear in the when it’s rendered (although in this case, the label we specified is actually the same one that would be generated automatically if we had omitted it).

The field’s maximum allowable length is defined by max_length. This does two things. It puts a maxlength="100" on the HTML (so the browser should prevent the user from entering more than that number of characters in the first place). It also means that when Django receives the form back from the browser, it will validate the length of the data.

A Form instance has an is_valid() method, which runs validation routines for all its fields. When this method is called, if all fields contain valid data, it will:

• return True

• place the form’s data in its cleaned_data attribute.

The whole form, when rendered for the first time, will look like:

<label for="your_name">Your name: label>

<input id="your_name" type="text" name="your_name" maxlength="100" required>

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



Note that it does not include the tags, or a submit button. We’ll have to provide those ourselves in the template.



The view



Form data sent back to a Django website is processed by a view, generally the same view which published the form. This allows us to reuse some of the same logic.

To handle the form we need to instantiate it in the view for the URL where we want it to be published:



Listing 11: views.py

from django.http import HttpResponseRedirect

from django.shortcuts import render



from .forms import NameForm



def get_name(request):

# if this is a POST request we need to process the form data if request.method == "POST":

# create a form instance and populate it with data from the request: form = NameForm(request.POST)

# check whether it's valid:

if form.is_valid():

# process the data in form.cleaned_data as required

# ...

# redirect to a new URL:

return HttpResponseRedirect("/thanks/")



# if a GET (or any other method) we'll create a blank form

else:

form = NameForm()



return render(request, "name.html", {"form": form})



If we arrive at this view with a GET request, it will create an empty form instance and place it in the template context to be rendered. This is what we can expect to happen the first time we visit the URL.

If the form is submitted using a POST request, the view will once again create a form instance and populate it with data from the request: form = NameForm(request.POST) This is called “binding data to the form” (it is now a bound form).

We call the form’s is_valid() method; if it’s not True, we go back to the template with the form. This time the form is no longer empty (unbound) so the HTML form will be populated with the data previously submitted, where it can be edited and corrected as required.

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



If is_valid() is True, we’ll now be able to find all the validated form data in its cleaned_data attribute. We can use this data to update the database or do other processing before sending an HTTP redirect to the browser telling it where to go next.



The template



We don’t need to do much in our name.html template:

<form action="/your-name/" method="post">

{% csrf_token %}

{{ form }}

<input type="submit" value="Submit">

form>



All the form’s fields and their attributes will be unpacked into HTML markup from that {{ form }} by Django’s template language.



Forms and Cross Site Request Forgery protection

Django ships with an easy-to-use protection against Cross Site Request Forgeries. When submitting a form

via POST with CSRF protection enabled you must use the csrf_token template tag as in the preceding ex-ample. However, since CSRF protection is not directly tied to forms in templates, this tag is omitted from the following examples in this document.



HTML5 input types and browser validation

If your form includes a URLField, an EmailField or any integer field type, Django will use the url, email and number HTML5 input types. By default, browsers may apply their own validation on these fields, which may be stricter than Django’s validation. If you would like to disable this behavior, set the novalidate attribute on the form tag, or specify a different widget on the field, like TextInput.



We now have a working web form, described by a Django Form, processed by a view, and rendered as an HTML .

That’s all you need to get started, but the forms framework puts a lot more at your fingertips. Once you understand the basics of the process described above, you should be prepared to understand other features of the forms system and ready to learn a bit more about the underlying machinery.



Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



3.4.5 More about Django Form classes



All form classes are created as subclasses of either django.forms.Form or django.forms.ModelForm. You can think of ModelForm as a subclass of Form. Form and ModelForm actually inherit common functionality from a (private) BaseForm class, but this implementation detail is rarely important.



Models and Forms

In fact if your form is going to be used to directly add or edit a Django model, a ModelForm can save you a great deal of time, effort, and code, because it will build a form, along with the appropriate fields and their attributes, from a Model class.



Bound and unbound form instances



The distinction between Bound and unbound forms is important:

• An unbound form has no data associated with it. When rendered to the user, it will be empty or will

contain default values.

• A bound form has submitted data, and hence can be used to tell if that data is valid. If an invalid bound

form is rendered, it can include inline error messages telling the user what data to correct.

The form’s is_bound attribute will tell you whether a form has data bound to it or not.



More on fields



Consider a more useful form than our minimal example above, which we could use to implement “contact me” functionality on a personal website:



Listing 12: forms.py

from django import forms



class ContactForm(forms.Form):

subject = forms.CharField(max_length=100)

message = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea)

sender = forms.EmailField()

cc_myself = forms.BooleanField(required=False)



Our earlier form used a single field, your_name, a CharField. In this case, our form has four fields: subject,

message, sender and cc_myself. CharField, EmailField and BooleanField are just three of the available

field types; a full list can be found in Form fields.

Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328



Widgets



Each form field has a corresponding Widget class, which in turn corresponds to an HTML form widget such as .

In most cases, the field will have a sensible default widget. For example, by default, a CharField will have a

TextInput widget, that produces an in the HTML. Likewise, fields such as <a href="index.html#page_1534"><i>IntegerField</i></a></p> <p>and <a href="index.html#page_1531"><i>FloatField</i></a> convert values to a Python int and float respectively.</p> <p>Here’s how the form data could be processed in the view that handles this form:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 13: views.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.mail</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">send_mail</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">subject</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cleaned_data[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"subject"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">message</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cleaned_data[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"message"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">sender</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cleaned_data[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"sender"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">cc_myself</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cleaned_data[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cc_myself"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">recipients</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"info@example.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cc_myself:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">recipients</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">append(sender)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">send_mail(subject, message, sender, recipients)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponseRedirect(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/thanks/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Tip: For more on sending email from Django, see <a href="index.html#page_634">Sending email.</a></p> <p id="page_337" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some field types need some extra handling. For example, files that are uploaded using a form need to be handled differently (they can be retrieved from request.FILES, rather than request.POST). For details of</p> <p>how to handle file uploads with your form, see <a href="index.html#page_1514">Binding uploaded files to a form</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.4.6 Working with form templates</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All you need to do to get your form into a template is to place the form instance into the template context. So if your form is called form in the context, {{ form }} will render its <label> and <input> elements appropriately.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Additional form template furniture</p> <p>Don’t forget that a form’s output does not include the surrounding <form> tags, or the form’s submit control. You will have to provide these yourself.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Reusable form templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The HTML output when rendering a form is itself generated via a template. You can control this by creating</p> <p>an appropriate template file and setting a custom <a href="index.html#page_1915"><i>FORM_RENDERER</i></a> to use that <a href="index.html#page_1551"><i>form_template_name</i></a> site-wide.</p> <p>You can also customize per-form by overriding the form’s <a href="index.html#page_1497"><i>template_name</i></a> attribute to render the form using</p> <p>the custom template, or by passing the template name directly to <a href="index.html#page_1497"><i>Form.render()</i></a>.</p> <p>The example below will result in {{ form }} being rendered as the output of the form_snippet.html tem-plate.</p> <p>In your templates:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># In your template:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># In form_snippet.html:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.label_tag</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}} {{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then you can configure the <a href="index.html#page_1915"><i>FORM_RENDERER</i></a> setting:</p> <p id="page_338"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 14: settings.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms.renderers</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplatesSetting</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomFormRenderer</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplatesSetting):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form_snippet.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">FORM_RENDERER</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"project.settings.CustomFormRenderer"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i> or for a single form:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form_snippet.html"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i> or for a single render of a form instance, passing in the template name to the <a href="index.html#page_1497"><i>Form.render()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1497">. </a>Here’s an example of this being used in a view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>index</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">rendered_form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">render(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"form_snippet.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"form"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: rendered_form}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"index.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1496">Outputting forms as HTML</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Reusable field group templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Each field is available as an attribute of the form, using {{ form.name_of_field }} in a template. A field</p> <p>has a <a href="index.html#page_1511"><i>as_field_group()</i></a> method which renders the related elements of the field as a group, its label, widget, errors, and help text.</p> <p>This allows generic templates to be written that arrange fields elements in the required layout. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.non_field_errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.subject.as_field_group</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.message.as_field_group</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_339" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.sender.as_field_group</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default Django uses the "django/forms/field.html" template which is designed for use with the default "django/forms/div.html" form style.</p> <p>The default template can be customized by setting <a href="index.html#page_1551"><i>field_template_name</i></a> in your project-level</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1915"><i>FORM_RENDERER</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms.renderers</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomFormRenderer</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplatesSetting):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span <p><i>. . .</i> or on a single field:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span <p><b>Rendering fields manually</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>More fine grained control over field rendering is also possible. <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Complete <label> elements can also be generated using the <a href="index.html#page_1511"><i>label_tag()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1511">. </a>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.subject</span> <span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Rendering form error messages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The price of this flexibility is a bit more work. Until now we haven’t had to worry about how to display form errors, because that’s taken care of for us. In this example we have had to make sure we take care of any errors for each field and any errors for the form as a whole. Note {{ form.non_field_errors }} at the top of the form and the template lookup for errors on each field.</p> <p>Using {{ form.name_of_field.errors }} displays a list of form errors, rendered as an unordered list. This might look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"errorlist"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Sender is required.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The list has a CSS class of errorlist to allow you to style its appearance. If you wish to further customize the display of errors you can do so by looping over them:</p> <p id="page_341" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.subject.errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ol</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">error</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.subject.errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">strong</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">error</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>|</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>escape</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">strong</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ol</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Non-field errors (and/or hidden field errors that are rendered at the top of the form when using helpers like form.as_p()) will be rendered with an additional class of nonfield to help distinguish them from field-specific errors. For example, {{ form.non_field_errors }} would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"errorlist nonfield"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Generic validation error</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1487">The Forms API</a> for more on errors, styling, and working with form attributes in templates.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Looping over the form’s fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using the same HTML for each of your form fields, you can reduce duplicate code by looping through each field in turn using a {% for %} loop:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Useful attributes on {{ field }} include:</p> <p><b>{{ field.errors }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Outputs a <ul class="errorlist"> containing any validation errors corresponding to this field. You can customize the presentation of the errors with a {% for error in field.errors %} loop. In this case, each object in the loop is a string containing the error message.</p> <p><b>{{ field.field }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1517"><i>Field</i></a> instance from the form class that this <a href="index.html#page_1507"><i>BoundField</i></a> wraps. You can use it to access <a href="index.html#page_1517"><i>Field</i></a> attributes, e.g. {{ char_field.field.max_length }}.</p> <p id="page_342"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>{{ field.help_text }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Any help text that has been associated with the field.</p> <p><b>{{ field.html_name }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The name of the field that will be used in the input element’s name field. This takes the form prefix into account, if it has been set.</p> <p><b>{{ field.id_for_label }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The ID that will be used for this field (id_email in the example above). If you are constructing the label manually, you may want to use this in lieu of label_tag. It’s also useful, for example, if you have some inline JavaScript and want to avoid hardcoding the field’s ID.</p> <p><b>{{ field.is_hidden }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This attribute is True if the form field is a hidden field and False otherwise. It’s not particularly useful as a template variable, but could be useful in conditional tests such as:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.is_hidden</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>{# Do something special #}</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>{{ field.label }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The label of the field, e.g. Email address.</p> <p><b>{{ field.label_tag }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The field’s label wrapped in the appropriate HTML <label> tag. <span style="float:right">This includes the form’s</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1503"><i>label_suffix</i> . </a>For example, the default label_suffix is a colon:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">label</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">for</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id_email"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Email address:</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">label</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>{{ field.legend_tag }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Similar to field.label_tag but uses a <legend> tag in place of <label>, for widgets with multiple inputs wrapped in a <fieldset>.</p> <p><b>{{ field.use_fieldset }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This attribute is True if the form field’s widget contains multiple inputs that should be semantically grouped in a <fieldset> with a <legend> to improve accessibility. An example use in a template:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.use_fieldset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fieldset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.label</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.legend_tag</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.label</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.label_tag</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p id="page_343" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>{{ field.value }}</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The value of the field. e.g someone@example.com.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>For a complete list of attributes and methods, see <a href="index.html#page_1507"><i>BoundField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Looping over hidden and visible fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re manually laying out a form in a template, as opposed to relying on Django’s default form layout, you might want to treat <input type="hidden"> fields differently from non-hidden fields. For example, because hidden fields don’t display anything, putting error messages “next to” the field could cause confusion for your users – so errors for those fields should be handled differently.</p> <p>Django provides two methods on a form that allow you to loop over the hidden and visible fields indepen-dently: hidden_fields() and visible_fields(). Here’s a modification of an earlier example that uses these two methods:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>{# Include the hidden fields #}</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">hidden</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.hidden_fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">hidden</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>{# Include the visible fields #}</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form.visible_fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fieldWrapper"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field.label_tag</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}} {{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example does not handle any errors in the hidden fields. Usually, an error in a hidden field is a sign of form tampering, since normal form interaction won’t alter them. However, you could easily insert some error displays for those form errors, as well.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.4.7 Further topics</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This covers the basics, but forms can do a whole lot more:</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_344"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Formsets</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BaseFormSet</b></p> <p>A formset is a layer of abstraction to work with multiple forms on the same page. It can be best compared to a data grid. Let’s say you have the following form:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ArticleForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">title</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pub_date</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You might want to allow the user to create several articles at once. To create a formset out of an ArticleForm you would do:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You now have created a formset class named ArticleFormSet. Instantiating the formset gives you the ability to iterate over the forms in the formset and display them as you would with a regular form:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(form)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-title">Title:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-title" id="id_form-</span><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0-title"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-pub_date">Pub date:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-pub_date" id=</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id_form-0-pub_date"></div></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As you can see it only displayed one empty form. The number of empty forms that is displayed is controlled</p> <p>by the extra parameter. By default, <a href="index.html#page_1550"><i>formset_factory()</i></a> defines one extra form; the following example will create a formset class to display two blank forms:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm, extra</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Formsets can be iterated and indexed, accessing forms in the order they were created. You can reorder the</p> <p>forms by overriding the default <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__iter__">iteration</a> and <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__getitem__">indexing</a> behavior if needed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_345" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using initial data with a formset</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Initial data is what drives the main usability of a formset. As shown above you can define the number of extra forms. What this means is that you are telling the formset how many additional forms to show in addition to the number of forms it generates from the initial data. Let’s take a look at an example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm, extra</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">initial</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"title"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Django is now open source"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"pub_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: datetime</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">date</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">today(),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(form)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-title">Title:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-title" value=</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Django is now open source" id="id_form-0-title"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-pub_date">Pub date:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-pub_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">␣</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">value="2023-02-11" id="id_form-0-pub_date"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-1-title">Title:</label><input type="text" name="form-1-title" id="id_form-</span><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1-title"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-1-pub_date">Pub date:</label><input type="text" name="form-1-pub_date" id=</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id_form-1-pub_date"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-2-title">Title:</label><input type="text" name="form-2-title" id="id_form-</span><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2-title"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-2-pub_date">Pub date:</label><input type="text" name="form-2-pub_date" id=</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id_form-2-pub_date"></div></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are now a total of three forms showing above. One for the initial data that was passed in and two extra forms. Also note that we are passing in a list of dictionaries as the initial data.</p> <p>If you use an initial for displaying a formset, you should pass the same initial when processing that formset’s submission so that the formset can detect which forms were changed by the user. For example, you might have something like: ArticleFormSet(request.POST, initial=[...]).</p> <p>See also:</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_379">Creating formsets from models with model formsets.</a></p> <p id="page_346"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Limiting the maximum number of forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The max_num parameter to <a href="index.html#page_1550"><i>formset_factory()</i></a> gives you the ability to limit the number of forms the formset will display:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm, extra</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, max_num</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(form)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-title">Title:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-title" id="id_form-</span><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0-title"></div></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><div><label for="id_form-0-pub_date">Pub date:</label><input type="text" name="form-0-pub_date" id=</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id_form-0-pub_date"></div></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the value of max_num is greater than the number of existing items in the initial data, up to extra additional blank forms will be added to the formset, so long as the total number of forms does not exceed max_num. For example, if extra=2 and max_num=2 and the formset is initialized with one initial item, a form for the initial item and one blank form will be displayed.</p> <p>If the number of items in the initial data exceeds max_num, all initial data forms will be displayed regardless of the value of max_num and no extra forms will be displayed. For example, if extra=3 and max_num=1 and the formset is initialized with two initial items, two forms with the initial data will be displayed.</p> <p>A max_num value of None (the default) puts a high limit on the number of forms displayed (1000). In practice this is equivalent to no limit.</p> <p>By default, max_num only affects how many forms are displayed and does not affect validation. If</p> <p>validate_max=True is passed to the <a href="index.html#page_1550"><i>formset_factory()</i>, </a>then max_num will affect validation. See <a href="index.html#page_352">vali-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_352">date_max.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Limiting the maximum number of instantiated forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The absolute_max parameter to <a href="index.html#page_1550"><i>formset_factory()</i></a> allows limiting the number of forms that can be in-stantiated when supplying POST data. This protects against memory exhaustion attacks using forged POST requests:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms.formsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm, absolute_max</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1500</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-TOTAL_FORMS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"1501"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_347" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-INITIAL_FORMS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet(data)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">len</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">forms)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1500</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">False</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">non_form_errors()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">['Please submit at most 1000 forms.']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When absolute_max is None, it defaults to max_num + 1000. (If max_num is None, it defaults to 2000).</p> <p>If absolute_max is less than max_num, a ValueError will be raised.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Formset validation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Validation with a formset is almost identical to a regular Form. There is an is_valid method on the formset to provide a convenient way to validate all forms in the formset:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset_factory(ArticleForm)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-TOTAL_FORMS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"1"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-INITIAL_FORMS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet(data)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We passed in no data to the formset which is resulting in a valid form. The formset is smart enough to ignore extra forms that were not changed. If we provide an invalid article:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As we can see, formset.errors is a list whose entries correspond to the forms in the formset. Validation was performed for each of the two forms, and the expected error message appears for the second item.</p> <p>Just like when using a normal Form, each field in a formset’s forms may include HTML attributes such as maxlength for browser validation. However, form fields of formsets won’t include the required attribute as that validation may be incorrect when adding and deleting forms.</p> <p>BaseFormSet.<b>total_error_count</b>()</p> <p>To check style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Understanding the ManagementForm</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You may have noticed the additional data (form-TOTAL_FORMS, form-INITIAL_FORMS) that was required in the formset’s data above. This data is required for the ManagementForm. This form is used by the formset to manage the collection of forms contained in the formset. If you don’t provide this management data, the formset will be invalid:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-0-title"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Test"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_349" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form-0-pub_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet(data)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">False</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is used to keep track of how many form instances are being displayed. If you are adding new forms via JavaScript, you should increment the count fields in this form as well. On the other hand, if you are using JavaScript to allow deletion of existing objects, then you need to ensure the ones being removed are properly marked for deletion by including form-#-DELETE in the POST data. It is expected that all forms are present in the POST data regardless.</p> <p>The management form is available as an attribute of the formset itself. When rendering a formset in a tem-plate, you can include all the management data by rendering {{ my_formset.management_form }} (substi-tuting the name of your formset as appropriate).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: As well as the form-TOTAL_FORMS and form-INITIAL_FORMS fields shown in the examples here, the management form also includes form-MIN_NUM_FORMS and form-MAX_NUM_FORMS fields. They are output with the rest of the management form, but only for the convenience of client-side code. These fields are not required and so are not shown in the example POST data.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>total_form_count and initial_form_count</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseFormSet has a couple of methods that are closely related to the ManagementForm, total_form_count and initial_form_count.</p> <p>total_form_count returns the total number of forms in this formset. initial_form_count returns the number of forms in the formset that were pre-filled, and is also used to determine how many forms are required. You will probably never need to override either of these methods, so please be sure you understand what they do before doing so.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>empty_form</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseFormSet provides an additional attribute empty_form which returns a form instance with a prefix of __prefix__ for easier use in dynamic forms with JavaScript.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_350"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>error_messages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The error_messages argument lets you override the default messages that the formset will raise. Pass in a dictionary with keys matching the error messages you want to override. Error message keys in-clude 'too_few_forms', 'too_many_forms', and 'missing_management_form'. The 'too_few_forms' and 'too_many_forms' error messages may contain %(num)d, which will be replaced with min_num and max_num, respectively.</p> <p>For example, here is the default error message when the management form is missing:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ArticleFormSet({})</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">False</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">formset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">non_form_errors()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">['ManagementForm data is missing or has been tampered with. clean method is called after all the Form.clean methods have been called. The errors will be found using the non_form_errors() method on the formset.</p> <p>Non-form errors will be rendered with an additional class of nonform to help distinguish them from form-specific errors. For example, {{ formset.non_form_errors }} would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"errorlist nonform"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Articles in a set must have distinct titles.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_352"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Validating the number of forms in a formset</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides a couple ways to validate the minimum or maximum number of submitted forms. style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In the rendered HTML, formsets include a prefix on each field’s name. By default, the prefix is 'form', but it can be customized using the formset’s prefix argument.</p> <p>For example, in the default case, you might see:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">label</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">for</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span
