For full details, see the <a href="index.html#page_949">class-based views reference documentation.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.1 Introduction to class-based views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Class-based views provide an alternative way to implement views as Python objects instead of functions. They do not replace function-based views, but have certain differences and advantages when compared to function-based views:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Organization of code related to specific HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.) can be addressed by separate</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">methods instead of conditional branching.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Object oriented techniques such as mixins (multiple inheritance) can be used to factor code into reusable</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">components.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The relationship and history of generic views, class-based views, and class-based generic views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In the beginning there was only the view function contract, Django passed your function an <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a></p> <p>and expected back an <a href="index.html#page_1871"><i>HttpResponse</i></a>. This was the extent of what Django provided.</p> <p>Early on it was recognized that there were common idioms and patterns found in view development. Function-based generic views were introduced to abstract these patterns and ease view development for the common cases.</p> <p>The problem with function-based generic views is that while they covered the simple cases well, there was no way to extend or customize them beyond some configuration options, limiting their usefulness in many</p> <p id="page_411" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>real-world applications.</p> <p>Class-based generic views were created with the same objective as function-based generic views, to make view development easier. However, the way the solution is implemented, through the use of mixins, provides a toolkit that results in class-based generic views being more extensible and flexible than their function-based counterparts.</p> <p>If you have tried function based generic views in the past and found them lacking, you should not think of class-based generic views as a class-based equivalent, but rather as a fresh approach to solving the original problems that generic views were meant to solve.</p> <p>The toolkit of base classes and mixins that Django uses to build class-based generic views are built for max-imum flexibility, and as such have many hooks in the form of default method implementations and at-tributes that you are unlikely to be concerned with in the simplest use cases. For example, instead of limiting you to a class-based attribute for form_class, the implementation uses a get_form method, which calls a get_form_class method, which in its default implementation returns the form_class attribute of the class. This gives you several options for specifying what form to use, from an attribute, to a fully dynamic, callable hook. These options seem to add hollow complexity for simple situations, but without them, more advanced designs would be limited.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using class-based views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>At its core, a class-based view allows you to respond to different HTTP request methods with different class instance methods, instead of with conditionally branching code inside a single view function.</p> <p>So where the code to handle HTTP GET in a view function would look something like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">method</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"GET"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># <view logic></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"result"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In a class-based view, this would become:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">View</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(View):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># <view logic></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"result"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p id="page_412"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because Django’s URL resolver expects to send the request and associated arguments to a callable function,</p> <p>not a class, class-based views have an <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> class method which returns a function that can be called when a request arrives for a URL matching the associated pattern. The function creates an instance of the</p> <p>class, calls <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>setup()</i></a> to initialize its attributes, and then calls its <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>dispatch()</i></a> method. dispatch looks at the request to determine whether it is a GET, POST, etc, and relays the request to a matching method if one is</p> <p>defined, or raises <a href="index.html#page_1877"><i>HttpResponseNotAllowed</i></a> if not:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># urls.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, MyView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is worth noting that what your method returns is identical to what you return from a function-based view,</p> <p>namely some form of <a href="index.html#page_1871"><i>HttpResponse</i></a>. This means that <a href="index.html#page_297">http shortcuts</a> or <a href="index.html#page_2054"><i>TemplateResponse</i></a> objects are valid to use inside a class-based view.</p> <p>While a minimal class-based view does not require any class attributes to perform its job, class attributes are useful in many class-based designs, and there are two ways to configure or set class attributes.</p> <p>The first is the standard Python way of subclassing and overriding attributes and methods in the subclass. So that if your parent class had an attribute greeting like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">View</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>GreetingView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(View):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">greeting</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Good Day"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">greeting)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can override that in a subclass:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MorningGreetingView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(GreetingView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">greeting</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Morning to ya"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another option is to configure class attributes as keyword arguments to the <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> call in the URLconf:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, GreetingView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view(greeting</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"G'day"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p id="page_413" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: While your class is instantiated for each request dispatched to it, class attributes set through the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> entry point are configured only once at the time your URLs are imported.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using mixins</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Mixins are a form of multiple inheritance where behaviors and attributes of multiple parent classes can be combined.</p> <p>For example, in the generic class-based views there is a mixin called <a href="index.html#page_979"><i>TemplateResponseMixin</i></a> whose pri-</p> <p>mary purpose is to define the method <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>render_to_response()</i>. </a>When combined with the behavior of the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_950"><i>View</i></a> base class, the result is a <a href="index.html#page_952"><i>TemplateView</i></a> class that will dispatch requests to the appropriate match-</p> <p>ing methods (a behavior defined in the View base class), and that has a <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>render_to_response()</i></a> method</p> <p>that uses a <a href="index.html#page_979"><i>template_name</i></a> attribute to return a <a href="index.html#page_2054"><i>TemplateResponse</i></a> object (a behavior defined in the TemplateResponseMixin).</p> <p>Mixins are an excellent way of reusing code across multiple classes, but they come with some cost. The more your code is scattered among mixins, the harder it will be to read a child class and know what exactly it is doing, and the harder it will be to know which methods from which mixins to override if you are subclassing something that has a deep inheritance tree.</p> <p>Note also that you can only inherit from one generic view - that is, only one parent class may inherit from</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_950"><i>View</i></a> and the rest (if any) should be mixins. Trying to inherit from more than one class that inherits from</p> <p>View- for example, trying to use a form at the top of a list and combining <a href="index.html#page_989"><i>ProcessFormView</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_957"><i>ListView</i></a>- won’t work as expected.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handling forms with class-based views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A basic function-based view that handles forms may look something like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponseRedirect</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>myview</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">method</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"POST"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm(request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">POST)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># <process form cleaned data></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponseRedirect(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/success/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_414"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm(initial</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"value"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form_template.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"form"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: form})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A similar class-based view might look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponseRedirect</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">View</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyFormView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(View):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_class</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyForm</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">initial</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"value"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"form_template.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_class(initial</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">initial)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"form"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: form})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>post</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_class(request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">POST)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_valid():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># <process form cleaned data></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponseRedirect(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/success/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"form"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: form})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This is a minimal case, but you can see that you would then have the option of customizing this view by over-riding any of the class attributes, e.g. form_class, via URLconf configuration, or subclassing and overriding one or more of the methods (or both!).</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_415" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Decorating class-based views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The extension of class-based views isn’t limited to using mixins. You can also use decorators. Since class-based views aren’t functions, decorating them works differently depending on if you’re using as_view() or creating a subclass.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Decorating in URLconf</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can adjust class-based views by decorating the result of the <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> method. The easiest place to do this is in the URLconf where you deploy your view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.decorators</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">login_required, permission_required</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplateView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">VoteView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, login_required(TemplateView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view(template_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"vote/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, permission_required(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"polls.can_vote"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)(VoteView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view())),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This approach applies the decorator on a per-instance basis. If you want every instance of a view to be decorated, you need to take a different approach.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Decorating the class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To decorate every instance of a class-based view, you need to decorate the class definition itself. To do this</p> <p>you apply the decorator to the <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>dispatch()</i></a> method of the class.</p> <p>A method on a class isn’t quite the same as a standalone function, so you can’t just apply a function decorator to the method – you need to transform it into a method decorator first. The method_decorator decorator transforms a function decorator into a method decorator so that it can be used on an instance method. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.decorators</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">login_required</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.decorators</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">method_decorator</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplateView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ProtectedView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@method_decorator(login_required)</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_416"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>dispatch</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dispatch(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Or, more succinctly, you can decorate the class instead and pass the name of the method to be decorated as the keyword argument name:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@method_decorator(login_required, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dispatch"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ProtectedView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have a set of common decorators used in several places, you can define a list or tuple of decorators and use this instead of invoking method_decorator() multiple times. These two classes are equivalent:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">decorators</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[never_cache, login_required]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@method_decorator(decorators, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dispatch"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ProtectedView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@method_decorator(never_cache, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dispatch"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@method_decorator(login_required, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dispatch"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ProtectedView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The decorators will process a request in the order they are passed to the decorator. In the example, never_cache() will process the request before login_required().</p> <p>In this example, every instance of ProtectedView will have login protection. These examples use</p> <p>login_required, however, the same behavior can be obtained by using <a href="index.html#page_541"><i>LoginRequiredMixin</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: method_decorator passes *args and **kwargs as parameters to the decorated method on the class. If your method does not accept a compatible set of parameters it will raise a TypeError exception.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_417" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.2 Built-in class-based generic views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Writing web applications can be monotonous, because we repeat certain patterns again and again. Django tries to take away some of that monotony at the model and template layers, but web developers also expe-rience this boredom at the view level.</p> <p>Django’s generic views were developed to ease that pain. They take certain common idioms and patterns found in view development and abstract them so that you can quickly write common views of data without having to write too much code.</p> <p>We can recognize certain common tasks, like displaying a list of objects, and write code that displays a list of any object. Then the model in question can be passed as an extra argument to the URLconf.</p> <p>Django ships with generic views to do the following:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Display list and detail pages for a single object. If we were creating an application to manage confer-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ences then a TalkListView and a RegisteredUserListView would be examples of list views. A single talk page is an example of what we call a “detail” view.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Present date-based objects in year/month/day archive pages, associated detail, and “latest” pages.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Allow users to create, update, and delete objects – with or without authorization.</p> <p>Taken together, these views provide interfaces to perform the most common tasks developers encounter.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Extending generic views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There’s no question that using generic views can speed up development substantially. In most projects, however, there comes a moment when the generic views no longer suffice. Indeed, the most common question asked by new Django developers is how to make generic views handle a wider array of situations.</p> <p>This is one of the reasons generic views were redesigned for the 1.3 release - previously, they were view functions with a bewildering array of options; now, rather than passing in a large amount of configuration in the URLconf, the recommended way to extend generic views is to subclass them, and override their attributes or methods.</p> <p>That said, generic views will have a limit. If you find you’re struggling to implement your view as a subclass of a generic view, then you may find it more effective to write just the code you need, using your own class-based or functional views.</p> <p>More examples of generic views are available in some third party applications, or you could write your own as needed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_418"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Generic views of objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_952"><i>TemplateView</i></a> certainly is useful, but Django’s generic views really shine when it comes to presenting views of your database content. Because it’s such a common task, Django comes with a handful of built-in generic views to help generate list and detail views of objects.</p> <p>Let’s start by looking at some examples of showing a list of objects or an individual object.</p> <p>We’ll be using these models:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># models.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Publisher</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">publication_date</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now we need to define a view:</p> <p id="page_419" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># views.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PublisherListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally hook that view into your urls:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># urls.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PublisherListView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"publishers/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, PublisherListView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That’s all the Python code we need to write. We still need to write a template, however. We could explicitly tell the view which template to use by adding a template_name attribute to the view, but in the absence of an explicit template Django will infer one from the object’s name. In this case, the inferred template will be "books/publisher_list.html" – the “books” part comes from the name of the app that defines the model, while the “publisher” bit is the lowercased version of the model’s name.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Thus, when (for example) the APP_DIRS option of a DjangoTemplates backend is set to True in</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1932"><i>TEMPLATES</i></a> , a template location could be: /path/to/project/books/templates/books/publisher_list.html</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This template will be rendered against a context containing a variable called object_list that contains all the publisher objects. A template might look like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>extends</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"base.html"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>block</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">content</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">h2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Publishers</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">h2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">publisher</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">object_list</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">publisher.name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endblock</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That’s really all there is to it. All the cool features of generic views come from changing the attributes set</p> <p>on the generic view. The <a href="index.html#page_949">generic views reference</a> documents all the generic views and their options in detail;</p> <p id="page_420"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>the rest of this document will consider some of the common ways you might customize and extend generic views.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Making “friendly” template contexts</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You might have noticed that our sample publisher list template stores all the publishers in a variable named object_list. While this works just fine, it isn’t all that “friendly” to template authors: they have to “just know” that they’re dealing with publishers here.</p> <p>Well, if you’re dealing with a model object, this is already done for you. When you are dealing with an object or queryset, Django is able to populate the context using the lowercased version of the model class’ name. This is provided in addition to the default object_list entry, but contains exactly the same data, i.e. publisher_list.</p> <p>If this still isn’t a good match, you can manually set the name of the context variable. <span style="float:right">The</span></p> <p>context_object_name attribute on a generic view specifies the context variable to use:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># views.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PublisherListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context_object_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_favorite_publishers"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Providing a useful context_object_name is always a good idea. Your coworkers who design templates will thank you.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Adding extra context</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Often you need to present some extra information beyond that provided by the generic view. For example,</p> <p>think of showing a list of all the books on each publisher detail page. The <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a> generic view provides the publisher to the context, but how do we get additional information in that template?</p> <p>The answer is to subclass <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a> and provide your own implementation of the get_context_data method. The default implementation adds the object being displayed to the template, but you can over-ride it to send more:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DetailView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book, Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PublisherDetailView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(DetailView):</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_421" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_context_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Call the base implementation first to get a context</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_context_data(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Add in a QuerySet of all the books</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"book_list"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Generally, get_context_data will merge the context data of all parent classes with those of the current class. To preserve this behavior in your own classes where you want to alter the context, you should be sure to call get_context_data on the super class. When no two classes try to define the same key, this will give the expected results. However if any class attempts to override a key after parent classes have set it (after the call to super), any children of that class will also need to explicitly set it after super if they want to be sure to override all parents. If you’re having trouble, review the method resolution order of your view.</p> <p>Another consideration is that the context data from class-based generic views will override data provided by</p> <p>context processors; see <a href="index.html#page_981"><i>get_context_data()</i></a> for an example.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Viewing subsets of objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now let’s take a closer look at the model argument we’ve been using all along. The model argument, which specifies the database model that the view will operate upon, is available on all the generic views that operate on a single object or a collection of objects. However, the model argument is not the only way to specify the objects that the view will operate upon – you can also specify the list of objects using the queryset argument:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DetailView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PublisherDetailView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(DetailView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context_object_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"publisher"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">queryset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Publisher</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Specifying model = Publisher is shorthand for saying queryset = Publisher.objects.all(). However, by using queryset to define a filtered list of objects you can be more specific about the objects that will be</p> <p>visible in the view (see <a href="index.html#page_143">Making queries</a> for more information about <a href="index.html#page_1709"><i>QuerySet</i></a> objects, and see the <a href="index.html#page_949">class-based</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_949">views reference</a> for the complete details).</p> <p>To pick an example, we might want to order a list of books by publication date, with the most recent first:</p> <p id="page_422"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>BookListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">queryset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">order_by(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"-publication_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context_object_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"book_list"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That’s a pretty minimal example, but it illustrates the idea nicely. You’ll usually want to do more than just reorder objects. If you want to present a list of books by a particular publisher, you can use the same technique:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AcmeBookListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context_object_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"book_list"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">queryset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(publisher__name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ACME Publishing"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"books/acme_list.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Notice that along with a filtered queryset, we’re also using a custom template name. If we didn’t, the generic view would use the same template as the “vanilla” object list, which might not be what we want.</p> <p>Also notice that this isn’t a very elegant way of doing publisher-specific books. If we want to add another publisher page, we’d need another handful of lines in the URLconf, and more than a few publishers would get unreasonable. We’ll deal with this problem in the next section.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you get a 404 when requesting /books/acme/, check to ensure you actually have a Publisher with</p> <p>the name ‘ACME Publishing’. Generic views have an allow_empty parameter for this case. See the <a href="index.html#page_949">class-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_949">based-views reference</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Dynamic filtering</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another common need is to filter down the objects given in a list page by some key in the URL. Earlier we hard-coded the publisher’s name in the URLconf, but what if we wanted to write a view that displayed all the books by some arbitrary publisher?</p> <p>Handily, the ListView has a <a href="index.html#page_984"><i>get_queryset()</i></a> method we can override. By default, it returns the value of the queryset attribute, but we can use it to add more logic.</p> <p>The key part to making this work is that when class-based views are called, various useful things are stored on self; as well as the request (self.request) this includes the positional (self.args) and name-based</p> <p id="page_423" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>(self.kwargs) arguments captured according to the URLconf.</p> <p>Here, we have a URLconf with a single captured group:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># urls.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PublisherBookListView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"books/<publisher>/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, PublisherBookListView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, we’ll write the PublisherBookListView view itself:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># views.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">get_object_or_404</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book, Publisher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PublisherBookListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"books/books_by_publisher.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_queryset</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">publisher</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">get_object_or_404(Publisher, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"publisher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(publisher</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">publisher)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Using get_queryset to add logic to the queryset selection is as convenient as it is powerful. For instance, if we wanted, we could use self.request.user to filter using the current user, or other more complex logic.</p> <p>We can also add the publisher into the context at the same time, so we can use it in the template:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_context_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Call the base implementation first to get a context</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_context_data(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Add in the publisher</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">context[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"publisher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">publisher</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_424"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Performing extra work</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The last common pattern we’ll look at involves doing some extra work before or after calling the generic view.</p> <p>Imagine we had a last_accessed field on our Author model that we were using to keep track of the last time anybody looked at that author:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># models.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Author</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">salutation</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">200</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">email</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">EmailField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">headshot</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ImageField(upload_to</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"author_headshots"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_accessed</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateTimeField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The generic DetailView class wouldn’t know anything about this field, but once again we could write a custom view to keep that field updated.</p> <p>First, we’d need to add an author detail bit in the URLconf to point to a custom view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthorDetailView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"authors/<int:pk>/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, AuthorDetailView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view(), name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"author-detail"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then we’d write our new view – get_object is the method that retrieves the object – so we override it and wrap the call:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DetailView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Author</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AuthorDetailView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(DetailView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">queryset</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Author</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_object</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_object()</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_425" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Record the last accessed date</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_accessed</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">now()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The URLconf here uses the named group pk- this name is the default name that DetailView uses to find the value of the primary key used to filter the queryset.</p> <p>If you want to call the group something else, you can set <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>pk_url_kwarg</i></a> on the view.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.3 Form handling with class-based views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Form processing generally has 3 paths:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Initial GET (blank or prepopulated form)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• POST with invalid data (typically redisplay form with errors)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• POST with valid data (process the data and typically redirect)</p> <p>Implementing this yourself often results in a lot of repeated boilerplate code (see <a href="index.html#page_333">Using a form in a view</a>). To help avoid this, Django provides a collection of generic class-based views for form processing.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Basic forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Given a contact form:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 15: forms.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ContactForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">message</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(widget</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>send_email</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># send email using the self.cleaned_data dictionary</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The view can be constructed using a FormView:</p> <p id="page_426"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 16: views.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContactForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic.edit</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FormView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ContactFormView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"contact.html"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_class</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContactForm</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">success_url</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/thanks/"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>form_valid</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># This method is called when valid form data has been POSTed.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># It should return an HttpResponse.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">send_email()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">form_valid(form)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Notes:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• FormView inherits <a href="index.html#page_979"><i>TemplateResponseMixin</i></a> so <a href="index.html#page_979"><i>template_name</i></a> can be used here.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The default implementation for <a href="index.html#page_987"><i>form_valid()</i></a> simply redirects to the <a href="index.html#page_987"><i>success_url</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Model forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Generic views really shine when working with models. These generic views will automatically create a</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_365"><i>ModelForm</i></a>, so long as they can work out which model class to use:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If the <a href="index.html#page_988"><i>model</i></a> attribute is given, that model class will be used.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If <a href="index.html#page_981"><i>get_object()</i></a> returns an object, the class of that object will be used.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If a <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>queryset</i></a> is given, the model for that queryset will be used.</p> <p>Model form views provide a <a href="index.html#page_989"><i>form_valid()</i></a> implementation that saves the model automatically. You can override this if you have any special requirements; see below for examples.</p> <p>You don’t even need to provide a success_url for <a href="index.html#page_961"><i>CreateView</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_962"><i>UpdateView</i></a>- they will use</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1703"><i>get_absolute_url()</i></a> on the model object if available.</p> <p>If you want to use a custom <a href="index.html#page_365"><i>ModelForm</i></a> (for instance to add extra validation), set <a href="index.html#page_987"><i>form_class</i></a> on your view.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: When specifying a custom form class, you must still specify the model, even though the <a href="index.html#page_987"><i>form_class</i></a></p> <p>may be a <a href="index.html#page_365"><i>ModelForm</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>First we need to add <a href="index.html#page_1703"><i>get_absolute_url()</i></a> to our Author class:</p> <p id="page_427" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 17: models.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_absolute_url</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">reverse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"author-detail"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, kwargs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pk})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then we can use <a href="index.html#page_1000"><i>CreateView</i></a> and friends to do the actual work. Notice how we’re just configuring the generic class-based views here; we don’t have to write any logic ourselves:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 18: loaded when the file is imported.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The fields attribute works the same way as the fields attribute on the inner Meta class on <a Unless you define the form class in another way, the attribute is required and the view will raise an</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>ImproperlyConfigured</i></a> exception if it’s not.</p> <p id="page_428"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you specify both the <a href="index.html#page_988"><i>fields</i></a> and <a style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1000"><i>CreateView</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1002"><i>UpdateView</i></a> use myapp/author_form.html</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1003"><i>DeleteView</i></a> uses myapp/author_confirm_delete.html</p> <p>If you wish to have separate templates for <a href="index.html#page_1000"><i>CreateView</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1002"><i>UpdateView</i></a> , you can set either <a href="index.html#page_979"><i>template_name</i></a></p> <p>or <a href="index.html#page_982"><i>template_name_suffix</i></a> on your view class.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Models and request.user</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To track the user that created an object using a <a href="index.html#page_1000"><i>CreateView</i></a>, you can use a custom <a href="index.html#page_365"><i>ModelForm</i></a> to do this. First, add the foreign key relation to the model:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 20: models.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(User, <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.mixins</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">instance</span><span
