style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">view(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>post</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_442"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">view</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthorInterestFormView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">view(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This approach can also be used with any other generic class-based views or your own class-based views</p> <p>inheriting directly from <a href="index.html#page_996"><i>View</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_996"><i>TemplateView</i></a>, as it keeps the different views as separate as possible.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>More than just HTML</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Where class-based views shine is when you want to do the same thing many times. Suppose you’re writing an API, and every view should return JSON instead of rendered HTML.</p> <p>We can create a mixin class to use in all of our views, handling the conversion to JSON once.</p> <p>For example, a JSON mixin might look something like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">JsonResponse</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>JSONResponseMixin</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">A mixin that can be used to render a JSON response.</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>render_to_json_response</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Returns a JSON response, transforming 'context' to make the payload.</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">JsonResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_data(context),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Returns an object that will be serialized as JSON by json.dumps().</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Note: This is *EXTREMELY* naive; in reality, you'll need</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># to do much more complex handling to ensure that arbitrary</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># objects -- such as Django model instances or querysets</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># -- can be serialized as JSON.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">context</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Check out the <a href="index.html#page_731">Serializing Django objects</a> documentation for more information on how to correctly transform Django models and querysets into JSON.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This mixin provides a render_to_json_response() <span style="float:right">method with the same signature as</span></p> <p id="page_443" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_980"><i>render_to_response()</i>. </a>To use it, we need to mix it into a TemplateView for example, and override render_to_response() to call render_to_json_response() instead:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplateView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>JSONView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(JSONResponseMixin, TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>render_to_response</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">render_to_json_response(context,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Equally we could use our mixin with one of the generic views. We can make our own version of <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a></p> <p>by mixing JSONResponseMixin with the <a href="index.html#page_956"><i>BaseDetailView</i></a> – (the <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a> before template rendering be-havior has been mixed in):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic.detail</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseDetailView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>JSONDetailView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(JSONResponseMixin, BaseDetailView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>render_to_response</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">render_to_json_response(context,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">response_kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This view can then be deployed in the same way as any other <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a> , with exactly the same behavior – except for the format of the response.</p> <p>If you want to be really adventurous, you could even mix a <a href="index.html#page_955"><i>DetailView</i></a> subclass that is able to return both HTML and JSON content, depending on some property of the HTTP request, such as a query argument</p> <p>or an HTTP header. Mix in both the JSONResponseMixin and a <a href="index.html#page_982"><i>SingleObjectTemplateResponseMixin</i></a>,</p> <p>and override the implementation of <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>render_to_response()</i></a> to defer to the appropriate rendering method depending on the type of response that the user requested:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic.detail</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SingleObjectTemplateResponseMixin</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>HybridDetailView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">JSONResponseMixin, SingleObjectTemplateResponseMixin, BaseDetailView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>render_to_response</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Look for a 'format=json' GET argument</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">GET</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"format"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">render_to_json_response(context)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">render_to_response(context)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because of the way that Python resolves method overloading, the call to super().</p> <p>render_to_response(context) ends up calling the <a href="index.html#page_980"><i>render_to_response()</i></a> implementation of <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_444"><a href="index.html#page_979"><i>TemplateResponseMixin</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.5 Basic examples</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides base view classes which will suit a wide range of applications. All views inherit from the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_950"><i>View</i></a> class, which handles linking the view into the URLs, HTTP method dispatching and other common</p> <p>features. <a href="index.html#page_953"><i>RedirectView</i></a> provides a HTTP redirect, and <a href="index.html#page_952"><i>TemplateView</i></a> extends the base class to make it also render a template.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.6 Usage in your URLconf</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The most direct way to use generic views is to create them directly in your URLconf. If you’re only changing</p> <p>a few attributes on a class-based view, you can pass them into the <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> method call itself:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplateView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, TemplateView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view(template_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any arguments passed to <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> will override attributes set on the class. In this example, we set template_name on the TemplateView. A similar overriding pattern can be used for the url attribute on</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_953"><i>RedirectView</i></a> .</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.7 Subclassing generic views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The second, more powerful way to use generic views is to inherit from an existing view and override attributes (such as the template_name) or methods (such as get_context_data) in your subclass to provide new values or methods. Consider, for example, a view that just displays one template, about.html. Django has a generic</p> <p>view to do this -<a href="index.html#page_952"><i>TemplateView</i></a>- so we can subclass it, and override the template name:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># some_app/views.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TemplateView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AboutView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TemplateView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">template_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"about.html"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then we need to add this new view into our URLconf. <a href="index.html#page_952"><i>TemplateView</i></a> is a class, not a function, so we point</p> <p>the URL to the <a href="index.html#page_950"><i>as_view()</i></a> class method instead, which provides a function-like entry to class-based views:</p> <p id="page_445" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># urls.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">some_app.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AboutView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, AboutView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For more information on how to use the built in generic views, consult the next topic on <a href="index.html#page_417">generic class-based</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_417">views.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Supporting other HTTP methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Suppose somebody wants to access our book library over HTTP using the views as an API. The API client would connect every now and then and download book data for the books published since last visit. But if no new books appeared since then, it is a waste of CPU time and bandwidth to fetch the books from the database, render a full response and send it to the client. It might be preferable to ask the API when the most recent book was published.</p> <p>We map the URL to book list view in the URLconf:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BookListView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"books/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, BookListView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>And the view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">books.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>BookListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>head</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_book</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_queryset()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">latest(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"publication_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># RFC 1123 date format.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">headers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Last-Modified"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: last_book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">publication_date</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">strftime(</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_446"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:8em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"%a, %d %b %Y %H:%M:%S GMT"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the view is accessed from a GET request, an object list is returned in the response (using the book_list.html template). But if the client issues a HEAD request, the response has an empty body and the Last-Modified header indicates when the most recent book was published. Based on this information, the client may or may not download the full object list.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.6.8 Asynchronous class-based views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As well as the synchronous (def) method handlers already shown, View subclasses may define asynchronous (async def) method handlers to leverage asynchronous code using await:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asyncio</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">View</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AsyncView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(View):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Perform io-blocking view logic using await, sleep for example.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asyncio</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sleep(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Hello async world!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Within a single view-class, all user-defined method handlers must be either synchronous, using def, or all asynchronous, using async def. An ImproperlyConfigured exception will be raised in as_view() if def and async def declarations are mixed.</p> <p>Django will automatically detect asynchronous views and run them in an asynchronous context. You can</p> <p>read more about Django’s asynchronous support, and how to best use async views, in <a href="index.html#page_764">Asynchronous support</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.7 Migrations</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations are Django’s way of propagating changes you make to your models (adding a field, deleting a model, etc.) into your database schema. They’re designed to be mostly automatic, but you’ll need to know when to make migrations, when to run them, and the common problems you might run into.</p> <p id="page_447" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.1 The Commands</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are several commands which you will use to interact with migrations and Django’s handling of database schema:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a>, which is responsible for applying and unapplying migrations.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a>, which is responsible for creating new migrations based on the changes you have made</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to your models.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1452"><i>sqlmigrate</i>, </a>which displays the SQL statements for a migration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1452"><i>showmigrations</i></a>, which lists a project’s migrations and their status.</p> <p>You should think of migrations as a version control system for your database schema. makemigrations is responsible for packaging up your model changes into individual migration files - analogous to commits -and migrate is responsible for applying those to your database.</p> <p>The migration files for each app live in a “migrations” directory inside of that app, and are designed to be committed to, and distributed as part of, its codebase. You should be making them once on your development machine and then running the same migrations on your colleagues’ machines, your staging machines, and eventually your production machines.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: It is possible to override the name of the package which contains the migrations on a per-app basis by</p> <p>modifying the <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIGRATION_MODULES</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations will run the same way on the same dataset and produce consistent results, meaning that what you see in development and staging is, under the same circumstances, exactly what will happen in production.</p> <p>Django will make migrations for any change to your models or fields - even options that don’t affect the database - as the only way it can reconstruct a field correctly is to have all the changes in the history, and you might need those options in some data migrations later on (for example, if you’ve set custom validators).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.2 Backend Support</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations are supported on all backends that Django ships with, as well as any third-party backends if they</p> <p>have programmed in support for schema alteration (done via the <a href="index.html#page_1883">SchemaEditor</a> class).</p> <p>However, some databases are more capable than others when it comes to schema migrations; some of the caveats are covered below.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_448"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostgreSQL is the most capable of all the databases here in terms of schema support.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MySQL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL lacks support for transactions around schema alteration operations, meaning that if a migration fails to apply you will have to manually unpick the changes in order to try again (it’s impossible to roll back to an earlier point).</p> <p>MySQL 8.0 introduced significant performance enhancements for <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/innodb-online-ddl-operations.html">DDL operations</a>, making them more ef-ficient and reducing the need for full table rebuilds. However, it cannot guarantee a complete absence of locks or interruptions. In situations where locks are still necessary, the duration of these operations will be proportionate to the number of rows involved.</p> <p>Finally, MySQL has a relatively small limit on the combined size of all columns an index covers. This means that indexes that are possible on other backends will fail to be created under MySQL.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SQLite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQLite has very little built-in schema alteration support, and so Django attempts to emulate it by:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Creating a new table with the new schema</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Copying the data across</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Dropping the old table</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Renaming the new table to match the original name</p> <p>This process generally works well, but it can be slow and occasionally buggy. It is not recommended that you run and migrate SQLite in a production environment unless you are very aware of the risks and its limitations; the support Django ships with is designed to allow developers to use SQLite on their local machines to develop less complex Django projects without the need for a full database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.3 Workflow</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django can create migrations for you. Make changes to your models - say, add a field and remove a model -</p> <p>and then run <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i>:</a></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py makemigrations</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migrations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'books'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">books/migrations/0003_auto.py:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">~ Alter field author on book</span></p> <p id="page_449" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Your models will be scanned and compared to the versions currently contained in your migration files, and then a new set of migrations will be written out. Make sure to read the output to see what makemigrations thinks you have changed - it’s not perfect, and for complex changes it might not be detecting what you expect.</p> <p>Once you have your new migration files, you should apply them to your database to make sure they work as expected:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py migrate</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Operations to perform:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Apply all migrations: books</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Running migrations:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Rendering model states... DONE</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Applying books.0003_auto... OK</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once the migration is applied, commit the migration and the models change to your version control system as a single commit - that way, when other developers (or your production servers) check out the code, they’ll get both the changes to your models and the accompanying migration at the same time.</p> <p>If you want to give the migration(s) a meaningful name instead of a generated one, you can use the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1445"><i>makemigrations --name</i></a> option:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py makemigrations --name changed_my_model your_app_label</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Version control</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because migrations are stored in version control, you’ll occasionally come across situations where you and another developer have both committed a migration to the same app at the same time, resulting in two migrations with the same number.</p> <p>Don’t worry - the numbers are just there for developers’ reference, Django just cares that each migration has a different name. Migrations specify which other migrations they depend on - including earlier migrations in the same app - in the file, so it’s possible to detect when there’s two new migrations for the same app that aren’t ordered.</p> <p>When this happens, Django will prompt you and give you some options. If it thinks it’s safe enough, it will offer to automatically linearize the two migrations for you. If not, you’ll have to go in and modify the</p> <p>migrations yourself - don’t worry, this isn’t difficult, and is explained more in <a href="index.html#page_451">Migration files</a> below.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_450"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.4 Transactions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On databases that support DDL transactions (SQLite and PostgreSQL), all migration operations will run inside a single transaction by default. In contrast, if a database doesn’t support DDL transactions (e.g. MySQL, Oracle) then all operations will run without a transaction.</p> <p>You can prevent a migration from running in a transaction by setting the atomic attribute to False. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">atomic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= False</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s also possible to execute parts of the migration inside a transaction using <a href="index.html#page_209"><i>atomic()</i></a> or by passing</p> <p>atomic=True to <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a>. See <a href="index.html#page_794">Non-atomic migrations</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.5 Dependencies</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While migrations are per-app, the tables and relationships implied by your models are too complex to be created for one app at a time. When you make a migration that requires something else to run - for exam-ple, you add a ForeignKey in your books app to your authors app - the resulting migration will contain a dependency on a migration in authors.</p> <p>This means that when you run the migrations, the authors migration runs first and creates the table the ForeignKey references, and then the migration that makes the ForeignKey column runs afterward and cre-ates the constraint. If this didn’t happen, the migration would try to create the ForeignKey column without the table it’s referencing existing and your database would throw an error.</p> <p>This dependency behavior affects most migration operations where you restrict to a single app. Restricting to a single app (either in makemigrations or migrate) is a best-efforts promise, and not a guarantee; any other apps that need to be used to get dependencies correct will be.</p> <p>Apps without migrations must not have relations (ForeignKey, ManyToManyField, etc.) to apps with migra-tions. Sometimes it may work, but it’s not supported.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_451" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Swappable dependencies</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django.db.migrations.<b>swappable_dependency</b>(value)</p> <p>The swappable_dependency() function is used in migrations to declare “swappable” dependencies on mi-grations in the app of the swapped-in model, currently, on the first migration of this app. As a consequence, the swapped-in model should be created in the initial migration. The argument value is a string "<app label>.<model>" describing an app label and a model name, e.g. "myapp.MyModel".</p> <p>By using swappable_dependency(), you inform the migration framework that the migration relies on an-other migration which sets up a swappable model, allowing for the possibility of substituting the model with a different implementation in the future. This is typically used for referencing models that are subject to customization or replacement, such as the custom user model (settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, which defaults to "auth.User") in Django’s authentication system.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.6 Migration files</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations are stored as an on-disk format, referred to here as “migration files”. These files are actually normal Python files with an agreed-upon object layout, written in a declarative style.</p> <p>A basic migration file looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations, models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">dependencies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"migrations"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0001_initial"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DeleteModel(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Tribble"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">AddField(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Author"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"rating"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">IntegerField(default</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>What Django looks for when it loads a migration file (as a Python module) is a subclass of django.db. migrations.Migration called Migration. It then inspects this object for four attributes, only two of which are used most of the time:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• dependencies, a list of migrations this one depends on.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• operations, a list of Operation classes that define what this migration does.</p> <p>The operations are the key; they are a set of declarative instructions which tell Django what schema changes need to be made. Django scans them and builds an in-memory representation of all of the schema changes to all apps, and uses this to generate the SQL which makes the schema changes.</p> <p>That in-memory structure is also used to work out what the differences are between your models and the current state of your migrations; Django runs through all the changes, in order, on an in-memory set of <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_452">models to come up with the state of your models last time you ran makemigrations. It then uses these models to compare against the ones in your models.py files to work out what you have changed.</p> <p>You should rarely, if ever, need to edit migration files by hand, but it’s entirely possible to write them man-ually if you need to. Some of the more complex operations are not autodetectable and are only available via a hand-written migration, so don’t be scared about editing them if you have to.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can’t modify the number of positional arguments in an already migrated custom field without raising a TypeError. The old migration will call the modified __init__ method with the old signature. So if you need a new argument, please create a keyword argument and add something like assert 'argument_name' in kwargs in the constructor.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Model managers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can optionally serialize managers into migrations and have them available in <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> operations. This is done by defining a use_in_migrations attribute on the manager class:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyManager</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Manager):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">use_in_migrations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= True</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyManager()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you are using the <a href="index.html#page_197"><i>from_queryset()</i></a> function to dynamically generate a manager class, you need to inherit from the generated class to make it importable:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyManager</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(MyBaseManager</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">from_queryset(CustomQuerySet)):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">use_in_migrations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= True</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyManager()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Please refer to the notes about <a href="index.html#page_455">Historical models</a> in migrations to see the implications that come along.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_453" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Initial migrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migration.<b>initial</b></p> <p>The “initial migrations” for an app are the migrations that create the first version of that app’s tables. Usually an app will have one initial migration, but in some cases of complex model interdependencies it may have two or more.</p> <p>Initial migrations are marked with an initial = True class attribute on the migration class. If an initial class attribute isn’t found, a migration will be considered “initial” if it is the first migration in the app (i.e. if it has no dependencies on any other migration in the same app).</p> <p>When the <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate --fake-initial</i></a> option is used, these initial migrations are treated specially. For an initial migration that creates one or more tables (CreateModel operation), Django checks that all of those tables already exist in the database and fake-applies the migration if so. Similarly, for an initial migration that adds one or more fields (AddField operation), Django checks that all of the respective columns already exist in the database and fake-applies the migration if so. Without--fake-initial, initial migrations are treated no differently from any other migration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>History consistency</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As previously discussed, you may need to linearize migrations manually when two development branches are joined. While editing migration dependencies, you can inadvertently create an inconsistent history state where a migration has been applied but some of its dependencies haven’t. This is a strong indication that the dependencies are incorrect, so Django will refuse to run migrations or make new migrations until it’s fixed.</p> <p>When using multiple databases, you can use the <a href="index.html#page_223"><i>allow_migrate()</i></a> method of <a href="index.html#page_223">database routers</a> to control</p> <p>which databases <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a> checks for consistent history.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.7 Adding migrations to apps</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>New apps come preconfigured to accept migrations, and so you can add migrations by running</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a> once you’ve made some changes.</p> <p>If your app already has models and database tables, and doesn’t have migrations yet (for example, you created it against a previous Django version), you’ll need to convert it to use migrations by running:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py makemigrations your_app_label</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will make a new initial migration for your app. Now, run python manage.py migrate--fake-initial, and Django will detect that you have an initial migration and that the tables it wants to</p> <p>create already exist, and will mark the migration as already applied. (Without the <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate --fake-initial</i></a> flag, the command would error out because the tables it wants to create already exist.)</p> <p>Note that this only works given two things:</p> <p id="page_454"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• You have not changed your models since you made their tables. For migrations to work, you must</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">make the initial migration first and then make changes, as Django compares changes against migration files, not the database.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• You have not manually edited your database - Django won’t be able to detect that your database</p> <p style="text-align:center">doesn’t match your models, you’ll just get errors when migrations try to modify those tables.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.8 Reversing migrations</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations can be reversed with <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> by passing the number of the previous migration. For example, to reverse migration books.0003:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py migrate books</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0002</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Operations to perform:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Target specific migration: 0002_auto, from books</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Running migrations:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Rendering model states... DONE</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Unapplying books.0003_auto... OK</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to reverse all migrations applied for an app, use the name zero:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py migrate books zero</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Operations to perform:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Unapply all migrations: books</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Running migrations:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Rendering model states... DONE</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Unapplying books.0002_auto... OK</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Unapplying books.0001_initial... OK</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A migration is irreversible if it contains any irreversible operations. Attempting to reverse such migrations will raise IrreversibleError:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py migrate books</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0002</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Operations to perform:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Target specific migration: 0002_auto, from books</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Running migrations:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Rendering model states... DONE</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Unapplying books.0003_auto...Traceback (most recent call last):</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.migrations.exceptions.IrreversibleError: Operation <RunSQL</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sql='DROP TABLE demo_books'></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">␣</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">in books.0003_auto is not reversible</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_455" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.9 Historical models</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you run migrations, Django is working from historical versions of your models stored in the migration</p> <p>files. If you write Python code using the <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> operation, or if you have allow_migrate methods on your database routers, you need to use these historical model versions rather than importing them directly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If you import models directly rather than using the historical models, your migrations may</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">work initially but will fail in the future when you try to rerun old migrations (commonly, when you set</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">up a new installation and run through all the migrations to set up the database).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">This means that historical model problems may not be immediately obvious. If you run into this kind of</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">failure, it’s OK to edit the migration to use the historical models rather than direct imports and commit</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">those changes.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because it’s impossible to serialize arbitrary Python code, these historical models will not have any custom methods that you have defined. They will, however, have the same fields, relationships, managers (limited to those with use_in_migrations = True) and Meta options (also versioned, so they may be different from your current ones).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: This means that you will NOT have custom save() methods called on objects when you</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">access them in migrations, and you will NOT have any custom constructors or instance methods. Plan</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">appropriately!</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>References to functions in field options such as upload_to and limit_choices_to and model manager dec-larations with managers having use_in_migrations = True are serialized in migrations, so the functions</p> <p>and classes will need to be kept around for as long as there is a migration referencing them. Any <a href="index.html#page_777">custom</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_777">model fields</a> will also need to be kept, since these are imported directly by migrations.</p> <p>In addition, the concrete base classes of the model are stored as pointers, so you must always keep base classes around for as long as there is a migration that contains a reference to them. On the plus side, methods and managers from these base classes inherit normally, so if you absolutely need access to these you can opt to move them into a superclass.</p> <p>To remove old references, you can <a href="index.html#page_459">squash migrations</a> or, if there aren’t many references, copy them into the migration files.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_456"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.10 Considerations when removing model fields</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Similar to the “references to historical functions” considerations described in the previous section, removing custom model fields from your project or third-party app will cause a problem if they are referenced in old migrations.</p> <p>To help with this situation, Django provides some model field attributes to assist with model field deprecation</p> <p>using the <a href="index.html#page_757">system checks framework.</a></p> <p>Add the system_check_deprecated_details attribute to your model field similar to the following:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>IPAddressField</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Field):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">system_check_deprecated_details</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"msg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: (</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"IPAddressField has been deprecated. Support for it (except "</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"in historical migrations) will be removed in Django 1.9."</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"hint"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Use GenericIPAddressField instead."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># optional</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields.W900"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># pick a unique ID for your field.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>After a deprecation period of your choosing (two or three feature releases for fields in Django itself), change the system_check_deprecated_details attribute to system_check_removed_details and update the dic-tionary similar to:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>IPAddressField</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Field):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">system_check_removed_details</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"msg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: (</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"IPAddressField has been removed except for support in "</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"historical migrations."</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"hint"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Use GenericIPAddressField instead."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"id"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields.E900"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># pick a unique ID for your field.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You should keep the field’s methods that are required for it to operate in database migrations such as __init__(), deconstruct(), and get_internal_type(). Keep this stub field for as long as any migrations which reference the field exist. For example, after squashing migrations and removing the old ones, you should be able to remove the field completely.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_457" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.11 Data Migrations</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As well as changing the database schema, you can also use migrations to change the data in the database itself, in conjunction with the schema if you want.</p> <p>Migrations that alter data are usually called “data migrations”; they’re best written as separate migrations, sitting alongside your schema migrations.</p> <p>Django can’t automatically generate data migrations for you, as it does with schema migrations, but it’s not</p> <p>very hard to write them. Migration files in Django are made up of <a href="index.html#page_1602">Operations</a>, and the main operation you</p> <p>use for data migrations is <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a>.</p> <p>To start, make an empty migration file you can work from (Django will put the file in the right place, suggest a name, and add dependencies for you):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py makemigrations --empty yourappname</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then, open up the file; it should look something like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Generated by Django A.B on YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">dependencies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"yourappname"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0001_initial"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now, all you need to do is create a new function and have <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> use it. <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> expects a callable as</p> <p>its argument which takes two arguments - the first is an <a href="index.html#page_921">app registry</a> that has the historical versions of all your</p> <p>models loaded into it to match where in your history the migration sits, and the second is a <a href="index.html#page_1883">SchemaEditor</a>, which you can use to manually effect database schema changes (but beware, doing this can confuse the migration autodetector!)</p> <p>Let’s write a migration that populates our new name field with the combined values of first_name and last_name (we’ve come to our senses and realized that not everyone has first and last names). All we need to do is use the historical model and iterate over the rows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>combine_names</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(apps, schema_editor):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># We can't import the Person model directly as it may be a newer</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># version than this migration expects. We use the historical version.</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_458"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Person</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_model(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"yourappname"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Person"</span><span
