style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">person</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f"{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">person</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">} {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">person</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">person</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">dependencies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"yourappname"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0001_initial"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">RunPython(combine_names),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once that’s done, we can run python manage.py migrate as normal and the data migration will run in place alongside other migrations.</p> <p>You can pass a second callable to <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> to run whatever logic you want executed when migrating back-wards. If this callable is omitted, migrating backwards will raise an exception.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Accessing models from other apps</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When writing a RunPython function that uses models from apps other than the one in which the migra-tion is located, the migration’s dependencies attribute should include the latest migration of each app that is involved, otherwise you may get an error similar to: LookupError: No installed app with label 'myappname' when you try to retrieve the model in the RunPython function using apps.get_model().</p> <p>In the following example, we have a migration in app1 which needs to use models in app2. We aren’t con-cerned with the details of move_m1 other than the fact it will need to access models from both apps. Therefore we’ve added a dependency that specifies the last migration of app2:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">dependencies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app1"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0001_initial"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># added dependency to enable using models from app2 in move_m1</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app2"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"0004_foobar"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">RunPython(move_m1),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p id="page_459" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>More advanced migrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re interested in the more advanced migration operations, or want to be able to write your own, see the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1602">migration operations reference</a> and the “how-to” on <a href="index.html#page_791">writing migrations</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.12 Squashing migrations</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You are encouraged to make migrations freely and not worry about how many you have; the migration code is optimized to deal with hundreds at a time without much slowdown. However, eventually you will want to move back from having several hundred migrations to just a few, and that’s where squashing comes in.</p> <p>Squashing is the act of reducing an existing set of many migrations down to one (or sometimes a few) migra-tions which still represent the same changes.</p> <p>Django does this by taking all of your existing migrations, extracting their Operations and putting them all in sequence, and then running an optimizer over them to try and reduce the length of the list - for example, it</p> <p>knows that <a href="index.html#page_1603"><i>CreateModel</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1603"><i>DeleteModel</i></a> cancel each other out, and it knows that <a href="index.html#page_1605"><i>AddField</i></a> can be rolled</p> <p>into <a href="index.html#page_1603"><i>CreateModel</i></a>.</p> <p>Once the operation sequence has been reduced as much as possible - the amount possible depends on how</p> <p>closely intertwined your models are and if you have any <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>RunSQL</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> operations (which can’t be optimized through unless they are marked as elidable) - Django will then write it back out into a new set of migration files.</p> <p>These files are marked to say they replace the previously-squashed migrations, so they can coexist with the old migration files, and Django will intelligently switch between them depending where you are in the history. If you’re still part-way through the set of migrations that you squashed, it will keep using them until it hits the end and then switch to the squashed history, while new installs will use the new squashed migration and skip all the old ones.</p> <p>This enables you to squash and not mess up systems currently in production that aren’t fully up-to-date yet. The recommended process is to squash, keeping the old files, commit and release, wait until all systems are upgraded with the new release (or if you’re a third-party project, ensure your users upgrade releases in order without skipping any), and then remove the old files, commit and do a second release.</p> <p>The command that backs all this is <a href="index.html#page_1453"><i>squashmigrations</i></a>- pass it the app label and migration name you want to squash up to, and it’ll get to work:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py squashmigrations myapp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0004</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Will squash the following migrations:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">- 0001_initial</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">- 0002_some_change</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">- 0003_another_change</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">- 0004_undo_something</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Do you wish to proceed?</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">y/N</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">y</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_460"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Optimizing...</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Optimized from</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">12</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">operations to</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">7</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">operations.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Created new squashed migration /home/andrew/Programs/DjangoTest/test/migrations/0001_squashed_0004_</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">undo_something.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">You should commit this migration but leave the old ones</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">place;</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">the new migration will be used</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">new installs. Once you are sure</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">all instances of the codebase have applied the migrations you squashed,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">you can delete them.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use the <a href="index.html#page_1453"><i>squashmigrations --squashed-name</i></a> option if you want to set the name of the squashed migration rather than use an autogenerated one.</p> <p>Note that model interdependencies in Django can get very complex, and squashing may result in migrations that do not run; either mis-optimized (in which case you can try again with--no-optimize, though you should also report an issue), or with a CircularDependencyError, in which case you can manually resolve it.</p> <p>To manually resolve a CircularDependencyError, break out one of the ForeignKeys in the circular depen-dency loop into a separate migration, and move the dependency on the other app with it. If you’re unsure, see</p> <p>how <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a> deals with the problem when asked to create brand new migrations from your models.</p> <p>In a future release of Django, <a href="index.html#page_1453"><i>squashmigrations</i></a> will be updated to attempt to resolve these errors itself.</p> <p>Once you’ve squashed your migration, you should then commit it alongside the migrations it replaces and distribute this change to all running instances of your application, making sure that they run migrate to store the change in their database.</p> <p>You must then transition the squashed migration to a normal migration by:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Deleting all the migration files it replaces.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Updating all migrations that depend on the deleted migrations to depend on the squashed migration</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">instead.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Removing the replaces attribute in the Migration class of the squashed migration (this is how Django</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tells that it is a squashed migration).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Once you’ve squashed a migration, you should not then re-squash that squashed migration until you have fully transitioned it to a normal migration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Pruning references to deleted migrations</p> <p>If it is likely that you may reuse the name of a deleted migration in the future, you should remove references</p> <p>to it from Django’s migrations table with the <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>migrate --prune</i></a> option.</p> <p id="page_461" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.13 Serializing values</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Migrations are Python files containing the old definitions of your models - thus, to write them, Django must take the current state of your models and serialize them out into a file.</p> <p>While Django can serialize most things, there are some things that we just can’t serialize out into a valid Python representation - there’s no Python standard for how a value can be turned back into code (repr() only works for basic values, and doesn’t specify import paths).</p> <p>Django can serialize the following:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• int, float, bool, str, bytes, None, NoneType</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• list, set, tuple, dict, range.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• datetime.date, datetime.time, and datetime.datetime instances (include those that are timezone-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">aware)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• decimal.Decimal instances</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• enum.Enum and enum.Flag instances</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• uuid.UUID instances</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.partial">functools.partial()</a> and <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.partialmethod">functools.partialmethod</a> instances which have serializable func, args,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">and keywords values.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Pure and concrete path objects from <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#module-pathlib">pathlib. </a>Concrete paths are converted to their pure path equiv-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">alent, e.g. <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.PosixPath">pathlib.PosixPath</a> to <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.PurePosixPath">pathlib.PurePosixPath</a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.PathLike">os.PathLike</a> instances, e.g. <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.DirEntry">os.DirEntry</a>, which are converted to str or bytes using <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.fspath">os.fspath()</a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• LazyObject instances which wrap a serializable value.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Enumeration types (e.g. TextChoices or IntegerChoices) instances.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Any Django field</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Any function or method reference (e.g. datetime.datetime.today) (must be in module’s top-level</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">scope)</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– Functions may be decorated if wrapped properly, i.e. using <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.wraps">functools.wraps()</a></p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– The <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.cache">functools.cache()</a> and <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.lru_cache">functools.lru_cache()</a> decorators are explicitly supported</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Unbound methods used from within the class body</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Any class reference (must be in module’s top-level scope)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Anything with a custom deconstruct() method (<a href="index.html#page_462">see below)</a></p> <p>Django cannot serialize:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Nested classes</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Arbitrary class instances (e.g. MyClass(4.3, 5.7))</p> <p id="page_462"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Lambdas</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom serializers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can serialize other types by writing a custom serializer. For example, if Django didn’t serialize <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/decimal.html#decimal.Decimal">Decimal</a> by default, you could do this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">decimal</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Decimal</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.migrations.serializer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseSerializer</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.migrations.writer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MigrationWriter</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>DecimalSerializer</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseSerializer):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>serialize</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">repr</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">value), {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"from decimal import Decimal"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">MigrationWriter</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register_serializer(Decimal, DecimalSerializer)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The first argument of MigrationWriter.register_serializer() is a type or iterable of types that should use the serializer.</p> <p>The serialize() method of your serializer must return a string of how the value should appear in migrations and a set of any imports that are needed in the migration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Adding a deconstruct() method</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can let Django serialize your own custom class instances by giving the class a deconstruct() method. It takes no arguments, and should return a tuple of three things (path, args, kwargs):</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• path should be the Python path to the class, with the class name included as the last part (for example,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">myapp.custom_things.MyClass). If your class is not available at the top level of a module it is not serializable.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• args should be a list of positional arguments to pass to your class’ __init__ method. Everything in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">this list should itself be serializable.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• kwargs should be a dict of keyword arguments to pass to your class’ __init__ method. Every value</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">should itself be serializable.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: This return value is different from the deconstruct() method <a href="index.html#page_781">for custom fields</a> which returns a tuple of four items.</p> <p id="page_463" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django will write out the value as an instantiation of your class with the given arguments, similar to the way it writes out references to Django fields.</p> <p>To prevent a new migration from being created each time <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a> is run, you should also add a __eq__() method to the decorated class. This function will be called by Django’s migration framework to detect changes between states.</p> <p>As long as all of the arguments to your class’ constructor are themselves serializable, you can use the @deconstructible class decorator from django.utils.deconstruct to add the deconstruct() method:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.deconstruct</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">deconstructible</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@deconstructible</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyCustomClass</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, foo</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">foo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">foo</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__eq__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, other):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">foo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">other</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">foo</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The decorator adds logic to capture and preserve the arguments on their way into your constructor, and then returns those arguments exactly when deconstruct() is called.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.7.14 Supporting multiple Django versions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you are the maintainer of a third-party app with models, you may need to ship migrations that support</p> <p>multiple Django versions. In this case, you should always run <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a> with the lowest Django version you wish to support.</p> <p>The migrations system will maintain backwards-compatibility according to the same policy as the rest of Django, so migration files generated on Django X.Y should run unchanged on Django X.Y+1. The migrations system does not promise forwards-compatibility, however. New features may be added, and migration files generated with newer versions of Django may not work on older versions.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1602">The Migrations Operations Reference</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Covers the schema operations API, special operations, and writing your own operations.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_791">The Writing Migrations “how-to”</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Explains how to structure and write database migrations for different scenarios you might encounter.</p> <p id="page_464"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.8 Managing files</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document describes Django’s file access APIs for files such as those uploaded by a user. The lower level APIs are general enough that you could use them for other purposes. If you want to handle “static files” (JS,</p> <p>CSS, etc.), see <a href="index.html#page_843">How to manage static files (e.g. images, JavaScript, CSS).</a></p> <p>By default, Django stores files locally, using the <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> settings. The examples below assume that you’re using these defaults.</p> <p>However, Django provides ways to write custom <a href="index.html#page_467">file storage systems</a> that allow you to completely customize where and how Django stores files. The second half of this document describes how these storage systems work.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.8.1 Using files in models</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you use a <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a>, Django provides a set of APIs you can use to deal with that file.</p> <p>Consider the following model, using an <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a> to store a photo:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Car</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DecimalField(max_digits</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">photo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ImageField(upload_to</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">FileField(upload_to</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">image</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><PIL.JpegImagePlugin.JpegImageFile image mode=RGB size=191x287 at 0x7F99A94E9048></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.8.2 The</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>File</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>object</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Internally, Django uses a <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>django.core.files.File</i></a> instance any time it needs to represent a file.</p> <p>Most of the time you’ll use a File that Django’s given you (i.e. a file attached to a model as above, or perhaps an uploaded file).</p> <p>If you need to construct a File yourself, the easiest way is to create one using a Python built-in file object:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">File</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myfile</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">File(f)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now you can use any of the documented attributes and methods of the <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> class.</p> <p>Be aware that files created in this way are not automatically closed. The following approach may be used to close files automatically:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">open</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/hello.world"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"w"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myfile</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">File(f)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myfile</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">write(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Hello World"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myfile</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">closed</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">closed</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Closing files is especially important when accessing file fields in a loop over a large number of objects. If files are not manually closed after accessing them, the risk of running out of file descriptors may arise. This may lead to the following error:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">OSError: [Errno 24] Too many open files</span></p> <p id="page_467" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.8.3 File storage</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Behind the scenes, Django delegates decisions about how and where to store files to a file storage system. This is the object that actually understands things like file systems, opening and reading files, etc.</p> <p>Django’s default file storage is <a href="index.html#page_1479">'<i>django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage</i>'</a>. If you don’t explicitly</p> <p>provide a storage system in the default key of the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> setting, this is the one that will be used.</p> <p>See below for details of the built-in default file storage system, and see <a href="index.html#page_901">How to write a custom storage class</a> for information on writing your own file storage system.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Storage objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Though most of the time you’ll want to use a File object (which delegates to the proper storage for that file), you can use file storage systems directly. You can create an instance of some custom file storage class, or – often more useful – you can use the global default storage system:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.base</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentFile</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"path/to/file"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, ContentFile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">b"new content"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'path/to/file'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">size(path)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">11</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">open(path)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">read()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">b'new content'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">delete(path)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">exists(path)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">False</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1479">File storage API</a> for the file storage API.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The built-in filesystem storage class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django ships with a <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage</i></a> class which implements basic local filesystem file storage.</p> <p>For example, the following code will store uploaded files under /media/photos regardless of what your</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> setting is:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FileSystemStorage</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_468"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">fs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FileSystemStorage(location</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/media/photos"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Car</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">photo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ImageField(storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_901">Custom storage systems</a> work the same way: you can pass them in as the storage argument to a <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using a callable</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can use a callable as the <a href="index.html#page_1632"><i>storage</i></a> parameter for <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a>. This allows you to modify the used storage at runtime, selecting different storages for different environments, for example.</p> <p>Your callable will be evaluated when your models classes are loaded, and must return an instance of <a href="index.html#page_1481"><i>Storage</i></a>.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.storages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyLocalStorage, MyRemoteStorage</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>select_storage</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyLocalStorage()</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEBUG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyRemoteStorage()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">my_file</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">FileField(storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">select_storage)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In order to set a storage defined in the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> setting you can use <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>storages</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>select_storage</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"mystorage"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">upload</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">FileField(storage</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">select_storage)</span></p> <p id="page_469" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.9 Testing in Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Automated testing is an extremely useful bug-killing tool for the modern web developer. You can use a collection of tests – a test suite – to solve, or avoid, a number of problems:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When you’re writing new code, you can use tests to validate your code works as expected.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When you’re refactoring or modifying old code, you can use tests to ensure your changes haven’t af-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">fected your application’s behavior unexpectedly.</p> <p>Testing a web application is a complex task, because a web application is made of several layers of logic – from HTTP-level request handling, to form validation and processing, to template rendering. With Django’s test-execution framework and assorted utilities, you can simulate requests, insert test data, inspect your application’s output and generally verify your code is doing what it should be doing.</p> <p>The preferred way to write tests in Django is using the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#module-unittest">unittest</a> module built-in to the Python standard</p> <p>library. This is covered in detail in the <a href="index.html#page_469">Writing and running tests</a> document.</p> <p>You can also use any other Python test framework; Django provides an API and tools for that kind of inte-</p> <p>gration. They are described in the <a href="index.html#page_524">Using different testing frameworks</a> section of <a href="index.html#page_515">Advanced testing topics</a><a href="index.html#page_515">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.9.1 Writing and running tests</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_58">testing tutorial, </a>the <a href="index.html#page_476">testing tools reference</a>, and the <a href="index.html#page_515">advanced testing topics</a><a href="index.html#page_515">.</a></p> <p>This document is split into two primary sections. First, we explain how to write tests with Django. Then, we explain how to run them.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s unit tests use a Python standard library module: <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#module-unittest">unittest. </a>This module defines tests using a class-based approach.</p> <p>Here is an example which subclasses from <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>django.test.TestCase</i></a>, which is a subclass of <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a> that runs each test inside a transaction to provide isolation:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TestCase</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AnimalTestCase</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>setUp</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"lion"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, sound</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"roar"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, sound</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"meow"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_470"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_animals_can_speak</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""Animals that can speak are correctly identified"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">lion</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"lion"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">cat</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertEqual(lion</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">speak(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'The lion says "roar"'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertEqual(cat</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">speak(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'The cat says "meow"'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you <a href="index.html#page_470">run your tests</a>, the default behavior of the test utility is to find all the test case classes (that is,</p> <p>subclasses of <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a>) in any file whose name begins with test, automatically build a test suite out of those test case classes, and run that suite.</p> <p>For more details about <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#module-unittest">unittest</a>, see the Python documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Where should the tests live?</p> <p>The default <a href="index.html#page_1454"><i>startapp</i></a> template creates a tests.py file in the new application. This might be fine if you only have a few tests, but as your test suite grows you’ll likely want to restructure it into a tests package so you can split your tests into different submodules such as test_models.py, test_views.py, test_forms.py, etc. Feel free to pick whatever organizational scheme you like.</p> <p>See also <a href="index.html#page_522">Using the Django test runner to test reusable applications</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If your tests rely on database access such as creating or querying models, be sure to create</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">your test classes as subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>django.test.TestCase</i></a> rather than <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Using <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a> avoids the cost of running each test in a transaction and flushing the database,</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">but if your tests interact with the database their behavior will vary based on the order that the test runner</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">executes them. This can lead to unit tests that pass when run in isolation but fail when run in a suite.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once you’ve written tests, run them using the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test</i></a> command of your project’s manage.py utility:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Test discovery is based on the unittest module’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest-test-discovery">built-in test discovery</a>. By default, this will discover tests in any file named test*.py under the current working directory.</p> <p>You can specify particular tests to run by supplying any number of “test labels” to ./manage.py test. Each test label can be a full Python dotted path to a package, module, TestCase subclass, or test method. For instance:</p> <p id="page_471" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Run all the tests in the animals.tests module</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">animals.tests</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Run all the tests found within the 'animals' package</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">animals</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Run just one test case class</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">animals.tests.AnimalTestCase</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Run just one test method</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">animals.tests.AnimalTestCase.test_animals_can_speak</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also provide a path to a directory to discover tests below that directory:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">animals/</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can specify a custom filename pattern match using the-p (or--pattern) option, if your test files are named differently from the test*.py pattern:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--pattern</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"tests_*.py"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you press Ctrl-C while the tests are running, the test runner will wait for the currently running test to complete and then exit gracefully. During a graceful exit the test runner will output details of any test failures, report on how many tests were run and how many errors and failures were encountered, and destroy</p> <p>any test databases as usual. Thus pressing Ctrl-C can be very useful if you forget to pass the<a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>--failfast</i></a> option, notice that some tests are unexpectedly failing and want to get details on the failures without waiting for the full test run to complete.</p> <p>If you do not want to wait for the currently running test to finish, you can press Ctrl-C a second time and the test run will halt immediately, but not gracefully. No details of the tests run before the interruption will be reported, and any test databases created by the run will not be destroyed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Test with warnings enabled</p> <p>It’s a good idea to run your tests with Python warnings enabled: python -Wa manage.py test. The-Wa flag tells Python to display deprecation warnings. Django, like many other Python libraries, uses these warnings to flag when features are going away. It also might flag areas in your code that aren’t strictly wrong but could benefit from a better implementation.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_472"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The test database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Tests that require a database (namely, model tests) will not use your “real” (production) database. Separate, blank databases are created for the tests.</p> <p>Regardless of whether the tests pass or fail, the test databases are destroyed when all the tests have been executed.</p> <p>You can prevent the test databases from being destroyed by using the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test --keepdb</i></a> option. This will preserve the test database between runs. If the database does not exist, it will first be created. Any migrations will also be applied in order to keep it up to date.</p> <p>As described in the previous section, if a test run is forcefully interrupted, the test database may not be</p> <p>destroyed. On the next run, you’ll be asked whether you want to reuse or destroy the database. Use the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>--noinput</i></a> option to suppress that prompt and automatically destroy the database. This can be useful when running tests on a continuous integration server where tests may be interrupted by a timeout, for example.</p> <p>The default test database names are created by prepending test_ to the value of each <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>. When using SQLite, the tests will use an in-memory database by default (i.e., the database will be created in</p> <p>memory, bypassing the filesystem entirely!). The <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>TEST</i></a> dictionary in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> offers a number of settings</p> <p>to configure your test database. For example, if you want to use a different database name, specify <a href="index.html#page_1901"><i>NAME</i></a> in</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>TEST</i></a> dictionary for any given database in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>.</p> <p>On PostgreSQL, <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a> will also need read access to the built-in postgres database.</p> <p>Aside from using a separate database, the test runner will otherwise use all of the same database settings you</p> <p>have in your settings file: <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>ENGINE</i></a> , <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> , etc. The test database is created by the user specified by <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a>, so you’ll need to make sure that the given user account has sufficient privileges to create a new database on the system.</p> <p>For fine-grained control over the character encoding of your test database, use the <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>CHARSET</i></a> TEST option. If</p> <p>you’re using MySQL, you can also use the <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>COLLATION</i></a> option to control the particular collation used by the</p> <p>test database. See the <a href="index.html#page_1887">settings documentation</a> for details of these and other advanced settings.</p> <p>If using an SQLite in-memory database with SQLite, <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/sharedcache.html">shared cache</a> is enabled, so you can write tests with ability to share the database between threads.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finding data from your production database when running tests?</p> <p>If your code attempts to access the database when its modules are compiled, this will occur before the test database is set up, with potentially unexpected results. For example, if you have a database query in module-level code and a real database exists, production data could pollute your tests. It is a bad idea to have such import-time database queries in your code anyway - rewrite your code so that it doesn’t do this.</p> <p>This also applies to customized implementations of <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i>.</a></p> <p id="page_473" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_518">advanced multi-db testing topics.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Order in which tests are executed</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In order to guarantee that all TestCase code starts with a clean database, the Django test runner reorders tests in the following way:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• All <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>TestCase</i></a> subclasses are run first.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Then, all other Django-based tests (test case classes based on <a href="index.html#page_490"><i>SimpleTestCase</i>, </a>including</p> <p style="text-align:center"><a href="index.html#page_491"><i>TransactionTestCase</i></a>) are run with no particular ordering guaranteed nor enforced among them.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Then any other <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a> tests (including doctests) that may alter the database without</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">restoring it to its original state are run.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The new ordering of tests may reveal unexpected dependencies on test case ordering. This is the case</p> <p>with doctests that relied on state left in the database by a given <a href="index.html#page_491"><i>TransactionTestCase</i></a> test, they must be updated to be able to run independently.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Failures detected when loading tests are ordered before all of the above for quicker feedback. This includes things like test modules that couldn’t be found or that couldn’t be loaded due to syntax errors.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You may randomize and/or reverse the execution order inside groups using the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test --shuffle</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>--reverse</i></a> options. This can help with ensuring your tests are independent from each other.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Rollback emulation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any initial data loaded in migrations will only be available in TestCase tests and not in TransactionTestCase tests, and additionally only on backends where transactions are supported (the most important exception being MyISAM). This is also true for tests which rely on TransactionTestCase</p> <p>such as <a href="index.html#page_493"><i>LiveServerTestCase</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1378"><i>StaticLiveServerTestCase</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1378">.</a></p> <p>Django can reload that data for you on a per-testcase basis by setting the serialized_rollback option to True in the body of the TestCase or TransactionTestCase, but note that this will slow down that test suite by approximately 3x.</p> <p>Third-party apps or those developing against MyISAM will need to set this; in general, however, you should be developing your own projects against a transactional database and be using TestCase for most tests, and thus not need this setting.</p> <p id="page_474"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The initial serialization is usually very quick, but if you wish to exclude some apps from this process (and</p> <p>speed up test runs slightly), you may add those apps to <a href="index.html#page_1934"><i>TEST_NON_SERIALIZED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p>To prevent serialized data from being loaded twice, setting serialized_rollback=True disables the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1961"><i>post_migrate</i></a> signal when flushing the test database.</p> <p>For <a href="index.html#page_491"><i>TransactionTestCase</i>, </a>serialized migration data is made available during setUpClass().</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Other test conditions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Regardless of the value of the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting in your configuration file, all Django tests run with <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> =False. This is to ensure that the observed output of your code matches what will be seen in a production setting.</p> <p>Caches are not cleared after each test, and running manage.py test fooapp can insert data from the tests into the cache of a live system if you run your tests in production because, unlike databases, a separate “test</p> <p>cache” is not used. This behavior <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/11505">may change</a> in the future.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Understanding the test output</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you run your tests, you’ll see a number of messages as the test runner prepares itself. You can control the level of detail of these messages with the verbosity option on the command line:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Creating</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">database...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Creating table myapp_animal</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Creating table myapp_mineral</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This tells you that the test runner is creating a test database, as described in the previous section.</p> <p>Once the test database has been created, Django will run your tests. If everything goes well, you’ll see some-thing like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">----------------------------------------------------------------------</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Ran</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">22</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">tests</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.221s</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">OK</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If there are test failures, however, you’ll see full details about which tests failed:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>======================================================================</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FAIL: test_was_published_recently_with_future_poll</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>(</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">polls.tests.PollMethodTests</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>)</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">----------------------------------------------------------------------</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Traceback</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>(</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">most recent call last</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>)</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">File</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/dev/mysite/polls/tests.py"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, line</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">16</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test_was_published_recently_with_future_poll</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self.assertIs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>(</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">future_poll.was_published_recently</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>()</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, False</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>)</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AssertionError: True is not False</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_475" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">----------------------------------------------------------------------</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Ran</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.003s</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">FAILED</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>(</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">failures</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>)</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A full explanation of this error output is beyond the scope of this document, but it’s pretty intuitive. You</p> <p>can consult the documentation of Python’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#module-unittest">unittest</a> library for details.</p> <p>Note that the return code for the test-runner script is 1 for any number of failed tests (whether the failure was caused by an error, a failed assertion, or an unexpected success). If all the tests pass, the return code is 0. This feature is useful if you’re using the test-runner script in a shell script and need to test for success or failure at that level.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Speeding up the tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running tests in parallel</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As long as your tests are properly isolated, you can run them in parallel to gain a speed up on multi-core</p> <p>hardware. See <a href="index.html#page_1458"><i>test --parallel</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Password hashing</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The default password hasher is rather slow by design. If you’re authenticating many users in your tests, you</p> <p>may want to use a custom settings file and set the <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> setting to a faster hashing algorithm:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.MD5PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Don’t forget to also include in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> any hashing algorithm used in fixtures, if any.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Preserving the test database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test --keepdb</i></a> option preserves the test database between test runs. It skips the create and destroy actions which can greatly decrease the time to run tests.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_476"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Avoiding disk access for media files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1480"><i>InMemoryStorage</i></a> is a convenient way to prevent disk access for media files. All data is kept in memory, then it gets discarded after tests run.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.9.2 Testing tools</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides a small set of tools that come in handy when writing tests.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The test client</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The test client is a Python class that acts as a dummy web browser, allowing you to test your views and interact with your Django-powered application programmatically.</p> <p>Some of the things you can do with the test client are:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Simulate GET and POST requests on a URL and observe the response – everything from low-level</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">HTTP (result headers and status codes) to page content.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• See the chain of redirects (if any) and check the URL and status code at each step.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Test that a given request is rendered by a given Django template, with a template context that contains</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">certain values.</p> <p>Note that the test client is not intended to be a replacement for <a href="https://www.selenium.dev/">Selenium</a> or other “in-browser” frameworks. Django’s test client has a different focus. In short:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Use Django’s test client to establish that the correct template is being rendered and that the template</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">is passed the correct context data.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Use <a href="index.html#page_515"><i>RequestFactory</i></a> to test view functions directly, bypassing the routing and middleware layers.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Use in-browser frameworks like <a href="https://www.selenium.dev/">Selenium</a> to test rendered HTML and the behavior of web pages,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">namely JavaScript functionality. Django also provides special support for those frameworks; see the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">section on <a href="index.html#page_493"><i>LiveServerTestCase</i></a> for more details.</p> <p>A comprehensive test suite should use a combination of all of these test types.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overview and a quick example</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To use the test client, instantiate django.test.Client and retrieve web pages:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">post(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/login/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"username"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"john"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"password"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"smith"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">status_code</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_477" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">200</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/customer/details/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">content</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">b'<!DOCTYPE html...'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As this example suggests, you can instantiate Client from within a session of the Python interactive inter-preter.</p> <p>Note a few important things about how the test client works:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The test client does not require the web server to be running. In fact, it will run just fine with no web</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">server running at all! That’s because it avoids the overhead of HTTP and deals directly with the Django framework. This helps make the unit tests run quickly.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When retrieving pages, remember to specify the path of the URL, not the whole domain. For example,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">this is correct:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/login/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This is incorrect:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"https://www.example.com/login/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The test client is not capable of retrieving web pages that are not powered by your Django project. If</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">you need to retrieve other web pages, use a Python standard library module such as <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.html#module-urllib">urllib</a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• To resolve URLs, the test client uses whatever URLconf is pointed-to by your <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>ROOT_URLCONF</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Although the above example would work in the Python interactive interpreter, some of the test client’s</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">functionality, notably the template-related functionality, is only available while tests are running.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The reason for this is that Django’s test runner performs a bit of black magic in order to determine which template was loaded by a given view. This black magic (essentially a patching of Django’s template system in memory) only happens during test running.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• By default, the test client will disable any CSRF checks performed by your site.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If, for some reason, you want the test client to perform CSRF checks, you can create an instance of the test client that enforces CSRF checks. To do this, pass in the enforce_csrf_checks argument when you construct your client:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_client</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client(enforce_csrf_checks</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p id="page_478"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Making requests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use the django.test.Client class to make requests.</p> <p><b>class Client</b>(enforce_csrf_checks=False, raise_request_exception=True,</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">json_encoder=DjangoJSONEncoder, *, headers=None, query_params=None, **defaults)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A testing HTTP client. Takes several arguments that can customize behavior.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">headers allows you to specify default headers that will be sent with every request.
