style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">XPATH,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'//input[@value="Log in"]'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">click()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, you may run the test as follows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.tests.MySeleniumTests.test_login</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example will automatically open Firefox then go to the login page, enter the credentials and press the “Log in” button. Selenium offers other drivers in case you do not have Firefox installed or wish to use another</p> <p id="page_495" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>browser. The example above is just a tiny fraction of what the Selenium client can do; check out the <a href="https://selenium-python.readthedocs.io/api.html">full</a></p> <p><a href="https://selenium-python.readthedocs.io/api.html">reference</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: When using an in-memory SQLite database to run the tests, the same database connection will be shared by two threads in parallel: the thread in which the live server is run and the thread in which the test case is run. It’s important to prevent simultaneous database queries via this shared connection by the two threads, as that may sometimes randomly cause the tests to fail. So you need to ensure that the two threads don’t access the database at the same time. In particular, this means that in some cases (for example, just after clicking a link or submitting a form), you might need to check that a response is received by Selenium and that the next page is loaded before proceeding with further test execution. Do this, for example, by making Selenium wait until the <body> HTML tag is found in the response (requires Selenium > 2.13):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_login</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">selenium.webdriver.support.wait</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WebDriverWait</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">timeout</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">selenium</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">find_element(By</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">XPATH,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'//input[@value="Log in"]'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">click()</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Wait until the response is received</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">WebDriverWait(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">selenium, timeout)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">until(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>lambda</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">driver: driver</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">find_element(By</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">TAG_NAME,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"body"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The tricky thing here is that there’s really no such thing as a “page load,” especially in modern web apps that generate HTML dynamically after the server generates the initial document. So, checking for the presence</p> <p>of <body> in the response might not necessarily be appropriate for all use cases. Please refer to the <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132110/http://code.google.com/p/selenium/wiki/FrequentlyAskedQuestions#Q:_WebDriver_fails_to_find_elements_/_Does_not_block_on_page_loa">Selenium</a></p> <p><a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20160129132110/http://code.google.com/p/selenium/wiki/FrequentlyAskedQuestions#Q:_WebDriver_fails_to_find_elements_/_Does_not_block_on_page_loa">FAQ</a> and <a href="https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/#explicit-waits">Selenium documentation</a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Test cases features</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Default test client</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>client</b></p> <p>Every test case in a django.test.*TestCase instance has access to an instance of a Django test client. This client can be accessed as self.client. This client is recreated for each test, so you don’t have to worry about state (such as cookies) carrying over from one test to another.</p> <p>This means, instead of instantiating a Client in each test:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">unittest</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Customizing the test client</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>client_class</b></p> <p>If you want to use a different Client class style="font-size:0.87em">call_some_test_code()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Fixture loading</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>TransactionTestCase.<b>fixtures</b></p> <p>A test case class for a database-backed website isn’t much use if there isn’t any data in the database. Tests</p> <p>are more readable and it’s more maintainable to create objects using the ORM, for example in <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>TestCase.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_492"><i>setUpTestData()</i>, </a>however, you can also use <a href="index.html#page_248">fixtures</a>.</p> <p>A fixture is a collection of data that Django knows how to import into a database. For example, if your site has user accounts, you might set up a fixture of fake user accounts in order to populate your database during tests.</p> <p>The most straightforward way of creating a fixture is to use the <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>manage.py dumpdata</i></a> command. This as-</p> <p>sumes you already have some data in your database. See the <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata documentation</i></a> for more details.</p> <p>Once you’ve created a fixture and placed it in a fixtures directory in one of your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>, you can</p> <p>use it in your unit tests by specifying a fixtures class attribute on your <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>django.test.TestCase</i></a> subclass:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TestCase</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Animal</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>AnimalTestCase</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fixtures</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"mammals.json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"birds"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>setUp</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Test definitions as before.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_setup_methods()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_fluffy_animals</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># A test that uses the fixtures.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_some_test_code()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here’s specifically what will happen:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• During setUpClass(), all the named fixtures are installed. In this example, Django will install any</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">JSON fixture named mammals, followed by any fixture named birds. See the <a href="index.html#page_248">Fixtures</a> topic for more details on defining and installing fixtures.</p> <p id="page_498"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For most unit tests using <a href="index.html#page_492"><i>TestCase</i></a>, Django doesn’t need to do anything else, because transactions are used</p> <p>to clean the database after each test for performance reasons. But for <a href="index.html#page_491"><i>TransactionTestCase</i>, </a>the following actions will take place:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• At the end of each test Django will flush the database, returning the database to the state it was in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">directly after <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> was called.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• For each subsequent test, the fixtures will be reloaded before setUp() is run.</p> <p>In any case, you can be certain that the outcome of a test will not be affected by another test or by the order of test execution.</p> <p>By default, fixtures are only loaded into the default database. If you are using multiple databases and set</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_498"><i>TransactionTestCase.databases</i>, </a>fixtures will be loaded into all specified databases.</p> <p>For <a href="index.html#page_491"><i>TransactionTestCase</i>, </a>fixtures were made available during setUpClass().</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>URLconf configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your application provides views, you may want to include tests that use the test client to exercise those views. However, an end user is free to deploy the views in your application at any URL of their choosing. This means that your tests can’t rely upon the fact that your views will be available at a particular URL. Decorate your test class or test method with @override_settings(ROOT_URLCONF=...) for URLconf configuration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Multi-database support</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>TransactionTestCase.<b>databases</b></p> <p>Django sets up a test database corresponding to every database that is defined in the <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> definition in your settings and referred to by at least one test through databases.</p> <p>However, a big part of the time taken to run a Django TestCase is consumed by the call to flush that ensures that you have a clean database at the start of each test run. If you have multiple databases, multiple flushes are required (one for each database), which can be a time consuming activity – especially if your tests don’t need to test multi-database activity.</p> <p>As an optimization, Django only flushes the default database at the start of each test run. If your setup contains multiple databases, and you have a test that requires every database to be clean, you can use the databases attribute on the test suite to request extra databases to be flushed.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TestMyViews</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TransactionTestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">databases</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"other"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_index_page_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_some_test_code()</span></p> <p id="page_499" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This test case class will flush the default and other test databases before running test_index_page_view. You can also use '__all__' to specify that all of the test databases must be flushed.</p> <p>The databases flag also controls which databases the <a href="index.html#page_497"><i>TransactionTestCase.fixtures</i></a> are loaded into. By default, fixtures are only loaded into the default database.</p> <p>Queries against databases not in databases will give assertion errors to prevent state leaking between tests.</p> <p>TestCase.<b>databases</b></p> <p>By default, only the default database will be wrapped in a transaction during a TestCase’s execution and attempts to query other databases will result in assertion errors to prevent state leaking between tests.</p> <p>Use the databases class attribute on the test class to request transaction wrapping against non-default databases.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>OtherDBTests</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">databases</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"other"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_other_db_query</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This test will only allow queries against the other database. Just like for <a href="index.html#page_490"><i>SimpleTestCase.databases</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_498"><i>TransactionTestCase.databases</i>, </a>the '__all__' constant can be used to specify that the test should allow queries to all databases.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overriding settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Use the functions below to temporarily alter the value of settings in tests. Don’t manipulate</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">django.conf.settings directly as Django won’t restore the original values after such manipulations.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>settings</b>()</p> <p>For testing purposes it’s often useful to change a setting temporarily and revert to the original value after</p> <p>running the testing code. For this use case Django provides a standard Python context manager (see <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0343/">PEP</a></p> <p><a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0343/">343</a>) called <a href="index.html#page_499"><i>settings()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_499">, </a>which can be used like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># First check for the default behavior</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_500"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">client</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/sekrit/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertRedirects(response,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/other/login/?next=/sekrit/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example will override the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>LOGIN_URL</i></a> setting for the code in the with block and reset its value to the previous state afterward.</p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>modify_settings</b>()</p> <p>It can prove unwieldy to redefine settings that contain a list of values. In practice, adding or removing values</p> <p>is often sufficient. Django provides the <a href="index.html#page_500"><i>modify_settings()</i></a> context manager for easier settings changes:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span <p>For each action, you can supply either a list of values or a string. When the value already exists in the list, append and prepend have no effect; neither does remove when the value doesn’t exist.</p> <p><b>override_settings</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p>In case you want to override a setting for a test method, Django provides the <a href="index.html#page_500"><i>override_settings()</i></a> decorator</p> <p>(see <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0318/">PEP 318</a>). It’s used like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TestCase, override_settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_501" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>LoginTestCase</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@override_settings(LOGIN_URL</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/other/login/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">client</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/sekrit/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">client</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/other/login/?next=/sekrit/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>modify_settings</b>(*args, **kwargs)</p> <p>Likewise, Django provides the <a href="index.html#page_501"><i>modify_settings()</i></a> decorator:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TestCase, modify_settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span <p>The decorator can also be applied to test case classes:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">client</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: When given a class, these decorators modify the class directly and return it; they don’t create and return a modified copy of it. So if you try to tweak the above examples to assign the return value to a different name than LoginTestCase or MiddlewareTestCase, you may be surprised to find that the original</p> <p>test case classes are still equally affected by the decorator. For a given class, <a href="index.html#page_501"><i>modify_settings()</i></a> is always</p> <p>applied after <a href="index.html#page_500"><i>override_settings()</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: The settings file contains some settings that are only consulted during initialization of Django</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">internals. If you change them with override_settings, the setting is changed if you access it via the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">django.conf.settings module, however, Django’s internals access it differently. Effectively, using</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="index.html#page_500"><i>override_settings()</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_501"><i>modify_settings()</i></a> with these settings is probably not going to do what you</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">expect it to do.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">We do not recommend altering the <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> setting. Altering the <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> setting is possible, but a</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">bit tricky if you are using internals that make using of caching, like <a href="index.html#page_311"><i>django.contrib.sessions</i></a>. For</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">example, you will have to reinitialize the session backend in a test that uses cached sessions and overrides</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> .</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Finally, avoid aliasing your settings as module-level constants as override_settings() won’t work on</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">such values since they are only evaluated the first time the module is imported.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also simulate the absence of a setting by deleting it after settings have been overridden, like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@override_settings()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_something</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>del</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGIN_URL</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When overriding settings, make sure to handle the cases in which your app’s code uses a cache or simi-</p> <p>lar feature that retains state even if the setting is changed. Django provides the <a href="index.html#page_1964"><i>django.test.signals.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1964"><i>setting_changed</i></a> signal that lets you register callbacks to clean up and otherwise reset state when settings are changed.</p> <p>Django itself uses this signal to reset various data:</p> <p id="page_503" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Overridden settings Data reset</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">USE_TZ, TIME_ZONE Databases timezone</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">TEMPLATES Template engines</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">FORM_RENDERER Default renderer</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">SERIALIZATION_MODULES Serializers cache</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">LOCALE_PATHS, LANGUAGE_CODE Default translation and loaded translations STATIC_ROOT, STATIC_URL, STORAGES Storages configuration</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Resetting the default renderer when the FORM_RENDERER setting is changed was added.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Isolating apps</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>utils.<b>isolate_apps</b>(*app_labels, attr_name=None, kwarg_name=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Registers the models defined within a wrapped context into their own isolated <a href="index.html#page_927"><i>apps</i></a> registry. This func-tionality is useful when creating model classes for tests, as the classes will be cleanly deleted afterward, and there is no risk of name collisions.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The app labels which the isolated registry should contain must be passed as individual arguments. You can use isolate_apps() as a decorator or a context manager. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SimpleTestCase</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test.utils</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">isolate_apps</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModelTests</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(SimpleTestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@isolate_apps(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app_label"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_model_definition</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TestModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><i>. . .</i> or:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>with</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">isolate_apps(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app_label"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TestModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The decorator form can also be applied to classes.</p> <p id="page_504"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Two optional keyword arguments can be specified:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• attr_name: attribute assigned the isolated registry if used as a class decorator.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• kwarg_name: keyword argument passing the isolated registry if used as a function decorator.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The temporary Apps instance used to isolate model registration can be retrieved as an attribute when used as a class decorator by using the attr_name parameter:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@isolate_apps(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app_label"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, attr_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"apps"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TestModelDefinition</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(SimpleTestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_model_definition</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TestModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertIs(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_model(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app_label"</span><span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Assertions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As Python’s normal <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a> class implements assertion methods such as <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase.assertTrue">assertTrue()</a> and</p> <p><a custom assertion methods that are useful for testing web applications:</p> <p>The failure messages given by most of these assertion methods can be customized with the msg_prefix ar-gument. This string will be prefixed to any failure message generated by the assertion. This allows you to provide additional details that may help you to identify the location and cause of a failure in your test suite.</p> <p id="page_505" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>assertRaisesMessage</b>(expected_exception, expected_message, callable, *args,</p> <p style="margin-left:14em">**kwargs)</p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>assertRaisesMessage</b>(expected_exception, expected_message)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Asserts that execution of callable raises expected_exception and that expected_message is found in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the exception’s message. Any other outcome is reported as a failure. expression.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If only the expected_exception and expected_message parameters are given, returns a context man-ager so that the code being tested can be written inline If present, the scheme in expected_url is the one used to make the comparisons to.</p> <p>SimpleTestCase.<b>assertHTMLEqual</b>(html1, html2, msg=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Asserts that the strings html1 and html2 are equal. The comparison is based on HTML semantics. The comparison takes following things into account:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Whitespace before and after HTML tags is ignored.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• All types of whitespace are considered equivalent.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• All open tags are closed implicitly, e.g. when a surrounding tag is closed or the HTML document</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">ends.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Empty tags are equivalent to their self-closing version.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• The ordering of attributes of an HTML element is not significant.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Boolean attributes (like checked) without an argument are equal to attributes that equal in name</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">and value (see the examples).</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Text, character references, and entity references that refer to the same character are equivalent.</p> <p id="page_508"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The following examples are valid tests and don’t raise any AssertionError:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertHTMLEqual(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"<p>Hello <b>'world'!</p>"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""<p></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Hello</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>'world'! </b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></p>"""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertHTMLEqual(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'<input type="checkbox" checked="checked" id="id_accept_terms" />'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'<input id="id_accept_terms" type="checkbox" checked>'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">html1 and html2 must contain HTML. style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Person</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Daniel"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Tagging tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can tag your tests so you can easily run a particular subset. For example, you might label fast or slow tests:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">tag</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SampleTestCase</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fast"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_fast</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"slow"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_slow</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"slow"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"core"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_slow_but_core</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also tag a test case class:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"slow"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"core"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SampleTestCase</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Subclasses inherit tags from superclasses, and methods inherit tags from their class. Given:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"foo"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SampleTestCaseChild</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(SampleTestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@tag(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"bar"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SampleTestCaseChild.test will be labeled with 'slow', 'core', 'bar', and 'foo'.</p> <p>Then you can choose which tests to run. For example, to run only fast tests:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--tag</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fast</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Or to run fast tests and the core one (even though it’s slow):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--tag</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fast --tag</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">core</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also exclude tests by tag. To run core tests if they are not slow:</p> <p id="page_511" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">./manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--tag</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">core --exclude-tag</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">slow</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>test --exclude-tag</i></a> has precedence over <a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>test --tag</i></a>, so if a test has two tags and you select one of them and exclude the other, the test won’t be run.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Testing asynchronous code</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you merely want to test the output of your asynchronous views, the standard test client will run them inside their own asynchronous loop without any extra work needed on your part.</p> <p>However, if you want to write fully-asynchronous tests for a Django project, you will need to take several things into account.</p> <p>Firstly, your tests must be async def methods on the test class (in order to give them an asynchronous context). Django will automatically detect any async def tests and wrap them so they run in their own event loop.</p> <p>If you are testing from an asynchronous function, you must also use the asynchronous test client. This is available as django.test.AsyncClient, or as self.async_client on any test.</p> <p><b>class AsyncClient</b>(enforce_csrf_checks=False, raise_request_exception=True, *, headers=None,</p> <p style="margin-left:8em">query_params=None, **defaults)</p> <p>AsyncClient has the same methods and signatures as the synchronous (normal) test client, with the following exceptions:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• In the initialization, arbitrary keyword arguments in defaults are added directly into the ASGI scope.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Headers passed as extra keyword arguments should not have the HTTP_ prefix required by the syn-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">chronous client (see <a href="index.html#page_478"><i>Client.get()</i></a>). For example, here is how to set an HTTP Accept header:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AsyncClient()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/customers/details/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fred"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"age"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">7</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}, ACCEPT</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"application/json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The query_params argument was added.</p> <p>Using AsyncClient any method that makes a request must be awaited:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>test_my_thing</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">async_client</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/some-url/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertEqual(response</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">status_code,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">200</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The asynchronous client can also call synchronous views; it runs through Django’s <a href="index.html#page_764">asynchronous request</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_764">path, </a>which supports both. Any view called through the AsyncClient will get an ASGIRequest object for its request rather than the WSGIRequest that the normal client creates.</p> <p id="page_512"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If you are using test decorators, they must be async-compatible to ensure they work correctly.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Django’s built-in decorators will behave correctly, but third-party ones may appear to not execute (they</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">will “wrap” the wrong part of the execution flow and not your test).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">If you need to use these decorators, then you should decorate your test methods with <a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">inside of them instead:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyTests</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(TestCase):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@mock</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span </p> <p><b>Email services</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If any of your Django views send email using <a href="index.html#page_634">Django’s email functionality, </a>you probably don’t want to send email each time you run a test using that view. For this reason, Django’s test runner automatically redirects all Django-sent email to a dummy outbox. This lets you test every aspect of sending email – from the number of messages sent to the contents of each message – without actually sending the messages.</p> <p>The test runner accomplishes this by transparently replacing the normal email backend with a testing back-end. (Don’t worry – this has no effect on any other email senders outside of Django, such as your machine’s mail server, if you’re running one.)</p> <p>django.core.mail.<b>outbox</b></p> <p>During test running, each outgoing email is saved in django.core.mail.outbox. This is a list of all</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_640"><i>EmailMessage</i></a> instances that have been sent. The outbox attribute is a special attribute that is created only</p> <p>when the locmem email backend is used. It doesn’t normally exist as part of the <a href="index.html#page_634"><i>django.core.mail</i></a> module and you can’t import it directly. The code below shows how to access this attribute correctly.</p> <p>Here’s an example test that examines django.core.mail.outbox for length and contents:</p> <p><span The output can be redirected into a StringIO instance:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">io</span> <span
