style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">sys</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">exit(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">bool</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(failures))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This is the script that you invoke to run the test suite. It sets up the Django environment, creates the test database and runs the tests.</p> <p>For the sake of clarity, this example contains only the bare minimum necessary to use the Django test runner. You may want to add command-line options for controlling verbosity, passing in specific test labels to run, etc.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_524"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 27: tests/test_settings.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SECRET_KEY</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fake-key"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INSTALLED_APPS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"tests"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This file contains the <a href="index.html#page_745">Django settings</a> required to run your app’s tests.</p> <p>Again, this is a minimal example; your tests may require additional settings to run.</p> <p>Since the tests package is included in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> when running your tests, you can define test-only models in its models.py file.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using different testing frameworks</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Clearly, <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#module-unittest">unittest</a> is not the only Python testing framework. While Django doesn’t provide explicit support for alternative frameworks, it does provide a way to invoke tests constructed for an alternative framework as if they were normal Django tests.</p> <p>When you run ./manage.py test, Django looks at the <a href="index.html#page_1934"><i>TEST_RUNNER</i></a> setting to determine what to do. By de-</p> <p>fault, <a href="index.html#page_1934"><i>TEST_RUNNER</i></a> points to 'django.test.runner.DiscoverRunner'. This class defines the default Django testing behavior. This behavior involves:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Performing global pre-test setup.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Looking for tests in any file below the current directory whose name matches the pattern test*.py.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Creating the test databases.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. Running migrate to install models and initial data into the test databases.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">5. Running the <a href="index.html#page_757">system checks.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">6. Running the tests that were found.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">7. Destroying the test databases.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">8. Performing global post-test teardown.</p> <p>If you define your own test runner class and point <a href="index.html#page_1934"><i>TEST_RUNNER</i></a> at that class, Django will execute your test runner whenever you run ./manage.py test. In this way, it is possible to use any test framework that can be executed from Python code, or to modify the Django test execution process to satisfy whatever testing requirements you may have.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_525" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Defining a test runner</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A test runner is a class defining a run_tests() method. Django ships with a DiscoverRunner class that defines the default Django testing behavior. This class defines the run_tests() entry point, plus a selection of other methods that are used by run_tests() to set up, execute and tear down the test suite.</p> <p><b>class DiscoverRunner</b>(pattern='test*.py', top_level=None, verbosity=1, interactive=True,</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">failfast=False, keepdb=False, reverse=False, debug_mode=False, debug_sql=False, parallel=0, tags=None, exclude_tags=None,</p> <p style="text-align:right">test_name_patterns=None, pdb=False, buffer=False, enable_faulthandler=True, timing=True, shuffle=False, logger=None, durations=None, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">DiscoverRunner will search for tests in any file matching pattern.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">top_level can be used to specify the directory containing your top-level Python modules. Usually Django can figure this out automatically, so it’s not necessary to specify this option. If specified, it should generally be the directory containing your manage.py file.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">verbosity determines the amount of notification and debug information that will be printed to the console; 0 is no output, 1 is normal output, and 2 is verbose output.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If interactive is True, the test suite has permission to ask the user for instructions when the test suite is executed. An example of this behavior would be asking for permission to delete an existing test database. If interactive is False, the test suite must be able to run without any manual intervention.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If failfast is True, the test suite will stop running after the first test failure is detected.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If keepdb is True, the test suite will use the existing database, or create one if necessary. If False, a new database will be created, prompting the user to remove the existing one, if present.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If reverse is True, test cases will be executed in the opposite order. This could be useful to debug tests</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">that aren’t properly isolated and have side effects. <a href="index.html#page_473">Grouping by test class</a> is preserved when using this option. This option can be used in conjunction with--shuffle to reverse the order for a particular random seed.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">debug_mode specifies what the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting should be set to prior to running tests.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">parallel specifies the number of processes. If parallel is greater than 1, the test suite will run in parallel processes. If there are fewer test case classes than configured processes, Django will reduce the number of processes accordingly. Each process gets its own database. This option requires the third-party tblib package to display tracebacks correctly.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tags can be used to specify a set of <a href="index.html#page_510">tags for filtering tests</a>. May be combined with exclude_tags.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">exclude_tags can be used to specify a set of <a href="index.html#page_510">tags for excluding tests</a>. May be combined with tags.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If debug_sql is True, failing test cases will output SQL queries logged to the <a href="index.html#page_1586">django.db.backends logger</a> as well as the traceback. If verbosity is 2, then queries in all tests are output.</p> <p id="page_526"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">test_name_patterns can be used to specify a set of patterns for filtering test methods and classes by their names.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If pdb is True, a debugger (pdb or ipdb) will be spawned at each test error or failure.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If buffer is True, outputs from passing tests will be discarded.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If enable_faulthandler is True, <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/faulthandler.html#module-faulthandler">faulthandler</a> will be enabled.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If timing is True, test timings, including database setup and total run time, will be shown.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If shuffle is an integer, test cases will be shuffled in a random order prior to execution, using the integer as a random seed. If shuffle is None, the seed will be generated randomly. In both cases, the seed will be logged and set to self.shuffle_seed prior to running tests. This option can be used to help detect</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tests that aren’t properly isolated. <a href="index.html#page_473">Grouping by test class</a> is preserved when using this option.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">logger can be used to pass a Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logger">Logger object</a>. If provided, the logger will be used to log mes-sages instead of printing to the console. The logger object will respect its logging level rather than the verbosity.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">durations will show a list of the N slowest test cases. Setting this option to 0 will result in the duration for all tests being shown. Requires Python 3.12+.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Django may, from time to time, extend the capabilities of the test runner by adding new arguments. The **kwargs declaration allows for this expansion. If you subclass DiscoverRunner or write your own test runner, ensure it accepts **kwargs.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Your test runner may also define additional command-line options. <span style="float:right">Create or override an</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">add_arguments(cls, parser) class method and add custom arguments by calling parser.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">add_argument() inside the method, so that the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test</i></a> command will be able to use those arguments.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Attributes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>test_suite</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The class used to build the test suite. By default it is set to unittest.TestSuite. This can be overridden if you wish to implement different logic for collecting tests.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>test_runner</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">This is the class of the low-level test runner which is used to execute the individual tests and format the results. By default it is set to unittest.TextTestRunner. Despite the unfortunate similarity in naming conventions, this is not the same type of class as DiscoverRunner, which covers a broader set of responsibilities. You can override this attribute to modify the way tests are run and reported.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>test_loader</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This is the class that loads tests, whether from TestCases or modules or otherwise and bundles them into test suites for the runner to execute. By default it is set to unittest.defaultTestLoader. You can override this attribute if your tests are going to be loaded in unusual ways.</p> <p id="page_527" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>run_tests</b>(test_labels, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Run the test suite.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">test_labels allows you to specify which tests to run and supports several formats (see</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_527"><i>DiscoverRunner.build_suite()</i></a> for a list of supported formats).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This method should return the number of tests that failed.</p> <p><b>classmethod</b> DiscoverRunner.<b>add_arguments</b>(parser)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Override this class method to add custom arguments accepted by the <a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>test</i></a> management command. See</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument">argparse.ArgumentParser.add_argument()</a> for details about adding arguments to a parser.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>setup_test_environment</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Sets up the test environment by calling <a href="index.html#page_528"><i>setup_test_environment()</i></a> and setting <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> to self. debug_mode (defaults to False).</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>build_suite</b>(test_labels=None, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Constructs a test suite that matches the test labels provided.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">test_labels is a list of strings describing the tests to be run. A test label can take one of four forms:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• path.to.test_module.TestCase.test_method – Run a single test method in a test case class.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• path.to.test_module.TestCase – Run all the test methods in a test case.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• path.to.module – Search for and run all tests in the named Python package or module.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• path/to/directory – Search for and run all tests below the named directory.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If test_labels has a value of None, the test runner will search for tests in all files below the current directory whose names match its pattern (see above).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a TestSuite instance ready to be run.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>setup_databases</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates the test databases by calling <a href="index.html#page_528"><i>setup_databases()</i>.</a></p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>run_checks</b>(databases)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Runs the <a href="index.html#page_757">system checks</a> on the test databases.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>run_suite</b>(suite, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Runs the test suite.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the result produced by the running the test suite.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>get_test_runner_kwargs</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the keyword arguments to instantiate the DiscoverRunner.test_runner with.</p> <p id="page_528"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>teardown_databases</b>(old_config, **kwargs)</p> <p style="text-align:center">Destroys the test databases, restoring pre-test conditions by calling <a href="index.html#page_528"><i>teardown_databases()</i>.</a></p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>teardown_test_environment</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Restores the pre-test environment.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>suite_result</b>(suite, result, **kwargs)</p> <p style="text-align:center">Computes and returns a return code based on a test suite, and the result from that test suite.</p> <p>DiscoverRunner.<b>log</b>(msg, level=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If a logger is set, logs the message at the given integer <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#levels">logging level</a> (e.g. logging.DEBUG, logging. INFO , or logging.WARNING). Otherwise, the message is printed to the console, respecting the current verbosity. For example, no message will be printed if the verbosity is 0, INFO and above will be printed if the verbosity is at least 1, and DEBUG will be printed if it is at least 2. The level defaults to logging.INFO .</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Testing utilities</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.test.utils</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To assist in the creation of your own test runner, Django provides a number of utility methods in the django. test.utils module.</p> <p><b>setup_test_environment</b>( debug=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Performs global pre-test setup, such as installing instrumentation for the template rendering system and setting up the dummy email outbox.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If debug isn’t None, the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting is updated to its value.</p> <p><b>teardown_test_environment</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Performs global post-test teardown, such as removing instrumentation from the template system and restoring normal email services.</p> <p><b>setup_databases</b>(verbosity, interactive, *, time_keeper=None, keepdb=False, debug_sql=False,</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">parallel=0, aliases=None, serialized_aliases=None, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates the test databases.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a data structure that provides enough detail to undo the changes that have been made. This</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">data will be provided to the <a href="index.html#page_528"><i>teardown_databases()</i></a> function at the conclusion of testing.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The aliases argument determines which <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> aliases test databases should be set up for. If it’s</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">not provided, it defaults to all of <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> aliases.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The serialized_aliases argument determines what subset of aliases test databases should have</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">their state serialized to allow usage of the <a href="index.html#page_473">serialized_rollback</a> feature. If it’s not provided, it defaults to aliases.</p> <p id="page_529" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>teardown_databases</b>(old_config, parallel=0, keepdb=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Destroys the test databases, restoring pre-test conditions.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">old_config is a data structure defining the changes in the database configuration that need to be re-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">versed. It’s the return value of the <a href="index.html#page_528"><i>setup_databases()</i></a> method.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.db.connection.creation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The creation module of the database backend also provides some utilities that can be useful during testing.</p> <p><b>create_test_db</b>(verbosity=1, autoclobber=False, serialize=True, keepdb=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a new test database and runs migrate against it.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">verbosity has the same behavior as in run_tests().</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">autoclobber describes the behavior that will occur if a database with the same name as the test database is discovered:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• If autoclobber is False, the user will be asked to approve destroying the existing database. sys.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">exit is called if the user does not approve.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• If autoclobber is True, the database will be destroyed without consulting the user.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">serialize determines if Django serializes the database into an in-memory JSON string before running tests (used to restore the database state between tests if you don’t have transactions). You can set this</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to False to speed up creation time if you don’t have any test classes with <a href="index.html#page_473">serialized_rollback=True</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">keepdb determines if the test run should use an existing database, or create a new one. If True, the existing database will be used, or created if not present. If False, a new database will be created, prompting the user to remove the existing one, if present.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the name of the test database that it created.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">create_test_db() has the side effect of modifying the value of <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> to match the name of the test database.</p> <p><b>destroy_test_db</b>(old_database_name, verbosity=1, keepdb=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Destroys the database whose name is the value of <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>, and sets <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> to the value of old_database_name .</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The verbosity argument has the same behavior as for <a href="index.html#page_525"><i>DiscoverRunner</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If the keepdb argument is True, then the connection to the database will be closed, but the database will not be destroyed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_530"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Integration with coverage.py</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Code coverage describes how much source code has been tested. It shows which parts of your code are being exercised by tests and which are not. It’s an important part of testing applications, so it’s strongly recom-mended to check the coverage of your tests.</p> <p>Django can be easily integrated with <a href="https://coverage.readthedocs.io/">coverage.py, </a>a tool for measuring code coverage of Python programs.</p> <p>First, install <a href="https://pypi.org/project/coverage/">coverage. </a>Next, run the following from your project folder containing manage.py:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">coverage run --source</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'.'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This runs your tests and collects coverage data of the executed files in your project. You can see a report of this data by typing following command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">coverage report</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that some Django code was executed while running tests, but it is not listed here because of the source flag passed to the previous command.</p> <p>For more options like annotated HTML listings detailing missed lines, see the <a href="https://coverage.readthedocs.io/">coverage.py</a> docs.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.10 User authentication in Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.10.1 Using the Django authentication system</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document explains the usage of Django’s authentication system in its default configuration. This con-figuration has evolved to serve the most common project needs, handling a reasonably wide range of tasks, and has a careful implementation of passwords and permissions. For projects where authentication needs</p> <p>differ from the default, Django supports extensive <a href="index.html#page_576">extension and customization</a> of authentication.</p> <p>Django authentication provides both authentication and authorization together and is generally referred to as the authentication system, as these features are somewhat coupled.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>User objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> objects are the core of the authentication system. They typically represent the people interacting with your site and are used to enable things like restricting access, registering user profiles, associating content</p> <p>with creators etc. Only one class of user exists in Django’s authentication framework, i.e., <a href="index.html#page_1103"><i>'superusers'</i></a> or</p> <p>admin <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>'staff'</i></a> users are just user objects with special attributes set, not different classes of user objects.</p> <p>The primary attributes of the default user are:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>username</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>password</i></a></p> <p id="page_531" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>email</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>first_name</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>last_name</i></a></p> <p>See the <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>full API documentation</i></a> for full reference, the documentation that follows is more task oriented.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The most direct way to create users is to use the included <a href="index.html#page_1106"><i>create_user()</i></a> helper function:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create_user(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"john"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"lennon@thebeatles.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"johnpassword"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># At this point, user is a User object that has already been saved</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"># to the database. You can continue to change its attributes</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"># if you want to change other fields.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Lennon"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have the Django admin installed, you can also <a href="index.html#page_561">create users interactively.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating superusers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Create superusers using the <a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>createsuperuser</i></a> command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py createsuperuser --username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">joe --email</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">joe@example.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You will be prompted for a password. After you enter one, the user will be created immediately. If you leave</p> <p>off the<a href="index.html#page_1462"><i>--username</i></a> or<a href="index.html#page_1462"><i>--email</i></a> options, it will prompt you for those values.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Changing passwords</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django does not store raw (clear text) passwords on the user model, but only a hash (see <a href="index.html#page_562">documentation of</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_562">how passwords are managed</a> for full details). Because of this, do not attempt to manipulate the password attribute of the user directly. This is why a helper function is used when creating a user.</p> <p>To change a user’s password, you have several options:</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>manage.py changepassword *username*</i></a> offers a method of changing a user’s password from the command line. It prompts you to change the password of a given user which you must enter twice. If they both match, the new password will be changed immediately. If you do not supply a user, the command will attempt to change the password whose username matches the current system user.</p> <p>You can also change a password programmatically, using <a href="index.html#page_1104"><i>set_password()</i>:</a></p> <p id="page_532"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">u</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"john"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">u</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set_password(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"new password"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">u</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have the Django admin installed, you can also change user’s passwords on the <a href="index.html#page_561">authentication system’s</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_561">admin pages.</a></p> <p>Django also provides <a href="index.html#page_548">views</a> and <a href="index.html#page_557">forms</a> that may be used to allow users to change their own passwords.</p> <p>Changing a user’s password will log out all their sessions. See <a href="index.html#page_547">Session invalidation on password change</a> for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authenticating users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>authenticate</b>(request=None, **credentials)</p> <p><b>aauthenticate</b>(request=None, **credentials)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Asynchronous version: aauthenticate()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Use <a href="index.html#page_532"><i>authenticate()</i></a> to verify a set of credentials. It takes credentials as keyword arguments, username</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">and password for the default case, checks them against each <a href="index.html#page_576">authentication backend</a>, and returns a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> object if the credentials are valid for a backend. If the credentials aren’t valid for any backend or</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">if a backend raises <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>PermissionDenied</i></a>, it returns None. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">authenticate</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">authenticate(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"john"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"secret"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>is not None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># A backend authenticated the credentials</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># No backend authenticated the credentials</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">request is an optional <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a> which is passed on the authenticate() method of the authenti-cation backends.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: <span style="float:right">This is a low level way to authenticate a set of credentials; for example, it’s used by the</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1600"><i>RemoteUserMiddleware</i></a>. Unless you are writing your own authentication system, you probably won’t</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">use this. Rather if you’re looking for a way to login a user, use the <a href="index.html#page_549"><i>LoginView</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_533" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Permissions and Authorization</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django comes with a built-in permissions system. It provides a way to assign permissions to specific users and groups of users.</p> <p>It’s used by the Django admin site, but you’re welcome to use it in your own code.</p> <p>The Django admin site uses permissions as follows:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Access to view objects is limited to users with the “view” or “change” permission for that type of object.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Access to view the “add” form and add an object is limited to users with the “add” permission for that</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">type of object.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Access to view the change list, view the “change” form and change an object is limited to users with the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">“change” permission for that type of object.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Access to delete an object is limited to users with the “delete” permission for that type of object.</p> <p>Permissions can be set not only per type of object, but also per specific object instance. <span style="float:right">By</span></p> <p>using the <a href="index.html#page_1072"><i>has_view_permission()</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1072"><i>has_add_permission()</i>, <i>has_change_permission()</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1072"><i>has_delete_permission()</i></a> methods provided by the <a href="index.html#page_1038"><i>ModelAdmin</i></a> class, it is possible to customize per-missions for different object instances of the same type.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> objects have two many-to-many fields: groups and user_permissions. <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> objects can access their</p> <p>related objects in the same way as any other <a href="index.html#page_115">Django model:</a></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">groups</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set([group_list])</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">groups</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add(group, group,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">groups</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">remove(group, group,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">groups</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">clear()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user_permissions</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set([permission_list])</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user_permissions</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add(permission, permission,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user_permissions</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">remove(permission, permission,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">myuser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user_permissions</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">clear()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Default permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When django.contrib.auth is listed in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting, it will ensure that four default per-missions – add, change, delete, and view – are created for each Django model defined in one of your installed applications.</p> <p>These permissions will be created when you run <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>manage.py migrate</i>; </a>the first time you run migrate after</p> <p>adding django.contrib.auth to <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>, the default permissions will be created for all previously-installed models, as well as for any new models being installed at that time. Afterward, it will create default</p> <p>permissions for new models each time you run <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>manage.py migrate</i></a> (the function that creates permissions is</p> <p>connected to the <a href="index.html#page_1961"><i>post_migrate</i></a> signal).</p> <p id="page_534"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Assuming you have an application with an <a href="index.html#page_1678"><i>app_label</i></a> foo and a model named Bar, to test for basic permis-sions you should use:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• add: user.has_perm('foo.add_bar')</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• change: user.has_perm('foo.change_bar')</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• delete: user.has_perm('foo.delete_bar')</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• view: user.has_perm('foo.view_bar')</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Permission</i></a> model is rarely accessed directly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Groups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>django.contrib.auth.models.Group</i></a> models are a generic way of categorizing users so you can apply per-missions, or some other label, to those users. A user can belong to any number of groups.</p> <p>A user in a group automatically has the permissions granted to that group. For example, if the group Site editors has the permission can_edit_home_page, any user in that group will have that permission.</p> <p>Beyond permissions, groups are a convenient way to categorize users to give them some label, or extended functionality. For example, you could create a group 'Special users', and you could write code that could, say, give them access to a members-only portion of your site, or send them members-only email messages.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Programmatically creating permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While <a href="index.html#page_581">custom permissions</a> can be defined within a model’s Meta class, you can also create permissions directly. For example, you can create the can_publish permission for a BlogPost model in myapp:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BlogPost</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Permission</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.contenttypes.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_for_model(BlogPost)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">permission</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Permission</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">codename</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"can_publish"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Can Publish Posts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The permission can then be assigned to a <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> via its user_permissions attribute or to a <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Group</i></a> via its permissions attribute.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Proxy models need their own content type</p> <p id="page_535" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to create <a href="index.html#page_536">permissions for a proxy model</a>, pass for_concrete_model=False to</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1117"><i>ContentTypeManager.get_for_model()</i></a> to get the appropriate ContentType:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_for_model(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">BlogPostProxy, for_concrete_model</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Permission caching</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1111"><i>ModelBackend</i></a> caches permissions on the user object after the first time they need to be fetched for a permissions check. This is typically fine for the request-response cycle since permissions aren’t typically checked immediately after they are added (in the admin, for example). If you are adding permissions and checking them immediately afterward, in a test or view for example, the easiest solution is to re-fetch the user from the database. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Permission, User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.contenttypes.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">get_object_or_404</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span
