To help prevent confusion with similar usernames, the form doesn’t allow usernames that differ only in case.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authentication data in templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The currently logged-in user and their permissions are made available in the <a href="index.html#page_2030">template context</a> when you use</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_2042"><i>RequestContext</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Technicality</p> <p>Technically, these variables are only made available in the template context if you use <a href="index.html#page_2042"><i>RequestContext</i></a> and the 'django.contrib.auth.context_processors.auth' context processor is enabled. It is in the default</p> <p>generated settings file. For more, see the <a href="index.html#page_2042">RequestContext docs</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When rendering a template <a href="index.html#page_2042"><i>RequestContext</i>, </a>the currently logged-in user, either a <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> instance or an</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1107"><i>AnonymousUser</i></a> instance, is stored in the template variable {{ user }}:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user.is_authenticated</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Welcome,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user.username</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">. Thanks for logging in.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>Welcome, new user. Please log in.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This template context variable is not available if a RequestContext is not being used.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The currently logged-in user’s permissions are stored in the template variable {{ perms }}. This is an in-stance of django.contrib.auth.context_processors.PermWrapper, which is a template-friendly proxy of permissions.</p> <p>Evaluating a single-attribute lookup of {{ perms }} as a boolean is a proxy to <a href="index.html#page_1106"><i>User.has_module_perms()</i></a>. For example, to check if the logged-in user has any permissions in the foo app:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms.foo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p id="page_561" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Evaluating a two-level-attribute lookup as a boolean is a proxy to <a href="index.html#page_1105"><i>User.has_perm()</i></a>. For example, to check if the logged-in user has the permission foo.add_vote:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms.foo.add_vote</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here’s a more complete example of checking permissions in a template:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms.foo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>You have permission to do something in the foo app.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms.foo.add_vote</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>You can vote!</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms.foo.add_driving</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>You can drive!</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>You don't have permission to do anything in the foo app.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is possible to also look permissions up by {% if in %} statements. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'foo'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'foo.add_vote'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">perms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>In lookup works, too.</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">p</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Managing users in the admin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you have both django.contrib.admin and django.contrib.auth installed, the admin provides a convenient way to view and manage users, groups, and permissions. Users can be created and deleted like any Django model. Groups can be created, and permissions can be assigned to users or groups. A log of user edits to models made within the admin is also stored and displayed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You should see a link to “Users” in the “Auth” section of the main admin index page. The “Add user” admin page is different than standard admin pages in that it requires you to choose a username and password before allowing you to edit the rest of the user’s fields. Alternatively, on this page, you can choose a username and disable password-based authentication for the user.</p> <p>Also note: if you want a user account to be able to create users using the Django admin site, you’ll need to give them permission to add users and change users (i.e., the “Add user” and “Change user” permissions). If an account has permission to add users but not to change them, that account won’t be able to add users.</p> <p id="page_562"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Why? Because if you have permission to add users, you have the power to create superusers, which can then, in turn, change other users. So Django requires add and change permissions as a slight security measure.</p> <p>Be thoughtful about how you allow users to manage permissions. If you give a non-superuser the ability to edit users, this is ultimately the same as giving them superuser status because they will be able to elevate permissions of users including themselves!</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Changing passwords</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>User passwords are not displayed in the admin (nor stored in the database), but the <a href="index.html#page_562">password storage details</a> are displayed. Included in the display of this information is a link to a password change form that allows admins to change or unset user passwords.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.10.2 Password management in Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Password management is something that should generally not be reinvented unnecessarily, and Django en-deavors to provide a secure and flexible set of tools for managing user passwords. This document describes how Django stores passwords, how the storage hashing can be configured, and some utilities to work with hashed passwords.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>Even though users may use strong passwords, attackers might be able to eavesdrop on their connections. Use</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_720">HTTPS</a> to avoid sending passwords (or any other sensitive data) over plain HTTP connections because they will be vulnerable to password sniffing.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How Django stores passwords</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides a flexible password storage system and uses PBKDF2 by default.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>password</i></a> attribute of a <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> object is a string in this format:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><algorithm>$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Those are the components used for storing a User’s password, separated by the dollar-sign character and consist of: the hashing algorithm, the number of algorithm iterations (work factor), the random salt, and the resulting password hash. The algorithm is one of a number of one-way hashing or password storage algorithms Django can use; see below. Iterations describe the number of times the algorithm is run over the hash. Salt is the random seed used and the hash is the result of the one-way function.</p> <p>By default, Django uses the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBKDF2">PBKDF2</a> algorithm with a SHA256 hash, a password stretching mechanism rec-</p> <p>ommended by <a href="https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-132.pdf">NIST. </a>This should be sufficient for most users: it’s quite secure, requiring massive amounts of computing time to break.</p> <p id="page_563" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>However, depending on your requirements, you may choose a different algorithm, or even use a custom algorithm to match your specific security situation. Again, most users shouldn’t need to do this – if you’re not sure, you probably don’t. If you do, please read on:</p> <p>Django chooses the algorithm to use by consulting the <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> setting. This is a list of hashing algorithm classes that this Django installation supports.</p> <p>For storing passwords, Django will use the first hasher in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a>. To store new passwords with</p> <p>a different algorithm, put your preferred algorithm first in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a>.</p> <p>For verifying passwords, Django will find the hasher in the list that matches the algorithm name in the stored</p> <p>password. If a stored password names an algorithm not found in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a>, trying to verify it will raise ValueError.</p> <p>The default for <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> is:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.ScryptPasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This means that Django will use <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBKDF2">PBKDF2</a> to store all passwords but will support checking passwords stored</p> <p>with PBKDF2SHA1, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2">argon2, </a>and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bcrypt">bcrypt</a><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bcrypt">.</a></p> <p>The next few sections describe a couple of common ways advanced users may want to modify this setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using Argon2 with Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2">Argon2</a> is the winner of the 2015 <a href="https://www.password-hashing.net/">Password Hashing Competition</a><a href="https://www.password-hashing.net/">, </a>a community organized open competition to select a next generation hashing algorithm. It’s designed not to be easier to compute on custom hardware than it is to compute on an ordinary CPU. The default variant for the Argon2 password hasher is Argon2id.</p> <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2">Argon2</a> is not the default for Django because it requires a third-party library. The Password Hashing Com-petition panel, however, recommends immediate use of Argon2 rather than the other algorithms supported by Django.</p> <p>To use Argon2id as your default storage algorithm, do the following:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Install the <a href="https://pypi.org/project/argon2-cffi/">argon2-cffi</a> package. This can be done by running python -m pip install</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">django[argon2], which is equivalent to python -m pip install argon2-cffi (along with any version requirement from Django’s pyproject.toml).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Modify <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> to list Argon2PasswordHasher first. That is, in your settings file, you’d put:</p> <p id="page_564"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.ScryptPasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Keep and/or add any entries in this list if you need Django to <a href="index.html#page_568">upgrade passwords.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using bcrypt with Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bcrypt">Bcrypt</a> is a popular password storage algorithm that’s specifically designed for long-term password storage. It’s not the default used by Django since it requires the use of third-party libraries, but since many people may want to use it Django supports bcrypt with minimal effort.</p> <p>To use Bcrypt as your default storage algorithm, do the following:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Install the <a href="https://pypi.org/project/bcrypt/">bcrypt</a> package. This can be done by running python -m pip install django[bcrypt],</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">which is equivalent to python -m pip install bcrypt (along with any version requirement from Django’s pyproject.toml).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Modify <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> to list BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher first. That is, in your settings file,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">you’d put:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.ScryptPasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Keep and/or add any entries in this list if you need Django to <a href="index.html#page_568">upgrade passwords.</a></p> <p>That’s it – now your Django install will use Bcrypt as the default storage algorithm.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using scrypt with Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrypt">scrypt</a> is similar to PBKDF2 and bcrypt in utilizing a set number of iterations to slow down brute-force attacks. However, because PBKDF2 and bcrypt do not require a lot of memory, attackers with sufficient</p> <p>resources can launch large-scale parallel attacks in order to speed up the attacking process. <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrypt">scrypt</a> is specifi-cally designed to use more memory compared to other password-based key derivation functions in order to</p> <p>limit the amount of parallelism an attacker can use, see <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7914.html">RFC 7914</a> for more details.</p> <p id="page_565" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To use <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrypt">scrypt</a> as your default storage algorithm, do the following:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Modify <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a> to list ScryptPasswordHasher first. That is, in your settings file:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.ScryptPasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Keep and/or add any entries in this list if you need Django to <a href="index.html#page_568">upgrade passwords.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: scrypt requires OpenSSL 1.1+.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Increasing the salt entropy</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Most password hashes include a salt along with their password hash in order to protect against rainbow table attacks. The salt itself is a random value which increases the size and thus the cost of the rainbow table and is currently set at 128 bits with the salt_entropy value in the BasePasswordHasher. As computing and storage costs decrease this value should be raised. When implementing your own password hasher you are free to override this value in order to use a desired entropy level for your password hashes. salt_entropy is measured in bits.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Implementation detail</p> <p>Due to the method in which salt values are stored the salt_entropy value is effectively a minimum value. For instance a value of 128 would provide a salt which would actually contain 131 bits of entropy.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Increasing the work factor</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PBKDF2 and bcrypt</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The PBKDF2 and bcrypt algorithms use a number of iterations or rounds of hashing. This deliberately slows down attackers, making attacks against hashed passwords harder. However, as computing power increases, the number of iterations needs to be increased. We’ve chosen a reasonable default (and will increase it with each release of Django), but you may wish to tune it up or down, depending on your security needs and available processing power. To do so, you’ll subclass the appropriate algorithm and override the iterations <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_566">parameter (use the rounds parameter when subclassing a bcrypt hasher). For example, to increase the num-ber of iterations used by the default PBKDF2 algorithm:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Create a subclass of django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.hashers</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PBKDF2PasswordHasher</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyPBKDF2PasswordHasher</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(PBKDF2PasswordHasher):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">A subclass of PBKDF2PasswordHasher that uses 100 times more iterations.</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">iterations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PBKDF2PasswordHasher</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">iterations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Save this somewhere in your project. For example, you might put this in a file like myproject/hashers. py.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Add your new hasher as the first entry in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a>:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD_HASHERS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"myproject.hashers.MyPBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.hashers.ScryptPasswordHasher"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That’s it – now your Django install will use more iterations when it stores passwords using PBKDF2.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: bcrypt rounds is a logarithmic work factor, e.g. 12 rounds means 2 ** 12 iterations.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Argon2</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Argon2 has the following attributes that can be customized:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. time_cost controls the number of iterations within the hash.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. memory_cost controls the size of memory that must be used during the computation of the hash.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. parallelism controls how many CPUs the computation of the hash can be parallelized on.</p> <p>The default values of these attributes are probably fine for you. If you determine that the password hash is too fast or too slow, you can tweak it as follows:</p> <p id="page_567" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Choose parallelism to be the number of threads you can spare computing the hash.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Choose memory_cost to be the KiB of memory you can spare.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Adjust time_cost and measure the time hashing a password takes. Pick a time_cost that takes an</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">acceptable time for you. If time_cost set to 1 is unacceptably slow, lower memory_cost.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>memory_cost</b> interpretation</p> <p>The argon2 command-line utility and some other libraries interpret the memory_cost parameter differently from the value that Django uses. The conversion is given by memory_cost == 2 ** memory_cost_commandline.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>scrypt</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrypt">scrypt</a> has the following attributes that can be customized:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. work_factor controls the number of iterations within the hash.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. block_size</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. parallelism controls how many threads will run in parallel.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. maxmem limits the maximum size of memory that can be used during the computation of the hash.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Defaults to 0, which means the default limitation from the OpenSSL library.</p> <p>We’ve chosen reasonable defaults, but you may wish to tune it up or down, depending on your security needs and available processing power.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Estimating memory usage</p> <p>The minimum memory requirement of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrypt">scrypt</a> is:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">work_factor</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">block_size</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">64</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>so you may need to tweak maxmem when changing the work_factor or block_size values.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_568"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Password upgrading</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When users log in, if their passwords are stored with anything other than the preferred algorithm, Django will automatically upgrade the algorithm to the preferred one. This means that old installs of Django will get automatically more secure as users log in, and it also means that you can switch to new (and better) storage algorithms as they get invented.</p> <p>However, Django can only upgrade passwords that use algorithms mentioned in <a href="index.html#page_1939"><i>PASSWORD_HASHERS</i></a>, so as you upgrade to new systems you should make sure never to remove entries from this list. If you do, users using unmentioned algorithms won’t be able to upgrade. Hashed passwords will be updated when increasing (or decreasing) the number of PBKDF2 iterations, bcrypt rounds, or argon2 attributes.</p> <p>Be aware that if all the passwords in your database aren’t encoded in the default hasher’s algorithm, you may be vulnerable to a user enumeration timing attack due to a difference between the duration of a login request for a user with a password encoded in a non-default algorithm and the duration of a login request</p> <p>for a nonexistent user (which runs the default hasher). You may be able to mitigate this by <a href="index.html#page_568">upgrading older</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_568">password hashes.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Password upgrading without requiring a login</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have an existing database with an older, weak hash such as MD5, you might want to upgrade those hashes yourself instead of waiting for the upgrade to happen when a user logs in (which may never happen if a user doesn’t return to your site). In this case, you can use a “wrapped” password hasher.</p> <p>For this example, we’ll migrate a collection of MD5 hashes to use PBKDF2(MD5(password)) and add the corresponding password hasher for checking if a user entered the correct password on login. We assume we’re using the built-in User model and that our project has an accounts app. You can modify the pattern to work with any algorithm or with a custom user model.</p> <p>First, we’ll add the custom hasher:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 28: accounts/hashers.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="text-indent:1em">• bcrypt_sha256</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• bcrypt</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• scrypt</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• md5</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing your own hasher</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you write your own password hasher that contains a work factor such as a number of iterations, you should implement a harden_runtime(self, password, encoded) method to bridge the runtime gap between the work factor supplied in the encoded password and the default work factor of the hasher. This prevents a user enumeration timing attack due to difference between a login request for a user with a password encoded in an older number of iterations and a nonexistent user (which runs the default hasher’s default number of iterations).</p> <p>Taking PBKDF2 as example, if encoded contains 20,000 iterations and the hasher’s default iterations is 30,000, the method should run password through another 10,000 iterations of PBKDF2.</p> <p id="page_571" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your hasher doesn’t have a work factor, implement the method as a no-op (pass).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Manually managing a user’s password</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_571"><i>django.contrib.auth.hashers</i></a> module provides a set of functions to create and validate hashed pass-words. You can use them independently from the User model.</p> <p><b>check_password</b>(password, encoded, setter=None, preferred='default')</p> <p><b>acheck_password</b>(password, encoded, asetter=None, preferred='default')</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Asynchronous version: acheck_password()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you’d like to manually authenticate a user by comparing a plain-text password to the hashed pass-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">word in the database, use the convenience function <a href="index.html#page_571"><i>check_password()</i></a>. It takes two mandatory argu-ments: the plain-text password to check, and the full value of a user’s password field in the database to check against. It returns True if they match, False otherwise. Optionally, you can pass a callable setter that takes the password and will be called when you need to regenerate it. You can also pass preferred to change a hashing algorithm if you don’t want to use the default (first entry of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">PASSWORD_HASHERS setting). See <a href="index.html#page_570">Included hashers</a> for the algorithm name of each hasher.</p> <p><b>make_password</b>(password, salt=None, hasher='default')</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a hashed password in the format used by this application. It takes one mandatory argument: the password in plain-text (string or bytes). Optionally, you can provide a salt and a hashing algorithm</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to use, if you don’t want to use the defaults (first entry of PASSWORD_HASHERS setting). See <a href="index.html#page_570">Included</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_570">hashers</a> for the algorithm name of each hasher. If the password argument is None, an unusable pass-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">word is returned (one that will never be accepted by <a href="index.html#page_571"><i>check_password()</i>).</a></p> <p><b>is_password_usable</b>(encoded_password)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns False if the password is a result of <a href="index.html#page_1104"><i>User.set_unusable_password()</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Password validation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Users often choose poor passwords. To help mitigate this problem, Django offers pluggable password vali-dation. You can configure multiple password validators at the same time. A few validators are included in Django, but you can write your own as well.</p> <p>Each password validator must provide a help text to explain the requirements to the user, validate a given password and return an error message if it does not meet the requirements, and optionally define a callback to be notified when the password for a user has been changed. Validators can also have optional settings to fine tune their behavior.</p> <p>Validation is controlled by the <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a> setting. The default for the setting is an empty</p> <p>list, which means no validators are applied. In new projects created with the default <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> template, a set of validators is enabled by default.</p> <p id="page_572"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, validators are used in the forms to reset or change passwords and in the <a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>createsuperuser</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>changepassword</i></a> management commands. Validators aren’t applied at the model level, for example in User. objects.create_user() and create_superuser(), because we assume that developers, not users, interact with Django at that level and also because model validation doesn’t automatically run as part of creating models.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Password validation can prevent the use of many types of weak passwords. However, the fact that a password passes all the validators doesn’t guarantee that it is a strong password. There are many factors that can weaken a password that are not detectable by even the most advanced password validators.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Enabling password validation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Password validation is configured in the <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a> setting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.password_validation.UserAttributeSimilarityValidator"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.password_validation.MinimumLengthValidator"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"min_length"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">9</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.password_validation.CommonPasswordValidator"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.password_validation.NumericPasswordValidator"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example enables all four included validators:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• UserAttributeSimilarityValidator, which checks the similarity between the password and a set of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">attributes of the user.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• MinimumLengthValidator, which checks whether the password meets a minimum length. This val-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">idator is configured with a custom option: it now requires the minimum length to be nine characters, instead of the default eight.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CommonPasswordValidator, which checks whether the password occurs in a list of common passwords.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">By default, it compares to an included list of 20,000 common passwords.</p> <p id="page_573" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• NumericPasswordValidator, which checks whether the password isn’t entirely numeric.</p> <p>For UserAttributeSimilarityValidator and CommonPasswordValidator, we’re using the default settings in this example. NumericPasswordValidator has no settings.</p> <p>The help texts and any errors from password validators are always returned in the order they are listed in</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a> .</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Included validators</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django includes four validators:</p> <p><b>class MinimumLengthValidator</b>(min_length=8)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Validates that the password is of a minimum length. The minimum length can be customized with the min_length parameter.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_error_message</b> ()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the ValidationError error message. Defaults to "This password is too short. It must contain at least <min_length> characters.".</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_help_text</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the validator’s help text. Defaults to "Your password must contain at least <min_length> characters.".</p> <p><b>class UserAttributeSimilarityValidator</b>(user_attributes=DEFAULT_USER_ATTRIBUTES,</p> <p style="text-align:center">max_similarity=0.7)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Validates that the password is sufficiently different from certain attributes of the user.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The user_attributes parameter should be an iterable of names of user attributes to compare to. If this argument is not provided, the default is used: 'username', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'email'. Attributes that don’t exist are ignored.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The maximum allowed similarity of passwords can be set on a scale of 0.1 to 1.0 with the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">max_similarity parameter. This is compared to the result of <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/difflib.html#difflib.SequenceMatcher.quick_ratio">difflib.SequenceMatcher.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/difflib.html#difflib.SequenceMatcher.quick_ratio">quick_ratio()</a>. A value of 0.1 rejects passwords unless they are substantially different from the user_attributes, whereas a value of 1.0 rejects only passwords that are identical to an attribute’s value.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_error_message</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the ValidationError error message. Defaults to "The password is too similar to the <user_attribute>.".</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_help_text</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the validator’s help text. Defaults to "Your password can’t be too similar to your other personal information.".</p> <p id="page_574"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CommonPasswordValidator</b>( password_list_path=DEFAULT_PASSWORD_LIST_PATH)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Validates that the password is not a common password. This converts the password to lowercase (to do a case-insensitive comparison) and checks it against a list of 20,000 common password created by</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://gist.github.com/roycewilliams/226886fd01572964e1431ac8afc999ce">Royce Williams</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The password_list_path can be set to the path of a custom file of common passwords. This file should contain one lowercase password per line and may be plain text or gzipped.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_error_message</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the ValidationError error message. Defaults to "This password is too common.".</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_help_text</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the validator’s help text. Defaults to "Your password can’t be a commonly used password." .</p> <p><b>class NumericPasswordValidator</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Validate that the password is not entirely numeric.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_error_message</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the ValidationError error message. Defaults to "This password is entirely numeric.".</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_help_text</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A hook for customizing the validator’s help text. Defaults to "Your password can’t be entirely numeric.".</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Integrating validation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are a few functions in django.contrib.auth.password_validation that you can call from your own forms or other code to integrate password validation. This can be useful if you use custom forms for password setting, or if you have API calls that allow passwords to be set, for example.</p> <p><b>validate_password</b>(password, user=None, password_validators=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Validates a password. If all validators find the password valid, returns None. If one or more validators</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">reject the password, raises a <a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>ValidationError</i></a> with all the error messages from the validators.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The user object is optional: if it’s not provided, some validators may not be able to perform any vali-dation and will accept any password.</p> <p><b>password_changed</b>( password, user=None, password_validators=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Informs all validators that the password has been changed. This can be used by validators such as one that prevents password reuse. This should be called once the password has been successfully changed.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>, the password field will be marked as “dirty” when calling</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_588"><i>set_password()</i></a> which triggers a call to password_changed() after the user is saved.</p> <p id="page_575" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>password_validators_help_texts</b>(password_validators=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a list of the help texts of all validators. These explain the password requirements to the user.</p> <p><b>password_validators_help_text_html</b>(password_validators=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an HTML string with all help texts in an <ul>. This is helpful when adding password validation to forms, as you can pass the output directly to the help_text parameter of a form field.</p> <p><b>get_password_validators</b>(validator_config)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a set of validator objects based on the validator_config parameter. By default, all functions</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">use the validators defined in <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a>, but by calling this function with an alternate set of validators and then passing the result into the password_validators parameter of the other functions, your custom set of validators will be used instead. This is useful when you have a typical set of validators to use for most scenarios, but also have a special situation that requires a custom set. If you always use the same set of validators, there is no need to use this function, as the configuration</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">from <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a> is used by default.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The structure of validator_config is identical to the structure of <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a>. The return value of this function can be passed into the password_validators parameter of the functions listed above.</p> <p>Note that where the password is passed to one of these functions, this should always be the clear text password- not a hashed password.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing your own validator</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If Django’s built-in validators are not sufficient, you can write your own password validators. Validators have a fairly small interface. They must implement two methods:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• validate(self, password, user=None): validate a password. Return None if the password is valid,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">or raise a <a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>ValidationError</i></a> with an error message if the password is not valid. You must be able to deal with user being None- if that means your validator can’t run, return None for no error.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• get_help_text(): provide a help text to explain the requirements to the user.</p> <p>Any items in the OPTIONS in <a href="index.html#page_1940"><i>AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS</i></a> for your validator will be passed to the constructor. All constructor arguments should have a default value.</p> <p>Here’s a basic example of a validator, with one optional setting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.exceptions</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ValidationError</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.translation</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">gettext</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">_</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MinimumLengthValidator</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, min_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">8</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">min_length</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">min_length</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_576"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>validate</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, password, user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">len</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(password)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b><</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">min_length:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>raise</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ValidationError(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">_(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"This password must contain at least %(min_length)d characters."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">code</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"password_too_short"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">params</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"min_length"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">min_length},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_help_text</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">_(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Your password must contain at least %(min_length)d characters."</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"min_length"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">min_length}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also implement password_changed(password, user=None), which will be called after a successful password change. That can be used to prevent password reuse, for example. However, if you decide to store a user’s previous passwords, you should never do so in clear text.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.10.3 Customizing authentication in Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The authentication that comes with Django is good enough for most common cases, but you may have needs not met by the out-of-the-box defaults. Customizing authentication in your projects requires understanding what points of the provided system are extensible or replaceable. This document provides details about how the auth system can be customized.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_576">Authentication backends</a> provide an extensible system for when a username and password stored with the user model need to be authenticated against a different service than Django’s default.</p> <p>You can give your models <a href="index.html#page_581">custom permissions</a> that can be checked through Django’s authorization system.</p> <p>You can <a href="index.html#page_582">extend</a> the default User model, or <a href="index.html#page_583">substitute</a> a completely customized model.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Other authentication sources</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There may be times you have the need to hook into another authentication source – that is, another source of usernames and passwords or authentication methods.</p> <p>For example, your company may already have an LDAP setup that stores a username and password for every employee. It’d be a hassle for both the network administrator and the users themselves if users had separate accounts in LDAP and the Django-based applications.</p> <p>So, to handle situations like this, the Django authentication system lets you plug in other authentication sources. You can override Django’s default database-based scheme, or you can use the default system in</p> <p id="page_577" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>tandem with other systems.</p> <p>See the <a href="index.html#page_1110">authentication backend reference</a> for information on the authentication backends included with Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Specifying authentication backends</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Behind the scenes, Django maintains a list of “authentication backends” that it checks for authentication.</p> <p>When somebody calls <a href="index.html#page_532"><i>django.contrib.auth.authenticate()</i></a> – as described in <a href="index.html#page_537">How to log a user in</a> – Django tries authenticating across all of its authentication backends. If the first authentication method fails, Django tries the second one, and so on, until all backends have been attempted.</p> <p>The list of authentication backends to use is specified in the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a> setting. This should be a list of Python path names that point to Python classes that know how to authenticate. These classes can be anywhere on your Python path.</p> <p>By default, <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a> is set to:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That’s the basic authentication backend that checks the Django users database and queries the built-in per-missions. It does not provide protection against brute force attacks via any rate limiting mechanism. You may either implement your own rate limiting mechanism in a custom auth backend, or use the mechanisms provided by most web servers.</p> <p>The order of <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a> matters, so if the same username and password is valid in multiple backends, Django will stop processing at the first positive match.</p> <p>If a backend raises a <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>PermissionDenied</i></a> exception, authentication will immediately fail. Django won’t check the backends that follow.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Once a user has authenticated, Django stores which backend was used to authenticate the user in the user’s session, and reuses the same backend for the duration of that session whenever access to the currently authenticated user is needed. This effectively means that authentication sources are cached on a per-session</p> <p>basis, so if you change <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a>, you’ll need to clear out session data if you need to force users to re-authenticate using different methods. A simple way to do that is to execute Session.objects. all().delete().</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_578"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing an authentication backend</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>An authentication backend is a class that implements two required methods: get_user(user_id) and</p> <p>authenticate(request, **credentials), as well as a set of optional permission related <a href="index.html#page_580">authorization</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_580">methods</a>.</p> <p>The get_user method takes a user_id – which could be a username, database ID or whatever, but has to be the primary key of your user object – and returns a user object or None.</p> <p>The authenticate method takes a request argument and credentials as keyword arguments. Most of the time, it’ll look like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.backends</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseBackend</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyBackend</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseBackend):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>authenticate</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request, username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Check the username/password and return a user.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>But it could also authenticate a token, like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.backends</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseBackend</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyBackend</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseBackend):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>authenticate</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request, token</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Check the token and return a user.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Either way, authenticate() should check the credentials it gets and return a user object that matches those credentials if the credentials are valid. If they’re not valid, it should return None.</p> <p>request is an <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a> and may be None if it wasn’t provided to <a href="index.html#page_532"><i>authenticate()</i></a> (which passes it on to the backend).</p> <p>The Django admin is tightly coupled to the Django <a href="index.html#page_530">User object</a>. For example, for a user to access the admin,</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User.is_staff</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User.is_active</i></a> must be True (see <a href="index.html#page_1093"><i>AdminSite.has_permission()</i></a> for details).</p> <p>The best way to deal with this is to create a Django User object for each user that exists for your backend (e.g., in your LDAP directory, your external SQL database, etc.). You can either write a script to do this in advance, or your authenticate method can do it the first time a user logs in.</p> <p>Here’s an example backend that authenticates against a username and password variable defined in your settings.py file and creates a Django User object the first time a user authenticates. In this example, the created Django User object is a superuser who will have full access to the admin:</p> <p id="page_579" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.backends</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseBackend</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.hashers</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">check_password</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SettingsBackend</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseBackend):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Authenticate against the settings ADMIN_LOGIN and ADMIN_PASSWORD.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Use the login name and a hash of the password. For example:</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">ADMIN_LOGIN = 'admin'</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">ADMIN_PASSWORD = 'pbkdf2_sha256$30000$Vo0VlMnkR4Bk$qEvtdyZRWTcOsCnI/oQ7fVOu1XAURIZYoOZ3iq8Dr4M=</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>authenticate</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request, username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">login_valid</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ADMIN_LOGIN</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">username</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pwd_valid</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">check_password(password, settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ADMIN_PASSWORD)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">login_valid</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>and</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pwd_valid:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>try</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">username)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>except</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DoesNotExist:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Create a new user. There's no need to set a password</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># because only the password from settings.py is checked.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">username)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># is_active defaults to True.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_staff</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= True</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_superuser</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= True</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return None</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_user</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, user_id):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>try</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user_id)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>except</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DoesNotExist:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return None</b></span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_580"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handling authorization in custom backends</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Custom auth backends can provide their own permissions.</p> <p>The user model and its manager will delegate permission lookup functions (<a href="index.html#page_1104"><i>get_user_permissions()</i></a>,</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1105"><i>get_group_permissions()</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1105"><i>get_all_permissions()</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1105"><i>has_perm()</i>,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1106"><i>has_module_perms()</i></a>, and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1107"><i>with_perm()</i></a>) to any authentication backend that implements these functions.</p> <p>The permissions given to the user will be the superset of all permissions returned by all backends. That is, Django grants a permission to a user that any one backend grants.</p> <p>If a backend raises a <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>PermissionDenied</i></a> exception in <a href="index.html#page_1105"><i>has_perm()</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1106"><i>has_module_perms()</i></a>, the authorization will immediately fail and Django won’t check the backends that follow.</p> <p>A backend could implement permissions for the magic admin like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.backends</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseBackend</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MagicAdminBackend</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseBackend):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>has_perm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, user_obj, perm, obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user_obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">username</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ADMIN_LOGIN</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This gives full permissions to the user granted access in the above example. Notice that in addition to the</p> <p>same arguments given to the associated <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>django.contrib.auth.models.User</i></a> functions, the backend auth functions all take the user object, which may be an anonymous user, as an argument.</p> <p>A full authorization implementation can be found in the ModelBackend class in</p> <p><a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/contrib/auth/backends.py">django/contrib/auth/backends.py, </a>which is the default backend and queries the auth_permission ta-ble most of the time.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authorization for anonymous users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>An anonymous user is one that is not authenticated i.e. they have provided no valid authentication details. However, that does not necessarily mean they are not authorized to do anything. At the most basic level, most websites authorize anonymous users to browse most of the site, and many allow anonymous posting of comments etc.</p> <p>Django’s permission framework does not have a place to store permissions for anonymous users. However, the</p> <p>user object passed to an authentication backend may be an <a href="index.html#page_1107"><i>django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser</i></a> object, allowing the backend to specify custom authorization behavior for anonymous users. This is especially useful for the authors of reusable apps, who can delegate all questions of authorization to the auth backend, rather than needing settings, for example, to control anonymous access.</p> <p id="page_581" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authorization for inactive users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>An inactive user is one that has its <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active</i></a> field set to False. The <a href="index.html#page_1111"><i>ModelBackend</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a> authentication backends prohibits these users from authenticating. If a custom user model doesn’t have an</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_587"><i>is_active</i></a> field, all users will be allowed to authenticate.</p> <p>You can use <a href="index.html#page_1112"><i>AllowAllUsersModelBackend</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>AllowAllUsersRemoteUserBackend</i></a> if you want to allow in-active users to authenticate.</p> <p>The support for anonymous users in the permission system allows for a scenario where anonymous users have permissions to do something while inactive authenticated users do not.</p> <p>Do not forget to test for the is_active attribute of the user in your own backend permission methods.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handling object permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s permission framework has a foundation for object permissions, though there is no implementation for it in the core. That means that checking for object permissions will always return False or an empty list (depending on the check performed). An authentication backend will receive the keyword parameters obj and user_obj for each object related authorization method and can return the object level permission as appropriate.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To create custom permissions for a given model object, use the permissions <a href="index.html#page_128">model Meta attribute.</a></p> <p>This example Task model creates two custom permissions, i.e., actions users can or cannot do with Task instances, specific to your application:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Task</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">permissions</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"change_task_status"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Can change the status of
