tasks"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"close_task"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Can remove a task by setting its status as closed"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The only thing this does is create those extra permissions when you run <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>manage.py migrate</i></a> (the function</p> <p>that creates permissions is connected to the <a href="index.html#page_1961"><i>post_migrate</i></a> signal). Your code is in charge of checking the value of these permissions when a user is trying to access the functionality provided by the application (changing the status of tasks or closing tasks.) Continuing the above example, the following checks if a user may close tasks:</p> <p id="page_582"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">has_perm(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app.close_task"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Extending the existing User model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are two ways to extend the default <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> model without substituting your own model. If the changes you need are purely behavioral, and don’t require any change to what is stored in the database, you can</p> <p>create a <a href="index.html#page_138">proxy model</a> based on <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a>. This allows for any of the features offered by proxy models including default ordering, custom managers, or custom model methods.</p> <p>If you wish to store information related to User, you can use a <a href="index.html#page_1652"><i>OneToOneField</i></a> to a model containing the fields for additional information. This one-to-one model is often called a profile model, as it might store non-auth related information about a site user. For example you might create an Employee model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Employee</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">OneToOneField(User, on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">department</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Assuming an existing Employee Fred Smith who has both a User and Employee model, you can access the related information using Django’s standard related model conventions:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">u</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fsmith"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">freds_department</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">u</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">employee</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">department</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To add a profile model’s fields to the user page in the admin, define an <a href="index.html#page_1077"><i>InlineModelAdmin</i></a> (for this example,</p> <p>we’ll use a <a href="index.html#page_1077"><i>StackedInline</i></a>) in your app’s admin.py and add it to a UserAdmin class which is registered with</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> class:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.admin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserAdmin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseUserAdmin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">my_user_profile_app.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Employee</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Define an inline admin descriptor for Employee model</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># which acts a bit like a singleton</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>EmployeeInline</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">StackedInline):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Employee</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">can_delete</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= False</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">verbose_name_plural</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"employee"</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_583" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Define a new User admin</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>UserAdmin</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseUserAdmin):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">inlines</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[EmployeeInline]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Re-register UserAdmin</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unregister(User)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(User, UserAdmin)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>These profile models are not special in any way - they are just Django models that happen to have a one-to-one</p> <p>link with a user model. As such, they aren’t auto created when a user is created, but a <a href="index.html#page_1956"><i>django.db.models.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1956"><i>signals.post_save</i></a> could be used to create or update related models as appropriate.</p> <p>Using related models results in additional queries or joins to retrieve the related data. Depending on your needs, a custom user model that includes the related fields may be your better option, however, existing relations to the default user model within your project’s apps may justify the extra database load.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Substituting a custom User model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some kinds of projects may have authentication requirements for which Django’s built-in <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> model is not always appropriate. For instance, on some sites it makes more sense to use an email address as your identification token instead of a username.</p> <p>Django allows you to override the default user model by providing a value for the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> setting that references a custom model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTH_USER_MODEL</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"myapp.MyUser"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This dotted pair describes the <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>label</i></a> of the Django app (which must be in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>), and the name of the Django model that you wish to use as your user model.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using a custom user model when starting a project</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re starting a new project, you can set up a custom user model that behaves identically to the default</p> <p>user model by subclassing <a href="index.html#page_589"><i>AbstractUser</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AbstractUser</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>User</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AbstractUser):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p id="page_584"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Don’t forget to point <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> to it. Do this before creating any migrations or running manage.py migrate for the first time.</p> <p>Also, register the model in the app’s admin.py:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.admin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserAdmin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(User, UserAdmin)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Changing to a custom user model mid-project</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Changing <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> after you’ve created database tables is possible, but can be complex, since it affects foreign keys and many-to-many relationships, for example.</p> <p>This change can’t be done automatically and requires manually fixing your schema, moving your data from</p> <p>the old user table, and possibly manually reapplying some migrations. See <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/25313">#25313</a> for an outline of the steps.</p> <p>Due to limitations of Django’s dynamic dependency feature for swappable models, the model referenced by</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> must be created in the first migration of its app (usually called 0001_initial); otherwise, you’ll have dependency issues.</p> <p>In addition, you may run into a CircularDependencyError when running your migrations as Django won’t be able to automatically break the dependency loop due to the dynamic dependency. If you see this error, you should break the loop by moving the models depended on by your user model into a second migration. (You can try making two normal models that have a ForeignKey to each other and seeing how makemigrations resolves that circular dependency if you want to see how it’s usually done.)</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Reusable apps and AUTH_USER_MODEL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Reusable apps shouldn’t implement a custom user model. A project may use many apps, and two reusable apps that implemented a custom user model couldn’t be used together. If you need to store per user informa-</p> <p>tion in your app, use a <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1652"><i>OneToOneField</i></a> to settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL as described below.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Referencing the User model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you reference <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> directly (for example, by referring to it in a foreign key), your code will not work in</p> <p>projects where the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> setting has been changed to a different user model.</p> <p><b>get_user_model</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Instead of referring to <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> directly, you should reference the user model using django.contrib.auth. get_user_model(). This method will return the currently active user model – the custom user model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">if one is specified, or <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> otherwise.</p> <p id="page_585" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When you define a foreign key or many-to-many relations to the user model, you should specify the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">custom model using the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> setting. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Article</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTH_USER_MODEL,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When connecting to signals sent by the user model, you should specify the custom model using the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> setting. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">post_save</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>post_save_receiver</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender, instance, created,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>pass</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">post_save</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(post_save_receiver, sender</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTH_USER_MODEL)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Generally speaking, it’s easiest to refer to the user model with the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a> setting in code that’s executed at import time, however, it’s also possible to call get_user_model() while Django is importing models, so you could use models.ForeignKey(get_user_model(), ...).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If your app is tested with multiple user models, using @override_settings(AUTH_USER_MODEL=...) for example, and you cache the result of get_user_model() in a module-level variable, you may need</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to listen to the <a href="index.html#page_1964"><i>setting_changed</i></a> signal to clear the cache. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">get_user_model</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">setting_changed</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.dispatch</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">receiver</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@receiver(setting_changed)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>user_model_swapped</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, setting,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">setting</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"AUTH_USER_MODEL"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">clear_cache()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">some_module</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_586"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">some_module</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">UserModel</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">get_user_model()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Specifying a custom user model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you start your project with a custom user model, stop to consider if this is the right choice for your project.</p> <p>Keeping all user related information in one model removes the need for additional or more complex database queries to retrieve related models. On the other hand, it may be more suitable to store app-specific user information in a model that has a relation with your custom user model. That allows each app to specify its own user data requirements without potentially conflicting or breaking assumptions by other apps. It also means that you would keep your user model as simple as possible, focused on authentication, and following the minimum requirements Django expects custom user models to meet.</p> <p>If you use the default authentication backend, then your model must have a single unique field that can be used for identification purposes. This can be a username, an email address, or any other unique attribute. A non-unique username field is allowed if you use a custom authentication backend that can support it.</p> <p>The easiest way to construct a compliant custom user model is to inherit from <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a> provides the core implementation of a user model, including hashed passwords and tok-enized password resets. You must then provide some key implementation details:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>CustomUser</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>USERNAME_FIELD</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A string describing the name of the field on the user model that is used as the unique identifier. This will usually be a username of some kind, but it can also be an email address, or any other unique identifier. The field must be unique (e.g. have unique=True set in its definition), unless you use a custom authentication backend that can support non-unique usernames.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">In the following example, the field identifier is used as the identifying field:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyUser</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AbstractBaseUser):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">identifier</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">40</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, unique</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">USERNAME_FIELD</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"identifier"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>EMAIL_FIELD</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A string describing the name of the email field on the User model. This value is returned by</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_588"><i>get_email_field_name()</i>.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>REQUIRED_FIELDS</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A list of the field names that will be prompted for when creating a user via the <a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>createsuperuser</i></a></p> <p id="page_587" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">management command. The user will be prompted to supply a value for each of these fields. It</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">must include any field for which <a href="index.html#page_1616"><i>blank</i></a> is False or undefined and may include additional fields you want prompted for when a user is created interactively. REQUIRED_FIELDS has no effect in other parts of Django, like creating a user in the admin.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">For example, here is the partial definition for a user model that defines two required fields - a date of birth and height:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyUser</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AbstractBaseUser):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">date_of_birth</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">height</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">FloatField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">REQUIRED_FIELDS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"date_of_birth"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"height"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Note: REQUIRED_FIELDS must contain all required fields on your user model, but should not contain the USERNAME_FIELD or password as these fields will always be prompted for.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>is_active</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A boolean attribute that indicates whether the user is considered “active”. This attribute is pro-vided as an attribute on AbstractBaseUser defaulting to True. How you choose to implement it</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">will depend on the details of your chosen auth backends. See the documentation of the <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>attribute on the built-in user model</i></a> for details.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_full_name</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Optional. A longer formal identifier for the user such as their full name. If implemented, this</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">appears alongside the username in an object’s history in <a href="index.html#page_1017"><i>django.contrib.admin</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_short_name</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Optional. A short, informal identifier for the user such as their first name. If implemented, this</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">replaces the username in the greeting to the user in the header of <a href="index.html#page_1017"><i>django.contrib.admin</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Importing <b>AbstractBaseUser</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">AbstractBaseUser and BaseUserManager are importable from django.contrib.auth.base_user so</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">that they can be imported without including django.contrib.auth in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following attributes and methods are available on any subclass of <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>AbstractBaseUser</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_username</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the value of the field nominated by USERNAME_FIELD.</p> <p id="page_588"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>clean</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Normalizes the username by calling <a href="index.html#page_588"><i>normalize_username()</i></a>. If you override this method, be sure to call super() to retain the normalization.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod get_email_field_name</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the name of the email field specified by the <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>EMAIL_FIELD</i></a> attribute. Defaults to 'email' if EMAIL_FIELD isn’t specified.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod normalize_username</b>(username)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Applies NFKC Unicode normalization to usernames so that visually identical characters with dif-ferent Unicode code points are considered identical.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>is_authenticated</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Read-only attribute which is always True (as opposed to AnonymousUser.is_authenticated which is always False). This is a way to tell if the user has been authenticated. This does not imply any permissions and doesn’t check if the user is active or has a valid session. Even though normally you will check this attribute on request.user to find out whether it has been populated</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">by the <a href="index.html#page_1599"><i>AuthenticationMiddleware</i></a> (representing the currently logged-in user), you should know</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">this attribute is True for any <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> instance.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>is_anonymous</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Read-only attribute which is always False. This is a way of differentiating <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> and</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1107"><i>AnonymousUser</i></a> objects. Generally, you should prefer using <a href="index.html#page_1103"><i>is_authenticated</i></a> to this attribute.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>set_password</b>( raw_password)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Sets the user’s password to the given raw string, taking care of the password hashing. Doesn’t save</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">the <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a> object.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">When the raw_password is None, the password will be set to an unusable password, as if</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_588"><i>set_unusable_password()</i></a> were used.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>check_password</b>(raw_password)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>acheck_password</b>(raw_password)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Asynchronous version: acheck_password()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True if the given raw string is the correct password for the user. (This takes care of the password hashing in making the comparison.)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>set_unusable_password</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Marks the user as having no password set. This isn’t the same as having a blank string for a pass-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">word. <a href="index.html#page_588"><i>check_password()</i></a> for this user will never return True. Doesn’t save the <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a> object.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">You may need this if authentication for your application takes place against an existing external source such as an LDAP directory.</p> <p id="page_589" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>has_usable_password</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns False if <a href="index.html#page_588"><i>set_unusable_password()</i></a> has been called for this user.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_session_auth_hash</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns an HMAC of the password field. Used for <a href="index.html#page_547">Session invalidation on password change</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_session_auth_fallback_hash</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Yields the HMAC of the password field using <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a>. Used by get_user().</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_589"><i>AbstractUser</i></a> subclasses <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>AbstractUser</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>clean</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Normalizes the email by calling <a href="index.html#page_590"><i>BaseUserManager.normalize_email()</i>. </a>If you override this method, be sure to call super() to retain the normalization.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing a manager for a custom user model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You should also define a custom manager for your user model. If your user model defines username, email, is_staff, is_active, is_superuser, last_login, and date_joined fields the same as Django’s default user,</p> <p>you can install Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1106"><i>UserManager</i></a> ; however, if your user model defines different fields, you’ll need to</p> <p>define a custom manager that extends <a href="index.html#page_590"><i>BaseUserManager</i></a> providing two additional methods:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>CustomUserManager</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>create_user</b>(username_field, password=None, **other_fields)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The prototype of create_user() should accept the username field, plus all required fields as argu-ments. For example, if your user model uses email as the username field, and has date_of_birth as a required field, then create_user should be defined as:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>create_user</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, email, date_of_birth, password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># create user here</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>create_superuser</b>(username_field, password=None, **other_fields)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The prototype of create_superuser() should accept the username field, plus all required fields as arguments. For example, if your user model uses email as the username field, and has date_of_birth as a required field, then create_superuser should be defined as:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>create_superuser</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, email, date_of_birth, password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># create superuser here</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For a <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> in <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>USERNAME_FIELD</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>REQUIRED_FIELDS</i></a>, these methods receive the value of the <a href="index.html#page_1648"><i>to_field</i></a></p> <p>(the <a href="index.html#page_1625"><i>primary_key</i></a> by default) of an existing instance.</p> <p id="page_590"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_590"><i>BaseUserManager</i></a> provides the following utility methods:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>BaseUserManager</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod normalize_email</b>(email)</p> <p style="text-align:center">Normalizes email addresses by lowercasing the domain portion of the email address.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_by_natural_key</b>( username)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>aget_by_natural_key</b>(username)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Asynchronous version: aget_by_natural_key()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Retrieves a user instance using the contents of the field nominated by USERNAME_FIELD.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">aget_by_natural_key() method was added.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Extending Django’s default User</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re entirely happy with Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> model, but you want to add some additional profile informa-</p> <p>tion, you could subclass <a href="index.html#page_589"><i>django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractUser</i></a> and add your custom profile fields,</p> <p>although we’d recommend a separate model as described in <a href="index.html#page_586">Specifying a custom user model.</a> AbstractUser</p> <p>provides the full implementation of the default <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> as an <a href="index.html#page_132">abstract model</a><a href="index.html#page_132">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom users and the built-in auth forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s built-in <a href="index.html#page_557">forms</a> and <a href="index.html#page_548">views</a> make certain assumptions about the user model that they are working with.</p> <p>The following forms are compatible with any subclass of <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_558"><i>AuthenticationForm</i></a>: Uses the username field specified by <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>USERNAME_FIELD</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_559"><i>SetPasswordForm</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_559"><i>PasswordChangeForm</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_557"><i>AdminPasswordChangeForm</i></a></p> <p>The following forms make assumptions about the user model and can be used as-is if those assumptions are met:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_559"><i>PasswordResetForm</i></a>: Assumes that the user model has a field that stores the user’s email address with</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the name returned by <a href="index.html#page_588"><i>get_email_field_name()</i></a> (email by default) that can be used to identify the user and a boolean field named is_active to prevent password resets for inactive users.</p> <p>Finally, the following forms are tied to <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> and need to be rewritten or extended to work with a custom user model:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_560"><i>UserCreationForm</i></a></p> <p id="page_591" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_559"><i>UserChangeForm</i></a></p> <p>If your custom user model is a subclass of AbstractUser, then you can extend these forms in this manner:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.forms</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserCreationForm</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomUserCreationForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(UserCreationForm):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(UserCreationForm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Meta):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CustomUser</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserCreationForm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Meta</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"custom_field"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom users and django.contrib.admin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want your custom user model to also work with the admin, your user model must define some addi-tional attributes and methods. These methods allow the admin to control access of the user to admin content:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>CustomUser</b></p> <p><b>is_staff</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the user is allowed to have access to the admin site.</p> <p><b>is_active</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the user account is currently active.</p> <p><b>has_perm(perm, obj=None):</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the user has the named permission. If obj is provided, the permission needs to be checked against a specific object instance.</p> <p><b>has_module_perms(app_label):</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the user has permission to access models in the given app.</p> <p>You will also need to register your custom user model with the admin. If your custom user model ex-tends django.contrib.auth.models.AbstractUser, you can use Django’s existing django.contrib.auth.</p> <p>admin.UserAdmin class. However, if your user model extends <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>AbstractBaseUser</i></a>, you’ll need to define a cus-tom ModelAdmin class. It may be possible to subclass the default django.contrib.auth.admin.UserAdmin; however, you’ll need to override any of the definitions that refer to fields on django.contrib.auth.models. AbstractUser that aren’t on your custom user class.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you are using a custom ModelAdmin which is a subclass of django.contrib.auth.admin.UserAdmin, then you need to add your custom fields to fieldsets (for fields to be used in editing users) and to add_fieldsets (for fields to be used when creating a user). For example:</p> <p id="page_592"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.admin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserAdmin</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomUserAdmin</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(UserAdmin):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fieldsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserAdmin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">fieldsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">((</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"custom_field"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]}),)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">add_fieldsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">UserAdmin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add_fieldsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">((</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"custom_field"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]}),)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_593">a full example</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom users and permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To make it easy to include Django’s permission framework into your own user class, Django provides</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_592"><i>PermissionsMixin</i>. </a>This is an abstract model you can include in the class hierarchy for your user model, giving you all the methods and database fields necessary to support Django’s permission model.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_592"><i>PermissionsMixin</i></a> provides the following methods and attributes:</p> <p><b>class</b> models.<b>PermissionsMixin</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>is_superuser</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">Boolean. Designates that this user has all permissions without explicitly assigning them.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_user_permissions</b>(obj=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a set of permission strings that the user has directly.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If obj is passed in, only returns the user permissions for this specific object.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_group_permissions</b>(obj=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a set of permission strings that the user has, through their groups.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If obj is passed in, only returns the group permissions for this specific object.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_all_permissions</b>(obj=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a set of permission strings that the user has, both through group and user permissions.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If obj is passed in, only returns the permissions for this specific object.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>has_perm</b>(perm, obj=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True if the user has the specified permission, where perm is in the format "<app label>.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><permission codename>" (see <a href="index.html#page_533">permissions</a>). If <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User.is_active</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1103"><i>is_superuser</i></a> are both True , this method always returns True.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If obj is passed in, this method won’t check for a permission for the model, but for this specific object.</p> <p id="page_593" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>has_perms</b>(perm_list, obj=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True if the user has each of the specified permissions, where each perm is in the format</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">"<app label>.<permission codename>". If <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User.is_active</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1103"><i>is_superuser</i></a> are both True, this method always returns True.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If obj is passed in, this method won’t check for permissions for the model, but for the specific object.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>has_module_perms</b>(package_name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True if the user has any permissions in the given package (the Django app label). If <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User.</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1103"><i>is_superuser</i></a> are both True, this method always returns True.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PermissionsMixin</b> and <b>ModelBackend</b></p> <p>If you don’t include the <a href="index.html#page_592"><i>PermissionsMixin</i></a>, you must ensure you don’t invoke the permissions methods on ModelBackend. ModelBackend assumes that certain fields are available on your user model. If your user model doesn’t provide those fields, you’ll receive database errors when you check permissions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom users and proxy models</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>One limitation of custom user models is that installing a custom user model will break any proxy model</p> <p>extending <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a>. Proxy models must be based on a concrete base class; by defining a custom user model, you remove the ability of Django to reliably identify the base class.</p> <p>If your project uses proxy models, you must either modify the proxy to extend the user model that’s in use</p> <p>in your project, or merge your proxy’s behavior into your <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> subclass.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>A full example</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here is an example of an admin-compliant custom user app. This user model uses an email address as the username, and has a required date of birth; it provides no permission checking beyond an admin flag on the user account. This model would be compatible with all the built-in auth forms and views, except for the user creation forms. This example illustrates how most of the components work together, but is not intended to be copied directly into projects for production use.</p> <p>This code would all live in a models.py file for a custom authentication app:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span
