This specifies which value to return if the object doesn’t exist in the cache:</p> <p id="page_616"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"has expired"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'has expired'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>add</b>( key, value, timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, version=None)</p> <p>To add a key only if it doesn’t already exist, use the add() method. It takes the same parameters as set(), but it will not attempt to update the cache if the key specified is already present:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"add_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Initial value"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"add_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"New value"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"add_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'Initial value'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to know whether add() stored a value in the cache, you can check the return value. It will return True if the value was stored, False otherwise.</p> <p>cache.<b>get_or_set</b>( key, default, timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, version=None)</p> <p>If you want to get a key’s value or set a value if the key isn’t in the cache, there is the get_or_set() method. It takes the same parameters as get() but the default is set as the new cache value for that key, rather than returned:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_new_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># returns None</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_or_set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_new_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"my new value"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'my new value'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also pass any callable as a default value:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_or_set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"some-timestamp-key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, datetime</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">now)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime.datetime(2014, 12, 11, 0, 15, 49, 457920)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>get_many</b>(keys, version=None)</p> <p>There’s also a get_many() interface that only hits the cache once. get_many() returns a dictionary with all the keys you asked for that actually exist in the cache (and haven’t expired):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"c"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">3</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_many([</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"c"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>set_many</b>(dict, timeout)</p> <p>To set multiple values more efficiently, use set_many() to pass a dictionary of key-value pairs:</p> <p id="page_617" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set_many({</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"c"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">3</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_many([</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"c"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Like cache.set(), set_many() takes an optional timeout parameter.</p> <p>On supported backends (memcached), set_many() returns a list of keys that failed to be inserted.</p> <p>cache.<b>delete</b>(key, version=None)</p> <p>You can delete keys explicitly with delete() to clear the cache for a particular object:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">delete(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>delete() returns True if the key was successfully deleted, False otherwise.</p> <p>cache.<b>delete_many</b>(keys, version=None)</p> <p>If you want to clear a bunch of keys at once, delete_many() can take a list of keys to be cleared:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">delete_many([</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"c"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>clear</b>()</p> <p>Finally, if you want to delete all the keys in the cache, use cache.clear(). Be careful with this; clear() will remove everything from the cache, not just the keys set by your application:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">clear()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>touch</b>(key, timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, version=None)</p> <p>cache.touch() sets a new expiration for a key. For example, to update a key to expire 10 seconds from now:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">touch(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"a"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Like other methods, the timeout argument is optional and defaults to the TIMEOUT option of the appropriate</p> <p>backend in the <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> setting.</p> <p>touch() returns True if the key was successfully touched, False otherwise.</p> <p>cache.<b>incr</b>(key, delta=1, version=None)</p> <p>cache.<b>decr</b>(key, delta=1, version=None)</p> <p>You can also increment or decrement a key that already exists using the incr() or decr() methods, re-spectively. By default, the existing cache value will be incremented or decremented by 1. Other incre-ment/decrement values can be specified by providing an argument to the increment/decrement call. A Val-ueError will be raised if you attempt to increment or decrement a nonexistent cache key:</p> <p id="page_618"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">incr(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">incr(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">12</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">decr(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">11</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">decr(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">6</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: incr()/decr() methods are not guaranteed to be atomic. On those backends that support atomic increment/decrement (most notably, the memcached backend), increment and decrement operations will be atomic. However, if the backend doesn’t natively provide an increment/decrement operation, it will be implemented using a two-step retrieve/update.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>cache.<b>close</b>()</p> <p>You can close the connection to your cache with close() if implemented by the cache backend.</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">close()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: For caches that don’t implement close methods it is a no-op.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The async variants of base methods are prefixed with a, e.g. cache.aadd() or cache.adelete_many().</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_621">Asynchronous support</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Cache key prefixing</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you are sharing a cache instance between servers, or between your production and development environ-ments, it’s possible for data cached by one server to be used by another server. If the format of cached data is different between servers, this can lead to some very hard to diagnose problems.</p> <p>To prevent this, Django provides the ability to prefix all cache keys used by a server. When a particular cache</p> <p>key is saved or retrieved, Django will automatically prefix the cache key with the value of the <a href="index.html#page_1890"><i>KEY_PREFIX</i></a> cache setting.</p> <p>By ensuring each Django instance has a different <a href="index.html#page_1890"><i>KEY_PREFIX</i></a> , you can ensure that there will be no collisions in cache values.</p> <p id="page_619" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Cache versioning</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you change running code that uses cached values, you may need to purge any existing cached values. The easiest way to do this is to flush the entire cache, but this can lead to the loss of cache values that are still valid and useful.</p> <p>Django provides a better way to target individual cache values. Django’s cache framework has a system-</p> <p>wide version identifier, specified using the <a href="index.html#page_1891"><i>VERSION</i></a> cache setting. The value of this setting is automatically combined with the cache prefix and the user-provided cache key to obtain the final cache key.</p> <p>By default, any key request will automatically include the site default cache key version. However, the primitive cache functions all include a version argument, so you can specify a particular cache key version to set or get. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Set version 2 of a cache key</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">set(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"hello world!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, version</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Get the default version (assuming version=1)</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">None</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Get version 2 of the same key</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, version</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'hello world!'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The version of a specific key can be incremented and decremented using the incr_version() and decr_version() methods. This enables specific keys to be bumped to a new version, leaving other keys unaffected. Continuing our previous example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Increment the version of 'my_key'</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">incr_version(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># The default version still isn't available</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">None</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># Version 2 isn't available, either</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, version</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">None</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># But version 3 *is* available</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, version</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">3</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'hello world!'</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_620"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Cache key transformation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As described in the previous two sections, the cache key provided by a user is not used verbatim – it is com-bined with the cache prefix and key version to provide a final cache key. By default, the three parts are joined using colons to produce a final string:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>make_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(key, key_prefix, version):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"%s:%s:%s"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(key_prefix, version, key)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to combine the parts in different ways, or apply other processing to the final key (e.g., taking a hash digest of the key parts), you can provide a custom key function.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1890"><i>KEY_FUNCTION</i></a> cache setting specifies a dotted-path to a function matching the prototype of make_key() above. If provided, this custom key function will be used instead of the default key combining function.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Cache key warnings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Memcached, the most commonly-used production cache backend, does not allow cache keys longer than 250 characters or containing whitespace or control characters, and using such keys will cause an exception. To encourage cache-portable code and minimize unpleasant surprises, the other built-in cache backends issue a warning (django.core.cache.backends.base.CacheKeyWarning) if a key is used that would cause an error on memcached.</p> <p>If you are using a production backend that can accept a wider range of keys (a custom backend, or one of the non-memcached built-in backends), and want to use this wider range without warnings, you can silence</p> <p>CacheKeyWarning with this code in the management module of one of your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">warnings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CacheKeyWarning</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">warnings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">simplefilter(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ignore"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, CacheKeyWarning)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to instead provide custom key validation logic for one of the built-in backends, you can subclass</p> <p>it, override just the validate_key method, and follow the instructions for <a href="index.html#page_607">using a custom cache backend</a>. For instance, to do this for the locmem backend, put this code in a module:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.cache.backends.locmem</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LocMemCache</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomLocMemCache</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(LocMemCache):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>validate_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, key):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""Custom validation, raising exceptions or warnings as needed."""</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p id="page_621" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i>and use the dotted Python path to this class in the <a href="index.html#page_1890"><i>BACKEND</i></a> portion of your <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.11.6 Asynchronous support</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django has developing support for asynchronous cache backends, but does not yet support asynchronous caching. It will be coming in a future release.</p> <p>django.core.cache.backends.base.BaseCache has async variants of <a href="index.html#page_615">all base methods</a>. By convention, the asynchronous versions of all methods are prefixed with a. By default, the arguments for both variants are the same:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">aset(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ahas_key(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"num"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.11.7 Downstream caches</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>So far, this document has focused on caching your own data. But another type of caching is relevant to web development, too: caching performed by “downstream” caches. These are systems that cache pages for users even before the request reaches your website.</p> <p>Here are a few examples of downstream caches:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When using HTTP, your ISP (Internet Service Provider) may cache certain pages, so if you requested</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a page from http://example.com/, your ISP would send you the page without having to access ex-ample.com directly. The maintainers of example.com have no knowledge of this caching; the ISP sits between example.com and your web browser, handling all of the caching transparently. Such caching is not possible under HTTPS as it would constitute a man-in-the-middle attack.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Your Django website may sit behind a proxy cache, such as Squid Web Proxy Cache <a href="http://www.squid-cache.org/">(http://www.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="http://www.squid-cache.org/">squid-cache.org/</a>), that caches pages for performance. In this case, each request first would be handled by the proxy, and it would be passed to your application only if needed.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Your web browser caches pages, too. If a web page sends out the appropriate headers, your browser</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">will use the local cached copy for subsequent requests to that page, without even contacting the web page again to see whether it has changed.</p> <p>Downstream caching is a nice efficiency boost, but there’s a danger to it: Many web pages’ contents differ based on authentication and a host of other variables, and cache systems that blindly save pages based purely on URLs could expose incorrect or sensitive data to subsequent visitors to those pages.</p> <p>For example, if you operate a web email system, then the contents of the “inbox” page depend on which user is logged in. If an ISP blindly cached your site, then the first user who logged in through that ISP would have their user-specific inbox page cached for subsequent visitors to the site. That’s not cool.</p> <p id="page_622"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Fortunately, HTTP provides a solution to this problem. A number of HTTP headers exist to instruct down-stream caches to differ their cache contents depending on designated variables, and to tell caching mecha-nisms not to cache particular pages. We’ll look at some of these headers in the sections that follow.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.11.8 Using</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>Vary</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>headers</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Vary header defines which request headers a cache mechanism should take into account when building its cache key. For example, if the contents of a web page depend on a user’s language preference, the page is said to “vary on language.”</p> <p>By default, Django’s cache system creates its cache keys using the requested fully-qualified URL – e.g., "https://www.example.com/stories/2005/?order_by=author". This means every request to that URL will use the same cached version, regardless of user-agent differences such as cookies or language prefer-ences. However, if this page produces different content based on some difference in request headers – such as a cookie, or a language, or a user-agent – you’ll need to use the Vary header to tell caching mechanisms that the page output depends on those things.</p> <p>To do this in Django, use the convenient <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>django.views.decorators.vary.vary_on_headers()</i></a> view deco-rator, like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.vary</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">vary_on_headers</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@vary_on_headers(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"User-Agent"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this case, a caching mechanism (such as Django’s own cache middleware) will cache a separate version of the page for each unique user-agent.</p> <p>The advantage to using the vary_on_headers decorator rather than manually setting the Vary header (using something like response.headers['Vary'] = 'user-agent') is that the decorator adds to the Vary header (which may already exist), rather than setting it from scratch and potentially overriding anything that was already in there.</p> <p>You can pass multiple headers to vary_on_headers():</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@vary_on_headers(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"User-Agent"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cookie"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This tells downstream caches to vary on both, which means each combination of user-agent and cookie will get its own cache value. For example, a request with the user-agent Mozilla and the cookie value foo=bar will be considered different from a request with the user-agent Mozilla and the cookie value foo=ham.</p> <p>Because varying on cookie is so common, there’s a <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>django.views.decorators.vary.vary_on_cookie()</i></a> decorator. These two views are equivalent:</p> <p id="page_623" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@vary_on_cookie</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@vary_on_headers(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cookie"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The headers you pass to vary_on_headers are not case sensitive; "User-Agent" is the same thing as "user-agent".</p> <p>You can also use a helper function, <a href="index.html#page_2073"><i>django.utils.cache.patch_vary_headers()</i></a>, directly. This function sets, or adds to, the Vary header. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">patch_vary_headers</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"template_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, context)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">patch_vary_headers(response, [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cookie"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>patch_vary_headers takes an <a href="index.html#page_1871"><i>HttpResponse</i></a> instance as its first argument and a list/tuple of case-insensitive header names as its second argument.</p> <p>For more on Vary headers, see the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-12.5.5">official Vary spec</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.11.9 Controlling cache: Using other headers</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Other problems with caching are the privacy of data and the question of where data should be stored in a cascade of caches.</p> <p>A user usually faces two kinds of caches: their own browser cache (a private cache) and their provider’s cache (a public cache). A public cache is used by multiple users and controlled by someone else. This poses problems with sensitive data–you don’t want, say, your bank account number stored in a public cache. So web applications need a way to tell caches which data is private and which is public.</p> <p>The solution is to indicate a page’s cache should be “private.” To do this in Django, use the <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>cache_control()</i></a> view decorator. Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache_control</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_624"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@cache_control(private</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This decorator takes care of sending out the appropriate HTTP header behind the scenes.</p> <p>Note that the cache control settings “private” and “public” are mutually exclusive. The decorator ensures that the “public” directive is removed if “private” should be set (and vice versa). An example use of the two directives would be a blog site that offers both private and public entries. Public entries may be cached on</p> <p>any shared cache. The following code uses <a href="index.html#page_2072"><i>patch_cache_control()</i>, </a>the manual way to modify the cache</p> <p>control header (it is internally called by the <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>cache_control()</i></a> decorator):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">patch_cache_control</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.vary</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">vary_on_cookie</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@vary_on_cookie</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>list_blog_entries_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_anonymous:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render_only_public_entries()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">patch_cache_control(response, public</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render_private_and_public_entries(request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">patch_cache_control(response, private</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can control downstream caches in other ways as well (see <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9111.html">RFC 9111</a> for details on HTTP caching). For example, even if you don’t use Django’s server-side cache framework, you can still tell clients to cache a view</p> <p>for a certain amount of time with the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.1">max-age</a> directive:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache_control</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@cache_control(max_age</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">3600</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>(If you do use the caching middleware, it already sets the max-age with the value of the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1892"><i>CACHE_MIDDLEWARE_SECONDS</i></a> setting. In that case, the custom max_age from the <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>cache_control()</i></a> deco-rator will take precedence, and the header values will be merged correctly.)</p> <p>Any valid Cache-Control response directive is valid in cache_control(). Here are some more examples:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• no_transform=True</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• must_revalidate=True</p> <p id="page_625" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• stale_while_revalidate=num_seconds</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• no_cache=True</p> <p>The full list of known directives can be found in the <a href="https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-cache-directives/http-cache-directives.xhtml">IANA registry</a> (note that not all of them apply to re-sponses).</p> <p>If you want to use headers to disable caching altogether, <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>never_cache()</i></a> is a view decorator that adds headers to ensure the response won’t be cached by browsers or other caches. Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">never_cache</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@never_cache</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>myview</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.11.10 Order of</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>MIDDLEWARE</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you use caching middleware, it’s important to put each half in the right place within the <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> setting. That’s because the cache middleware needs to know which headers by which to vary the cache storage. Middleware always adds something to the Vary response header when it can.</p> <p>UpdateCacheMiddleware runs during the response phase, where middleware is run in reverse order, so an item at the top of the list runs last during the response phase. Thus, you need to make sure that UpdateCacheMiddleware appears before any other middleware that might add something to the Vary header. The following middleware modules do so:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• SessionMiddleware adds Cookie</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• GZipMiddleware adds Accept-Encoding</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• LocaleMiddleware adds Accept-Language</p> <p>FetchFromCacheMiddleware, on the other hand, runs during the request phase, where middleware is applied first-to-last, so an item at the top of the list runs first during the request phase. The FetchFromCacheMiddleware also needs to run after other middleware updates the Vary header, so FetchFromCacheMiddleware must be after any item that does so.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.12 Conditional View Processing</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>HTTP clients can send a number of headers to tell the server about copies of a resource that they have already seen. This is commonly used when retrieving a web page (using an HTTP GET request) to avoid sending all the data for something the client has already retrieved. However, the same headers can be used for all HTTP methods (POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.).</p> <p id="page_626"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For each page (response) that Django sends back from a view, it might provide two HTTP headers: the ETag header and the Last-Modified header. These headers are optional on HTTP responses. They can be set by</p> <p>your view function, or you can rely on the <a href="index.html#page_1593"><i>ConditionalGetMiddleware</i></a> middleware to set the ETag header.</p> <p>When the client next requests the same resource, it might send along a header such as either <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.3">If-Modified-</a></p> <p><a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.3">Since</a> or <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.4">If-Unmodified-Since</a>, containing the date of the last modification time it was sent, or either <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.1">If-Match</a></p> <p>or <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.2">If-None-Match, </a>containing the last ETag it was sent. If the current version of the page matches the ETag sent by the client, or if the resource has not been modified, a 304 status code can be sent back, instead of a full response, telling the client that nothing has changed. Depending on the header, if the page has been modified or does not match the ETag sent by the client, a 412 status code (Precondition Failed) may be returned.</p> <p>When you need more fine-grained control you may use per-view conditional processing functions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.12.1 The</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>condition</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>decorator</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Sometimes (in fact, quite often) you can create functions to rapidly compute the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.3">ETag</a> value or the last-modified time for a resource, without needing to do all the computations needed to construct the full view. Django can then use these functions to provide an “early bailout” option for the view processing. Telling the client that the content has not been modified since the last request, perhaps.</p> <p>These two functions are passed as parameters to the django.views.decorators.http.condition decorator. This decorator uses the two functions (you only need to supply one, if you can’t compute both quantities easily and quickly) to work out if the headers in the HTTP request match those on the resource. If they don’t match, a new copy of the resource must be computed and your normal view is called.</p> <p>The condition decorator’s signature looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">condition(etag_func</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, last_modified_func</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The two functions, to compute the ETag and the last modified time, will be passed the incoming request object and the same parameters, in the same order, as the view function they are helping to wrap. The function passed last_modified_func should return a standard datetime value specifying the last time the resource was modified, or None if the resource doesn’t exist. The function passed to the etag decorator should return a string representing the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.3">ETag</a> for the resource, or None if it doesn’t exist.</p> <p>The decorator sets the ETag and Last-Modified headers on the response if they are not already set by the view and if the request’s method is safe (GET or HEAD).</p> <p>Using this feature usefully is probably best explained with an example. Suppose you have this pair of models, representing a small blog system:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_627" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Blog</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Entry</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">blog</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(Blog, on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">published</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateTimeField(default</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">now)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the front page, displaying the latest blog entries, only changes when you add a new blog entry, you can compute the last modified time very quickly. You need the latest published date for every entry associated with that blog. One way to do this would be:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>latest_entry</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request, blog_id):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(blog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">blog_id)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">latest(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"published"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">published</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can then use this function to provide early detection of an unchanged page for your front page view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">condition</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@condition(last_modified_func</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">latest_entry)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>front_page</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request, blog_id):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Be careful with the order of decorators</p> <p>When condition() returns a conditional response, any decorators below it will be skipped and won’t apply to the response. Therefore, any decorators that need to apply to both the regular view response and a con-</p> <p>ditional response must be above condition(). In particular, <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>vary_on_cookie()</i>, <i>vary_on_headers()</i></a>, and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_289"><i>cache_control()</i></a> should come first because <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-15.4.5">RFC 9110</a> requires that the headers they set be present on 304 responses.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.12.2 Shortcuts for only computing one value</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As a general rule, if you can provide functions to compute both the ETag and the last modified time, you should do so. You don’t know which headers any given HTTP client will send you, so be prepared to handle both. However, sometimes only one value is easy to compute and Django provides decorators that handle only ETag or only last-modified computations.</p> <p>The django.views.decorators.http.etag and django.views.decorators.http.last_modified decora-tors are passed the same type of functions as the condition decorator. Their signatures are:</p> <p id="page_628"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">etag(etag_func)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_modified(last_modified_func)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We could write the earlier example, which only uses a last-modified function, using one of these decorators:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@last_modified(latest_entry)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>front_page</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request, blog_id):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i>or:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>front_page</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request, blog_id):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">front_page</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">last_modified(latest_entry)(front_page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Use condition when testing both conditions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It might look nicer to some people to try and chain the etag and last_modified decorators if you want to test both preconditions. However, this would lead to incorrect behavior.</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Bad code. Don't do this!</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@etag(etag_func)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@last_modified(last_modified_func)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># End of bad code.</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The first decorator doesn’t know anything about the second and might answer that the response is not mod-ified even if the second decorators would determine otherwise. The condition decorator uses both callback functions simultaneously to work out the right action to take.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.12.3 Using the decorators with other HTTP methods</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The condition decorator is useful for more than only GET and HEAD requests (HEAD requests are the same as GET in this situation). It can also be used to provide checking for POST, PUT and DELETE requests. In these situations, the idea isn’t to return a “not modified” response, but to tell the client that the resource they are trying to change has been altered in the meantime.</p> <p>For example, consider the following exchange between the client and server:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Client requests /foo/.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Server responds with some content with an ETag of "abcd1234".</p> <p id="page_629" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Client sends an HTTP PUT request to /foo/ to update the resource. It also sends an If-Match:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">"abcd1234" header to specify the version it is trying to update.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. Server checks to see if the resource has changed, by computing the ETag the same way it does for a GET</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">request (using the same function). If the resource has changed, it will return a 412 status code, meaning “precondition failed”.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">5. Client sends a GET request to /foo/, after receiving a 412 response, to retrieve an updated version of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the content before updating it.</p> <p>The important thing this example shows is that the same functions can be used to compute the ETag and last modification values in all situations. In fact, you should use the same functions, so that the same values are returned every time.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Validator headers with non-safe request methods</p> <p>The condition decorator only sets validator headers (ETag and Last-Modified) for safe HTTP methods, i.e.</p> <p>GET and HEAD. If you wish to return them in other cases, set them in your view. See <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.4">RFC 9110#section-9.3.4</a> to learn about the distinction between setting a validator header in response to requests made with PUT versus POST.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.12.4 Comparison with middleware conditional processing</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides conditional GET handling via <a href="index.html#page_1593"><i>django.middleware.http.ConditionalGetMiddleware</i></a>. While being suitable for many situations, the middleware has limitations for advanced usage:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It’s applied globally to all views in your project.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It doesn’t save you from generating the response, which may be expensive.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It’s only appropriate for HTTP GET requests.</p> <p>You should choose the most appropriate tool for your particular problem here. If you have a way to compute ETags and modification times quickly and if some view takes a while to generate the content, you should consider using the condition decorator described in this document. If everything already runs fairly quickly, stick to using the middleware and the amount of network traffic sent back to the clients will still be reduced if the view hasn’t changed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_630"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.13 Cryptographic signing</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The golden rule of web application security is to never trust data from untrusted sources. Sometimes it can be useful to pass data through an untrusted medium. Cryptographically signed values can be passed through an untrusted channel safe in the knowledge that any tampering will be detected.</p> <p>Django provides both a low-level API for signing values and a high-level API for setting and reading signed cookies, one of the most common uses of signing in web applications.</p> <p>You may also find signing useful for the following:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Generating “recover my account” URLs for sending to users who have lost their password.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Ensuring data stored in hidden form fields has not been tampered with.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Generating one-time secret URLs for allowing temporary access to a protected resource, for example a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">downloadable file that a user has paid for.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.13.1 Protecting</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>SECRET_KEY</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>and</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you create a new Django project using <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i>, </a>the settings.py file is generated automatically</p> <p>and gets a random <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> value. This value is the key to securing signed data – it is vital you keep this secure, or attackers could use it to generate their own signed values.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a> can be used to rotate secret keys. The values will not be used to sign data, but if specified, they will be used to validate signed data and must be kept secure.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.13.2 Using the low-level API</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s signing methods live in the django.core.signing module. To sign a value, first instantiate a Signer instance:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signing</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Signer</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Signer()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">value</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"My string"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">value</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'My string:v9G-nxfz3iQGTXrePqYPlGvH79WTcIgj1QIQSUODTW0'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The signature is appended to the end of the string, following the colon. You can retrieve the original value using the unsign method:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">original</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unsign(value)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">original</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'My string'</span></p> <p id="page_631" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you pass a non-string value to sign, the value will be forced to string before being signed, and the unsign result will give you that string value:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signed</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2.5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">original</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unsign(signed)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">original</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'2.5'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you wish to protect a list, tuple, or dictionary you can do so using the sign_object() and unsign_object() methods:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signed_obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign_object({</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"message"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Hello!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signed_obj</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'eyJtZXNzYWdlIjoiSGVsbG8hIn0:bzb48DBkB-bwLaCnUVB75r5VAPUEpzWJPrTb80JMIXM'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unsign_object(signed_obj)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{'message': 'Hello!'}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_633">Protecting complex data structures</a> for more details.</p> <p>If the signature or value have been altered in any way, a django.core.signing.BadSignature exception will be raised:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signing</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">value</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"m"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>try</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">original</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unsign(value)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>except</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signing</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">BadSignature:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Tampering detected!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, the Signer class uses the <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> setting to generate signatures. You can use a different secret by passing it to the Signer constructor:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Signer(key</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my-other-secret"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">value</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"My string"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">value</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'My string:o3DrrsT6JRB73t-HDymfDNbTSxfMlom2d8TiUlb1hWY'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Signer</b>(*, key=None, sep=':', salt=None, algorithm=None, fallback_keys=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a signer which uses key to generate signatures and sep to separate values. sep cannot be in the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648.html#section-5">URL safe base64 alphabet</a>. This alphabet contains alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and underscores.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">algorithm must be an algorithm supported by <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html#module-hashlib">hashlib, </a>it defaults to 'sha256'. fallback_keys is a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">list of additional values used to validate signed data, defaults to <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_632"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using the salt argument</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you do not wish for every occurrence of a particular string to have the same signature hash, you can use the optional salt argument to the Signer class. Using a salt will seed the signing hash function with both</p> <p>the salt and your <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> :</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Signer()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"My string"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'My string:v9G-nxfz3iQGTXrePqYPlGvH79WTcIgj1QIQSUODTW0'</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sign_object({</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"message"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'eyJtZXNzYWdlIjoiSGVsbG8hIn0:bzb48DBkB-bwLaCnUVB75r5VAPUEpzWJPrTb80JMIXM'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Signer(salt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"extra"</span><span <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unsign_object(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"eyJtZXNzYWdlIjoiSGVsbG8hIn0:-UWSLCE-oUAHzhkHviYz3SOZYBjFKllEOyVZNuUtM-I"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span different namespaces. A signature that comes from one namespace (a particular salt value) cannot be used to validate the same plaintext string in a different namespace that is using a different salt setting. The result is to prevent an attacker from using a signed string generated in one place in the code as input to another piece of code that is generating (and verifying) signatures using a different salt.</p> <p>Unlike your <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> , your salt argument does not need to stay secret.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Verifying timestamped values</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>TimestampSigner is a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_631"><i>Signer</i></a> that appends a signed timestamp to the value. otherwise raises</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">SignatureExpired. Checks max_age (in seconds) if given.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.14 Sending email</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Although Python provides a mail sending interface via the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/smtplib.html#module-smtplib">smtplib</a> module, Django provides a couple of light wrappers over it. These wrappers are provided to make sending email extra quick, to help test email sending during development, and to provide support for platforms that can’t use SMTP.</p> <p>The code lives in the django.core.mail module.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.14.1 Quick examples</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use <a href="index.html#page_636"><i>send_mail()</i></a> for straightforward email sending. For example, to send a plain text message:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.mail</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">send_mail</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">send_mail(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Subject here"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Here is the message."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"from@example.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"to@example.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span
