tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='America/New_York'))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">As this example shows, the same datetime has a different date, depending on the time zone in which it is represented. But the real problem is more fundamental.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A datetime represents a point in time. It’s absolute: it doesn’t depend on anything. On the contrary, a date is a calendaring concept. It’s a period of time whose bounds depend on the time zone in which the date is considered. As you can see, these two concepts are fundamentally different, and converting a datetime to a date isn’t a deterministic operation.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">What does this mean in practice?</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Generally, you should avoid converting a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> to <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.date">date</a><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.date">. </a>For instance, you can use the <a href="index.html#page_2006"><i>date</i></a> tem-plate filter to only show the date part of a datetime. This filter will convert the datetime into the current time zone before formatting it, ensuring the results appear correctly.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you really need to do the conversion yourself, you must ensure the datetime is converted to the appropriate time zone first. Usually, this will be the current timezone:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">activate(zoneinfo</span><span style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"># For this example, we set the time zone to Singapore, but here's how</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"># you would obtain the current time zone in the general case.</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">current_tz</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_current_timezone()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">local</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">paris</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">local</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime.datetime(2012, 3, 3, 8, 30, tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='Asia/Singapore'))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">local</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">date()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime.date(2012, 3, 3)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. I get an error “Are time zone definitions for your database installed?”</p> <p id="page_705" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you are using MySQL, see the <a href="index.html#page_1419">Time zone definitions</a> section of the MySQL notes for instructions on loading time zone definitions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Usage</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. I have a string "2012-02-21 10:28:45" and I know it’s in the "Europe/Helsinki" time zone. How do</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">I turn that into an aware datetime?</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Here you need to create the required ZoneInfo instance and attach it to the naïve datetime:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">zoneinfo</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.dateparse</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">parse_datetime</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">naive</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">parse_datetime(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"2012-02-21 10:28:45"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">naive</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">replace(tzinfo</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">zoneinfo</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ZoneInfo(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Europe/Helsinki"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime.datetime(2012, 2, 21, 10, 28, 45, tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='Europe/Helsinki'))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. How can I obtain the local time in the current time zone?</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Well, the first question is, do you really need to?</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You should only use local time when you’re interacting with humans, and the template layer provides</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_697">filters and tags</a> to convert datetimes to the time zone of your choice.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Furthermore, Python knows how to compare aware datetimes, taking into account UTC offsets when necessary. It’s much easier (and possibly faster) to write all your model and view code in UTC. So, in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">most circumstances, the datetime in UTC returned by <a href="index.html#page_2088"><i>django.utils.timezone.now()</i></a> will be suffi-cient.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For the sake of completeness, though, if you really want the local time in the current time zone, here’s how you can obtain it:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">timezone</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">localtime(timezone</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">now())</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">datetime.datetime(2012, 3, 3, 20, 10, 53, 873365, tzinfo=zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(key='Europe/Paris</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In this example, the current time zone is "Europe/Paris".</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. How can I see all available time zones?</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/zoneinfo.html#zoneinfo.available_timezones">zoneinfo.available_timezones()</a> provides the set of all valid keys for IANA time zones available to your system. See the docs for usage considerations.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_706"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.15.4 Overview</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The goal of internationalization and localization is to allow a single web application to offer its content in languages and formats tailored to the audience.</p> <p>Django has full support for <a href="index.html#page_649">translation of text,</a> <a href="index.html#page_689">formatting of dates, times and numbers</a><a href="index.html#page_689">, </a>and <a href="index.html#page_693">time zones</a><a href="index.html#page_693">.</a></p> <p>Essentially, Django does two things:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It allows developers and template authors to specify which parts of their apps should be translated or</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">formatted for local languages and cultures.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It uses these hooks to localize web apps for particular users according to their preferences.</p> <p>Translation depends on the target language, and formatting usually depends on the target country. This information is provided by browsers in the Accept-Language header. However, the time zone isn’t readily available.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.15.5 Definitions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The words “internationalization” and “localization” often cause confusion; here’s a simplified definition:</p> <p>internationalization</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Preparing the software for localization. Usually done by developers.</p> <p>localization</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Writing the translations and local formats. Usually done by translators.</p> <p>More details can be found in the <a href="https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-i18n">W3C Web Internationalization FAQ</a>, the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalization_and_localization">Wikipedia article</a> or the <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/manual/gettext.html#Concepts">GNU</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/manual/gettext.html#Concepts">gettext documentation</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Translation is controlled by the <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_I18N</i></a> setting. However, it involves internationalization</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">and localization. The name of the setting is an unfortunate result of Django’s history.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here are some other terms that will help us to handle a common language:</p> <p>locale name</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A locale name, either a language specification of the form ll or a combined language and country specification of the form ll_CC. Examples: it, de_AT, es, pt_BR, sr_Latn. The language part is always in lowercase. The country part is in titlecase if it has more than 2 characters, otherwise it’s in uppercase. The separator is an underscore.</p> <p>language code</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Represents the name of a language. Browsers send the names of the languages they accept in the Accept-Language HTTP header using this format. Examples: it, de-at, es, pt-br. Language codes</p> <p id="page_707" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">are generally represented in lowercase, but the HTTP Accept-Language header is case-insensitive. The separator is a dash.</p> <p>message file</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A message file is a plain-text file, representing a single language, that contains all available <a href="index.html#page_707">transla-</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_707">tion strings</a> and how they should be represented in the given language. Message files have a .po file extension.</p> <p>translation string</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A literal that can be translated.</p> <p>format file</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A format file is a Python module that defines the data formats for a given locale.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.16 Logging</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_847">How to configure and use logging</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1582">Django logging reference</a></p> <p>Python programmers will often use print() in their code as a quick and convenient debugging tool. Using the logging framework is only a little more effort than that, but it’s much more elegant and flexible. As well as being useful for debugging, logging can also provide you with more - and better structured - information about the state and health of your application.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.16.1 Overview</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django uses and extends Python’s builtin <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#module-logging">logging</a> module to perform system logging. This module is dis-cussed in detail in Python’s own documentation; this section provides a quick overview.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The cast of players</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A Python logging configuration consists of four parts:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_708">Loggers</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_708">Handlers</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_709">Filters</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_709">Formatters</a></p> <p id="page_708"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Loggers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A logger is the entry point into the logging system. Each logger is a named bucket to which messages can be written for processing.</p> <p>A logger is configured to have a log level. This log level describes the severity of the messages that the logger will handle. Python defines the following log levels:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• DEBUG: Low level system information for debugging purposes</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• INFO: General system information</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• WARNING: Information describing a minor problem that has occurred.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• ERROR: Information describing a major problem that has occurred.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CRITICAL: Information describing a critical problem that has occurred.</p> <p>Each message that is written to the logger is a Log Record. Each log record also has a log level indicating the severity of that specific message. A log record can also contain useful metadata that describes the event that is being logged. This can include details such as a stack trace or an error code.</p> <p>When a message is given to the logger, the log level of the message is compared to the log level of the logger. If the log level of the message meets or exceeds the log level of the logger itself, the message will undergo further processing. If it doesn’t, the message will be ignored.</p> <p>Once a logger has determined that a message needs to be processed, it is passed to a Handler.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handlers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The handler is the engine that determines what happens to each message in a logger. It describes a particular logging behavior, such as writing a message to the screen, to a file, or to a network socket.</p> <p>Like loggers, handlers also have a log level. If the log level of a log record doesn’t meet or exceed the level of the handler, the handler will ignore the message.</p> <p>A logger can have multiple handlers, and each handler can have a different log level. In this way, it is possible to provide different forms of notification depending on the importance of a message. For example, you could install one handler that forwards ERROR and CRITICAL messages to a paging service, while a second handler logs all messages (including ERROR and CRITICAL messages) to a file for later analysis.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_709" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Filters</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A filter is used to provide additional control over which log records are passed from logger to handler.</p> <p>By default, any log message that meets log level requirements will be handled. However, by installing a filter, you can place additional criteria on the logging process. For example, you could install a filter that only allows ERROR messages from a particular source to be emitted.</p> <p>Filters can also be used to modify the logging record prior to being emitted. For example, you could write a filter that downgrades ERROR log records to WARNING records if a particular set of criteria are met.</p> <p>Filters can be installed on loggers or on handlers; multiple filters can be used in a chain to perform multiple filtering actions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Formatters</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Ultimately, a log record needs to be rendered as text. Formatters describe the exact format of that text. A</p> <p>formatter usually consists of a Python formatting string containing <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logrecord-attributes">LogRecord attributes; </a>however, you can also write custom formatters to implement specific formatting behavior.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.16.2 Security implications</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The logging system handles potentially sensitive information. For example, the log record may contain information about a web request or a stack trace, while some of the data you collect in your own loggers may also have security implications. You need to be sure you know:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• what information is collected</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• where it will subsequently be stored</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• how it will be transferred</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• who might have access to it.</p> <p>To help control the collection of sensitive information, you can explicitly designate certain sensitive infor-</p> <p>mation to be filtered out of error reports – read more about how to <a href="index.html#page_855">filter error reports.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>AdminEmailHandler</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The built-in <a href="index.html#page_1588"><i>AdminEmailHandler</i></a> deserves a mention in the context of security. If its include_html option is enabled, the email message it sends will contain a full traceback, with names and values of local variables at each level of the stack, plus the values of your Django settings (in other words, the same level of detail that</p> <p>is exposed in a web page when <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is True).</p> <p>It’s generally not considered a good idea to send such potentially sensitive information over email. Consider instead using one of the many third-party services to which detailed logs can be sent to get the best of multiple <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_710">worlds – the rich information of full tracebacks, clear management of who is notified and has access to the information, and so on.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.16.3 Configuring logging</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Python’s logging library provides several techniques to configure logging, ranging from a programmatic</p> <p>interface to configuration files. By default, Django uses the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema">dictConfig format</a>.</p> <p>In order to configure logging, you use <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOGGING</i></a> to define a dictionary of logging settings. These settings describe the loggers, handlers, filters and formatters that you want in your logging setup, and the log levels and other properties that you want those components to have.</p> <p>By default, the <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOGGING</i></a> setting is merged with <a href="index.html#page_1583">Django’s default logging configuration</a> using the following scheme.</p> <p>If the disable_existing_loggers key in the <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOGGING</i></a> dictConfig is set to True (which is the dictConfig default if the key is missing) then all loggers from the default configuration will be disabled. Dis-abled loggers are not the same as removed; the logger will still exist, but will silently discard any-thing logged to it, not even propagating entries to a parent logger. Thus you should be very care-ful using 'disable_existing_loggers': True; it’s probably not what you want. Instead, you can set disable_existing_loggers to False and redefine some or all of the default loggers; or you can set</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>LOGGING_CONFIG</i></a> to None and <a href="index.html#page_715">handle logging config yourself</a>.</p> <p>Logging is configured as part of the general Django setup() function. Therefore, you can be certain that loggers are always ready for use in your project code.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Examples</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The full documentation for <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema">dictConfig format</a> is the best source of information about logging configuration dictionaries. However, to give you a taste of what is possible, here are several examples.</p> <p>To begin, here’s a small configuration that will allow you to output all log messages to the console:</p> <p send messages with the WARNING level and higher to the console handler. By adjusting the level to INFO or DEBUG you can display more messages. This may be useful during development.</p> <p>Next we can add more fine-grained logging. Here’s an example of how to make the logging system print more</p> <p>messages from just the <a href="index.html#page_1585">django</a> named logger:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p With this config, however, you can also set the environment variable DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG to see all of Django’s debug logging which is very verbose as it includes all database queries.</p> <p>You don’t have to log to the console. Here’s a configuration which writes all logging from the <a href="index.html#page_1585">django</a> named <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> Django application.</p> <p>Finally, here’s an example of a fairly complex logging setup:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 34: settings.py</p> <p><span [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"console"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"propagate"</span><span <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.request"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"handlers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"mail_admins"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"ERROR"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"propagate"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"myproject.custom"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"handlers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"console"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"mail_admins"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"INFO"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"filters"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"special"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This logging configuration does the following things:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Identifies the configuration as being in ‘dictConfig version 1’ format. At present, this is the only dict-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Config format version.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Defines two formatters:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– simple, that outputs the log level name (e.g., DEBUG) and the log message.</p> <p id="page_714"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The format string is a normal Python formatting string describing the details that are to be output</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">on each logging line. The full list of detail that can be output can be found in <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#formatter-objects">Formatter Objects</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– verbose, that outputs the log level name, the log message, plus the time, process, thread and</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">module that generate the log message.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Defines two filters:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– project.logging.SpecialFilter, using the alias special. If this filter required additional argu-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">ments, they can be provided as additional keys in the filter configuration dictionary. In this case, the argument foo will be given a value of bar when instantiating SpecialFilter.</p> <p style="text-align:center">– django.utils.log.RequireDebugTrue, which passes on records when <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is True.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Defines two handlers:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– console, a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.handlers.html#logging.StreamHandler">StreamHandler</a>, which prints any INFO (or higher) message to sys.stderr. This han-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">dler uses the simple output format.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– mail_admins, an <a href="index.html#page_1588"><i>AdminEmailHandler</i></a>, which emails any ERROR (or higher) message to the site</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> . This handler uses the special filter.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Configures three loggers:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– django, which passes all messages to the console handler.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– django.request, which passes all ERROR messages to the mail_admins handler. In addition, this</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">logger is marked to not propagate messages. This means that log messages written to django. request will not be handled by the django logger.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">– myproject.custom, which passes all messages at INFO or higher that also pass the special filter</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">to two handlers – the console, and mail_admins. This means that all INFO level messages (or higher) will be printed to the console; ERROR and CRITICAL messages will also be output via email.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom logging configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you don’t want to use Python’s dictConfig format to configure your logger, you can specify your own configuration scheme.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>LOGGING_CONFIG</i></a> setting defines the callable that will be used to configure Django’s loggers. By default,</p> <p>it points at Python’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging.config.dictConfig">logging.config.dictConfig()</a> function. However, if you want to use a different con-</p> <p>figuration process, you can use any other callable that takes a single argument. The contents of <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOGGING</i></a> will be provided as the value of that argument when logging is configured.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_715" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Disabling logging configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you don’t want to configure logging at all (or you want to manually configure logging using your own</p> <p>approach), you can set <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>LOGGING_CONFIG</i></a> to None. This will disable the configuration process for <a href="index.html#page_1583">Django’s</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1583">default logging</a>.</p> <p>Setting <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>LOGGING_CONFIG</i></a> to None only means that the automatic configuration process is disabled, not logging itself. If you disable the configuration process, Django will still make logging calls, falling back to whatever default logging behavior is defined.</p> <p>Here’s an example that disables Django’s logging configuration and then manually configures logging:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 35: settings.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING_CONFIG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= None</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">logging.config</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logging</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">config</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dictConfig(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that the default configuration process only calls <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>LOGGING_CONFIG</i></a> once settings are fully-loaded. In contrast, manually configuring the logging in your settings file will load your logging config immediately. As such, your logging config must appear after any settings on which it depends.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.17 Pagination</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides high-level and low-level ways to help you manage paginated data – that is, data that’s split across several pages, with “Previous/Next” links.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.17.1 The</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>Paginator</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>class</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Under the hood, all methods of pagination use the <a href="index.html#page_1855"><i>Paginator</i></a> class. It does all the heavy lifting of actually</p> <p>splitting a QuerySet into <a href="index.html#page_1858"><i>Page</i></a> objects.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span When determining the number of objects contained in the passed object, Paginator will first try calling count(), then fallback to using len() if the passed object has no count() method. This allows objects such as Django’s QuerySet to use a more efficient count() method when available.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.17.3 Paginating a</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>ListView</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_957"><i>django.views.generic.list.ListView</i></a> provides a builtin way to paginate the displayed list. You can do</p> <p>this by adding a <a href="index.html#page_984"><i>paginate_by</i></a> attribute to your view class, for example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.generic</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ListView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Contact</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ContactListView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ListView):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">paginate_by</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Contact</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This limits the number of objects per page and adds a paginator and page_obj to the context. To allow your users to navigate between pages, add links to the next and previous page, in your template like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">contact</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>{# Each "contact" is a Contact model object. #}</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">contact.full_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>|</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>upper</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">br</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pagination"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">span</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"step-links"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.has_previous</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">href</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"?page=1"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">«</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">first</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">href</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"?page=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.previous_page_number</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>previous</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">span</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">class</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"current"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Page</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.number</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">of</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.paginator.num_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">span</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.has_next</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">href</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"?page=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.next_page_number</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>next</</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">href</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"?page=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj.paginator.num_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>last</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">»</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_718"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endif</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">span</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">div</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.17.4 Using</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>Paginator</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>in a view function</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here’s an example using <a href="index.html#page_1855"><i>Paginator</i></a> in a view function to paginate a queryset:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.paginator</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Paginator</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Contact</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>listing</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">contact_list</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Contact</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">paginator</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Paginator(contact_list,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">25</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Show 25 contacts per page.</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">page_number</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">GET</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"page"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">page_obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">paginator</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_page(page_number)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"list.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"page_obj"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: page_obj})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In the template list.html, you can include navigation between pages in the same way as in the template for the ListView above.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.18 Security in Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document is an overview of Django’s security features. It includes advice on securing a Django-powered site.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.1 Cross site scripting (XSS) protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>XSS attacks allow a user to inject client side scripts into the browsers of other users. This is usually achieved by storing the malicious scripts in the database where it will be retrieved and displayed to other users, or by getting users to click a link which will cause the attacker’s JavaScript to be executed by the user’s browser. However, XSS attacks can originate from any untrusted source of data, such as cookies or web services, whenever the data is not sufficiently sanitized before including in a page.</p> <p>Using Django templates protects you against the majority of XSS attacks. However, it is important to under-stand what protections it provides and its limitations.</p> <p id="page_719" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django templates <a href="index.html#page_1973">escape specific characters</a> which are particularly dangerous to HTML. While this protects users from most malicious input, it is not entirely foolproof. For example, it will not protect the following:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><style class={{ var }}>...</style></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If var is set to 'class1 onmouseover=javascript:func()', this can result in unauthorized JavaScript exe-cution, depending on how the browser renders imperfect HTML. (Quoting the attribute value would fix this case.)</p> <p>It is also important to be particularly careful when using is_safe with custom template tags, the <a href="index.html#page_2019"><i>safe</i></a> tem-</p> <p>plate tag, <a href="index.html#page_2086"><i>mark_safe</i></a>, and when autoescape is turned off.</p> <p>In addition, if you are using the template system to output something other than HTML, there may be entirely separate characters and words which require escaping.</p> <p>You should also be very careful when storing HTML in the database, especially when that HTML is retrieved and displayed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.2 Cross site request forgery (CSRF) protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>CSRF attacks allow a malicious user to execute actions using the credentials of another user without that user’s knowledge or consent.</p> <p>Django has built-in protection against most types of CSRF attacks, providing you have <a href="index.html#page_889">enabled and used</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_889">it</a> where appropriate. However, as with any mitigation technique, there are limitations. For example, it is possible to disable the CSRF module globally or for particular views. You should only do this if you know</p> <p>what you are doing. There are other <a href="index.html#page_1408">limitations</a> if your site has subdomains that are outside of your control.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1406">CSRF protection works</a> by checking for a secret in each POST request. This ensures that a malicious user cannot “replay” a form POST to your website and have another logged in user unwittingly submit that form. The malicious user would have to know the secret, which is user specific (using a cookie).</p> <p>When deployed with <a href="index.html#page_720">HTTPS</a>, CsrfViewMiddleware will check that the HTTP referer header is set to a URL on the same origin (including subdomain and port). Because HTTPS provides additional security, it is imperative to ensure connections use HTTPS where it is available by forwarding insecure connection requests and using HSTS for supported browsers.</p> <p>Be very careful with marking views with the csrf_exempt decorator unless it is absolutely necessary.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_720"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.3 SQL injection protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQL injection is a type of attack where a malicious user is able to execute arbitrary SQL code on a database. This can result in records being deleted or data leakage.</p> <p>Django’s querysets are protected from SQL injection since their queries are constructed using query param-eterization. A query’s SQL code is defined separately from the query’s parameters. Since parameters may be user-provided and therefore unsafe, they are escaped by the underlying database driver.</p> <p>Django also gives developers power to write <a href="index.html#page_201">raw queries</a> or execute <a href="index.html#page_205">custom sql</a>. These capabilities should be used sparingly and you should always be careful to properly escape any parameters that the user can control.</p> <p>In addition, you should exercise caution when using <a href="index.html#page_1732"><i>extra()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1799"><i>RawSQL</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1799">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.4 Clickjacking protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Clickjacking is a type of attack where a malicious site wraps another site in a frame. This attack can result in an unsuspecting user being tricked into performing unintended actions on the target site.</p> <p>Django contains <a href="index.html#page_1015">clickjacking protection</a> in the form of the <a href="index.html#page_1601"><i>X-Frame-Options middleware</i></a> which in a sup-porting browser can prevent a site from being rendered inside a frame. It is possible to disable the protection on a per view basis or to configure the exact header value sent.</p> <p>The middleware is strongly recommended for any site that does not need to have its pages wrapped in a frame by third party sites, or only needs to allow that for a small section of the site.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.5 SSL/HTTPS</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is always better for security to deploy your site behind HTTPS. Without this, it is possible for malicious network users to sniff authentication credentials or any other information transferred between client and server, and in some cases – active network attackers – to alter data that is sent in either direction.</p> <p>If you want the protection that HTTPS provides, and have enabled it on your server, there are some additional steps you may need:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If necessary, set <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER</i></a>, ensuring that you have understood the warnings there</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">thoroughly. Failure to do this can result in CSRF vulnerabilities, and failure to do it correctly can also be dangerous!</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Set <a href="index.html#page_1929"><i>SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT</i></a> to True, so that requests over HTTP are redirected to HTTPS.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Please note the caveats under <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER</i></a>. For the case of a reverse proxy, it may be easier or more secure to configure the main web server to do the redirect to HTTPS.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Use ‘secure’ cookies.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If a browser connects initially via HTTP, which is the default for most browsers, it is possible for</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">existing cookies to be leaked. For this reason, you should set your <a href="index.html#page_1944"><i>SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE</i></a> and</p> <p id="page_721" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE</i></a> settings to True. This instructs the browser to only send these cookies over HTTPS connections. Note that this will mean that sessions will not work over HTTP, and the CSRF pro-tection will prevent any POST data being accepted over HTTP (which will be fine if you are redirecting all HTTP traffic to HTTPS).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Use <a href="index.html#page_1595">HTTP Strict Transport Security</a> (HSTS)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">HSTS is an HTTP header that informs a browser that all future connections to a particular site should always use HTTPS. Combined with redirecting requests over HTTP to HTTPS, this will ensure that connections always enjoy the added security of SSL provided one successful connection has occurred.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">HSTS may either be configured with <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS</i></a> , and</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD</i></a> , or on the web server.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.6 Host header validation</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django uses the Host header provided by the client to construct URLs in certain cases. While these values are sanitized to prevent Cross Site Scripting attacks, a fake Host value can be used for Cross-Site Request Forgery, cache poisoning attacks, and poisoning links in emails.</p> <p>Because even seemingly-secure web server configurations are susceptible to fake Host headers, Django</p> <p>validates Host headers against the <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ALLOWED_HOSTS</i></a> setting in the <a href="index.html#page_1864"><i>django.http.HttpRequest.get_host()</i></a> method.</p> <p>This validation only applies via <a href="index.html#page_1864"><i>get_host()</i></a>; if your code accesses the Host header directly from request. META you are bypassing this security protection.</p> <p>For more details see the full <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ALLOWED_HOSTS</i></a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Previous versions of this document recommended configuring your web server to ensure it</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">validates incoming HTTP Host headers. While this is still recommended, in many common web servers a</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">configuration that seems to validate the Host header may not in fact do so. For instance, even if Apache</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">is configured such that your Django site is served from a non-default virtual host with the ServerName</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">set, it is still possible for an HTTP request to match this virtual host and supply a fake Host header.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Thus, Django now requires that you set <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ALLOWED_HOSTS</i></a> explicitly rather than relying on web server</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">configuration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Additionally, Django requires you to explicitly enable support for the X-Forwarded-Host header (via the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_X_FORWARDED_HOST</i></a> setting) if your configuration requires it.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_722"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.7 Referrer policy</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Browsers use the Referer header as a way to send information to a site about how users got there. By setting a Referrer Policy you can help to protect the privacy of your users, restricting under which circumstances</p> <p>the Referer header is set. See <a href="index.html#page_1596">the referrer policy section of the security middleware reference</a> for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.8 Cross-origin opener policy</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The cross-origin opener policy (COOP) header allows browsers to isolate a top-level window from other doc-uments by putting them in a different context group so that they cannot directly interact with the top-level window. If a document protected by COOP opens a cross-origin popup window, the popup’s window.opener</p> <p>property will be null. COOP protects against cross-origin attacks. See <a href="index.html#page_1597">the cross-origin opener policy section</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1597">of the security middleware reference</a> for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.9 Session security</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Similar to the <a href="index.html#page_1408">CSRF limitations</a> requiring a site to be deployed such that untrusted users don’t have access</p> <p>to any subdomains, <a href="index.html#page_311"><i>django.contrib.sessions</i></a> also has limitations. See <a href="index.html#page_324">the session topic guide section on</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_324">security</a> for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.10 User-uploaded content</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Consider <a href="index.html#page_886">serving static files from a cloud service or CDN</a> to avoid some of these issues.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If your site accepts file uploads, it is strongly advised that you limit these uploads in your web server</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">configuration to a reasonable size in order to prevent denial of service (DOS) attacks. In Apache, this</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">can be easily set using the <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/core.html#limitrequestbody">LimitRequestBody</a> directive.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If you are serving your own static files, be sure that handlers like Apache’s mod_php, which would</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">execute static files as code, are disabled. You don’t want users to be able to execute arbitrary code by uploading and requesting a specially crafted file.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Django’s media upload handling poses some vulnerabilities when that media is served in ways that do</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">not follow security best practices. Specifically, an HTML file can be uploaded as an image if that file contains a valid PNG header followed by malicious HTML. This file will pass verification of the library</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">that Django uses for <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a> image processing (Pillow). When this file is subsequently displayed to a user, it may be displayed as HTML depending on the type and configuration of your web server.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">No bulletproof technical solution exists at the framework level to safely validate all user uploaded file content, however, there are some other steps you can take to mitigate these attacks:</p> <p id="page_723" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">1. One class of attacks can be prevented by always serving user uploaded content from a distinct top-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">level or second-level domain. This prevents any exploit blocked by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-origin_policy">same-origin policy</a> protections such as cross site scripting. For example, if your site runs on example.com, you would want to</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">serve uploaded content (the <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> setting) from something like usercontent-example.com. It’s not sufficient to serve content from a subdomain like usercontent.example.com.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">2. Beyond this, applications may choose to define a list of allowable file extensions for user uploaded</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">files and configure the web server to only serve such files.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.18.11 Additional security topics</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While Django provides good security protection out of the box, it is still important to properly deploy your application and take advantage of the security protection of the web server, operating system and other components.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Make sure that your Python code is outside of the web server’s root. This will ensure that your Python</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">code is not accidentally served as plain text (or accidentally executed).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Take care with any <a href="index.html#page_1633">user uploaded files</a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Django does not throttle requests to authenticate users. To protect against brute-force attacks against</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the authentication system, you may consider deploying a Django plugin or web server module to throt-tle these requests.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Keep your <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> , and <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a> if in use, secret.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It is a good idea to limit the accessibility of your caching system and database using a firewall.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Take a look at the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) <a href="https://owasp.org/Top10/">Top 10 list</a> which identifies some</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">common vulnerabilities in web applications. While Django has tools to address some of the issues, other issues must be accounted for in the design of your project.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Mozilla discusses various topics regarding <a href="https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security.html">web security. </a>Their pages also include security principles</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">that apply to any system.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.19 Performance and optimization</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document provides an overview of techniques and tools that can help get your Django code running more efficiently - faster, and using fewer system resources.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_724"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.1 Introduction</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Generally one’s first concern is to write code that works, whose logic functions as required to produce the expected output. Sometimes, however, this will not be enough to make the code work as efficiently as one would like.</p> <p>In this case, what’s needed is something - and in practice, often a collection of things - to improve the code’s performance without, or only minimally, affecting its behavior.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.2 General approaches</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>What are you optimizing</b> <i><b>for</b></i><b>?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s important to have a clear idea what you mean by ‘performance’. There is not just one metric of it.</p> <p>Improved speed might be the most obvious aim for a program, but sometimes other performance improve-ments might be sought, such as lower memory consumption or fewer demands on the database or network.</p> <p>Improvements in one area will often bring about improved performance in another, but not always; some-times one can even be at the expense of another. For example, an improvement in a program’s speed might cause it to use more memory. Even worse, it can be self-defeating - if the speed improvement is so memory-hungry that the system starts to run out of memory, you’ll have done more harm than good.</p> <p>There are other trade-offs to bear in mind. Your own time is a valuable resource, more precious than CPU time. Some improvements might be too difficult to be worth implementing, or might affect the portability or maintainability of the code. Not all performance improvements are worth the effort.</p> <p>So, you need to know what performance improvements you are aiming for, and you also need to know that you have a good reason for aiming in that direction - and for that you need:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Performance benchmarking</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s no good just guessing or assuming where the inefficiencies lie in your code.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Django tools</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-debug-toolbar/">django-debug-toolbar</a> is a very handy tool that provides insights into what your code is doing and how much time it spends doing it. In particular it can show you all the SQL queries your page is generating, and how long each one has taken.</p> <p>Third-party panels are also available for the toolbar, that can (for example) report on cache performance and template rendering times.</p> <p id="page_725" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Third-party services</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are a number of free services that will analyze and report on the performance of your site’s pages from the perspective of a remote HTTP client, in effect simulating the experience of an actual user.</p> <p>These can’t report on the internals of your code, but can provide a useful insight into your site’s overall per-formance, including aspects that can’t be adequately measured from within Django environment. Examples include:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://yslow.org/">Yahoo’s Yslow</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://developers.google.com/speed/">Google PageSpeed</a></p> <p>There are also several paid-for services that perform a similar analysis, including some that are Django-aware and can integrate with your codebase to profile its performance far more comprehensively.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Get things right from the start</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some work in optimization involves tackling performance shortcomings, but some of the work can be built-in to what you’d do anyway, as part of the good practices you should adopt even before you start thinking about improving performance.</p> <p>In this respect Python is an excellent language to work with, because solutions that look elegant and feel right usually are the best performing ones. As with most skills, learning what “looks right” takes practice, but one of the most useful guidelines is:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Work at the appropriate level</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django offers many different ways of approaching things, but just because it’s possible to do something in a certain way doesn’t mean that it’s the most appropriate way to do it. For example, you might find that you could calculate the same thing - the number of items in a collection, perhaps - in a QuerySet, in Python, or in a template.</p> <p>However, it will almost always be faster to do this work at lower rather than higher levels. At higher levels the system has to deal with objects through multiple levels of abstraction and layers of machinery.</p> <p>That is, the database can typically do things faster than Python can, which can do them faster than the template language can:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># QuerySet operation on the database</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># fast, because that's what databases are good at</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">my_bicycles</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">count()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># counting Python objects</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># slower, because it requires a database query anyway, and processing</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_726"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># of the Python objects</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">len</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(my_bicycles)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><!--</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>Django template filter</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>slower still, because it will have to count them in Python anyway,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>and because of template language overheads</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>--></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">my_bicycles</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>|</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>length</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Generally speaking, the most appropriate level for the job is the lowest-level one that it is comfortable to code for.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The example above is merely illustrative.</p> <p>Firstly, in a real-life case you need to consider what is happening before and after your count to work out what’s an optimal way of doing it in that particular context. The database optimization document describes</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_241">a case where counting in the template would be better.</a></p> <p>Secondly, there are other options to consider: in a real-life case, {{ my_bicycles.count }}, which invokes the QuerySet count() method directly from the template, might be the most appropriate choice.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.3 Caching</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Often it is expensive (that is, resource-hungry and slow) to compute a value, so there can be huge benefit in saving the value to a quickly accessible cache, ready for the next time it’s required.</p> <p>It’s a sufficiently significant and powerful technique that Django includes a comprehensive caching frame-work, as well as other smaller pieces of caching functionality.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The caching framework</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_599">caching framework</a> offers very significant opportunities for performance gains, by saving dynamic content so that it doesn’t need to be calculated for each request.</p> <p>For convenience, Django offers different levels of cache granularity: you can cache the output of specific views, or only the pieces that are difficult to produce, or even an entire site.</p> <p>Implementing caching should not be regarded as an alternative to improving code that’s performing poorly because it has been written badly. It’s one of the final steps toward producing well-performing code, not a shortcut.</p> <p id="page_727" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>cached_property</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s common to have to call a class instance’s method more than once. If that function is expensive, then doing so can be wasteful.</p> <p>Using the <a href="index.html#page_2079"><i>cached_property</i></a> decorator saves the value returned by a property; the next time the function is called on that instance, it will return the saved value rather than re-computing it. Note that this only works on methods that take self as their only argument and that it changes the method to a property.</p> <p>Certain Django components also have their own caching functionality; these are discussed below in the sec-tions related to those components.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.4 Understanding laziness</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Laziness is a strategy complementary to caching. Caching avoids recomputation by saving results; laziness delays computation until it’s actually required.</p> <p>Laziness allows us to refer to things before they are instantiated, or even before it’s possible to instantiate them. This has numerous uses.</p> <p>For example, <a href="index.html#page_655">lazy translation</a> can be used before the target language is even known, because it doesn’t take place until the translated string is actually required, such as in a rendered template.</p> <p>Laziness is also a way to save effort by trying to avoid work in the first place. That is, one aspect of laziness is not doing anything until it has to be done, because it may not turn out to be necessary after all. Laziness can therefore have performance implications, and the more expensive the work concerned, the more there is to gain through laziness.</p> <p>Python provides a number of tools for lazy evaluation, particularly through the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator">generator</a> and <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator-expression">generator</a></p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator-expression">expression</a> constructs. It’s worth reading up on laziness in Python to discover opportunities for making use of lazy patterns in your code.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Laziness in Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django is itself quite lazy. A good example of this can be found in the evaluation of QuerySets. <a href="index.html#page_148">QuerySets are</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_148">lazy</a>. Thus a QuerySet can be created, passed around and combined with other QuerySets, without actually incurring any trips to the database to fetch the items it describes. What gets passed around is the QuerySet object, not the collection of items that - eventually - will be required from the database.</p> <p>On the other hand, <a href="index.html#page_1706">certain operations will force the evaluation of a QuerySet</a>. Avoiding the premature eval-uation of a QuerySet can save making an expensive and unnecessary trip to the database.</p> <p>Django also offers a <a href="index.html#page_2081"><i>keep_lazy()</i></a> decorator. This allows a function that has been called with a lazy argument to behave lazily itself, only being evaluated when it needs to be. Thus the lazy argument - which could be an expensive one - will not be called upon for evaluation until it’s strictly required.</p> <p id="page_728"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.5 Databases</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database optimization</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s database layer provides various ways to help developers get the best performance from their</p> <p>databases. The <a href="index.html#page_236">database optimization documentation</a> gathers together links to the relevant documentation and adds various tips that outline the steps to take when attempting to optimize your database usage.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Other database-related tips</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Enabling <a href="index.html#page_1411">Persistent connections</a> can speed up connections to the database accounts for a significant part of the request processing time.</p> <p>This helps a lot on virtualized hosts with limited network performance, for example.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.6 HTTP performance</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Middleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django comes with a few helpful pieces of <a href="index.html#page_1591">middleware</a> that can help optimize your site’s performance. They include:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ConditionalGetMiddleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Adds support for modern browsers to conditionally GET responses based on the ETag and Last-Modified headers. It also calculates and sets an ETag if needed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GZipMiddleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Compresses responses for all modern browsers, saving bandwidth and transfer time. Note that GZipMiddle-ware is currently considered a security risk, and is vulnerable to attacks that nullify the protection provided</p> <p>by TLS/SSL. See the warning in <a href="index.html#page_1593"><i>GZipMiddleware</i></a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Sessions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using cached sessions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_312">Using cached sessions</a> may be a way to increase performance by eliminating the need to load session data from a slower storage source like the database and instead storing frequently used session data in memory.</p> <p id="page_729" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Static files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Static files, which by definition are not dynamic, make an excellent target for optimization gains.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ManifestStaticFilesStorage</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By taking advantage of web browsers’ caching abilities, you can eliminate network hits entirely for a given file after the initial download.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1374"><i>ManifestStaticFilesStorage</i></a> appends a content-dependent tag to the filenames of <a href="index.html#page_1369">static files</a> to make it safe for browsers to cache them long-term without missing future changes - when a file changes, so will the tag, so browsers will reload the asset automatically.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>“Minification”</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Several third-party Django tools and packages provide the ability to “minify” HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
