They remove unnecessary whitespace, newlines, and comments, and shorten variable names, and thus reduce the size of the documents that your site publishes.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.7 Template performance</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• using {% block %} is faster than using {% include %}</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• heavily-fragmented templates, assembled from many small pieces, can affect performance</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The cached template loader</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Enabling the <a href="index.html#page_2048"><i>cached template loader</i></a> often improves performance drastically, as it avoids compiling each template every time it needs to be rendered.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.19.8 Using different versions of available software</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It can sometimes be worth checking whether different and better-performing versions of the software that you’re using are available.</p> <p>These techniques are targeted at more advanced users who want to push the boundaries of performance of an already well-optimized Django site.</p> <p>However, they are not magic solutions to performance problems, and they’re unlikely to bring better than marginal gains to sites that don’t already do the more basic things the right way.</p> <p id="page_730"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: It’s worth repeating: reaching for alternatives to software you’re already using is never the first answer to performance problems. When you reach this level of optimization, you need a formal benchmarking solution.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Newer is often - but not always - better</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s fairly rare for a new release of well-maintained software to be less efficient, but the maintainers can’t anticipate every possible use-case - so while being aware that newer versions are likely to perform better, don’t assume that they always will.</p> <p>This is true of Django itself. Successive releases have offered a number of improvements across the system, but you should still check the real-world performance of your application, because in some cases you may find that changes mean it performs worse rather than better.</p> <p>Newer versions of Python, and also of Python packages, will often perform better too - but measure, rather than assume.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Unless you’ve encountered an unusual performance problem in a particular version, you’ll generally find better features, reliability, and security in a new release and that these benefits are far more significant than any performance you might win or lose.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Alternatives to Django’s template language</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For nearly all cases, Django’s built-in template language is perfectly adequate. However, if the bottlenecks in your Django project seem to lie in the template system and you have exhausted other opportunities to remedy this, a third-party alternative may be the answer.</p> <p><a href="https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/">Jinja2</a> can offer performance improvements, particularly when it comes to speed.</p> <p>Alternative template systems vary in the extent to which they share Django’s templating language.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you experience performance issues in templates, the first thing to do is to understand exactly why. Using an alternative template system may prove faster, but the same gains may also be available without going to that trouble - for example, expensive processing and logic in your templates could be done more efficiently in your views.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_731" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Alternative software implementations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It may be worth checking whether Python software you’re using has been provided in a different implemen-tation that can execute the same code faster.</p> <p>However: most performance problems in well-written Django sites aren’t at the Python execution level, but rather in inefficient database querying, caching, and templates. If you’re relying on poorly-written Python code, your performance problems are unlikely to be solved by having it execute faster.</p> <p>Using an alternative implementation may introduce compatibility, deployment, portability, or maintenance issues. It goes without saying that before adopting a non-standard implementation you should ensure it provides sufficient performance gains for your application to outweigh the potential risks.</p> <p>With these caveats in mind, you should be aware of:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PyPy</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://www.pypy.org/">PyPy</a> is an implementation of Python in Python itself (the ‘standard’ Python implementation is in C). PyPy can offer substantial performance gains, typically for heavyweight applications.</p> <p>A key aim of the PyPy project is <a href="https://www.pypy.org/compat.html">compatibility</a> with existing Python APIs and libraries. Django is compatible, but you will need to check the compatibility of other libraries you rely on.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>C implementations of Python libraries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some Python libraries are also implemented in C, and can be much faster. They aim to offer the same APIs. Note that compatibility issues and behavior differences are not unknown (and not always immediately evi-dent).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.20 Serializing Django objects</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s serialization framework provides a mechanism for “translating” Django models into other formats. Usually these other formats will be text-based and used for sending Django data over a wire, but it’s possible for a serializer to handle any format (text-based or not).</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>If you just want to get some data from your tables into a serialized form, you could use the <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata</i></a> man-agement command.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_732"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.20.1 Serializing data</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>At the highest level, you can serialize data like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, SomeModel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all())</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The arguments to the serialize function are the format to serialize the data to (see <a href="index.html#page_734">Serialization formats</a>)</p> <p>and a <a href="index.html#page_1709"><i>QuerySet</i></a> to serialize. (Actually, the second argument can be any iterator that yields Django model instances, but it’ll almost always be a QuerySet).</p> <p>django.core.serializers.<b>get_serializer</b>(format)</p> <p>You can also use a serializer object directly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">XMLSerializer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_serializer(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">xml_serializer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">XMLSerializer()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">xml_serializer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(queryset)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">xml_serializer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">getvalue()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This is useful if you want to serialize data directly to a file-like object (which includes an <a href="index.html#page_1871"><i>HttpResponse</i></a>):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>with</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">open</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"file.xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"w"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">out:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">xml_serializer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(SomeModel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all(), stream</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">out)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Calling <a href="index.html#page_732"><i>get_serializer()</i></a> with an unknown <a href="index.html#page_734">format</a> will raise a django.core.serializers. SerializerDoesNotExist exception.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Subset of fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you only want a subset of fields to be serialized, you can specify a fields argument to the serializer:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, SomeModel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all(), fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"size"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this example, only the name and size attributes of each model will be serialized. The primary key is always serialized as the pk element in the resulting output; it never appears in the fields part.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Depending on your model, you may find that it is not possible to deserialize a model that only serializes a subset of its fields. If a serialized object doesn’t specify all the fields that are required by a model, the</p> <p id="page_733" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>deserializer will not be able to save deserialized instances.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Inherited models</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have a model that is defined using an <a href="index.html#page_132">abstract base class, </a>you don’t have to do anything special to serialize that model. Call the serializer on the object (or objects) that you want to serialize, and the output will be a complete representation of the serialized object.</p> <p>However, if you have a model that uses <a href="index.html#page_136">multi-table inheritance</a>, you also need to serialize all of the base classes for the model. This is because only the fields that are locally defined on the model will be serialized. For example, consider the following models:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Place</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">50</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Restaurant</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Place):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">serves_hot_dogs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">BooleanField(default</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you only serialize the Restaurant model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, Restaurant</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all())</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>the fields on the serialized output will only contain the serves_hot_dogs attribute. The name attribute of the base class will be ignored.</p> <p>In order to fully serialize your Restaurant instances, you will need to serialize the Place models as well:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">all_objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Restaurant</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Place</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, all_objects)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.20.2 Deserializing data</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Deserializing data is very similar to serializing it:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">do_something_with(obj)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As you can see, the deserialize function takes the same format argument as serialize, a string or stream of data, and returns an iterator.</p> <p>However, here it gets slightly complicated. The objects returned by the deserialize iterator aren’t regular Django objects. Instead, they are special DeserializedObject instances that wrap a created – but unsaved – object and any associated relationship data.</p> <p id="page_734"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Calling DeserializedObject.save() saves the object to the database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If the pk attribute in the serialized data doesn’t exist or is null, a new instance will be saved to the database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This ensures that deserializing is a non-destructive operation even if the data in your serialized representation doesn’t match what’s currently in the database. Usually, working with these DeserializedObject instances looks something like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialized_object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">object_should_be_saved(deserialized_object):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialized_object</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In other words, the usual use is to examine the deserialized objects to make sure that they are “appropriate” for saving before doing so. If you trust your data source you can instead save the object directly and move on.</p> <p>The Django object itself can be inspected as deserialized_object.object. If fields in the serialized data do not exist on a model, a DeserializationError will be raised unless the ignorenonexistent argument is passed in as True:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data, ignorenonexistent</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.20.3 Serialization formats</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports a number of serialization formats, some of which require you to install third-party Python modules:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Identi- Information</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">fier</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">xml Serializes to and from a simple XML dialect.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">json Serializes to and from <a href="https://json.org/">JSON</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">jsonl Serializes to and from <a href="https://jsonlines.org/">JSONL</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">yaml <span style="float:right">Serializes to YAML (YAML Ain’t a Markup Language). This serializer is only available if</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="https://pyyaml.org/">PyYAML</a> is installed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_735" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>XML</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The basic XML serialization format looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b><?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?></b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><django-objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">version=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"1.0"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pk=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"123"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">model=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"sessions.session"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">type=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DateTimeField"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">name=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"expire_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2013-01-16T08:16:59.844560+00:00</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></field></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><!-- ... --></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></object></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></django-objects></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The whole collection of objects that is either serialized or deserialized is represented by a <django-objects>-tag which contains multiple <object>-elements. Each such object has two attributes: “pk” and “model”, the latter being represented by the name of the app (“sessions”) and the lowercase name of the model (“session”) separated by a dot.</p> <p>Each field of the object is serialized as a <field>-element sporting the fields “type” and “name”. The text content of the element represents the value that should be stored.</p> <p>Foreign keys and other relational fields are treated a little bit differently:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pk=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"27"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">model=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth.permission"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><!-- ... --></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">to=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"contenttypes.contenttype"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">name=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"content_type"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rel=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ManyToOneRel"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">9</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></field></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><!-- ... --></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></object></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this example we specify that the auth.Permission object with the PK 27 has a foreign key to the contenttypes.ContentType instance with the PK 9.</p> <p>ManyToMany-relations are exported for the model that binds them. For instance, the auth.User model has such a relation to the auth.Permission model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pk=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"1"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">model=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth.user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><!-- ... --></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><field</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">to=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth.permission"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">name=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"user_permissions"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rel=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ManyToManyRel"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pk=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"46"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></object></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pk=</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"47"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></object></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"></field></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></object></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example links the given user with the permission models with PKs 46 and 47.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Control characters</p> <p id="page_736"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the content to be serialized contains control characters that are not accepted in the XML 1.0 standard, the</p> <p>serialization will fail with a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#ValueError">ValueError</a> exception. Read also the W3C’s explanation of <a href="https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-controls">HTML, XHTML,</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-controls">XML and Control Codes</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>JSON</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When staying with the same example data as before it would be serialized as JSON in the following way:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"4b678b301dfd8a4e0dad910de3ae245b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"sessions.session"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"expire_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"2013-01-16T08:16:59.844Z"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The formatting here is a bit simpler than with XML. The whole collection is just represented as an array and the objects are represented by JSON objects with three properties: “pk”, “model” and “fields”. “fields” is again an object containing each field’s name and value as property and property-value respectively.</p> <p>Foreign keys have the PK of the linked object as property value. ManyToMany-relations are serialized for the model that defines them and are represented as a list of PKs.</p> <p>Be aware that not all Django output can be passed unmodified to <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#module-json">json. </a>For example, if you have some custom</p> <p>type in an object to be serialized, you’ll have to write a custom <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#module-json">json</a> encoder for it. Something like this will work:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.serializers.json</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DjangoJSONEncoder</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>LazyEncoder</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(DjangoJSONEncoder):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>default</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, obj):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">isinstance</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(obj, YourCustomType):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">str</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(obj)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">default(obj)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can then pass cls=LazyEncoder to the serializers.serialize() function:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.serializers</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, SomeModel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cls</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">LazyEncoder)</span></p> <p id="page_737" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Also note that GeoDjango provides a <a href="index.html#page_1276">customized GeoJSON serializer.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DjangoJSONEncoder</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class</b> django.core.serializers.json.<b>DjangoJSONEncoder</b></p> <p>The JSON serializer uses DjangoJSONEncoder for encoding. A subclass of <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.JSONEncoder">JSONEncoder</a>, it handles these additional types:</p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime"><b>datetime</b></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string of the form YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sss+HH:MM as defined in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://262.ecma-international.org/5.1/#sec-15.9.1.15">ECMA-262.</a></p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.date"><b>date</b></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string of the form YYYY-MM-DD as defined in <a href="https://262.ecma-international.org/5.1/#sec-15.9.1.15">ECMA-262</a>.</p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.time"><b>time</b></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string of the form HH:MM:ss.sss as defined in <a href="https://262.ecma-international.org/5.1/#sec-15.9.1.15">ECMA-262.</a></p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.timedelta"><b>timedelta</b></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string representing a duration as defined in ISO-8601. For example, timedelta(days=1, hours=2, seconds=3.4) is represented as 'P1DT02H00M03.400000S'.</p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/decimal.html#decimal.Decimal"><b>Decimal</b>,</a> <b>Promise</b> (<b>django.utils.functional.lazy()</b> objects), <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/uuid.html#uuid.UUID"><b>UUID</b></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string representation of the object.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>JSONL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>JSONL stands for JSON Lines. With this format, objects are separated by new lines, and each line contains a valid JSON object. JSONL serialized data looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"4b678b301dfd8a4e0dad910de3ae245b"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"sessions.session"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}}</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"88bea72c02274f3c9bf1cb2bb8cee4fc"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"sessions.session"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}}</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"9cf0e26691b64147a67e2a9f06ad7a53"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"sessions.session"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>JSONL can be useful for populating large databases, since the data can be processed line by line, rather than being loaded into memory all at once.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_738"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>YAML</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>YAML serialization looks quite similar to JSON. The object list is serialized as a sequence mappings with the keys “pk”, “model” and “fields”. Each field is again a mapping with the key being name of the field and the value the value:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">-</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: sessions.session</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: 4b678b301dfd8a4e0dad910de3ae245b</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">expire_date</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: 2013-01-16 08:16:59.844560+00:00</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Referential fields are again represented by the PK or sequence of PKs.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom serialization formats</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to the default formats, you can create a custom serialization format.</p> <p>For example, let’s consider a csv serializer and deserializer. First, define a Serializer and a Deserializer class. <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">(serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">python</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span href="index.html#page_1930"><i>SERIALIZATION_MODULES</i></a> setting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SERIALIZATION_MODULES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.core.serializers.json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A Deserializer class definition was added to each of the provided serialization formats.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_740"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.20.4 Natural keys</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The default serialization strategy for foreign keys and many-to-many relations is to serialize the value of the primary key(s) of the objects in the relation. This strategy works well for most objects, but it can cause difficulty in some circumstances.</p> <p>Consider the case of a list of objects that have a foreign key referencing <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i>. </a>If you’re going to serialize an object that refers to a content type, then you need to have a way to refer to that content type to begin with. Since ContentType objects are automatically created by Django during the database synchro-nization process, the primary key of a given content type isn’t easy to predict; it will depend on how and when</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> was executed. This is true for all models which automatically generate objects, notably including</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Permission</i></a> , <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Group</i>, </a>and <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: You should never include automatically generated objects in a fixture or other serialized</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">data. By chance, the primary keys in the fixture may match those in the database and loading the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">fixture will have no effect. In the more likely case that they don’t match, the fixture loading will fail</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">with an <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>IntegrityError</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There is also the matter of convenience. An integer id isn’t always the most convenient way to refer to an object; sometimes, a more natural reference would be helpful.</p> <p>It is for these reasons that Django provides natural keys. A natural key is a tuple of values that can be used to uniquely identify an object instance without using the primary key value.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Deserialization of natural keys</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Consider the following two models:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Person</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">birthdate</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">constraints</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">UniqueConstraint(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"unique_first_last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_741" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Book</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(Person, on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Ordinarily, serialized data for Book would use an integer to refer to the author. For example, in JSON, a Book might be serialized as:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"store.book"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Mostly Harmless"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"author"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">42</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}}</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This isn’t a particularly natural way to refer to an author. It requires that you know the primary key value for the author; it also requires that this primary key value is stable and predictable.</p> <p>However, if we add natural key handling to Person, the fixture becomes much more humane. To add natural key handling, you define a default Manager for Person with a get_by_natural_key() method. In the case of a Person, a good natural key might be the pair of first and last name:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PersonManager</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Manager):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_by_natural_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, first_name, last_name):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(first_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name, last_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Person</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">birthdate</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PersonManager()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">constraints</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">UniqueConstraint(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"unique_first_last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now books can use that natural key to refer to Person objects:</p> <p id="page_742"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"store.book"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Mostly Harmless"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"author"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Douglas"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Adams"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you try to load this serialized data, Django will use the get_by_natural_key() method to resolve ["Douglas", "Adams"] into the primary key of an actual Person object.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Whatever fields you use for a natural key must be able to uniquely identify an object. This will usually mean that your model will have a uniqueness clause (either unique=True on a single field, or a UniqueConstraint or unique_together over multiple fields) for the field or fields in your natural key. How-ever, uniqueness doesn’t need to be enforced at the database level. If you are certain that a set of fields will be effectively unique, you can still use those fields as a natural key.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Deserialization of objects with no primary key will always check whether the model’s manager has a get_by_natural_key() method and if so, use it to populate the deserialized object’s primary key.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serialization of natural keys</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>So how do you get Django to emit a natural key when serializing an object? Firstly, you need to add another method – this time to the model itself:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Person</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">birthdate</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DateField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PersonManager()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">constraints</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">UniqueConstraint(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"unique_first_last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>natural_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name)</span></p> <p id="page_743" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>That method should always return a natural key tuple – in this example, (first name, last name). Then, when you call serializers.serialize(), you provide use_natural_foreign_keys=True or use_natural_primary_keys=True arguments:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">serialize(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"json"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[book1, book2],</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">indent</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">use_natural_foreign_keys</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">use_natural_primary_keys</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When use_natural_foreign_keys=True is specified, Django will use the natural_key() method to serialize any foreign key reference to objects of the type that defines the method.</p> <p>When use_natural_primary_keys=True is specified, Django will not provide the primary key in the serial-ized data of this object since it can be calculated during deserialization:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"store.person"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Douglas"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Adams"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"birth_date"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"1952-03-11"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This can be useful when you need to load serialized data into an existing database and you cannot guarantee that the serialized primary key value is not already in use, and do not need to ensure that deserialized objects retain the same primary keys.</p> <p>If you are using <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata</i></a> to generate serialized data, use the <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>dumpdata --natural-foreign</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>dumpdata</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>--natural-primary</i></a> command line flags to generate natural keys.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: You don’t need to define both natural_key() and get_by_natural_key(). If you don’t want Django to output natural keys during serialization, but you want to retain the ability to load natural keys, then you can opt to not implement the natural_key() method.</p> <p>Conversely, if (for some strange reason) you want Django to output natural keys during serialization, but not be able to load those key values, just don’t define the get_by_natural_key() method.</p> <p id="page_744"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Natural keys and forward references</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Sometimes when you use <a href="index.html#page_740">natural foreign keys</a> you’ll need to deserialize data where an object has a foreign key referencing another object that hasn’t yet been deserialized. This is called a “forward reference”.</p> <p>For instance, suppose you have the following objects in your fixture:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"store.book"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Mostly Harmless"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"author"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Douglas"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Adams"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"store.person"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Douglas"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Adams"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}},</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In order to handle this situation, you need to pass handle_forward_references=True to serializers. deserialize(). This will set the deferred_fields attribute on the DeserializedObject instances. You’ll need to keep track of DeserializedObject instances where this attribute isn’t None and later call save_deferred_fields() on them.</p> <p>Typical usage looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">objs_with_deferred_fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">serializers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">deserialize(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data, handle_forward_references</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">deferred_fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>is not None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">objs_with_deferred_fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">append(obj)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">objs_with_deferred_fields:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save_deferred_fields()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For this to work, the ForeignKey on the referencing model must have null=True.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Dependencies during serialization</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s often possible to avoid explicitly having to handle forward references by taking care with the ordering of objects within a fixture.</p> <p>To help with this, calls to <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata</i></a> that use the <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>dumpdata --natural-foreign</i></a> option will serialize any model with a natural_key() method before serializing standard primary key objects.</p> <p>However, this may not always be enough. If your natural key refers to another object (by using a foreign key or natural key to another object as part of a natural key), then you need to be able to ensure that the objects on which a natural key depends occur in the serialized data before the natural key requires them.</p> <p id="page_745" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To control this ordering, you can define dependencies on your natural_key() methods. You do this by setting a dependencies attribute on the natural_key() method itself.</p> <p>For example, let’s add a natural key to the Book model from the example above:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Book</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(Person, on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>natural_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name,)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">natural_key()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The natural key for a Book is a combination of its name and its author. This means that Person must be serialized before Book. To define this dependency, we add one extra line:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>natural_key</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name,)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">natural_key()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">natural_key</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dependencies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"example_app.person"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This definition ensures that all Person objects are serialized before any Book objects. In turn, any object referencing Book will be serialized after both Person and Book have been serialized.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.21 Django settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A Django settings file contains all the configuration of your Django installation. This document explains how settings work and which settings are available.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.1 The basics</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A settings file is just a Python module with module-level variables.</p> <p>Here are a couple of example settings:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">ALLOWED_HOSTS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"www.example.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEBUG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= False</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"webmaster@example.com"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you set <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> to False, you also need to properly set the <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ALLOWED_HOSTS</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because a settings file is a Python module, the following apply:</p> <p id="page_746"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It doesn’t allow for Python syntax errors.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It can assign settings dynamically using normal Python syntax. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">MY_SETTING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">str</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(i)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">i</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">range</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">30</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• It can import values from other settings files.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.2 Designating the settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</b></p> <p>When you use Django, you have to tell it which settings you’re using. Do this by using an environment</p> <p>variable, <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a>.</p> <p>The value of <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> should be in Python path syntax, e.g. mysite.settings. Note that</p> <p>the settings module should be on the Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.path">sys.path.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The django-admin utility</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When using <a href="index.html#page_1433">django-admin, </a>you can either set the environment variable once, or explicitly pass in the settings module each time you run the utility.</p> <p>Example (Unix Bash shell):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite.settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin runserver</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Example (Windows shell):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">set DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=mysite.settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin runserver</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use the--settings command-line argument to specify the settings manually:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin runserver --settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite.settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>On the server (mod_wsgi)</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In your live server environment, you’ll need to tell your WSGI application what settings file to use. Do that with os.environ:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"mysite.settings"</span></p> <p id="page_747" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Read the <a href="index.html#page_868">Django mod_wsgi documentation</a> for more information and other common elements to a Django WSGI application.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.3 Default settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A Django settings file doesn’t have to define any settings if it doesn’t need to. Each setting has a sensible</p> <p>default value. These defaults live in the module <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/conf/global_settings.py">django/conf/global_settings.py.</a></p> <p>Here’s the algorithm Django uses in compiling settings:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Load settings from global_settings.py.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Load settings from the specified settings file, overriding the global settings as necessary.</p> <p>Note that a settings file should not import from global_settings, because that’s redundant.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Seeing which settings you’ve changed</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The command python manage.py diffsettings displays differences between the current settings file and Django’s default settings.</p> <p>For more, see the <a href="index.html#page_1437"><i>diffsettings</i></a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.4 Using settings in Python code</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In your Django apps, use settings by importing the object django.conf.settings. Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEBUG:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Do something</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that django.conf.settings isn’t a module – it’s an object. So importing individual settings is not possible:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf.settings</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DEBUG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># This won't work.</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Also note that your code should not import from either global_settings or your own settings file. django. conf.settings abstracts the concepts of default settings and site-specific settings; it presents a single inter-face. It also decouples the code that uses settings from the location of your settings.</p> <p id="page_748"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.5 Altering settings at runtime</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You shouldn’t alter settings in your applications at runtime. For example, don’t do this in a view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEBUG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= True</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Don't do this!</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The only place you should assign to settings is in a settings file.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.6 Security</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because a settings file contains sensitive information, such as the database password, you should make every attempt to limit access to it. For example, change its file permissions so that only you and your web server’s user can read it. This is especially important in a shared-hosting environment.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.7 Available settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For a full list of available settings, see the <a href="index.html#page_1887">settings reference.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.8 Creating your own settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There’s nothing stopping you from creating your own settings, for your own Django apps, but follow these guidelines:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Setting names must be all uppercase.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Don’t reinvent an already-existing setting.</p> <p>For settings that are sequences, Django itself uses lists, but this is only a convention.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.21.9 Using settings without setting</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In some cases, you might want to bypass the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable. For example, if you’re using the template system by itself, you likely don’t want to have to set up an environment variable pointing to a settings module.</p> <p>In these cases, you can configure Django’s settings manually.
