Do this by calling:</p> <p>django.conf.settings.<b>configure</b>(default_settings, **settings)</p> <p>Example:</p> <p id="page_749" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configure(DEBUG</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Pass configure() as many keyword arguments as you’d like, with each keyword argument representing a setting and its value. Each argument name should be all uppercase, with the same name as the settings described above. If a particular setting is not passed to configure() and is needed at some later point, Django will use the default setting value.</p> <p>Configuring Django in this fashion is mostly necessary – and, indeed, recommended – when you’re using a piece of the framework inside a larger application.</p> <p>Consequently, when configured via settings.configure(), Django will not make any modifications to the</p> <p>process environment variables (see the documentation of <a href="index.html#page_1935"><i>TIME_ZONE</i></a> for why this would normally occur). It’s assumed that you’re already in full control of your environment in these cases.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom default settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’d like default values to come from somewhere other than django.conf.global_settings, you can pass in a module or class that provides the default settings as the default_settings argument (or as the first positional argument) in the call to configure().</p> <p>In this example, default settings are taken from myapp_defaults, and the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting is set to True, re-gardless of its value in myapp_defaults:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp_defaults</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configure(default_settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp_defaults, DEBUG</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following example, which uses myapp_defaults as a positional argument, is equivalent:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configure(myapp_defaults, DEBUG</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Normally, you will not need to override the defaults in this fashion. The Django defaults are sufficiently tame that you can safely use them. Be aware that if you do pass in a new default module, it entirely replaces the Django defaults, so you must specify a value for every possible setting that might be used in the code you are importing. Check in django.conf.settings.global_settings for the full list.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_750"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Either configure() or DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE is required</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re not setting the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable, you must call configure() at some point before using any code that reads settings.</p> <p>If you don’t set <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> and don’t call configure(), Django will raise an ImportError exception the first time a setting is accessed.</p> <p>If you set <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a>, access settings values somehow, then call configure(), Django will raise a RuntimeError indicating that settings have already been configured. There is a property for this purpose:</p> <p>django.conf.settings.<b>configured</b></p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if not</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configured:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configure(myapp_defaults, DEBUG</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Also, it’s an error to call configure() more than once, or to call configure() after any setting has been accessed.</p> <p>It boils down to this: Use exactly one of either configure() or <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a>. Not both, and not neither.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Calling django.setup() is required for “standalone” Django usage</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using components of Django “standalone” – for example, writing a Python script which loads some Django templates and renders them, or uses the ORM to fetch some data – there’s one more step you’ll need in addition to configuring settings.</p> <p>After you’ve either set <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> or called configure(), you’ll need to call <a href="index.html#page_928"><i>django.setup()</i></a> to load your settings and populate Django’s application registry. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp_defaults</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">configure(default_settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp_defaults, DEBUG</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">setup()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Now this script or any imported module can use any part of Django it needs.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p id="page_751" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that calling django.setup() is only necessary if your code is truly standalone. When invoked by your</p> <p>web server, or through <a href="index.html#page_1433">django-admin</a>, Django will handle this for you.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.setup()</b> may only be called once.</p> <p>Therefore, avoid putting reusable application logic in standalone scripts so that you have to import from the script elsewhere in your application. If you can’t avoid that, put the call to django.setup() inside an if block:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">__name__</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"__main__"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">setup()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1887">The Settings Reference</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Contains the complete list of core and contrib app settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.22 Signals</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django includes a “signal dispatcher” which helps decoupled applications get notified when actions occur elsewhere in the framework. In a nutshell, signals allow certain senders to notify a set of receivers that some action has taken place. They’re especially useful when many pieces of code may be interested in the same events.</p> <p>For example, a third-party app can register to be notified of settings changes:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AppConfig</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">setting_changed</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_callback</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Setting changed!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyAppConfig</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AppConfig):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ready</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">setting_changed</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(my_callback)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1953">built-in signals</a> let user code get notified of certain actions.</p> <p id="page_752"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also define and send your own custom signals. See <a href="index.html#page_755">Defining and sending signals</a> below.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Signals give the appearance of loose coupling, but they can quickly lead to code that is hard</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">to understand, adjust and debug.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Where possible you should opt for directly calling the handling code, rather than dispatching via a signal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.22.1 Listening to signals</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To receive a signal, register a receiver function using the <a href="index.html#page_752"><i>Signal.connect()</i></a> method. The receiver function is called when the signal is sent. All of the signal’s receiver functions are called one at a time, in the order they were registered.</p> <p>Signal.<b>connect</b>(receiver, sender=None, weak=True, dispatch_uid=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Parameters</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>receiver</b> – The callback function which will be connected to this signal. See <a href="index.html#page_752">Receiver</a></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><a href="index.html#page_752">functions</a> for more information.</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>sender</b> – Specifies a particular sender to receive signals from. See <a href="index.html#page_754">Connecting to</a></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><a href="index.html#page_754">signals sent by specific senders</a> for more information.</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>weak</b> – Django stores signal handlers as weak references by default. Thus, if your</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">receiver is a local function, it may be garbage collected. To prevent this, pass weak=False when you call the signal’s connect() method.</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>dispatch_uid</b> – A unique identifier for a signal receiver in cases where duplicate</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">signals may be sent. See <a href="index.html#page_755">Preventing duplicate signals</a> for more information.</p> <p>Let’s see how this works by registering a signal that gets called after each HTTP request is finished. We’ll be</p> <p>connecting to the <a href="index.html#page_1963"><i>request_finished</i></a> signal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Receiver functions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>First, we need to define a receiver function. A receiver can be any Python function or method:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_callback</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Request finished!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Notice that the function takes a sender argument, along with wildcard keyword arguments (**kwargs); all signal handlers must take these arguments.</p> <p>We’ll look at senders <a href="index.html#page_754">a bit later, </a>but right now look at the **kwargs argument. All signals send keyword</p> <p>arguments, and may change those keyword arguments at any time. In the case of <a href="index.html#page_1963"><i>request_finished</i></a>, it’s</p> <p id="page_753" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>documented as sending no arguments, which means we might be tempted to write our signal handling as my_callback(sender).</p> <p>This would be wrong – in fact, Django will throw an error if you do so. That’s because at any point arguments could get added to the signal and your receiver must be able to handle those new arguments.</p> <p>Receivers may also be asynchronous functions, with the same signature but declared using async def:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_callback</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asyncio</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sleep(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Request finished!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Signals can be sent either synchronously or asynchronously, and receivers will automatically be adapted to</p> <p>the correct call-style. See <a href="index.html#page_756">sending signals</a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connecting receiver functions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are two ways you can connect a receiver to a signal. You can take the manual connect route:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(my_callback)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Alternatively, you can use a <a href="index.html#page_753"><i>receiver()</i></a> decorator:</p> <p><b>receiver</b>(signal, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Parameters</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>signal</b> – A signal or a list of signals to connect a function to.</p> <p style="margin-left:6em">• <b>kwargs</b> – Wildcard keyword arguments to pass to a <a href="index.html#page_752">function</a>.</p> <p>Here’s how you connect with the decorator:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.dispatch</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">receiver</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@receiver(request_finished)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_callback</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Request finished!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now, our my_callback function will be called each time a request finishes.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Where should this code live?</p> <p id="page_754"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Strictly speaking, signal handling and registration code can live anywhere you like, although it’s recom-mended to avoid the application’s root module and its models module to minimize side-effects of importing code.</p> <p>In practice, signal handlers are usually defined in a signals submodule of the application they relate to.</p> <p>Signal receivers are connected in the <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> method of your application <a href="index.html#page_922">configuration class</a>. If you’re using</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_753"><i>receiver()</i></a> decorator, import the signals submodule inside <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_925">, </a>this will implicitly connect signal handlers:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AppConfig</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyAppConfig</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AppConfig):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ready</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Implicitly connect signal handlers decorated with @receiver.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">signals</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Explicitly connect a signal handler.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(signals</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">my_callback)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> method may be executed more than once during testing, so you may want to <a href="index.html#page_755">guard your</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_755">signals from duplication, </a>especially if you’re planning to send them within tests.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connecting to signals sent by specific senders</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some signals get sent many times, but you’ll only be interested in receiving a certain subset of those sig-</p> <p>nals. For example, consider the <a href="index.html#page_1955"><i>django.db.models.signals.pre_save</i></a> signal sent before a model gets saved. Most of the time, you don’t need to know when any model gets saved – just when one specific model is saved.</p> <p>In these cases, you can register to receive signals sent only by particular senders. In the case of <a href="index.html#page_1955"><i>django.db.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1955"><i>models.signals.pre_save</i></a> , the sender will be the model class being saved, so you can indicate that you only want signals sent by some model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pre_save</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.dispatch</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">receiver</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyModel</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_755" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@receiver(pre_save, sender</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">MyModel)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_handler</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(sender,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The my_handler function will only be called when an instance of MyModel is saved.</p> <p>Different signals use different objects as their senders; you’ll need to consult the <a href="index.html#page_1953">built-in signal documentation</a> for details of each particular signal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Preventing duplicate signals</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In some circumstances, the code connecting receivers to signals may run multiple times. This can cause your receiver function to be registered more than once, and thus called as many times for a signal event. For</p> <p>example, the <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> method may be executed more than once during testing. More generally, this occurs everywhere your project imports the module where you define the signals, because signal registration runs as many times as it is imported.</p> <p>If this behavior is problematic (such as when using signals to send an email whenever a model is saved), pass a unique identifier as the dispatch_uid argument to identify your receiver function. This identifier will usually be a string, although any hashable object will suffice. The end result is that your receiver function will only be bound to the signal once for each unique dispatch_uid value:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">request_finished</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(my_callback, dispatch_uid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_unique_identifier"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.22.2 Defining and sending signals</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Your applications can take advantage of the signal infrastructure and provide its own signals.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When to use custom signals</p> <p>Signals are implicit function calls which make debugging harder. If the sender and receiver of your custom signal are both within your project, you’re better off using an explicit function call.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_756"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Defining signals</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Signal</b></p> <p>All signals are <a href="index.html#page_756"><i>django.dispatch.Signal</i></a> instances.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.dispatch</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">pizza_done</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dispatch</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Signal()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This declares a pizza_done signal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Sending signals</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are two ways to send signals synchronously in Django.</p> <p>Signal.<b>send</b>(sender, **kwargs)</p> <p>Signal.<b>send_robust</b>(sender, **kwargs)</p> <p>Signals may also be sent asynchronously.</p> <p>Signal.<b>asend</b>(sender, **kwargs)</p> <p>Signal.<b>asend_robust</b>(sender, **kwargs)</p> <p>To send a signal, call either <a href="index.html#page_756"><i>Signal.send()</i>, <i>Signal.send_robust()</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_756"><i>await Signal.asend()</i>, </a>or <a href="index.html#page_756"><i>await</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_756"><i>Signal.asend_robust()</i>. </a>You must provide the sender argument (which is a class most of the time) and may provide as many other keyword arguments as you like.</p> <p>For example, here’s how sending our pizza_done signal might look:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PizzaStore</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>send_pizza</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, toppings, size):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pizza_done</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">send(sender</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__class__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, toppings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">toppings, size</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">size)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All four methods return a list of tuple pairs [(receiver, response), ...], representing the list of called receiver functions and their response values.</p> <p>send() differs from send_robust() in how exceptions raised by receiver functions are handled. send() does not catch any exceptions raised by receivers; it simply allows errors to propagate. Thus not all receivers may be notified of a signal in the face of an error.</p> <p id="page_757" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>send_robust() catches all errors derived from Python’s Exception class, and ensures all receivers are noti-fied of the signal. If an error occurs, the error instance is returned in the tuple pair for the receiver that raised the error.</p> <p>The tracebacks are present on the __traceback__ attribute of the errors returned when calling send_robust().</p> <p>asend() is similar to send(), but it is a coroutine that must be awaited:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>asend_pizza</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, toppings, size):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pizza_done</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">asend(sender</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__class__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, toppings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">toppings, size</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">size)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Whether synchronous or asynchronous, receivers will be correctly adapted to whether send() or asend() is</p> <p>used. Synchronous receivers will be called using <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> when invoked via asend(). Asynchronous</p> <p>receivers will be called using <a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a> when invoked via sync(). Similar to the <a href="index.html#page_767">case for middleware</a>, there is a small performance cost to adapting receivers in this way. Note that in order to reduce the number of sync/async calling-style switches within a send() or asend() call, the receivers are grouped by whether or not they are async before being called. This means that an asynchronous receiver registered before a syn-chronous receiver may be executed after the synchronous receiver. In addition, async receivers are executed concurrently using asyncio.gather().</p> <p>All built-in signals, except those in the async request-response cycle, are dispatched using <a href="index.html#page_756"><i>Signal.send()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.22.3 Disconnecting signals</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Signal.<b>disconnect</b>(receiver=None, sender=None, dispatch_uid=None)</p> <p>To disconnect a receiver from a signal, call <a href="index.html#page_757"><i>Signal.disconnect()</i>. </a>The arguments are as described in</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_752"><i>Signal.connect()</i>. </a>The method returns True if a receiver was disconnected and False if not. When sender is passed as a lazy reference to <app label>.<model>, this method always returns None.</p> <p>The receiver argument indicates the registered receiver to disconnect. It may be None if dispatch_uid is used to identify the receiver.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.23 System check framework</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The system check framework is a set of static checks for validating Django projects. It detects common problems and provides hints for how to fix them. The framework is extensible so you can easily add your own checks.</p> <p>Checks can be triggered explicitly via the <a href="index.html#page_1434"><i>check</i></a> command. Checks are triggered implicitly before most com-</p> <p>mands, including <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1446">. </a>For performance reasons, checks are not run as part of the WSGI stack that is used in deployment. If you need to run system checks on your deployment server, trigger them</p> <p>explicitly using <a href="index.html#page_1434"><i>check</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_758"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Serious errors will prevent Django commands (such as <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a>) from running at all. Minor problems are reported to the console. If you have inspected the cause of a warning and are happy to ignore it, you can</p> <p>hide specific warnings using the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>SILENCED_SYSTEM_CHECKS</i></a> setting in your project settings file.</p> <p>A full list of all checks that can be raised by Django can be found in the <a href="index.html#page_930">System check reference</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.23.1 Writing your own checks</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The framework is flexible and allows you to write functions that perform any other kind of check you may require. The following is an example stub check function:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.checks</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Error, register</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@register()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>example_check</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(app_configs,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ... your check logic here</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">check_failed:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">errors</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">append(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Error(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"an error"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">hint</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"A hint."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">obj</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">checked_object,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">id</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"myapp.E001"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">errors</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The check function must accept an app_configs argument; this argument is the list of applications that should be inspected. If None, the check must be run on all installed apps in the project.</p> <p>The check will receive a databases keyword argument. This is a list of database aliases whose connec-tions may be used to inspect database level configuration. If databases is None, the check must not use any database connections.</p> <p>The **kwargs argument is required for future expansion.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_759" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Messages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The function must return a list of messages. If no problems are found as a result of the check, the check function must return an empty list.</p> <p>The warnings and errors raised by the check method must be instances of <a href="index.html#page_930"><i>CheckMessage</i></a>. An instance of</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_930"><i>CheckMessage</i></a> encapsulates a single reportable error or warning. It also provides context and hints applicable to the message, and a unique identifier that is used for filtering purposes.</p> <p>The concept is very similar to messages from the <a href="index.html#page_1287">message framework</a> or the <a href="index.html#page_707">logging framework</a>. Messages are tagged with a level indicating the severity of the message.</p> <p>There are also shortcuts to make creating messages with common levels easier. When using these classes you can omit the level argument because it is implied by the class name.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_931"><i>Debug</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_931"><i>Info</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_931"><i>Warning</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_931"><i>Error</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_931"><i>Critical</i></a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Registering and labeling checks</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Lastly, your check function must be registered explicitly with system check registry. Checks should be regis-</p> <p>tered in a file that’s loaded when your application is loaded; for example, in the <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>AppConfig.ready()</i></a> method.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>register</b>(*tags)(function)</p> <p>You can pass as many tags to register as you want in order to label your check. Tagging checks is useful since it allows you to run only a certain group of checks. For example, to register a compatibility check, you would make the following call:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.checks</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">register, Tags</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@register(Tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compatibility)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_check</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(app_configs,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ... perform compatibility checks and collect errors</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">errors</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can register “deployment checks” that are only relevant to a production settings file like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@register(Tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">security, deploy</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_check</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(app_configs,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p id="page_760"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>These checks will only be run if the <a href="index.html#page_1435"><i>check --deploy</i></a> option is used.</p> <p>You can also use register as a function rather than a decorator by passing a callable object (usually a function) as the first argument to register.</p> <p>The code below is equivalent to the code above:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_check</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(app_configs,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(my_check, Tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">security, deploy</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Field, model, manager, template engine, and database checks</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In some cases, you won’t need to register your check function – you can piggyback on an existing registration.</p> <p>Fields, models, model managers, template engines, and database backends all implement a check() method that is already registered with the check framework. If you want to add extra checks, you can extend the implementation on the base class, perform any extra checks you need, and append any messages to those generated by the base class. It’s recommended that you delegate each check to separate methods.</p> <p>Consider an example where you are implementing a custom field named RangedIntegerField. This field adds min and max arguments to the constructor of IntegerField. You may want to add a check to ensure that users provide a min value that is less than or equal to the max value. <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">max</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span the superclass</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">errors</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span the check is a classmethod, not an instance method:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyModel</b></span><span didn’t implement a check() method.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Messages are comparable. That allows you to easily write tests:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.checks</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_762"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">assertEqual(errors, expected_errors)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing integration tests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Given the need to register certain checks when the application loads, it can be useful to test their integration</p> <p>within the system checks framework. This can be accomplished by using the <a href="index.html#page_1468"><i>call_command()</i></a> function.</p> <p>For example, this test demonstrates that the <a deploy</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span
