style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.24 External packages</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django ships with a variety of extra, optional tools that solve common problems (contrib.*). For easier maintenance and to trim the size of the codebase, a few of those applications have been moved out to separate projects.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.24.1 Localflavor</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django-localflavor is a collection of utilities for particular countries and cultures.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://github.com/django/django-localflavor">GitHub</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://django-localflavor.readthedocs.io/">Documentation</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-localflavor/">PyPI</a></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_764"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.24.2 Comments</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django-contrib-comments can be used to attach comments to any model, so you can use it for comments on blog entries, photos, book chapters, or anything else. Most users will be better served with a custom solution, or a hosted product like Disqus.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://github.com/django/django-contrib-comments">GitHub</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://django-contrib-comments.readthedocs.io/">Documentation</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-contrib-comments/">PyPI</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.24.3 Formtools</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django-formtools is a collection of assorted utilities to work with forms.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://github.com/jazzband/django-formtools/">GitHub</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://django-formtools.readthedocs.io/">Documentation</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-formtools/">PyPI</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>3.25 Asynchronous support</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django has support for writing asynchronous (“async”) views, along with an entirely async-enabled request</p> <p>stack if you are running under <a href="index.html#page_875">ASGI. </a>Async views will still work under WSGI, but with performance penalties, and without the ability to have efficient long-running requests.</p> <p>We’re still working on async support for the ORM and other parts of Django. You can expect to see this</p> <p>in future releases. For now, you can use the <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> adapter to interact with the sync parts of Django. There is also a whole range of async-native Python libraries that you can integrate with.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.25.1 Async views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any view can be declared async by making the callable part of it return a coroutine - commonly, this is done using async def. For a function-based view, this means declaring the whole view using async def. For a class-based view, this means declaring the HTTP method handlers, such as get() and post() as async def (not its __init__(), or as_view()).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Django uses asgiref.sync.iscoroutinefunction to test if your view is asynchronous or not. If you implement your own method of returning a coroutine, ensure you use asgiref.sync. markcoroutinefunction so this function returns True.</p> <p id="page_765" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Under a WSGI server, async views will run in their own, one-off event loop. This means you can use async features, like concurrent async HTTP requests, without any issues, but you will not get the benefits of an async stack.</p> <p>The main benefits are the ability to service hundreds of connections without using Python threads. This allows you to use slow streaming, long-polling, and other exciting response types.</p> <p>If you want to use these, you will need to deploy Django using <a href="index.html#page_875">ASGI</a> instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: You will only get the benefits of a fully-asynchronous request stack if you have no syn-</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">chronous middleware loaded into your site. If there is a piece of synchronous middleware, then Django</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">must use a thread per request to safely emulate a synchronous environment for it.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Middleware can be built to support <a href="index.html#page_308">both sync and async</a> contexts. Some of Django’s middleware is built</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">like this, but not all. To see what middleware Django has to adapt for, you can turn on debug logging</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">for the django.request logger and look for log messages about “Asynchronous handler adapted for</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">middleware <i>. . .</i>”.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In both ASGI and WSGI mode, you can still safely use asynchronous support to run code concurrently rather than serially. This is especially handy when dealing with external APIs or data stores.</p> <p>If you want to call a part of Django that is still synchronous, you will need to wrap it in a <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> call. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asgiref.sync</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">results</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async(sync_function, thread_sensitive</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)(pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">123</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you accidentally try to call a part of Django that is synchronous-only from an async view, you will trigger</p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_768">asynchronous safety protection</a> to protect your data from corruption.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Decorators</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following decorators can be used with both synchronous and asynchronous view functions:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>cache_control()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>never_cache()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>no_append_slash()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_exempt()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_protect()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1409"><i>ensure_csrf_cookie()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>requires_csrf_token()</i></a></p> <p id="page_766"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_855"><i>sensitive_variables()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_856"><i>sensitive_post_parameters()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>gzip_page()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>condition()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• conditional_page()</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>etag()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>last_modified()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_287"><i>require_http_methods()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>require_GET()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>require_POST()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_288"><i>require_safe()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>vary_on_cookie()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_289"><i>vary_on_headers()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• xframe_options_deny()</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• xframe_options_sameorigin()</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• xframe_options_exempt()</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">never_cache</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@never_cache</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_sync_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@never_cache</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_async_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Queries & the ORM</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>With some exceptions, Django can run ORM queries asynchronously as well:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Author</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(name__startswith</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"A"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">book</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">author</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">books</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">afirst()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Detailed notes can be found in <a href="index.html#page_159">Asynchronous queries, </a>but in short:</p> <p id="page_767" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• All QuerySet methods that cause an SQL query to occur have an a-prefixed asynchronous variant.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• async for is supported on all QuerySets (including the output of values() and values_list().)</p> <p>Django also supports some asynchronous model methods that use the database:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>make_book</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">book</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">asave(using</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"secondary"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>make_book_with_tags</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(tags,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">book</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">acreate(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">book</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">aset(tags)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Transactions do not yet work in async mode. If you have a piece of code that needs transactions behavior,</p> <p>we recommend you write that piece as a single synchronous function and call it using <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Performance</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When running in a mode that does not match the view (e.g. an async view under WSGI, or a traditional sync view under ASGI), Django must emulate the other call style to allow your code to run. This context-switch causes a small performance penalty of around a millisecond.</p> <p>This is also true of middleware. Django will attempt to minimize the number of context-switches between sync and async. If you have an ASGI server, but all your middleware and views are synchronous, it will switch just once, before it enters the middleware stack.</p> <p>However, if you put synchronous middleware between an ASGI server and an asynchronous view, it will have to switch into sync mode for the middleware and then back to async mode for the view. Django will also hold the sync thread open for middleware exception propagation. This may not be noticeable at first, but adding this penalty of one thread per request can remove any async performance advantage.</p> <p>You should do your own performance testing to see what effect ASGI versus WSGI has on your code. In some cases, there may be a performance increase even for a purely synchronous codebase under ASGI because the request-handling code is still all running asynchronously. In general you will only want to enable ASGI mode if you have asynchronous code in your project.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_768"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handling disconnects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For long-lived requests, a client may disconnect before the view returns a response. In this case, an asyncio. CancelledError will be raised in the view. You can catch this error and handle it if you need to perform any cleanup:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>try</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Do some work</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>except</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asyncio</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CancelledError:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Handle disconnect</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>raise</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also <a href="index.html#page_1881">handle client disconnects in streaming responses.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.25.2 Async safety</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE</b></p> <p>Certain key parts of Django are not able to operate safely in an async environment, as they have global state that is not coroutine-aware. These parts of Django are classified as “async-unsafe”, and are protected from execution in an async environment. The ORM is the main example, but there are other parts that are also protected in this way.</p> <p>If you try to run any of these parts from a thread where there is a running event loop, you will get a</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>SynchronousOnlyOperation</i></a> error. Note that you don’t have to be inside an async function directly to have this error occur. If you have called a sync function directly from an async function, without using</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> or similar, then it can also occur. This is because your code is still running in a thread with an active event loop, even though it may not be declared as async code.</p> <p>If you encounter this error, you should fix your code to not call the offending code from an async context. Instead, write your code that talks to async-unsafe functions in its own, sync function, and call that using</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_770"><i>asgiref.sync.sync_to_async()</i></a> (or any other way of running sync code in its own thread).</p> <p>The async context can be imposed upon you by the environment in which you are running your Django code.</p> <p>For example, <a href="https://jupyter.org/">Jupyter</a> notebooks and <a href="https://ipython.org">IPython</a> interactive shells both transparently provide an active event loop so that it is easier to interact with asynchronous APIs.</p> <p>If you’re using an IPython shell, you can disable this event loop by running:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">%autoawait off</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>as a command at the IPython prompt. This will allow you to run synchronous code without generating</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>SynchronousOnlyOperation</i></a> errors; however, you also won’t be able to await asynchronous APIs. To turn the event loop back on, run:</p> <p id="page_769" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">%autoawait on</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re in an environment other than IPython (or you can’t turn off autoawait in IPython for some reason), you are certain there is no chance of your code being run concurrently, and you absolutely need to run your sync code from an async context, then you can disable the warning by setting the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_768"><i>DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE</i></a> environment variable to any value.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If you enable this option and there is concurrent access to the async-unsafe parts of Django,</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">you may suffer data loss or corruption. Be very careful and do not use this in production environments.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to do this from within Python, do that with os.environ:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"true"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>3.25.3 Async adapter functions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is necessary to adapt the calling style when calling sync code from an async context, or vice-versa. For this</p> <p>there are two adapter functions, from the asgiref.sync module: <a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a>. They are used to transition between the calling styles while preserving compatibility.</p> <p>These adapter functions are widely used in Django. The <a href="https://pypi.org/project/asgiref/">asgiref</a> package itself is part of the Django project, and it is automatically installed as a dependency when you install Django with pip.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>async_to_sync()</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>async_to_sync</b>(async_function, force_new_loop=False)</p> <p>Takes an async function and returns a sync function that wraps it. Can be used as either a direct wrapper or a decorator:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asgiref.sync</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">async_to_sync</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_get_data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">async_to_sync(get_data)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_770"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@async_to_sync</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>async def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_other_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The async function is run in the event loop for the current thread, if one is present. If there is no current event loop, a new event loop is spun up specifically for the single async invocation and shut down again once it completes. In either situation, the async function will execute on a different thread to the calling code.</p> <p>Threadlocals and contextvars values are preserved across the boundary in both directions.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a> is essentially a more powerful version of the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-runner.html#asyncio.run">asyncio.run()</a> function in Python’s stan-dard library. As well as ensuring threadlocals work, it also enables the thread_sensitive mode of</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> when that wrapper is used below it.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sync_to_async()</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sync_to_async</b>(sync_function, thread_sensitive=True)</p> <p>Takes a sync function and returns an async function that wraps it. Can be used as either a direct wrapper or a decorator:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asgiref.sync</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">async_function</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async(sync_function, thread_sensitive</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">async_function</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async(sensitive_sync_function, thread_sensitive</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sync_to_async</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>sync_function</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Threadlocals and contextvars values are preserved across the boundary in both directions.</p> <p>Sync functions tend to be written assuming they all run in the main thread, so <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>sync_to_async()</i></a> has two threading modes:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• thread_sensitive=True (the default): the sync function will run in the same thread as all other</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">thread_sensitive functions. This will be the main thread, if the main thread is synchronous and</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">you are using the <a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a> wrapper.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• thread_sensitive=False: the sync function will run in a brand new thread which is then closed once</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the invocation completes.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: asgiref version 3.3.0 changed the default value of the thread_sensitive parameter to</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">True. This is a safer default, and in many cases interacting with Django the correct value, but be sure to</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">evaluate uses of sync_to_async() if updating asgiref from a prior version.</p> <p id="page_771" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Thread-sensitive mode is quite special, and does a lot of work to run all functions in the same thread. Note,</p> <p>though, that it relies on usage of <a href="index.html#page_769"><i>async_to_sync()</i></a> above it in the stack to correctly run things on the main thread. If you use asyncio.run() or similar, it will fall back to running thread-sensitive functions in a single, shared thread, but this will not be the main thread.</p> <p>The reason this is needed in Django is that many libraries, specifically database adapters, require that they are accessed in the same thread that they were created in. Also a lot of existing Django code assumes it all runs in the same thread, e.g. middleware adding things to a request for later use in views.</p> <p>Rather than introduce potential compatibility issues with this code, we instead opted to add this mode so that all existing Django sync code runs in the same thread and thus is fully compatible with async mode. Note that sync code will always be in a different thread to any async code that is calling it, so you should avoid passing raw database handles or other thread-sensitive references around.</p> <p>In practice this restriction means that you should not pass features of the database connection object when calling sync_to_async(). Doing so will trigger the thread safety checks:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=settings.py python -m asyncio</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asyncio</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">asgiref.sync</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># In an async context so you cannot use the database directly:</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cursor()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.exceptions.SynchronousOnlyOperation: You cannot call this from</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">an async context - use a thread or sync_to_async.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Nor can you pass resolved connection attributes across threads:</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>await</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sync_to_async(connection</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">cursor)()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.utils.DatabaseError: DatabaseWrapper objects created in a thread</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">can only be used in that same thread. The object with alias 'default' was</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">created in thread id 4371465600 and this is thread id 6131478528.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Rather, you should encapsulate all database access within a helper function that can be called with sync_to_async() without relying on the connection object in the calling code.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_772"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <h2 id="page_773" style="text-align:right"><b>CHAPTER</b></h2> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>FOUR</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>HOW-TO GUIDES</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Practical guides covering common tasks and problems.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>4.1 Models, data and databases</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.1.1 How to provide initial data for models</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s sometimes useful to prepopulate your database with hard-coded data when you’re first setting up an app. You can provide initial data with migrations or fixtures.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Provide initial data with migrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To automatically load initial data for an app, create a <a href="index.html#page_457">data migration</a>. Migrations are run when setting up</p> <p>the test database, so the data will be available there, subject to <a href="index.html#page_473">some limitations.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Provide data with fixtures</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also provide data using <a href="index.html#page_248">fixtures</a>, however, this data isn’t loaded automatically, except if you use</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_497"><i>TransactionTestCase.fixtures</i>.</a></p> <p>A fixture is a collection of data that Django knows how to import into a database. The most straightforward</p> <p>way of creating a fixture if you’ve already got some data is to use the <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>manage.py dumpdata</i></a> command. Or,</p> <p>you can write fixtures by hand; fixtures can be written as JSON, XML or YAML (with <a href="https://pyyaml.org/">PyYAML</a> installed)</p> <p>documents. The <a href="index.html#page_731">serialization documentation</a> has more details about each of these supported <a href="index.html#page_734">serialization</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_734">formats.</a></p> <p>As an example, though, here’s what a fixture for a Person model might look like in JSON:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"myapp.person"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_774"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"John"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Lennon"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"model"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"myapp.person"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fields"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"first_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Paul"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"last_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"McCartney"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>And here’s that same fixture as YAML:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">-</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: myapp.person</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: 1</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: John</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: Lennon</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">-</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">model</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: myapp.person</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: 2</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: Paul</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">last_name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: McCartney</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You’ll store this data in a fixtures directory inside your app.</p> <p>You can load data by calling <a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>manage.py loaddata</i></a> <fixturename>, where <fixturename> is the name of the</p> <p>fixture file you’ve created. Each time you run <a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>loaddata</i></a>, the data will be read from the fixture and reloaded into the database. Note this means that if you change one of the rows created by a fixture and then run</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>loaddata</i></a> again, you’ll wipe out any changes you’ve made.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_775" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Tell Django where to look for fixture files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, Django looks for fixtures in the fixtures directory inside each app, so the command loaddata sample will find the file my_app/fixtures/sample.json. This works with relative paths as well, so loaddata my_app/sample will find the file my_app/fixtures/my_app/sample.json.</p> <p>Django also looks for fixtures in the list of directories provided in the <a href="index.html#page_1915"><i>FIXTURE_DIRS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>To completely prevent default search from happening, use an absolute path to specify the location of your fixture file, e.g. loaddata /path/to/sample.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Namespace your fixture files</p> <p>Django will use the first fixture file it finds whose name matches, so if you have fixture files with the same name in different applications, you will be unable to distinguish between them in your loaddata commands. The easiest way to avoid this problem is by namespacing your fixture files. That is, by putting them inside a directory named for their application, as in the relative path example above.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>Fixtures are also used by the <a href="index.html#page_497">testing framework</a> to help set up a consistent test environment.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.1.2 How to integrate Django with a legacy database</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While Django is best suited for developing new applications, it’s quite possible to integrate it into legacy databases. Django includes a couple of utilities to automate as much of this process as possible.</p> <p>This document assumes you know the Django basics, as covered in the <a href="index.html#page_21">tutorial.</a></p> <p>Once you’ve got Django set up, you’ll follow this general process to integrate with an existing database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Give Django your database parameters</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You’ll need to tell Django what your database connection parameters are, and what the name of the database</p> <p>is. Do that by editing the <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> setting and assigning values to the following keys for the 'default' connection:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>ENGINE</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PASSWORD</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a></p> <p id="page_776"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Auto-generate the models</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django comes with a utility called <a href="index.html#page_1440"><i>inspectdb</i></a> that can create models by introspecting an existing database. You can view the output by running this command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py inspectdb</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Save this as a file by using standard Unix output redirection:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py inspectdb > models.py</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This feature is meant as a shortcut, not as definitive model generation. See the <a href="index.html#page_1440"><i>documentation of</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1440"><i>inspectdb</i></a> for more information.</p> <p>Once you’ve cleaned up your models, name the file models.py and put it in the Python package that holds</p> <p>your app. Then add the app to your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>By default, <a href="index.html#page_1440"><i>inspectdb</i></a> creates unmanaged models. That is, managed = False in the model’s Meta class tells Django not to manage each table’s creation, modification, and deletion:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Person</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">id</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">IntegerField(primary_key</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">first_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">70</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">managed</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= False</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">db_table</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"CENSUS_PERSONS"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you do want to allow Django to manage the table’s lifecycle, you’ll need to change the <a href="index.html#page_1681"><i>managed</i></a> option above to True (or remove it because True is its default value).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Install the core Django tables</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, run the <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> command to install any extra needed database records such as admin permissions and content types:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ python manage.py migrate</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_777" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Test and tweak</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Those are the basic steps – from here you’ll want to tweak the models Django generated until they work the way you’d like. Try accessing your data via the Django database API, and try editing objects via Django’s admin site, and edit the models file accordingly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.1.3 How to create custom model fields</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Introduction</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_115">model reference</a> documentation explains how to use Django’s standard field classes – <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a>,</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>DateField</i></a>, etc. For many purposes, those classes are all you’ll need. Sometimes, though, the Django ver-sion won’t meet your precise requirements, or you’ll want to use a field that is entirely different from those shipped with Django.</p> <p>Django’s built-in field types don’t cover every possible database column type – only the common types, such as VARCHAR and INTEGER. For more obscure column types, such as geographic polygons or even user-created</p> <p>types such as <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtype.html">PostgreSQL custom types</a>, you can define your own Django Field subclasses.</p> <p>Alternatively, you may have a complex Python object that can somehow be serialized to fit into a standard database column type. This is another case where a Field subclass will help you use your object with your models.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Our example object</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Creating custom fields requires a bit of attention to detail. To make things easier to follow, we’ll use a consis-tent example throughout this document: wrapping a Python object representing the deal of cards in a hand</p> <p>of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_bridge">Bridge. </a>Don’t worry, you don’t have to know how to play Bridge to follow this example. You only need to know that 52 cards are dealt out equally to four players, who are traditionally called north, east, south and west. Our class looks something like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Hand</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"""A hand of cards (bridge style)"""</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, north, east, south, west):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Input parameters are lists of cards ('Ah', '9s', etc.)</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">north</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">north</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">east</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">east</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">south</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">south</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">west</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">west</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ... (other possibly useful methods omitted) ...</i></span></p> <p id="page_778"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This is an ordinary Python class, with nothing Django-specific about it. We’d like to be able to do things like this in our models (we assume the hand attribute on the model is an instance of Hand):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">example</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyModel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(example</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">hand</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">north)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">new_hand</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Hand(north, east, south, west)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">example</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">hand</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">new_hand</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">example</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We assign to and retrieve from the hand attribute in our model just like any other Python class. The trick is to tell Django how to handle saving and loading such an object.</p> <p>In order to use the Hand class in our models, we do not have to change this class at all. This is ideal, because it means you can easily write model support for existing classes where you cannot change the source code.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: You might only be wanting to take advantage of custom database column types and deal with the data as standard Python types in your models; strings, or floats, for example. This case is similar to our Hand example and we’ll note any differences as we go along.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Background theory</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database storage</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Let’s start with model fields. If you break it down, a model field provides a way to take a normal Python object – string, boolean, datetime, or something more complex like Hand – and convert it to and from a format that is useful when dealing with the database. (Such a format is also useful for serialization, but as we’ll see later, that is easier once you have the database side under control).</p> <p>Fields in a model must somehow be converted to fit into an existing database column type. Different databases provide different sets of valid column types, but the rule is still the same: those are the only types you have to work with. Anything you want to store in the database must fit into one of those types.</p> <p>Normally, you’re either writing a Django field to match a particular database column type, or you will need a way to convert your data to, say, a string.</p> <p>For our Hand example, we could convert the card data to a string of 104 characters by concatenating all the cards together in a predetermined order – say, all the north cards first, then the east, south and west cards. So Hand objects can be saved to text or character columns in the database.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_779" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>What does a field class do?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All of Django’s fields (and when we say fields in this document, we always mean model fields and not <a href="index.html#page_1517">form</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1517">fields) </a>are subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>django.db.models.Field</i></a>. Most of the information that Django records about a field is common to all fields – name, help text, uniqueness and so forth. Storing all that information is handled by Field. We’ll get into the precise details of what Field can do later on; for now, suffice it to say that everything descends from Field and then customizes key pieces of the class behavior.</p> <p>It’s important to realize that a Django field class is not what is stored in your model attributes. The model attributes contain normal Python objects. The field classes you define in a model are actually stored in the Meta class when the model class is created (the precise details of how this is done are unimportant here). This is because the field classes aren’t necessary when you’re just creating and modifying attributes. Instead, they provide the machinery for converting between the attribute value and what is stored in the database or sent to the <a href="index.html#page_731">serializer</a>.</p> <p>Keep this in mind when creating your own custom fields. The Django Field subclass you write provides the machinery for converting between your Python instances and the database/serializer values in various ways (there are differences between storing a value and using a value for lookups, for example). If this sounds a bit tricky, don’t worry – it will become clearer in the examples below. Just remember that you will often end up creating two classes when you want a custom field:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The first class is the Python object that your users will manipulate. They will assign it to the model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">attribute, they will read from it for displaying purposes, things like that. This is the Hand class in our example.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The second class is the Field subclass. This is the class that knows how to convert your first class back</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">and forth between its permanent storage form and the Python form.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing a field subclass</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When planning your <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> subclass, first give some thought to which existing <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> class your new field is most similar to. Can you subclass an existing Django field and save yourself some work? If not, you should</p> <p>subclass the <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> class, from which everything is descended.</p> <p>Initializing your new field is a matter of separating out any arguments that are specific to your case from the</p> <p>common arguments and passing the latter to the __init__() method of <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> (or your parent class).</p> <p>In our example, we’ll call our field HandField. (It’s a good idea to call your <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> subclass <Something>Field,</p> <p>so it’s easily identifiable as a <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> subclass.) It doesn’t behave like any existing field, so we’ll subclass directly</p> <p>from <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>HandField</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Field):</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_780"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">description</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"A hand of cards (bridge style)"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"max_length"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">104</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Our HandField accepts most of the standard field options (see the list below), but we ensure it has a fixed length, since it only needs to hold 52 card values plus their suits; 104 characters in total.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Many of Django’s model fields accept options that they don’t do anything with. For example, you</p> <p>can pass both <a href="index.html#page_1624"><i>editable</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>auto_now</i></a> to a <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>django.db.models.DateField</i></a> and it will ignore the <a href="index.html#page_1624"><i>editable</i></a></p> <p>parameter <a href="index.html#page_1628">(<i>auto_now</i></a> being set implies editable=False). No error is raised in this case.</p> <p>This behavior simplifies the field classes, because they don’t need to check for options that aren’t necessary. They pass all the options to the parent class and then don’t use them later on. It’s up to you whether you want your fields to be more strict about the options they select, or to use the more permissive behavior of the current fields.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Field.__init__() method takes the following parameters:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>verbose_name</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• name</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1625"><i>primary_key</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>max_length</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1625"><i>unique</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1616"><i>blank</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1615"><i>null</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1623"><i>db_index</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• rel: Used for related fields (like <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a>). For advanced use only.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1623"><i>default</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1624"><i>editable</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• serialize: If False, the field will not be serialized when the model is passed to Django’s <a href="index.html#page_731">serializers</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Defaults to True.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1625"><i>unique_for_date</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>unique_for_month</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>unique_for_year</i></a></p> <p id="page_781" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1616"><i>choices</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1624"><i>help_text</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1622"><i>db_column</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1623"><i>db_tablespace</i></a>: Only for index creation, if the backend supports <a href="index.html#page_235">tablespaces</a><a href="index.html#page_235">. </a>You can usually ignore</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">this option.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1659"><i>auto_created</i>:</a> True if the field was automatically created, as for the <a href="index.html#page_1652"><i>OneToOneField</i></a> used by model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">inheritance. For advanced use only.</p> <p>All of the options without an explanation in the above list have the same meaning they do for normal Django</p> <p>fields. See the <a href="index.html#page_1615">field documentation</a> for examples and details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Field deconstruction</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The counterpoint to writing your __init__() method is writing the <a href="index.html#page_1658"><i>deconstruct()</i></a> method. It’s used during</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_446">model migrations</a> to tell Django how to take an instance of your new field and reduce it to a serialized form- in particular, what arguments to pass to __init__() to recreate it.</p> <p>If you haven’t added any extra options on top of the field you inherited from, then there’s no need to write a new deconstruct() method. If, however, you’re changing the arguments passed in __init__() (like we are in HandField), you’ll need to supplement the values being passed.</p> <p>deconstruct() returns a tuple of four items: the field’s attribute name, the full import path of the field class, the positional arguments (as a list), and the keyword arguments (as a dict). Note this is different from the</p> <p>deconstruct() method <a href="index.html#page_462">for custom classes</a> which returns a tuple of three things.</p> <p>As a custom field author, you don’t need to care about the first two values; the base Field class has all the code to work out the field’s attribute name and import path. You do, however, have to care about the positional and keyword arguments, as these are likely the things you are changing.</p> <p>For example, in our HandField class we’re always forcibly setting max_length in __init__(). The deconstruct() method on the base Field class will see this and try to return it in the keyword arguments; thus, we can drop it from the keyword arguments for readability:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>HandField</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Field):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"max_length"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">104</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p kwargs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span keyword argument, you need to write code in deconstruct() that puts its value into kwargs yourself. You should also omit the value from kwargs when it isn’t necessary to reconstruct the state of the field, such as when the default value is being used:</p> <p><span
