For complete details on all the set-</p> <p>tings, commands, template tags, and other pieces included in <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.contrib.staticfiles</i></a>, see <a href="index.html#page_1369">the static-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1369">files reference.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.3.2 How to configure and use logging</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1582">Django logging reference</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_707">Django logging overview</a></p> <p>Django provides a working <a href="index.html#page_1583">default logging configuration</a> that is readily extended.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Make a basic logging call</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To send a log message from within your code, you place a logging call into it.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Don’t be tempted to use logging calls in <b>settings.py</b>.</p> <p>The way that Django logging is configured as part of the setup() function means that logging calls placed in settings.py may not work as expected, because logging will not be set up at that point. To explore logging, use a view function as suggested in the example below.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>First, import the Python logging library, and then obtain a logger instance with <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.getLogger">logging.getLogger()</a>. Provide the getLogger() method with a name to identify it and the records it emits. A good option is to use</p> <p>__name__ (see <a href="index.html#page_851">Use logger namespacing</a> below for more on this) which will provide the name of the current Python module as a dotted path:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">logging</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">logging</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">getLogger(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__name__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s a good convention to perform this declaration at module level.</p> <p>And then in a function, for example in a view, send a record to the logger:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>some_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">some_risky_state:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">warning(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Platform is running at risk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p id="page_848"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When this code is executed, a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.LogRecord">LogRecord</a> containing that message will be sent to the logger. If you’re using Django’s default logging configuration, the message will appear in the console.</p> <p>The WARNING level used in the example above is one of several <a href="index.html#page_708">logging severity levels</a>: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. So, another example might be:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">critical(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Payment system is not responding"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Important: Records with a level lower than WARNING will not appear in the console by default. Changing this behavior requires additional configuration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Customize logging configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Although Django’s logging configuration works out of the box, you can control exactly how your logs are sent to various destinations - to log files, external services, email and so on - with some additional configuration.</p> <p>You can configure:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• logger mappings, to determine which records are sent to which handlers</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• handlers, to determine what they do with the records they receive</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• filters, to provide additional control over the transfer of records, and even modify records in-place</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• formatters, to convert <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.LogRecord">LogRecord</a> objects to a string or other form for consumption by human beings</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">or another system</p> <p>There are various ways of configuring logging. In Django, the <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOGGING</i></a> setting is most commonly used. The</p> <p>setting uses the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema">dictConfig format</a>, and extends the <a href="index.html#page_1583">default logging configuration</a><a href="index.html#page_1583">.</a></p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_710">Configuring logging</a> for an explanation of how your custom settings are merged with Django’s defaults.</p> <p>See the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#module-logging.config">Python logging documentation</a> for details of other ways of configuring logging. For the sake of simplicity, this documentation will only consider configuration via the LOGGING setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Basic logging configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When configuring logging, it makes sense to</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_849" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Create a LOGGING dictionary</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In your settings.py:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"version"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># the dictConfig format version</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"disable_existing_loggers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># retain the default loggers</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It nearly always makes sense to retain and extend the default logging configuration by setting disable_existing_loggers to False.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configure a handler</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example configures a single handler named file, that uses Python’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.handlers.html#logging.FileHandler">FileHandler</a> to save logs of level DEBUG and higher to the file general.log (at the project root):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"handlers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"file"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"class"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"logging.FileHandler"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"filename"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"general.log"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Different handler classes take different configuration options. For more information on available handler</p> <p>classes, see the <a href="index.html#page_1588"><i>AdminEmailHandler</i></a> provided by Django and the various <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.handlers.html#module-logging.handlers">handler classes</a> provided by Python.</p> <p>Logging levels can also be set on the handlers (by default, they accept log messages of all levels). Using the example above, adding:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"class"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"logging.FileHandler"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"filename"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"general.log"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"DEBUG"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>would define a handler configuration that only accepts records of level DEBUG and higher.</p> <p id="page_850"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configure a logger mapping</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To send records to this handler, configure a logger mapping to use it for example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"loggers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"DEBUG"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"handlers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"file"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The mapping’s name determines which log records it will process. This configuration ('') is unnamed. That</p> <p>means that it will process records from all loggers (see <a href="index.html#page_851">Use logger namespacing</a> below on how to use the mapping name to determine the loggers for which it will process records).</p> <p>It will forward messages of levels DEBUG and higher to the handler named file.</p> <p>Note that a logger can forward messages to multiple handlers, so the relation between loggers and handlers is many-to-many.</p> <p>If you execute:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">debug(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Attempting to connect to API"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>in your code, you will find that message in the file general.log in the root of the project.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configure a formatter</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, the final log output contains the message part of each <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.LogRecord">log record</a>. Use a formatter if you want to include additional data. First name and define your formatters - this example defines formatters named verbose and simple:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"formatters"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"verbose"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"format"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{name} {levelname} {asctime} {module} {process:d} {thread:d} {message}"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"style"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"simple"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"format"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{levelname} {message}"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"style"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_851" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The style keyword allows you to specify { for <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.format">str.format()</a> or $ for <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/string.html#string.Template">string.Template</a> formatting; the default is $.</p> <p>See <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logrecord-attributes">LogRecord attributes</a> for the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.LogRecord">LogRecord</a> attributes you can include.</p> <p>To apply a formatter to a handler, add a formatter entry to the handler’s dictionary referring to the for-matter by name, for example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"handlers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"file"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"class"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"logging.FileHandler"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"filename"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"general.log"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"formatter"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"verbose"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Use logger namespacing</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The unnamed logging configuration '' captures logs from any Python application. A named logging config-uration will capture logs only from loggers with matching names.</p> <p>The namespace of a logger instance is defined using <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.getLogger">getLogger()</a>. For example in views.py of my_app:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">logging</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">getLogger(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__name__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>will create a logger in the my_app.views namespace. __name__ allows you to organize log messages accord-ing to their provenance within your project’s applications automatically. It also ensures that you will not experience name collisions.</p> <p>A logger mapping named my_app.views will capture records from this logger:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"loggers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_app.views"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A logger mapping named my_app will be more permissive, capturing records from loggers anywhere within the my_app namespace (including my_app.views, my_app.utils, and so on):</p> <p id="page_852"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"loggers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_app"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also define logger namespacing explicitly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">logger</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">logging</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">getLogger(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"project.payment"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>and set up logger mappings accordingly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using logger hierarchies and propagation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Logger naming is hierarchical. my_app is the parent of my_app.views, which is the parent of my_app.views. private. Unless specified otherwise, logger mappings will propagate the records they process to their parents- a record from a logger in the my_app.views.private namespace will be handled by a mapping for both my_app and my_app.views.</p> <p>To manage this behavior, set the propagation key on the mappings you define:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LOGGING</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"loggers"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_app"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_app.views"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_app.views.private"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"propagate"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>propagate defaults to True. In this example, the logs from my_app.views.private will not be handled by the parent, but logs from my_app.views will.</p> <p id="page_853" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configure responsive logging</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Logging is most useful when it contains as much information as possible, but not information that you don’t need - and how much you need depends upon what you’re doing. When you’re debugging, you need a level of information that would be excessive and unhelpful if you had to deal with it in production.</p> <p>You can configure logging to provide you with the level of detail you need, when you need it. Rather than manually change configuration to achieve this, a better way is to apply configuration automatically according to the environment.</p> <p>For example, you could set an environment variable DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL appropriately in your development and staging environments, and make use of it in a logger mapping thus:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">getenv(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"WARNING"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>- so that unless the environment specifies a lower log level, this configuration will only forward records of severity WARNING and above to its handler.</p> <p>Other options in the configuration (such as the level or formatter option of handlers) can be similarly managed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.3.3 How to manage error reporting</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you’re running a public site you should always turn off the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting. That will make your server run much faster, and will also prevent malicious users from seeing details of your application that can be revealed by the error pages.</p> <p>However, running with <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> set to False means you’ll never see errors generated by your site – everyone will instead see your public error pages. You need to keep track of errors that occur in deployed sites, so Django can be configured to create reports with details about those errors.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Email reports</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Server errors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is False, Django will email the users listed in the <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> setting whenever your code raises an unhandled exception and results in an internal server error (strictly speaking, for any response with an HTTP status code of 500 or greater). This gives the administrators immediate notification of any errors. The</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> will get a description of the error, a complete Python traceback, and details about the HTTP request that caused the error.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: In order to send email, Django requires a few settings telling it how to connect to your mail server. At</p> <p>the very least, you’ll need to specify <a href="index.html#page_1911"><i>EMAIL_HOST</i></a> and possibly <a href="index.html#page_1911"><i>EMAIL_HOST_USER</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1911"><i>EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD</i></a>, <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_854">though other settings may be also required depending on your mail server’s configuration. Consult <a href="index.html#page_1887">the Django</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1887">settings documentation</a> for a full list of email-related settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, Django will send email from <a href="mailto:root@localhost">root@localhost. </a>However, some mail providers reject all email from</p> <p>this address. To use a different sender address, modify the <a href="index.html#page_1930"><i>SERVER_EMAIL</i></a> setting.</p> <p>To activate this behavior, put the email addresses of the recipients in the <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>Server error emails are sent using the logging framework, so you can customize this behavior by <a href="index.html#page_707">customizing</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_707">your logging configuration</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>404 errors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django can also be configured to email errors about broken links (404 “page not found” errors). Django sends emails about 404 errors when:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is False;</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> setting includes <a href="index.html#page_1592"><i>django.middleware.common.BrokenLinkEmailsMiddleware</i></a>.</p> <p>If those conditions are met, Django will email the users listed in the <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MANAGERS</i></a> setting whenever your code raises a 404 and the request has a referer. It doesn’t bother to email for 404s that don’t have a referer – those are usually people typing in broken URLs or broken web bots. It also ignores 404s when the referer is equal to the requested URL, since this behavior is from broken web bots too.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: <a href="index.html#page_1592"><i>BrokenLinkEmailsMiddleware</i></a> must appear before other middleware that intercepts 404 errors, such</p> <p>as <a href="index.html#page_1594"><i>LocaleMiddleware</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1126"><i>FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1126">. </a>Put it toward the top of your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can tell Django to stop reporting particular 404s by tweaking the <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>IGNORABLE_404_URLS</i></a> setting. It should be a list of compiled regular expression objects. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">IGNORABLE_404_URLS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"\.(php|cgi)$"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"^/phpmyadmin/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this example, a 404 to any URL ending with .php or .cgi will not be reported. Neither will any URL starting with /phpmyadmin/.</p> <p>The following example shows how to exclude some conventional URLs that browsers and crawlers often request:</p> <p id="page_855" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">IGNORABLE_404_URLS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"^/apple-touch-icon.*\.png$"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"^/favicon\.ico$"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"^/robots\.txt$"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>(Note that these are regular expressions, so we put a backslash in front of periods to escape them.)</p> <p>If you’d like to customize the behavior of <a href="index.html#page_1592"><i>django.middleware.common.BrokenLinkEmailsMiddleware</i></a> fur-ther (for example to ignore requests coming from web crawlers), you should subclass it and override its methods.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>404 errors are logged using the logging framework. By default, these log records are ignored, but you can use</p> <p>them for error reporting by writing a handler and <a href="index.html#page_707">configuring logging</a> appropriately.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Filtering error reports</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Filtering sensitive data is a hard problem, and it’s nearly impossible to guarantee that sensitive</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">data won’t leak into an error report. Therefore, error reports should only be available to trusted team</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">members and you should avoid transmitting error reports unencrypted over the internet (such as through</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">email).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Filtering sensitive information</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Error reports are really helpful for debugging errors, so it is generally useful to record as much relevant</p> <p>information about those errors as possible. For example, by default Django records the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_trace">full traceback</a> for the</p> <p>exception raised, each <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_frame">traceback frame’s </a>local variables, and the <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a>’s <a href="index.html#page_1859">attributes</a><a href="index.html#page_1859">.</a></p> <p>However, sometimes certain types of information may be too sensitive and thus may not be appropriate to be kept track of, for example a user’s password or credit card number. So in addition to filtering out settings that</p> <p>appear to be sensitive as described in the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> documentation, Django offers a set of function decorators to help you control which information should be filtered out of error reports in a production environment (that</p> <p>is, where <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is set to False): <a href="index.html#page_855"><i>sensitive_variables()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_856"><i>sensitive_post_parameters()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_856">.</a></p> <p><b>sensitive_variables</b>(*variables)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If a function (either a view or any regular callback) in your code uses local variables susceptible to contain sensitive information, you may prevent the values of those variables from being included in error reports using the sensitive_variables decorator:</p> <p id="page_856"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.debug</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sensitive_variables</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sensitive_variables(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"pw"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"cc"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>process_info</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(user):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pw</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pass_word</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">cc</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">credit_card_number</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In the above example, the values for the user, pw and cc variables will be hidden and replaced with stars (**********) in the error reports, whereas the value of the name variable will be disclosed.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To systematically hide all local variables of a function from error logs, do not provide any argument to the sensitive_variables decorator:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sensitive_variables()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_function</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">():</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When using multiple decorators</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If the variable you want to hide is also a function argument (e.g. ‘user’ in the following example), and if the decorated function has multiple decorators, then make sure to place @sensitive_variables at the top of the decorator chain. This way it will also hide the function argument as it gets passed through the other decorators:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sensitive_variables(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"pw"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"cc"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@some_decorator</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@another_decorator</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>process_info</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(user):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sensitive_post_parameters</b>(*parameters)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If one of your views receives an <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a> object with <a href="index.html#page_1861"><i>POST parameters</i></a> susceptible to contain sen-sitive information, you may prevent the values of those parameters from being included in the error reports using the sensitive_post_parameters decorator:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.debug</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sensitive_post_parameters</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sensitive_post_parameters(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pass_word"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"credit_card_number"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>record_user_profile</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">UserProfile</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_857" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">password</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">POST[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pass_word"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">credit_card</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">POST[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"credit_card_number"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">POST[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In the above example, the values for the pass_word and credit_card_number POST parameters will be hidden and replaced with stars (**********) in the request’s representation inside the error reports, whereas the value of the name parameter will be disclosed.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To systematically hide all POST parameters of a request in error reports, do not provide any argument to the sensitive_post_parameters decorator:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@sensitive_post_parameters()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">All POST parameters are systematically filtered out of error reports for certain <a href="index.html#page_548"><i>django.</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_548"><i>contrib.auth.views</i></a> views (login, password_reset_confirm, password_change, and add_view and user_change_password in the auth admin) to prevent the leaking of sensitive information such as user passwords.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom error reports</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All <a href="index.html#page_855"><i>sensitive_variables()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_856"><i>sensitive_post_parameters()</i></a> do is, respectively, annotate the decorated function with the names of sensitive variables and annotate the HttpRequest object with the names of sensitive POST parameters, so that this sensitive information can later be filtered out of reports when an error occurs. The actual filtering is done by Django’s default error reporter filter: <a href="index.html#page_858"><i>django.views.debug.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_858"><i>SafeExceptionReporterFilter</i></a> . This filter uses the decorators’ annotations to replace the corresponding values with stars (**********) when the error reports are produced. If you wish to override or customize this default behavior for your entire site, you need to define your own filter class and tell Django to use it via</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1910"><i>DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER_FILTER</i></a> setting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER_FILTER</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"path.to.your.CustomExceptionReporterFilter"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You may also control in a more granular way which filter to use within any given view by setting the HttpRequest’s exception_reporter_filter attribute:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_authenticated:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">exception_reporter_filter</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CustomExceptionReporterFilter()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p id="page_858"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Your custom filter class needs to inherit from <a href="index.html#page_858"><i>django.views.debug.SafeExceptionReporterFilter</i></a> and may override the following attributes and methods:</p> <p><b>class SafeExceptionReporterFilter</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>cleansed_substitute</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The string value to replace sensitive value with. By default it replaces the values of sensitive variables with stars (**********).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>hidden_settings</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A compiled regular expression object used to match settings and request.META values considered as sensitive. By default equivalent to:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">compile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"API|AUTH|TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASS|SIGNATURE|HTTP_COOKIE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, flags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">re</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">IGNORECASE)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The term AUTH was added.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>is_active</b>(request)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True to activate the filtering in <a href="index.html#page_858"><i>get_post_parameters()</i></a> and</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_858"><i>get_traceback_frame_variables()</i></a>. By default the filter is active if <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is False. Note that sensitive request.META values are always filtered along with sensitive setting values, as</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">described in the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> documentation.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_post_parameters</b>(request)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the filtered dictionary of POST parameters. <span style="float:right">Sensitive values are replaced with</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_858"><i>cleansed_substitute</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_traceback_frame_variables</b>(request, tb_frame)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the filtered dictionary of local variables for the given traceback frame. Sensitive values</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">are replaced with <a href="index.html#page_858"><i>cleansed_substitute</i></a>.</p> <p>If you need to customize error reports beyond filtering you may specify a custom error reporter class by</p> <p>defining the <a href="index.html#page_1910"><i>DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER</i></a> setting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"path.to.your.CustomExceptionReporter"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The exception reporter is responsible for compiling the exception report data, and formatting it as text or</p> <p>HTML appropriately. (The exception reporter uses <a href="index.html#page_1910"><i>DEFAULT_EXCEPTION_REPORTER_FILTER</i></a> when preparing the exception report data.)</p> <p>Your custom reporter class needs to inherit from <a href="index.html#page_858"><i>django.views.debug.ExceptionReporter</i></a> .</p> <p><b>class ExceptionReporter</b></p> <p id="page_859" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>html_template_path</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Property that returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path">pathlib.Path</a> representing the absolute filesystem path to a template for rendering the HTML representation of the exception. Defaults to the Django provided template.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>text_template_path</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Property that returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path">pathlib.Path</a> representing the absolute filesystem path to a template for rendering the plain-text representation of the exception. Defaults to the Django provided template.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_traceback_data</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Return a dictionary containing traceback information.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">This is the main extension point for customizing exception reports, for example:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.debug</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ExceptionReporter</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomExceptionReporter</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(ExceptionReporter):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_traceback_data</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_traceback_data()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ... remove/add something here ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_traceback_html</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Return HTML version of exception report.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Used for HTML version of debug 500 HTTP error page.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_traceback_text</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Return plain text version of exception report.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Used for plain text version of debug 500 HTTP error page and email reports.</p> <p>As with the filter class, you may control which exception reporter class to use within any given view by setting the HttpRequest’s exception_reporter_class attribute:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">is_authenticated:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">exception_reporter_class</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CustomExceptionReporter()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>You can also set up custom error reporting by writing a custom piece of <a href="index.html#page_306">exception middleware</a>. If you do write custom error handling, it’s a good idea to emulate Django’s built-in error handling and only report/log</p> <p>errors if <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is False.</p> <p id="page_860"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.3.4 How to delete a Django application</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides the ability to group sets of features into Python packages called <a href="index.html#page_921">applications. </a>When re-quirements change, apps may become obsolete or unnecessary. The following steps will help you delete an application safely.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Remove all references to the app (imports, foreign keys etc.).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Remove all models from the corresponding models.py file.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Create relevant migrations by running <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i>. </a>This step generates a migration that deletes</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tables for the removed models, and any other required migration for updating relationships connected to those models.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. <a href="index.html#page_459">Squash</a> out references to the app in other apps’ migrations.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">5. Apply migrations locally, runs tests, and verify the correctness of your project.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">6. Deploy/release your updated Django project.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">7. Remove the app from <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">8. Finally, remove the app’s directory.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>4.4 Installing, deploying and upgrading</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.4.1 How to upgrade Django to a newer version</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While it can be a complex process at times, upgrading to the latest Django version has several benefits:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• New features and improvements are added.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Bugs are fixed.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Older version of Django will eventually no longer receive security updates. (see <a href="index.html#page_2833">Supported versions).</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Upgrading as each new Django release is available makes future upgrades less painful by keeping your</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">code base up to date.</p> <p>Here are some things to consider to help make your upgrade process as smooth as possible.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_861" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Required Reading</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If it’s your first time doing an upgrade, it is useful to read the <a href="index.html#page_2831">guide on the different release processes</a>.</p> <p>Afterward, you should familiarize yourself with the changes that were made in the new Django version(s):</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Read the <a href="index.html#page_2115">release notes</a> for each ‘final’ release from the one after your current Django version, up to and</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">including the version to which you plan to upgrade.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Look at the <a href="index.html#page_2835">deprecation timeline</a> for the relevant versions.</p> <p>Pay particular attention to backwards incompatible changes to get a clear idea of what will be needed for a successful upgrade.</p> <p>If you’re upgrading through more than one feature version (e.g. 2.0 to 2.2), it’s usually easier to upgrade through each feature release incrementally (2.0 to 2.1 to 2.2) rather than to make all the changes for each feature release at once. For each feature release, use the latest patch release (e.g. for 2.1, use 2.1.15).</p> <p>The same incremental upgrade approach is recommended when upgrading from one LTS to the next.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Dependencies</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In most cases it will be necessary to upgrade to the latest version of your Django-related dependencies as well. If the Django version was recently released or if some of your dependencies are not well-maintained, some of your dependencies may not yet support the new Django version. In these cases you may have to wait until new versions of your dependencies are released.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Resolving deprecation warnings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Before upgrading, it’s a good idea to resolve any deprecation warnings raised by your project while using your current version of Django. Fixing these warnings before upgrading ensures that you’re informed about areas of the code that need altering.</p> <p>In Python, deprecation warnings are silenced by default. You must turn them on using the-Wa Python</p> <p>command line option or the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONWARNINGS">PYTHONWARNINGS</a> environment variable. For example, to show warnings while running tests:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -Wa manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re not using the Django test runner, you may need to also ensure that any console output is not captured</p> <p>which would hide deprecation warnings. For example, if you use <a href="https://docs.pytest.org/">pytest:</a></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PYTHONWARNINGS</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">always pytest tests --capture</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">no</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Resolve any deprecation warnings with your current version of Django before continuing the upgrade pro-cess.</p> <p id="page_862"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Third party applications might use deprecated APIs in order to support multiple versions of Django, so dep-recation warnings in packages you’ve installed don’t necessarily indicate a problem. If a package doesn’t support the latest version of Django, consider raising an issue or sending a pull request for it.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once you’re ready, it is time to <a href="index.html#page_111">install the new Django version</a>. If you are using a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html#module-venv">virtual environment</a> and it is a major upgrade, you might want to set up a new environment with all the dependencies first.</p> <p>If you installed Django with <a href="https://pip.pypa.io/">pip</a>, you can use the--upgrade or-U flag:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install -U Django</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Testing</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When the new environment is set up, <a href="index.html#page_469">run the full test suite</a> for your application. Again, it’s useful to turn on deprecation warnings on so they’re shown in the test output (you can also use the flag if you test your app manually using manage.py runserver):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -Wa manage.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">test</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>After you have run the tests, fix any failures. While you have the release notes fresh in your mind, it may also be a good time to take advantage of new features in Django by refactoring your code to eliminate any deprecation warnings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Deployment</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you are sufficiently confident your app works with the new version of Django, you’re ready to go ahead</p> <p>and <a href="index.html#page_865">deploy</a> your upgraded Django project.</p> <p>If you are using caching provided by Django, you should consider clearing your cache after upgrading. Oth-erwise you may run into problems, for example, if you are caching pickled objects as these objects are not guaranteed to be pickle-compatible across Django versions. A past instance of incompatibility was caching</p> <p>pickled <a href="index.html#page_1871"><i>HttpResponse</i></a> objects, either directly or indirectly via the <a href="index.html#page_611"><i>cache_page()</i></a> decorator.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.4.2 How to install Django on Windows</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document will guide you through installing Python 3.13 and Django on Windows. It also provides instructions for setting up a virtual environment, which makes it easier to work on Python projects. This is meant as a beginner’s guide for users working on Django projects and does not reflect how Django should be installed when developing changes for Django itself.</p> <p id="page_863" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The steps in this guide have been tested with Windows 10. In other versions, the steps would be similar. You will need to be familiar with using the Windows command prompt.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Install Python</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django is a Python web framework, thus requiring Python to be installed on your machine. At the time of writing, Python 3.13 is the latest version.</p> <p>To install Python on your machine go to <a href="https://www.python.org/downloads/">https://www.python.org/downloads/</a>. The website should offer you a download button for the latest Python version. Download the executable installer and run it. Check the boxes next to “Install launcher for all users (recommended)” then click “Install Now”.</p> <p>After installation, open the command prompt and check that the Python version matches the version you installed by executing:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">py --version</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>py</b> is not recognized or found</p> <p>Depending on how you’ve installed Python (such as via the Microsoft Store), py may not be available in the command prompt.</p> <p>You will then need to use python instead of py when entering commands.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>For more details, see <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html">Using Python on Windows</a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>About pip</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://pypi.org/project/pip/">pip</a> is a package manager for Python and is included by default with the Python installer. It helps to install and uninstall Python packages (such as Django!). For the rest of the installation, we’ll use pip to install Python packages from the command line.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting up a virtual environment</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It is best practice to provide a dedicated environment for each Django project you create. There are many op-tions to manage environments and packages within the Python ecosystem, some of which are recommended</p> <p>in the <a href="https://packaging.python.org/guides/tool-recommendations/">Python documentation</a>. Python itself comes with <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/venv.html">venv</a> for managing environments which we will use for this guide.</p> <p>To create a virtual environment for your project, open a new command prompt, navigate to the folder where you want to create your project and then enter the following:</p> <p id="page_864"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">py -m venv project-name</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will create a folder called ‘project-name’ if it does not already exist and set up the virtual environment. To activate the environment, run:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">project-name\Scripts\activate.bat</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The virtual environment will be activated and you’ll see “(project-name)” next to the command prompt to designate that. Each time you start a new command prompt, you’ll need to activate the environment again.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Install Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django can be installed easily using pip within your virtual environment.</p> <p>In the command prompt, ensure your virtual environment is active, and execute the following command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">py -m pip install Django</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will download and install the latest Django release.</p> <p>After the installation has completed, you can verify your Django installation by executing django-admin--version in the command prompt.</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_112">Get your database running</a> for information on database installation with Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Colored terminal output</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A quality-of-life feature adds colored (rather than monochrome) output to the terminal. In modern termi-nals this should work for both CMD and PowerShell. If for some reason this needs to be disabled, set the</p> <p>environmental variable <a href="index.html#page_1465"><i>DJANGO_COLORS</i></a> to nocolor.</p> <p>On older Windows versions, or legacy terminals, <a href="https://pypi.org/project/colorama/">colorama</a> 0.4.6+ must be installed to enable syntax coloring:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">py -m pip install</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"colorama >= 0.4.6"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1465">Syntax coloring</a> for more information on color settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Common pitfalls</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If django-admin only displays the help text no matter what arguments it is given, there is probably a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">problem with the file association in Windows. Check if there is more than one environment variable set for running Python scripts in PATH. This usually occurs when there is more than one Python version installed.</p> <p id="page_865" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If you are connecting to the internet behind a proxy, there might be problems in running the command</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">py -m pip install Django . Set the environment variables for proxy configuration in the command prompt as follows:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>set</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">http_proxy</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">=http://username:password@proxyserver:proxyport</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>set</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">https_proxy</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">=https://username:password@proxyserver:proxyport</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• In general, Django assumes that UTF-8 encoding is used for I/O. This may cause problems if your system</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">is set to use a different encoding. Recent versions of Python allow setting the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONUTF8">PYTHONUTF8</a> environment variable in order to force a UTF-8 encoding. Windows 10 also provides a system-wide setting by check-ing Use Unicode UTF-8 for worldwide language support in Language ‣ Administrative Language Settings ‣ Change system locale in system settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.4.3 How to deploy Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django is full of shortcuts to make web developers’ lives easier, but all those tools are of no use if you can’t easily deploy your sites. Since Django’s inception, ease of deployment has been a major goal.</p> <p>There are many options for deploying your Django application, based on your architecture or your particular business needs, but that discussion is outside the scope of what Django can give you as guidance.</p> <p>Django, being a web framework, needs a web server in order to operate. And since most web servers don’t</p> <p>natively speak Python, we need an interface to make that communication happen. The <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command starts a lightweight development server, which is not suitable for production.</p> <p>Django currently supports two interfaces: WSGI and ASGI.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://wsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">WSGI</a> is the main Python standard for communicating between web servers and applications, but it</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">only supports synchronous code.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">ASGI</a> is the new, asynchronous-friendly standard that will allow your Django site to use asynchronous</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Python features, and asynchronous Django features as they are developed.</p> <p>You should also consider how you will handle <a href="index.html#page_885">static files</a> for your application, and how to handle <a href="index.html#page_853">error re-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_853">porting</a>.</p> <p>Finally, before you deploy your application to production, you should run through our <a href="index.html#page_879">deployment checklist</a> to ensure that your configurations are suitable.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_866"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to deploy with WSGI</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s primary deployment platform is <a href="https://wsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">WSGI</a>, the Python standard for web servers and applications.</p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> management command sets up a minimal default WSGI configuration for you, which you can tweak as needed for your project, and direct any WSGI-compliant application server to use.</p> <p>Django includes getting-started documentation for the following WSGI servers:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with Gunicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://gunicorn.org/">Gunicorn</a> (‘Green Unicorn’) is a pure-Python WSGI server for UNIX. It has no dependencies and can be in-stalled using pip.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing Gunicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Install gunicorn by running python -m pip install gunicorn. For more details, see the <a href="https://docs.gunicorn.org/en/latest/install.html">gunicorn docu-</a></p> <p><a href="https://docs.gunicorn.org/en/latest/install.html">mentation.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running Django in Gunicorn as a generic WSGI application</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Gunicorn is installed, a gunicorn command is available which starts the Gunicorn server process. The simplest invocation of gunicorn is to pass the location of a module containing a WSGI application object named application, which for a typical Django project would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">gunicorn myproject.wsgi</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will start one process running one thread listening on 127.0.0.1:8000. It requires that your project be on the Python path; the simplest way to ensure that is to run this command from the same directory as your manage.py file.</p> <p>See Gunicorn’s <a href="https://docs.gunicorn.org/en/latest/deploy.html">deployment documentation</a> for additional tips.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with uWSGI</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/">uWSGI</a> is a fast, self-healing and developer/sysadmin-friendly application container server coded in pure C.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>The uWSGI docs offer a <a href="https://uwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/Django_and_nginx.html">tutorial</a> covering Django, nginx, and uWSGI (one possible deployment setup of many). The docs below are focused on how to integrate Django with uWSGI.</p> <p id="page_867" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Prerequisite: uWSGI</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The uWSGI wiki describes several <a href="https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Install.html">installation procedures</a>. Using pip, the Python package manager, you can install any uWSGI version with a single command. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">#</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Install current stable version.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install uwsgi</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">#</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Or install LTS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>(</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">long term support</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>)</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install https://projects.unbit.it/downloads/uwsgi-lts.tar.gz</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>uWSGI model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>uWSGI operates on a client-server model. Your web server (e.g., nginx, Apache) communicates with a django-uwsgi “worker” process to serve dynamic content.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configuring and starting the uWSGI server for Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>uWSGI supports multiple ways to configure the process. See uWSGI’s <a href="https://uwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Configuration.html">configuration documentation.</a></p> <p>Here’s an example command to start a uWSGI server:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">uwsgi --chdir</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/your/project</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--module</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite.wsgi:application</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--env</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite.settings</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--master --pidfile</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/tmp/project-master.pid</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--socket</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">127</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.0.0.1:49152</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># can also be a file</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--processes</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># number of worker processes</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--uid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1000</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--gid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2000</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># if root, uwsgi can drop privileges</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--harakiri</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">20</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># respawn processes taking more than 20 seconds</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--max-requests</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5000</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># respawn processes after serving 5000 requests</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--vacuum</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># clear environment on exit</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--home</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/virtual/env</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># optional path to a virtual environment</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--daemonize</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/var/log/uwsgi/yourproject.log</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># background the process</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This assumes you have a top-level project package named mysite, and within it a module mysite/wsgi. py that contains a WSGI application object. This is the layout you’ll have if you ran django-admin startproject mysite (using your own project name in place of mysite) with a recent version of Django.</p> <p>If this file doesn’t exist, you’ll need to create it. See the <a href="index.html#page_866">How to deploy with WSGI</a> documentation for the default contents you should put in this file and what else you can add to it.</p> <p>The Django-specific options here are:</p> <p id="page_868"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• chdir: The path to the directory that needs to be on Python’s import path – i.e., the directory containing</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the mysite package.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• module: The WSGI module to use – probably the mysite.wsgi module that <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> creates.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• env: Should probably contain at least <a
