href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• home: Optional path to your project virtual environment.</p> <p>Example ini configuration file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[uwsgi]</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">chdir</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/your/project</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">module</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite.wsgi:application</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">master</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">pidfile</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/tmp/project-master.pid</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">vacuum</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">max-requests</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5000</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">daemonize</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/var/log/uwsgi/yourproject.log</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Example ini configuration file usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">uwsgi --ini uwsgi.ini</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Fixing <b>UnicodeEncodeError</b> for file uploads</p> <p>If you get a UnicodeEncodeError when uploading files with file names that contain non-ASCII characters, make sure uWSGI is configured to accept non-ASCII file names by adding this to your uwsgi.ini:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">env</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LANG=en_US.UTF-8</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See the <a href="index.html#page_2062">Files</a> section of the Unicode reference guide for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See the uWSGI docs on <a href="https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Management.html">managing the uWSGI process</a> for information on starting, stopping and reloading the uWSGI workers.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with Apache and mod_wsgi</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Deploying Django with <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/">Apache</a> and <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/">mod_wsgi</a> is a tried and tested way to get Django into production.</p> <p>mod_wsgi is an Apache module which can host any Python <a href="https://wsgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">WSGI</a> application, including Django. Django will work with any version of Apache which supports mod_wsgi.</p> <p>The <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/">official mod_wsgi documentation</a> is your source for all the details about how to use mod_wsgi. You’ll</p> <p>probably want to start with the <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/installation.html">installation and configuration documentation</a>.</p> <p id="page_869" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Basic configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once you’ve got mod_wsgi installed and activated, edit your Apache server’s <a href="https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/httpd/DistrosDefaultLayout">httpd.conf</a> file and add the following.</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIScriptAlias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIPythonHome</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/venv</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIPythonPath</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Directory</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Files</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wsgi.py</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>all</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">granted</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Files></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Directory></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The first bit in the WSGIScriptAlias line is the base URL path you want to serve your application at (/ indicates the root url), and the second is the location of a “WSGI file” – see below – on your system, usually inside of your project package (mysite in this example). This tells Apache to serve any request below the given URL using the WSGI application defined in that file.</p> <p>If you install your project’s Python dependencies inside a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html#module-venv">virtual environment</a>, add the path using</p> <p>WSGIPythonHome. See the <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/user-guides/virtual-environments.html">mod_wsgi virtual environment guide</a> for more details.</p> <p>The WSGIPythonPath line ensures that your project package is available for import on the Python path; in other words, that import mysite works.</p> <p>The <Directory> piece ensures that Apache can access your wsgi.py file.</p> <p>Next we’ll need to ensure this wsgi.py with a WSGI application object exists. As of Django version 1.4,</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> will have created one for you; otherwise, you’ll need to create it. See the <a href="index.html#page_866">WSGI overview</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_866">documentation</a> for the default contents you should put in this file, and what else you can add to it.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If multiple Django sites are run in a single mod_wsgi process, all of them will use the settings</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">of whichever one happens to run first. This can be solved by changing:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">setdefault(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{{ project_name }}.settings"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">in wsgi.py, to:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"{{ project_name }}.settings"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">or by <a href="index.html#page_870">using mod_wsgi daemon mode</a> and ensuring that each site runs in its own daemon process.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Fixing <b>UnicodeEncodeError</b> for file uploads</p> <p>If you get a UnicodeEncodeError when uploading or writing files with file names or content that contains non-ASCII characters, make sure Apache is configured to support UTF-8 encoding:</p> <p id="page_870"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LANG</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'en_US.UTF-8'</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LC_ALL</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'en_US.UTF-8'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A common location to put this configuration is /etc/apache2/envvars.</p> <p>Alternatively, if you are <a href="index.html#page_870">using mod_wsgi daemon mode</a> you can add lang and locale options to the WSGIDaemonProcess directive:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIDaemonProcess example.com lang='en_US.UTF-8' locale='en_US.UTF-8'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See the <a href="index.html#page_2062">Files</a> section of the Unicode reference guide for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using mod_wsgi daemon mode</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>“Daemon mode” is the recommended mode for running mod_wsgi (on non-Windows platforms). To create the required daemon process group and delegate the Django instance to run in it, you will need to add ap-propriate WSGIDaemonProcess and WSGIProcessGroup directives. A further change required to the above configuration if you use daemon mode is that you can’t use WSGIPythonPath; instead you should use the python-path option to WSGIDaemonProcess, for example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIDaemonProcess</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">example.com python-home=/path/to/venv python-path=/path/to/mysite.com</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIProcessGroup</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">example.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to serve your project in a subdirectory (https://example.com/mysite in this example), you can add WSGIScriptAlias to the configuration above:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIScriptAlias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/mysite /path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">process-group=example.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See the official mod_wsgi documentation for <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/user-guides/quick-configuration-guide.html#delegation-to-daemon-process">details on setting up daemon mode.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django doesn’t serve files itself; it leaves that job to whichever web server you choose.</p> <p>We recommend using a separate web server – i.e., one that’s not also running Django – for serving media. Here are some good choices:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://nginx.org/en/">Nginx</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• A stripped-down version of <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/">Apache</a></p> <p>If, however, you have no option but to serve media files on the same Apache VirtualHost as Django, you can set up Apache to serve some URLs as static media, and others using the mod_wsgi interface to Django.</p> <p id="page_871" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example sets up Django at the site root, but serves robots.txt, favicon.ico, and anything in the /static/ and /media/ URL space as a static file. All other URLs will be served using mod_wsgi:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Alias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/robots.txt /path/to/mysite.com/static/robots.txt</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Alias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/favicon.ico /path/to/mysite.com/static/favicon.ico</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Alias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/media/ /path/to/mysite.com/media/</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Alias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/static/ /path/to/mysite.com/static/</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Directory</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/static</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>all</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">granted</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Directory></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Directory</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/media</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>all</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">granted</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Directory></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIScriptAlias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Directory</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Files</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wsgi.py</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>all</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">granted</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Files></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Directory></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving the admin files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.contrib.staticfiles</i></a> is in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>, the Django development server automatically serves the static files of the admin app (and any other installed apps). This is however not the case when you use any other server arrangement. You’re responsible for setting up Apache, or whichever web server you’re using, to serve the admin files.</p> <p>The admin files live in <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/contrib/admin/static/admin">(django/contrib/admin/static/admin</a>) of the Django distribution.</p> <p>We strongly recommend using <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.contrib.staticfiles</i></a> to handle the admin files (along with a web</p> <p>server as outlined in the previous section; this means using the <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> management command</p> <p>to collect the static files in <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> , and then configuring your web server to serve <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> at</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1946"><i>STATIC_URL</i></a>), but here are three other approaches:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Create a symbolic link to the admin static files from within your document root (this may require</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">+FollowSymLinks in your Apache configuration).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Use an Alias directive, as demonstrated above, to alias the appropriate URL (probably <a href="index.html#page_1946"><i>STATIC_URL</i></a> +</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">admin/) to the actual location of the admin files.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Copy the admin static files so that they live within your Apache document root.</p> <p id="page_872"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authenticating against Django’s user database from Apache</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides a handler to allow Apache to authenticate users directly against Django’s authentication</p> <p>backends. See the <a href="index.html#page_872">mod_wsgi authentication documentation</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to authenticate against Django’s user database from Apache</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Since keeping multiple authentication databases in sync is a common problem when dealing with Apache,</p> <p>you can configure Apache to authenticate against Django’s <a href="index.html#page_530">authentication system</a> directly. This requires Apache version >= 2.2 and mod_wsgi >= 2.0. For example, you could:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Serve static/media files directly from Apache only to authenticated users.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Authenticate access to a <a href="https://subversion.apache.org/">Subversion</a> repository against Django users with a certain permission.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Allow certain users to connect to a WebDAV share created with <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.2/mod/mod_dav.html">mod_dav.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you have installed a <a href="index.html#page_583">custom user model</a> and want to use this default auth handler, it must support an is_active attribute. If you want to use group based authorization, your custom user must have a relation named ‘groups’, referring to a related object that has a ‘name’ field. You can also specify your own custom mod_wsgi auth handler if your custom cannot conform to these requirements.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authentication with mod_wsgi</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The use of WSGIApplicationGroup %{GLOBAL} in the configurations below presumes that your Apache instance is running only one Django application. If you are running more than one Django appli-</p> <p>cation, please refer to the <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/user-guides/configuration-guidelines.html#defining-application-groups">Defining Application Groups</a> section of the mod_wsgi docs for more information about this setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Make sure that mod_wsgi is installed and activated and that you have followed the steps to set up <a href="index.html#page_868">Apache</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_868">with mod_wsgi</a>.</p> <p>Next, edit your Apache configuration to add a location that you want only authenticated users to be able to view:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIScriptAlias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIPythonPath</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIProcessGroup</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">%{GLOBAL}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIApplicationGroup</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">%{GLOBAL}</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_873" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Location</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/secret"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthType</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Basic</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthName</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Top Secret"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">valid-user</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthBasicProvider</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wsgi</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIAuthUserScript</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Location></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The WSGIAuthUserScript directive tells mod_wsgi to execute the check_password function in specified wsgi script, passing the user name and password that it receives from the prompt. In this example, the</p> <p>WSGIAuthUserScript is the same as the WSGIScriptAlias that defines your application <a href="index.html#page_866">that is created by</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_866">django-admin startproject.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Using Apache 2.2 with authentication</p> <p>Make sure that mod_auth_basic and mod_authz_user are loaded.</p> <p>These might be compiled statically into Apache, or you might need to use LoadModule to load them dynam-ically in your httpd.conf:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LoadModule</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">auth_basic_module modules/mod_auth_basic.so</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LoadModule</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">authz_user_module modules/mod_authz_user.so</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, edit your WSGI script mysite.wsgi to tie Apache’s authentication to your site’s authentication mech-anisms by importing the check_password function:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"mysite.settings"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.handlers.modwsgi</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">check_password</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.handlers.wsgi</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIHandler</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">application</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIHandler()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Requests beginning with /secret/ will now require a user to authenticate.</p> <p>The mod_wsgi <a href="https://modwsgi.readthedocs.io/en/develop/user-guides/access-control-mechanisms.html">access control mechanisms documentation</a> provides additional details and information about alternative methods of authentication.</p> <p id="page_874"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Authorization with mod_wsgi and Django groups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>mod_wsgi also provides functionality to restrict a particular location to members of a group.</p> <p>In this case, the Apache configuration should look like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIScriptAlias</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIProcessGroup</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">%{GLOBAL}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIApplicationGroup</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">%{GLOBAL}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><Location</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/secret"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthType</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Basic</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthName</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Top Secret"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AuthBasicProvider</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wsgi</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIAuthUserScript</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGIAuthGroupScript</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/path/to/mysite.com/mysite/wsgi.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>group</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">secret-agents</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Require</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">valid-user</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></Location></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To support the WSGIAuthGroupScript directive, the same WSGI script mysite.wsgi must also import the groups_for_user function which returns a list groups the given user belongs to.</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.handlers.modwsgi</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">check_password, groups_for_user</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Requests for /secret/ will now also require user to be a member of the “secret-agents” group.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The application object</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The key concept of deploying with WSGI is the application callable which the application server uses to communicate with your code. It’s commonly provided as an object named application in a Python module accessible to the server.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> command creates a file <project_name>/wsgi.py that contains such an application callable.</p> <p>It’s used both by Django’s development server and in production WSGI deployments.</p> <p>WSGI servers obtain the path to the application callable from their configuration. Django’s built-in server,</p> <p>namely the <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command, reads it from the <a href="index.html#page_1937"><i>WSGI_APPLICATION</i></a> setting. By default, it’s set to <project_name>.wsgi.application, which points to the application callable in <project_name>/wsgi. py.</p> <p id="page_875" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configuring the settings module</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When the WSGI server loads your application, Django needs to import the settings module — that’s where your entire application is defined.</p> <p>Django uses the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable to locate the appropriate settings module. It must contain the dotted path to the settings module. You can use a different value for development and production; it all depends on how you organize your settings.</p> <p>If this variable isn’t set, the default wsgi.py sets it to mysite.settings, where mysite is the name of your</p> <p>project. That’s how <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> discovers the default settings file by default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Since environment variables are process-wide, this doesn’t work when you run multiple Django sites in the same process. This happens with mod_wsgi.</p> <p>To avoid this problem, use mod_wsgi’s daemon mode with each site in its own daemon process, or over-ride the value from the environment by enforcing os.environ["DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"] = "mysite. settings" in your wsgi.py.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Applying WSGI middleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To apply <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-3333/#middleware-components-that-play-both-sides">WSGI middleware</a> you can wrap the application object. For instance you could add these lines at the bottom of wsgi.py:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">helloworld.wsgi</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HelloWorldApplication</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">application</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HelloWorldApplication(application)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You could also replace the Django WSGI application with a custom WSGI application that later delegates to the Django WSGI application, if you want to combine a Django application with a WSGI application of another framework.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to deploy with ASGI</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>As well as WSGI, Django also supports deploying on <a href="https://asgi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">ASGI, </a>the emerging Python standard for asynchronous web servers and applications.</p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> management command sets up a default ASGI configuration for you, which you can tweak as needed for your project, and direct any ASGI-compliant application server to use.</p> <p>Django includes getting-started documentation for the following ASGI servers:</p> <p id="page_876"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with Daphne</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://pypi.org/project/daphne/">Daphne</a> is a pure-Python ASGI server for UNIX, maintained by members of the Django project. It acts as the reference server for ASGI.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing Daphne</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can install Daphne with pip:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install daphne</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running Django in Daphne</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Daphne is installed, a daphne command is available which starts the Daphne server process. At its simplest, Daphne needs to be called with the location of a module containing an ASGI application object, followed by what the application is called (separated by a colon).</p> <p>For a typical Django project, invoking Daphne would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">daphne myproject.asgi:application</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will start one process listening on 127.0.0.1:8000. It requires that your project be on the Python path; to ensure that run this command from the same directory as your manage.py file.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Integration with runserver</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Daphne provides a <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command to serve your site under ASGI during development.</p> <p>This can be enabled by adding daphne to the start of your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> and adding an ASGI_APPLICATION setting pointing to your ASGI application object:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INSTALLED_APPS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"daphne"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">ASGI_APPLICATION</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"myproject.asgi.application"</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_877" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with Hypercorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://hypercorn.readthedocs.io/">Hypercorn</a> is an ASGI server that supports HTTP/1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 with an emphasis on protocol support.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing Hypercorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can install Hypercorn with pip:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install hypercorn</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running Django in Hypercorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When <a href="https://pypi.org/project/Hypercorn/">Hypercorn</a> is installed, a hypercorn command is available which runs ASGI applications. Hypercorn needs to be called with the location of a module containing an ASGI application object, followed by what the application is called (separated by a colon).</p> <p>For a typical Django project, invoking Hypercorn would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">hypercorn myproject.asgi:application</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will start one process listening on 127.0.0.1:8000. It requires that your project be on the Python path; to ensure that run this command from the same directory as your manage.py file.</p> <p>For more advanced usage, please read the <a href="https://hypercorn.readthedocs.io/">Hypercorn documentation</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to use Django with Uvicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://www.uvicorn.org/">Uvicorn</a> is an ASGI server based on uvloop and httptools, with an emphasis on speed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing Uvicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can install Uvicorn with pip:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install uvicorn</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_878"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Running Django in Uvicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Uvicorn is installed, a uvicorn command is available which runs ASGI applications. Uvicorn needs to be called with the location of a module containing an ASGI application object, followed by what the appli-cation is called (separated by a colon).</p> <p>For a typical Django project, invoking Uvicorn would look like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m uvicorn myproject.asgi:application</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will start one process listening on 127.0.0.1:8000. It requires that your project be on the Python path; to ensure that run this command from the same directory as your manage.py file.</p> <p>In development mode, you can add--reload to cause the server to reload any time a file is changed on disk.</p> <p>For more advanced usage, please read the <a href="https://www.uvicorn.org/">Uvicorn documentation.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Deploying Django using Uvicorn and Gunicorn</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://gunicorn.org/">Gunicorn</a> is a robust web server that implements process monitoring and automatic restarts. This can be useful when running Uvicorn in a production environment.</p> <p>To install Uvicorn and Gunicorn, use the following:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install uvicorn uvicorn-worker gunicorn</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then start Gunicorn using the Uvicorn worker class like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m gunicorn myproject.asgi:application -k uvicorn_worker.UvicornWorker</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The application object</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Like WSGI, ASGI has you supply an application callable which the application server uses to communicate with your code. It’s commonly provided as an object named application in a Python module accessible to the server.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a> command creates a file <project_name>/asgi.py that contains such an application callable.</p> <p>It’s not used by the development server (runserver), but can be used by any ASGI server either in develop-ment or in production.</p> <p>ASGI servers usually take the path to the application callable as a string; for most Django projects, this will look like myproject.asgi:application.</p> <p id="page_879" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: While Django’s default ASGI handler will run all your code in a synchronous thread, if you</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">choose to run your own async handler you must be aware of async-safety.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Do not call blocking synchronous functions or libraries in any async code. Django prevents you from</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">doing this with the parts of Django that are not async-safe, but the same may not be true of third-party</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">apps or Python libraries.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configuring the settings module</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When the ASGI server loads your application, Django needs to import the settings module — that’s where your entire application is defined.</p> <p>Django uses the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable to locate the appropriate settings module. It must contain the dotted path to the settings module. You can use a different value for development and production; it all depends on how you organize your settings.</p> <p>If this variable isn’t set, the default asgi.py sets it to mysite.settings, where mysite is the name of your project.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Applying ASGI middleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To apply ASGI middleware, or to embed Django in another ASGI application, you can wrap Django’s application object in the asgi.py file. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">some_asgi_library</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AmazingMiddleware</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">application</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AmazingMiddleware(application)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Deployment checklist</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The internet is a hostile environment. Before deploying your Django project, you should take some time to review your settings, with security, performance, and operations in mind.</p> <p>Django includes many <a href="index.html#page_718">security features</a>. Some are built-in and always enabled. Others are optional be-cause they aren’t always appropriate, or because they’re inconvenient for development. For example, forcing HTTPS may not be suitable for all websites, and it’s impractical for local development.</p> <p>Performance optimizations are another category of trade-offs with convenience. For instance, caching is useful in production, less so for local development. Error reporting needs are also widely different.</p> <p>The following checklist includes settings that:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• must be set properly for Django to provide the expected level of security;</p> <p id="page_880"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• are expected to be different in each environment;</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• enable optional security features;</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• enable performance optimizations;</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• provide error reporting.</p> <p>Many of these settings are sensitive and should be treated as confidential. If you’re releasing the source code for your project, a common practice is to publish suitable settings for development, and to use a private settings module for production.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Run manage.py check --deploy</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some of the checks described below can be automated using the <a href="index.html#page_1435"><i>check --deploy</i></a> option. Be sure to run it against your production settings file as described in the option’s documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Switch away from manage.py runserver</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command is not designed for a production setting. Be sure to switch to a production-ready</p> <p>WSGI or ASGI server. For a few common options, see <a href="index.html#page_866">WSGI servers</a> or <a href="index.html#page_875">ASGI servers</a><a href="index.html#page_875">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Critical settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SECRET_KEY</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The secret key must be a large random value and it must be kept secret.</p> <p>Make sure that the key used in production isn’t used anywhere else and avoid committing it to source control. This reduces the number of vectors from which an attacker may acquire the key.</p> <p>Instead of hardcoding the secret key in your settings module, consider loading it from an environment vari-able:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SECRET_KEY</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"SECRET_KEY"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>or from a file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>with</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">open</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/etc/secret_key.txt"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">SECRET_KEY</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">read()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">strip()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If rotating secret keys, you may use <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a>:</p> <p id="page_881" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SECRET_KEY</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"CURRENT_SECRET_KEY"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">os</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">environ[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OLD_SECRET_KEY"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Ensure that old secret keys are removed from SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS in a timely manner.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DEBUG</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You must never enable debug in production.</p> <p>You’re certainly developing your project with <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG = True</i></a>, since this enables handy features like full trace-backs in your browser.</p> <p>For a production environment, though, this is a really bad idea, because it leaks lots of information about your project: excerpts of your source code, local variables, settings, libraries used, etc.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Environment-specific settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ALLOWED_HOSTS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG = False</i></a>, Django doesn’t work at all without a suitable value for <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ALLOWED_HOSTS</i></a>.</p> <p>This setting is required to protect your site against some CSRF attacks. If you use a wildcard, you must perform your own validation of the Host HTTP header, or otherwise ensure that you aren’t vulnerable to this category of attacks.</p> <p>You should also configure the web server that sits in front of Django to validate the host. It should respond with a static error page or ignore requests for incorrect hosts instead of forwarding the request to Django. This way you’ll avoid spurious errors in your Django logs (or emails if you have error reporting configured that way). For example, on nginx you might set up a default server to return “444 No Response” on an unrecognized host:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>server</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>listen</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">80</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">default_server</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">444</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_882"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CACHES</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using a cache, connection parameters may be different in development and in production. Django</p> <p>defaults to per-process <a href="index.html#page_606">local-memory caching</a> which may not be desirable.</p> <p>Cache servers often have weak authentication. Make sure they only accept connections from your application servers.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DATABASES</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Database connection parameters are probably different in development and in production.</p> <p>Database passwords are very sensitive. You should protect them exactly like <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> .</p> <p>For maximum security, make sure database servers only accept connections from your application servers.</p> <p>If you haven’t set up backups for your database, do it right now!</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>EMAIL_BACKEND and related settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your site sends emails, these values need to be set correctly.</p> <p>By default, Django sends email from <a href="mailto:webmaster@localhost">webmaster@localhost</a> and <a href="mailto:root@localhost">root@localhost</a><a href="mailto:root@localhost">.</a> <span style="float:right">However, some</span></p> <p>mail providers reject email from these addresses. <span style="float:right">To use different sender addresses, modify the</span></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1910"><i>DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1930"><i>SERVER_EMAIL</i></a> settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>STATIC_ROOT and STATIC_URL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Static files are automatically served by the development server. In production, you must define a</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> directory where <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> will copy them.</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_843">How to manage static files (e.g. images, JavaScript, CSS)</a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MEDIA_ROOT and MEDIA_URL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Media files are uploaded by your users. They’re untrusted! Make sure your web server never attempts to interpret them. For instance, if a user uploads a .php file, the web server shouldn’t execute it.</p> <p>Now is a good time to check your backup strategy for these files.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_883" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>HTTPS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any website which allows users to log in should enforce site-wide HTTPS to avoid transmitting access tokens in clear. In Django, access tokens include the login/password, the session cookie, and password reset tokens. (You can’t do much to protect password reset tokens if you’re sending them by email.)</p> <p>Protecting sensitive areas such as the user account or the admin isn’t sufficient, because the same session cookie is used for HTTP and HTTPS. Your web server must redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS, and only transmit HTTPS requests to Django.</p> <p>Once you’ve set up HTTPS, enable the following settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Set this to True to avoid transmitting the CSRF cookie over HTTP accidentally.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Set this to True to avoid transmitting the session cookie over HTTP accidentally.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Performance optimizations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Setting <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG = False</i></a> disables several features that are only useful in development. In addition, you can tune the following settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Sessions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Consider using <a href="index.html#page_312">cached sessions</a> to improve performance.</p> <p>If using database-backed sessions, regularly <a href="index.html#page_323">clear old sessions</a> to avoid storing unnecessary data.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CONN_MAX_AGE</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Enabling <a href="index.html#page_1411">persistent database connections</a> can result in a nice speed-up when connecting to the database accounts for a significant part of the request processing time.</p> <p>This helps a lot on virtualized hosts with limited network performance.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_884"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TEMPLATES</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Enabling the cached template loader often improves performance drastically, as it avoids compiling each</p> <p>template every time it needs to be rendered. When <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG = False</i>, </a>the cached template loader is enabled</p> <p>automatically. See <a href="index.html#page_2048"><i>django.template.loaders.cached.Loader</i></a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Error reporting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By the time you push your code to production, it’s hopefully robust, but you can’t rule out unexpected errors. Thankfully, Django can capture errors and notify you accordingly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>LOGGING</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Review your logging configuration before putting your website in production, and check that it works as expected as soon as you have received some traffic.</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_707">Logging</a> for details on logging.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ADMINS and MANAGERS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> will be notified of 500 errors by email.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MANAGERS</i></a> will be notified of 404 errors. <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>IGNORABLE_404_URLS</i></a> can help filter out spurious reports.</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_853">How to manage error reporting</a> for details on error reporting by email.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Error reporting by email doesn’t scale very well</p> <p>Consider using an error monitoring system such as <a href="https://docs.sentry.io/">Sentry</a> before your inbox is flooded by reports. Sentry can also aggregate logs.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Customize the default error views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django includes default views and templates for several HTTP error codes. You may want to override the default templates by creating the following templates in your root template directory: 404.html, 500.html,</p> <p>403.html, and 400.html. The <a href="index.html#page_2100">default error views</a> that use these templates should suffice for 99% of web</p> <p>applications, but you can <a href="index.html#page_285">customize them</a> as well.</p> <p id="page_885" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.4.4 How to deploy static files</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>For an introduction to the use of <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.contrib.staticfiles</i>, </a>see <a href="index.html#page_843">How to manage static files (e.g. images,</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_843">JavaScript, CSS)</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving static files in production</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The basic outline of putting static files into production consists of two steps: run the <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> com-</p> <p>mand when static files change, then arrange for the collected static files directory <a href="index.html#page_1945">(<i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> ) to be moved</p> <p>to the static file server and served. Depending on the staticfiles <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> alias, files may need to be moved</p> <p>to a new location manually or the <a href="index.html#page_1373"><i>post_process</i></a> method of the Storage class might take care of that.</p> <p>As with all deployment tasks, the devil’s in the details. Every production setup will be a bit different, so you’ll need to adapt the basic outline to fit your needs. Below are a few common patterns that might help.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving the site and your static files from the same server</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you want to serve your static files from the same server that’s already serving your site, the process may look something like:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Push your code up to the deployment server.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• On the server, run <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> to copy all the static files into <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> .</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Configure your web server to serve the files in <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> under the URL <a href="index.html#page_1946"><i>STATIC_URL</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1946">. </a>For example,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">here’s <a href="index.html#page_870">how to do this with Apache and mod_wsgi.</a></p> <p>You’ll probably want to automate this process, especially if you’ve got multiple web servers.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving static files from a dedicated server</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Most larger Django sites use a separate web server – i.e., one that’s not also running Django – for serving static files. This server often runs a different type of web server – faster but less full-featured. Some common choices are:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://nginx.org/en/">Nginx</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• A stripped-down version of <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/">Apache</a></p> <p>Configuring these servers is out of scope of this document; check each server’s respective documentation for instructions.</p> <p>Since your static file server won’t be running Django, you’ll need to modify the deployment strategy to look something like:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When your static files change, run <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> locally.</p> <p id="page_886"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Push your local <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> up to the static file server into the directory that’s being served. <a href="https://rsync.samba.org/">rsync</a> is</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a common choice for this step since it only needs to transfer the bits of static files that have changed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving static files from a cloud service or CDN</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another common tactic is to serve static files from a cloud storage provider like Amazon’s S3 and/or a CDN (content delivery network). This lets you ignore the problems of serving static files and can often make for faster-loading web pages (especially when using a CDN).</p> <p>When using these services, the basic workflow would look a bit like the above, except that instead of using rsync to transfer your static files to the server you’d need to transfer the static files to the storage provider or CDN.</p> <p>There’s any number of ways you might do this, but if the provider has an API, you can use a <a href="index.html#page_901">custom file</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_901">storage backend</a> to integrate the CDN with your Django project. If you’ve written or are using a 3rd party</p> <p>custom storage backend, you can tell <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> to use it by setting staticfiles in <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a>.</p> <p>For example, if you’ve written an S3 storage backend in myproject.storage.S3Storage you could use it with:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">STORAGES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"staticfiles"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"BACKEND"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"myproject.storage.S3Storage"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Once that’s done, all you have to do is run <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>collectstatic</i></a> and your static files would be pushed through your storage package up to S3. If you later needed to switch to a different storage provider, you may only</p> <p>have to change staticfiles in the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> setting.</p> <p>For details on how you’d write one of these backends, see <a href="index.html#page_901">How to write a custom storage class. </a>There are 3rd party apps available that provide storage backends for many common file storage APIs. A good starting</p> <p>point is the <a href="https://djangopackages.org/grids/g/storage-backends/">overview at djangopackages.org</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Learn more</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For complete details on all the settings, commands, template tags, and other pieces included in <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>contrib.staticfiles</i></a>, see <a href="index.html#page_1369">the staticfiles reference.</a></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_887" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>4.5 Other guides</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.5.1 How to authenticate using</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>REMOTE_USER</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This document describes how to make use of external authentication sources (where the web server sets the REMOTE_USER environment variable) in your Django applications. This type of authentication solution is typ-ically seen on intranet sites, with single sign-on solutions such as IIS and Integrated Windows Authentication</p> <p>or Apache and <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/docs/current/mod/mod_authnz_ldap.html">mod_authnz_ldap,</a> <a href="https://www.apereo.org/projects/cas">CAS</a>, <a href="https://uit.stanford.edu/service/authentication">WebAuth</a>, <a href="https://sourceforge.net/projects/mod-auth-sspi">mod_auth_sspi</a><a href="https://sourceforge.net/projects/mod-auth-sspi">, </a>etc.</p> <p>When the web server takes care of authentication it typically sets the REMOTE_USER environment variable</p> <p>for use in the underlying application. In Django, REMOTE_USER is made available in the <a href="index.html#page_1861"><i>request.META</i></a> at-tribute. Django can be configured to make use of the REMOTE_USER value using the RemoteUserMiddleware</p> <p>or PersistentRemoteUserMiddleware, and <a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a> classes found in <a href="index.html#page_598"><i>django.contrib.auth</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>First, you must add the <a href="index.html#page_1600"><i>django.contrib.auth.middleware.RemoteUserMiddleware</i></a> to the <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> set-</p> <p>ting after the <a href="index.html#page_1599"><i>django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">MIDDLEWARE</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"..."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.middleware.RemoteUserMiddleware"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"..."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, you must replace the <a href="index.html#page_1111"><i>ModelBackend</i></a> with <a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a> in the <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a> set-ting:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth.backends.RemoteUserBackend"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>With this setup, RemoteUserMiddleware will detect the username in request.META['REMOTE_USER'] and</p> <p>will authenticate and auto-login that user using the <a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a>.</p> <p>Be aware that this particular setup disables authentication with the default ModelBackend. This means that if the REMOTE_USER value is not set then the user is unable to log in, even using Django’s admin interface. Adding 'django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend' to the AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS list will use ModelBackend as a fallback if REMOTE_USER is absent, which will solve these issues.</p> <p>Django’s user management, such as the views in contrib.admin and the <a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>createsuperuser</i></a> management command, doesn’t integrate with remote users. These interfaces work with users stored in the database regardless of AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS.</p> <p id="page_888"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Since the RemoteUserBackend inherits from ModelBackend, you will still have all of the same permis-sions checking that is implemented in ModelBackend.</p> <p>Users with <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active=False</i></a> won’t be allowed to authenticate. Use <a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>AllowAllUsersRemoteUserBackend</i></a> if you want to allow them to.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your authentication mechanism uses a custom HTTP header and not REMOTE_USER, you can subclass RemoteUserMiddleware and set the header attribute to the desired request.META key. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.middleware</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">RemoteUserMiddleware</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CustomHeaderMiddleware</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(RemoteUserMiddleware):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">header</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"HTTP_AUTHUSER"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Be very careful if using a RemoteUserMiddleware subclass with a custom HTTP header.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">You must be sure that your front-end web server always sets or strips that header based on the ap-</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">propriate authentication checks, never permitting an end-user to submit a fake (or “spoofed”) header</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">value. Since the HTTP headers X-Auth-User and X-Auth_User (for example) both normalize to the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">HTTP_X_AUTH_USER key in request.META, you must also check that your web server doesn’t allow a</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">spoofed header using underscores in place of dashes.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">This warning doesn’t apply to RemoteUserMiddleware in its default configuration with header =</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">'REMOTE_USER', since a key that doesn’t start with HTTP_ in request.META can only be set by your WSGI</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">server, not directly from an HTTP request header.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need more control, you can create your own authentication backend that inherits from</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a> and override one or more of its attributes and methods.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using REMOTE_USER on login pages only</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The RemoteUserMiddleware authentication middleware assumes that the HTTP request header REMOTE_USER is present with all authenticated requests. That might be expected and practical when Basic HTTP Auth with htpasswd or similar mechanisms are used, but with Negotiate (GSSAPI/Kerberos) or other resource intensive authentication methods, the authentication in the front-end HTTP server is usually only set up for one or a few login URLs, and after successful authentication, the application is supposed to maintain the authenticated session itself.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1600"><i>PersistentRemoteUserMiddleware</i></a> provides support for this use case. It will maintain the authenti-cated session until explicit logout by the user. The class can be used as a drop-in replacement of</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1600"><i>RemoteUserMiddleware</i></a> in the documentation above.</p> <p id="page_889" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.5.2 How to use Django’s CSRF protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To take advantage of CSRF protection in your views, follow these steps:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. The CSRF middleware is activated by default in the <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> setting. If you override that setting,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">remember that 'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware' should come before any view mid-dleware that assume that CSRF attacks have been dealt with.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you disabled it, which is not recommended, you can use <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_protect()</i></a> on particular views you want to protect (see below).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. In any template that uses a POST form, use the <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> tag inside the <form> element if the form</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">is for an internal URL, e.g.:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">method</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>csrf_token</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This should not be done for POST forms that target external URLs, since that would cause the CSRF token to be leaked, leading to a vulnerability.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. In the corresponding view functions, ensure that <a href="index.html#page_2042"><i>RequestContext</i></a> is used to render the response so that</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">{% csrf_token %} will work properly. If you’re using the <a href="index.html#page_297"><i>render()</i></a> function, generic views, or contrib apps, you are covered already since these all use RequestContext.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using CSRF protection with AJAX</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>While the above method can be used for AJAX POST requests, it has some inconveniences: you have to remember to pass the CSRF token in as POST data with every POST request. For this reason, there is an alternative method: on each XMLHttpRequest, set a custom X-CSRFToken header (as specified by the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_HEADER_NAME</i></a> setting) to the value of the CSRF token. This is often easier because many JavaScript frameworks provide hooks that allow headers to be set on every request.</p> <p>First, you must get the CSRF token. How to do that depends on whether or not the <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_USE_SESSIONS</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY</i></a> settings are enabled.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Acquiring the token if CSRF_USE_SESSIONS and CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY are False</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The recommended source for the token is the csrftoken cookie, which will be set if you’ve enabled CSRF protection for your views as outlined above.</p> <p>The CSRF token cookie is named csrftoken by default, but you can control the cookie name via the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_NAME</i></a> setting.</p> <p>You can acquire the token like this:</p> <p id="page_890"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>function</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">getCookie(name) {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>let</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookieValue</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= null</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">document</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.cookie</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>&&</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">document</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.cookie</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>!==</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">''</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">) {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookies</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">document</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.cookie.split(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">';'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">);</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>let</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">i</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">; i</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b><</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookies.length; i</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>++</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">) {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookie</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookies[i].trim();</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>// Does this cookie string begin with the name we want?</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(cookie.substring(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, name.length</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>===</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'='</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)) {</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">cookieValue</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">decodeURIComponent</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(cookie.substring(name.length</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">));</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>break</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cookieValue;</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrftoken</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">getCookie(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'csrftoken'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">);</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The above code could be simplified by using the <a href="https://github.com/js-cookie/js-cookie/">JavaScript Cookie library</a> to replace getCookie:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrftoken</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Cookies.get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'csrftoken'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">);</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The CSRF token is also present in the DOM in a masked form, but only if explicitly included using</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> in a template. The cookie contains the canonical, unmasked token. The <a href="index.html#page_1601"><i>CsrfViewMiddleware</i></a></p> <p>will accept either. However, in order to protect against <a href="https://www.breachattack.com/">BREACH</a> attacks, it’s recommended to use a masked token.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If your view is not rendering a template containing the <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> template tag, Django</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">might not set the CSRF token cookie. This is common in cases where forms are dynamically added to</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">the page. To address this case, Django provides a view decorator which forces setting of the cookie:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="index.html#page_1409"><i>ensure_csrf_cookie()</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Acquiring the token if CSRF_USE_SESSIONS or CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY is True</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you activate <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_USE_SESSIONS</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY</i></a> , you must include the CSRF token in your HTML and read the token from the DOM with JavaScript:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>csrf_token</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">script</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrftoken</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">document</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">.querySelector(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'[name=csrfmiddlewaretoken]'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">).value;</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">script</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p id="page_891" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting the token on the AJAX request</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, you’ll need to set the header on your AJAX request. Using the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch">fetch()</a> API:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>const</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">request</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= new</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Request(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>/* URL */</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">method</span><span
