style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'POST'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">headers</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'X-CSRFToken'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrftoken},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">mode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>:</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'same-origin'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>// Do not send CSRF token to another domain.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">);</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">fetch(request).then(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>function</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(response) {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i>// ...</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">});</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using CSRF protection in Jinja2 templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s <a href="index.html#page_408"><i>Jinja2</i></a> template backend adds {{ csrf_input }} to the context of all templates which is equiva-lent to {% csrf_token %} in the Django template language. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">form</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">method</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_input</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using the decorator method</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Rather than adding CsrfViewMiddleware as a blanket protection, you can use the <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_protect()</i></a> decora-tor, which has exactly the same functionality, on particular views that need the protection. It must be used both on views that insert the CSRF token in the output, and on those that accept the POST form data. (These are often the same view function, but not always).</p> <p>Use of the decorator by itself is not recommended, since if you forget to use it, you will have a security hole. The ‘belt and braces’ strategy of using both is fine, and will incur minimal overhead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Handling rejected requests</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, a ‘403 Forbidden’ response is sent to the user if an incoming request fails the checks performed by CsrfViewMiddleware. This should usually only be seen when there is a genuine Cross Site Request Forgery, or when, due to a programming error, the CSRF token has not been included with a POST form.</p> <p>The error page, however, is not very friendly, so you may want to provide your own view for handling this</p> <p>condition. To do this, set the <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW</i></a> setting.</p> <p>CSRF failures are logged as warnings to the <a href="index.html#page_1587">django.security.csrf</a> logger.</p> <p id="page_892"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using CSRF protection with caching</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> template tag is used by a template (or the get_token function is called some other way), CsrfViewMiddleware will add a cookie and a Vary: Cookie header to the response. This means that the middleware will play well with the cache middleware if it is used as instructed (UpdateCacheMiddleware goes before all other middleware).</p> <p>However, if you use cache decorators on individual views, the CSRF middleware will not yet have been able to set the Vary header or the CSRF cookie, and the response will be cached without either one. In this case,</p> <p>on any views that will require a CSRF token to be inserted you should use the <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>django.views.decorators.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf.csrf_protect()</i></a> decorator first:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.cache</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cache_page</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.csrf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_protect</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@cache_page(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">60</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">15</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@csrf_protect</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you are using class-based views, you can refer to <a href="index.html#page_415">Decorating class-based views</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Testing and CSRF protection</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The CsrfViewMiddleware will usually be a big hindrance to testing view functions, due to the need for the CSRF token which must be sent with every POST request. For this reason, Django’s HTTP client for tests has been modified to set a flag on requests which relaxes the middleware and the csrf_protect decorator so that they no longer rejects requests. In every other respect (e.g. sending cookies etc.), they behave the same.</p> <p>If, for some reason, you want the test client to perform CSRF checks, you can create an instance of the test client that enforces CSRF checks:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.test</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_client</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Client(enforce_csrf_checks</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Edge cases</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Certain views can have unusual requirements that mean they don’t fit the normal pattern envisaged here. A number of utilities can be useful in these situations. The scenarios they might be needed in are described in the following section.</p> <p id="page_893" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Disabling CSRF protection for just a few views</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Most views requires CSRF protection, but a few do not.</p> <p>Solution: rather than disabling the middleware and applying csrf_protect to all the views that need it,</p> <p>enable the middleware and use <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_exempt()</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting the token when CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view() is not used</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are cases when CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view may not have run before your view is run - 404 and 500 handlers, for example - but you still need the CSRF token in a form.</p> <p>Solution: use <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>requires_csrf_token()</i></a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Including the CSRF token in an unprotected view</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There may be some views that are unprotected and have been exempted by csrf_exempt, but still need to include the CSRF token.</p> <p>Solution: use <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_exempt()</i></a> followed by <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>requires_csrf_token()</i>. </a>(i.e. requires_csrf_token should be the innermost decorator).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Protecting a view for only one path</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A view needs CSRF protection under one set of conditions only, and mustn’t have it for the rest of the time.</p> <p>Solution: use <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_exempt()</i></a> for the whole view function, and <a href="index.html#page_1408"><i>csrf_protect()</i></a> for the path within it that needs protection. Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.csrf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_exempt, csrf_protect</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">@csrf_exempt</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@csrf_protect</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>protected_path</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">do_something()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">some_condition():</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">protected_path(request)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>else</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">do_something_else()</span></p> <p id="page_894"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Protecting a page that uses AJAX without an HTML form</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A page makes a POST request via AJAX, and the page does not have an HTML form with a <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> that would cause the required CSRF cookie to be sent.</p> <p>Solution: use <a href="index.html#page_1409"><i>ensure_csrf_cookie()</i></a> on the view that sends the page.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CSRF protection in reusable applications</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because it is possible for the developer to turn off the CsrfViewMiddleware, all relevant views in contrib apps use the csrf_protect decorator to ensure the security of these applications against CSRF. It is recom-mended that the developers of other reusable apps that want the same guarantees also use the csrf_protect decorator on their views.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.5.3 How to create custom</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>django-admin</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>commands</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Applications can register their own actions with manage.py. For example, you might want to add a manage. py action for a Django app that you’re distributing. In this document, we will be building a custom closepoll</p> <p>command for the polls application from the <a href="index.html#page_21">tutorial</a>.</p> <p>To do this, add a management/commands directory to the application. Django will register a manage.py com-mand for each Python module in that directory whose name doesn’t begin with an underscore. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">polls/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">__init__.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">models.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">management/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">__init__.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">commands/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">__init__.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">_private.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">closepoll.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">tests.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">views.py</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this example, the closepoll command will be made available to any project that includes the polls</p> <p>application in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p>The _private.py module will not be available as a management command.</p> <p>The closepoll.py module has only one requirement – it must define a class Command that extends</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a> or one of its <a href="index.html#page_900">subclasses</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Standalone scripts</p> <p id="page_895" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Custom management commands are especially useful for running standalone scripts or for scripts that are periodically executed from the UNIX crontab or from Windows scheduled tasks control panel.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To implement the command, edit polls/management/commands/closepoll.py to look like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.management.base</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseCommand, CommandError</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">polls.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Question</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Poll</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Command</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseCommand):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">help</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Closes the specified poll for voting"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>add_arguments</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, parser):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">parser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add_argument(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"poll_ids"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, nargs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"+"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">int</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>handle</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">poll_id</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">options[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"poll_ids"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>try</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">poll</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Poll</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">poll_id)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>except</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Poll</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DoesNotExist:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>raise</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CommandError(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'Poll "%s" does not exist'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">poll_id)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">poll</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">opened</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>= False</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">poll</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">stdout</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">write(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">style</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SUCCESS(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'Successfully closed poll "%s"'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">poll_id)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: When you are using management commands and wish to provide console output, you should write to self.stdout and self.stderr, instead of printing to stdout and stderr directly. By using these proxies, it becomes much easier to test your custom command. Note also that you don’t need to end messages with a newline character, it will be added automatically, unless you specify the ending parameter:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">stdout</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">write(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Unterminated line"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, ending</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The new custom command can be called using python manage.py closepoll <poll_ids>.</p> <p>The handle() method takes one or more poll_ids and sets poll.opened to False for each one. If the user</p> <p>referenced any nonexistent polls, a <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>CommandError</i></a> is raised. The poll.opened attribute does not exist in the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_27">tutorial</a> and was added to polls.models.Question for this example.</p> <p id="page_896"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Accepting optional arguments</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The same closepoll could be easily modified to delete a given poll instead of closing it by accepting ad-</p> <p>ditional command line options. These custom options can be added in the <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>add_arguments()</i></a> method like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Command</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseCommand):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>add_arguments</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, parser):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Positional arguments</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">parser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add_argument(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"poll_ids"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, nargs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"+"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">int</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Named (optional) arguments</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">parser</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">add_argument(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"--delete"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">action</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"store_true"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">help</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Delete poll instead of closing it"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>handle</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">options[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"delete"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">poll</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">delete()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The option (delete in our example) is available in the options dict parameter of the handle method. See the</p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#module-argparse">argparse</a> Python documentation for more about add_argument usage.</p> <p>In addition to being able to add custom command line options, all <a href="index.html#page_1433">management commands</a> can accept some</p> <p>default options such as<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--verbosity</i></a> and<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--traceback</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Management commands and locales</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, management commands are executed with the current active locale.</p> <p>If, for some reason, your custom management command must run without an active locale (for exam-ple, to prevent translated content from being inserted into the database), deactivate translations using the</p> <p>@no_translations decorator on your <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>handle()</i></a> method:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.management.base</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">BaseCommand, no_translations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Command</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseCommand):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_897" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@no_translations</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>handle</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Since translation deactivation requires access to configured settings, the decorator can’t be used for com-mands that work without configured settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Testing</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Information on how to test custom management commands can be found in the <a href="index.html#page_513">testing docs</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overriding commands</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django registers the built-in commands and then searches for commands in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> in reverse. During the search, if a command name duplicates an already registered command, the newly discovered command overrides the first.</p> <p>In other words, to override a command, the new command must have the same name and its app must be</p> <p>before the overridden command’s app in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p>Management commands from third-party apps that have been unintentionally overridden can be made available under a new name by creating a new command in one of your project’s apps (ordered before the</p> <p>third-party app in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>) which imports the Command of the overridden command.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Command objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BaseCommand</b></p> <p>The base class from which all management commands ultimately derive.</p> <p>Use this class if you want access to all of the mechanisms which parse the command-line arguments and work out what code to call in response; if you don’t need to change any of that behavior, consider using one of its</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_900">subclasses</a>.</p> <p>Subclassing the <a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a> class requires that you implement the <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>handle()</i></a> method.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Attributes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All attributes can be set in your derived class and can be used in <a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a>’s <a href="index.html#page_900">subclasses</a><a href="index.html#page_900">.</a></p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>help</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A short description of the command, which will be printed in the help message when the user runs the command python manage.py help <command>.</p> <p id="page_898"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>missing_args_message</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If your command defines mandatory positional arguments, you can customize the message error re-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">turned in the case of missing arguments. The default is output by <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#module-argparse">argparse</a> (“too few arguments”).</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>output_transaction</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A boolean indicating whether the command outputs SQL statements; if True, the output will automat-ically be wrapped with BEGIN; and COMMIT;. Default value is False.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>requires_migrations_checks</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A boolean; if True, the command prints a warning if the set of migrations on disk don’t match the migrations in the database. A warning doesn’t prevent the command from executing. Default value is False .</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>requires_system_checks</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A list or tuple of tags, e.g. [Tags.staticfiles, Tags.models]. System checks <a href="index.html#page_759">registered in the chosen</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_759">tags</a> will be checked for errors prior to executing the command. The value '__all__' can be used to specify that all system checks should be performed. Default value is '__all__'.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>style</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">An instance attribute that helps create colored output when writing to stdout or stderr. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">stdout</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">write(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">style</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SUCCESS(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"..."</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">See <a href="index.html#page_1465">Syntax coloring</a> to learn how to modify the color palette and to see the available styles (use upper-cased versions of the “roles” described in that section).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you pass the<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--no-color</i></a> option when running your command, all self.style() calls will return the original string uncolored.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>suppressed_base_arguments</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The default command options to suppress in the help output. This should be a set of option names (e.g. '--verbosity'). The default values for the suppressed options are still passed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a> has a few methods that can be overridden but only the <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>handle()</i></a> method must be implemented.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Implementing a constructor in a subclass</p> <p>If you implement __init__ in your subclass of <a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a>, you must call <a href="index.html#page_897"><i>BaseCommand</i></a>’s __init__:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Command</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(BaseCommand):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">super</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p id="page_899" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>create_parser</b>(prog_name, subcommand, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a CommandParser instance, which is an <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#argparse.ArgumentParser">ArgumentParser</a> subclass with a few customizations for Django.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You can customize the instance by overriding this method and calling super() with kwargs of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html#argparse.ArgumentParser">ArgumentParser</a> parameters.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>add_arguments</b>(parser)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Entry point to add parser arguments to handle command line arguments passed to the command. Cus-tom commands should override this method to add both positional and optional arguments accepted by the command. Calling super() is not needed when directly subclassing BaseCommand.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>get_version</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the Django version, which should be correct for all built-in Django commands. User-supplied commands can override this method to return their own version.</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>execute</b>(*args, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Tries to execute this command, performing system checks if needed (as controlled by the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_898"><i>requires_system_checks</i></a> attribute). If the command raises a <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>CommandError</i></a>, it’s intercepted and printed to stderr.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Calling a management command in your code</p> <p>execute() should not be called directly from your code to execute a command. Use <a href="index.html#page_1468"><i>call_command()</i></a> instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>handle</b>(*args, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The actual logic of the command. Subclasses must implement this method.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It may return a string which will be printed to stdout (wrapped by BEGIN; and COMMIT; if</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_898"><i>output_transaction</i></a> is True).</p> <p>BaseCommand.<b>check</b>(app_configs=None, tags=None, display_num_errors=False,</p> <p style="text-align:right">include_deployment_checks=False, fail_level=checks.ERROR, databases=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Uses the system check framework to inspect the entire Django project for potential problems. Serious</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">problems are raised as a <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>CommandError</i></a>; warnings are output to stderr; minor notifications are output to stdout.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If app_configs and tags are both None, all system checks are performed except deployment and database related checks. tags can be a list of check tags, like compatibility or models.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You can pass include_deployment_checks=True to also perform deployment checks, and list of database aliases in the databases to run database related checks against them.</p> <p id="page_900"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BaseCommand subclasses</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class AppCommand</b></p> <p>A management command which takes one or more installed application labels as arguments, and does some-thing with each of them.</p> <p>Rather than implementing <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>handle()</i></a>, subclasses must implement <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>handle_app_config()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_900">, </a>which will be called once for each application.</p> <p>AppCommand.<b>handle_app_config</b>(app_config, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Perform the command’s actions for app_config, which will be an <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> instance corresponding to an application label given on the command line.</p> <p><b>class LabelCommand</b></p> <p>A management command which takes one or more arbitrary arguments (labels) on the command line, and does something with each of them.</p> <p>Rather than implementing <a href="index.html#page_899"><i>handle()</i>, </a>subclasses must implement <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>handle_label()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_900">, </a>which will be called once for each label.</p> <p>LabelCommand.<b>label</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A string describing the arbitrary arguments passed to the command. The string is used in the usage text and error messages of the command. Defaults to 'label'.</p> <p>LabelCommand.<b>handle_label</b>(label, **options)</p> <p style="text-align:center">Perform the command’s actions for label, which will be the string as given on the command line.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Command exceptions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception CommandError</b>( returncode=1)</p> <p>Exception class indicating a problem while executing a management command.</p> <p>If this exception is raised during the execution of a management command from a command line console, it will be caught and turned into a nicely-printed error message to the appropriate output stream (i.e., stderr); as a result, raising this exception (with a sensible description of the error) is the preferred way to indicate that something has gone wrong in the execution of a command. It accepts the optional returncode argument to customize the exit status for the management command to exit with, using <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.exit">sys.exit().</a></p> <p>If a management command is called from code through <a href="index.html#page_1468"><i>call_command()</i></a>, it’s up to you to catch the exception when needed.</p> <p id="page_901" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>4.5.4 How to write a custom storage class</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to provide custom file storage – a common example is storing files on some remote system – you can do so by defining a custom storage class. You’ll need to follow these steps:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Your custom storage system must be a subclass of django.core.files.storage.Storage:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Storage</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyStorage</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(Storage):</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Django must be able to instantiate your storage system without any arguments. This means that any</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">settings should be taken from django.conf.settings:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.conf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Storage</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyStorage</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Storage):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__init__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, option</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=None</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>if not</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">option:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:7em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">option</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">settings</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CUSTOM_STORAGE_OPTIONS</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Your storage class must implement the <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>_open()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>_save()</i></a> methods, along with any other methods</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">appropriate to your storage class. See below for more on these methods.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In addition, if your class provides local file storage, it must override the path() method.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. Your storage class must be <a href="index.html#page_462">deconstructible</a> so it can be serialized when it’s used on a field in a migration.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">As long as your field has arguments that are themselves <a href="index.html#page_461">serializable</a>, you can use the django.utils. deconstruct.deconstructible class decorator for this (that’s what Django uses on FileSystemStor-age).</p> <p>By default, the following methods raise NotImplementedError and will typically have to be overridden:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1481"><i>Storage.delete()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1481"><i>Storage.exists()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1482"><i>Storage.listdir()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1482"><i>Storage.size()</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1482"><i>Storage.url()</i></a></p> <p>Note however that not all these methods are required and may be deliberately omitted. As it happens, it is possible to leave each method unimplemented and still have a working Storage.</p> <p id="page_902"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By way of example, if listing the contents of certain storage backends turns out to be expensive, you might decide not to implement Storage.listdir().</p> <p>Another example would be a backend that only handles writing to files. In this case, you would not need to implement any of the above methods.</p> <p>Ultimately, which of these methods are implemented is up to you. Leaving some methods unimplemented will result in a partial (possibly broken) interface.</p> <p>You’ll also usually want to use hooks specifically designed for custom storage objects. These are:</p> <p><b>_open</b>(name, mode='rb')</p> <p>Required.</p> <p>Called by Storage.open(), this is the actual mechanism the storage class uses to open the file. This must return a File object, though in most cases, you’ll want to return some subclass here that implements logic spe-</p> <p>cific to the backend storage system. The <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#FileNotFoundError">FileNotFoundError</a> exception should be raised when a file doesn’t exist.</p> <p><b>_save</b>(name, content)</p> <p>Called by Storage.save(). The name will already have gone through get_valid_name() and get_available_name(), and the content will be a File object itself.</p> <p>Should return the actual name of the file saved (usually the name passed in, but if the storage needs to change the file name return the new name instead).</p> <p><b>get_valid_name</b>(name)</p> <p>Returns a filename suitable for use with the underlying storage system. The name argument passed to this method is either the original filename sent to the server or, if upload_to is a callable, the filename returned by that method after any path information is removed. Override this to customize how non-standard characters are converted to safe filenames.</p> <p>The code provided on Storage retains only alpha-numeric characters, periods and underscores from the original filename, removing everything else.</p> <p><b>get_alternative_name</b>(file_root, file_ext)</p> <p>Returns an alternative filename based on the file_root and file_ext parameters. By default, an under-score plus a random 7 character alphanumeric string is appended to the filename before the extension.</p> <p><b>get_available_name</b>(name, max_length=None)</p> <p>Returns a filename that is available in the storage mechanism, possibly taking the provided filename into account. The name argument passed to this method will have already cleaned to a filename valid for the storage system, according to the get_valid_name() method described above.</p> <p>The length of the filename will not exceed max_length, if provided. If a free unique filename cannot be</p> <p>found, a <a href="index.html#page_1471"><i>SuspiciousFileOperation</i></a> exception is raised.</p> <p id="page_903" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If a file with name already exists, get_alternative_name() is called to obtain an alternative name.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Use your custom storage engine</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The first step to using your custom storage with Django is to tell Django about the file storage backend you’ll</p> <p>be using. This is done using the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> setting. This setting maps storage aliases, which are a way to refer to a specific storage throughout Django, to a dictionary of settings for that specific storage backend. The</p> <p>settings in the inner dictionaries are described fully in the <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> documentation.</p> <p>Storages are then accessed by alias from the <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>django.core.files.storage.storages</i></a> dictionary:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">example_storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"example"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also:</p> <p>The <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/community/">Django community aggregator, </a>where we aggregate content from the global Django community. Many writers in the aggregator write this sort of how-to material.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_904"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <h2 id="page_905" style="text-align:right"><b>CHAPTER</b></h2> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>FIVE</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>DJANGO FAQ</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.1 FAQ: General</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.1 Why does this project exist?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django grew from a very practical need: World Online, a newspaper web operation, is responsible for building intensive web applications on journalism deadlines. In the fast-paced newsroom, World Online often has only a matter of hours to take a complicated web application from concept to public launch.</p> <p>At the same time, the World Online web developers have consistently been perfectionists when it comes to following best practices of web development.</p> <p>In fall 2003, the World Online developers (Adrian Holovaty and Simon Willison) ditched PHP and began using Python to develop its websites. As they built intensive, richly interactive sites such as Lawrence.com, they began to extract a generic web development framework that let them build web applications more and more quickly. They tweaked this framework constantly, adding improvements over two years.</p> <p>In summer 2005, World Online decided to open-source the resulting software, Django. Django would not be</p> <p>possible without a whole host of open-source projects – <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/">Apache</a>, <a href="https://www.python.org/">Python</a>, and <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/">PostgreSQL</a> to name a few – and we’re thrilled to be able to give something back to the open-source community.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.2 What does “Django” mean, and how do you pronounce it?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django is named after <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Django_Reinhardt">Django Reinhardt</a>, a jazz manouche guitarist from the 1930s to early 1950s. To this day, he’s considered one of the best guitarists of all time.</p> <p>Listen to his music. You’ll like it.</p> <p>Django is pronounced JANG-oh. Rhymes with FANG-oh. The “D” is silent.</p> <p>We’ve also recorded an <a href="https://www.red-bean.com/~adrian/django_pronunciation.mp3">audio clip of the pronunciation</a>.</p> <p id="page_906"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.3 Is Django stable?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Yes, it’s quite stable. Companies like Disqus, Instagram, Pinterest, and Mozilla have been using Django for many years. Sites built on Django have weathered traffic spikes of over 50 thousand hits per second.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.4 Does Django scale?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Yes. Compared to development time, hardware is cheap, and so Django is designed to take advantage of as much hardware as you can throw at it.</p> <p>Django uses a “shared-nothing” architecture, which means you can add hardware at any level – database servers, caching servers or web/application servers.</p> <p>The framework cleanly separates components such as its database layer and application layer. And it ships</p> <p>with a simple-yet-powerful <a href="index.html#page_599">cache framework.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.5 Who’s behind this?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django was originally developed at World Online, the web department of a newspaper in Lawrence, Kansas,</p> <p>USA. Django’s now run by an international <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/foundation/teams/">team of volunteers</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.6 How is Django licensed?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django is distributed under <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/LICENSE">the 3-clause BSD license</a>. This is an open source license granting broad permissions to modify and redistribute Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.7 Why does Django include Python’s license file?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django includes code from the Python standard library. Python is distributed under a permissive open source</p> <p>license. <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/LICENSE.python">A copy of the Python license</a> is included with Django for compliance with Python’s terms.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.8 Which sites use Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://builtwithdjango.com/projects/">BuiltWithDjango.com</a> features a constantly growing list of Django-powered sites.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_907" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.9 Django appears to be a MVC framework, but you call the Controller the “view”,</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>and the View the “template”. How come you don’t use the standard names?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Well, the standard names are debatable.</p> <p>In our interpretation of MVC, the “view” describes the data that gets presented to the user. It’s not necessarily how the data looks, but which data is presented. The view describes which data you see, not how you see it. It’s a subtle distinction.</p> <p>So, in our case, a “view” is the Python callback function for a particular URL, because that callback function describes which data is presented.</p> <p>Furthermore, it’s sensible to separate content from presentation – which is where templates come in. In Django, a “view” describes which data is presented, but a view normally delegates to a template, which describes how the data is presented.</p> <p>Where does the “controller” fit in, then? In Django’s case, it’s probably the framework itself: the machinery that sends a request to the appropriate view, according to the Django URL configuration.</p> <p>If you’re hungry for acronyms, you might say that Django is a “MTV” framework – that is, “model”, “tem-plate”, and “view.” That breakdown makes much more sense.</p> <p>At the end of the day, it comes down to getting stuff done. And, regardless of how things are named, Django gets stuff done in a way that’s most logical to us.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.10 <Framework X> does <feature Y> – why doesn’t Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We’re well aware that there are other awesome web frameworks out there, and we’re not averse to borrowing ideas where appropriate. However, Django was developed precisely because we were unhappy with the status quo, so please be aware that “because <Framework X> does it” is not going to be sufficient reason to add a given feature to Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.11 Why did you write all of Django from scratch, instead of using other Python</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>libraries?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Django was originally written, Adrian and Simon spent quite a bit of time exploring the various Python web frameworks available.</p> <p>In our opinion, none of them were completely up to snuff.</p> <p>We’re picky. You might even call us perfectionists. (With deadlines.)</p> <p>Over time, we stumbled across open-source libraries that did things we’d already implemented. It was reas-suring to see other people solving similar problems in similar ways, but it was too late to integrate outside code: We’d already written, tested and implemented our own framework bits in several production settings – and our own code met our needs delightfully.</p> <p id="page_908"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In most cases, however, we found that existing frameworks/tools inevitably had some sort of fundamental, fatal flaw that made us squeamish. No tool fit our philosophies 100%.</p> <p>Like we said: We’re picky.</p> <p>We’ve documented our philosophies on the <a href="index.html#page_2104">design philosophies page</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.12 Is Django a content-management-system (CMS)?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>No, Django is not a CMS, or any sort of “turnkey product” in and of itself. It’s a web framework; it’s a programming tool that lets you build websites.</p> <p>For example, it doesn’t make much sense to compare Django to something like <a href="https://www.drupal.org/">Drupal, </a>because Django is something you use to create things like Drupal.</p> <p>Yes, Django’s automatic admin site is fantastic and timesaving – but the admin site is one module of Django the framework. Furthermore, although Django has special conveniences for building “CMS-y” apps, that doesn’t mean it’s not just as appropriate for building “non-CMS-y” apps (whatever that means!).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.13 How can I download the Django documentation to read it offline?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Django docs are available in the docs directory of each Django tarball release. These docs are in reST (reStructuredText) format, and each text file corresponds to a web page on the official Django site.</p> <p>Because the documentation is <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/docs">stored in revision control</a>, you can browse documentation changes just like you can browse code changes.</p> <p>Technically, the docs on Django’s site are generated from the latest development versions of those reST documents, so the docs on the Django site may offer more information than the docs that come with the latest Django release.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.1.14 How do I cite Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>It’s difficult to give an official citation format, for two reasons: citation formats can vary wildly between publications, and citation standards for software are still a matter of some debate.</p> <p>For example, <a href="https://apastyle.apa.org/">APA style, </a>would dictate something like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Django (Version 1.5) [Computer Software]. (2013). Retrieved from https://www.djangoproject.com/.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>However, the only true guide is what your publisher will accept, so get a copy of those guidelines and fill in the gaps as best you can.</p> <p>If your referencing style guide requires a publisher name, use “Django Software Foundation”.</p> <p>If you need a publishing location, use “Lawrence, Kansas”.</p> <p id="page_909" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need a web address, use <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/">https://www.djangoproject.com/.</a></p> <p>If you need a name, just use “Django”, without any tagline.</p> <p>If you need a publication date, use the year of release of the version you’re referencing (e.g., 2013 for v1.5)</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.2 FAQ: Installation</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.2.1 How do I get started?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/download/">Download the code</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Install Django (read the <a href="index.html#page_20">installation guide</a>).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Walk through the <a href="index.html#page_21">tutorial</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. Check out the rest of the <a href="index.html#page_7">documentation</a>, and <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/community/">ask questions</a> if you run into trouble.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.2.2 What are Django’s prerequisites?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django requires Python. See the table in the next question for the versions of Python that work with each version of Django. Other Python libraries may be required for some use cases, but you’ll receive an error about them as they’re needed.</p> <p>For a development environment – if you just want to experiment with Django – you don’t need to have a separate web server installed or database server.</p> <p>Django comes with its own <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>lightweight development server</i></a>. For a production environment, Django fol-</p> <p>lows the WSGI spec, <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-3333/">PEP 3333</a>, which means it can run on a variety of web servers. See <a href="index.html#page_865">Deploying Django</a> for more information.</p> <p>Django runs <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/">SQLite</a> by default, which is included in Python installations. For a production environment, we</p> <p>recommend <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/">PostgreSQL; </a>but we also officially support <a href="https://mariadb.org/">MariaDB</a>, <a href="https://www.mysql.com/">MySQL</a><a href="https://www.mysql.com/">,</a> <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/">SQLite</a><a href="https://www.sqlite.org/">, </a>and <a href="https://www.oracle.com/">Oracle</a>. See <a href="index.html#page_1410">Supported</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1410">Databases</a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.2.3 What Python version can I use with Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:9em">Django version Python versions</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">4.2 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 (added in 4.2.8)</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">5.0 3.10, 3.11, 3.12</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">5.1 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 (added in 5.1.3)</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">5.2 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13</p> <p id="page_910"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For each version of Python, only the latest micro release (A.B.C) is officially supported. You can find the</p> <p>latest micro version for each series on the <a href="https://www.python.org/downloads/">Python download page</a>.</p> <p>Typically, we will support a Python version up to and including the first Django LTS release whose security support ends after security support for that version of Python ends. For example, Python 3.9 security support ends in October 2025 and Django 4.2 LTS security support ends in April 2026. Therefore Django 4.2 is the last version to support Python 3.9.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.2.4 What Python version should I use with Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Since newer versions of Python are often faster, have more features, and are better supported, the latest version of Python 3 is recommended.</p> <p>You don’t lose anything in Django by using an older release, but you don’t take advantage of the improve-ments and optimizations in newer Python releases. Third-party applications for use with Django are free to set their own version requirements.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.2.5 Should I use the stable version or development version?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Generally, if you’re using code in production, you should be using a stable release. The Django project pub-lishes a full stable release every eight months or so, with bugfix updates in between. These stable releases contain the API that is covered by our backwards compatibility guarantees; if you write code against stable releases, you shouldn’t have any problems upgrading when the next official version is released.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.3 FAQ: Using Django</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.3.1 Why do I get an error about importing</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</b></span><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Make sure that:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The environment variable <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> is set to a fully-qualified Python module (i.e.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">mysite.settings).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Said module is on sys.path (import mysite.settings should work).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The module doesn’t contain syntax errors.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_911" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.3.2 I can’t stand your template language. Do I have to use it?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We happen to think our template engine is the best thing since chunky bacon, but we recognize that choosing a template language runs close to religion. There’s nothing about Django that requires using the template language, so if you’re attached to Jinja2, Mako, or whatever, feel free to use those.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.3.3 Do I have to use your model/database layer?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Nope. Just like the template system, the model/database layer is decoupled from the rest of the framework.</p> <p>The one exception is: If you use a different database library, you won’t get to use Django’s automatically-generated admin site. That app is coupled to the Django database layer.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.3.4 How do I use image and file fields?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Using a <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField</i></a> or an <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a> in a model takes a few steps:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. In your settings file, you’ll need to define <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> as the full path to a directory where you’d like</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Django to store uploaded files. (For performance, these files are not stored in the database.) Define</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> as the base public URL of that directory. Make sure that this directory is writable by the web server’s user account.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Add the <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a> to your model, defining the <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>upload_to</i></a> option to specify a subdirec-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tory of <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> to use for uploaded files.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. All that will be stored in your database is a path to the file (relative to <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> ). You’ll most likely</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">want to use the convenience <a href="index.html#page_1634"><i>url</i></a> attribute provided by Django. For example, if your <a href="index.html#page_1638"><i>ImageField</i></a> is called mug_shot, you can get the absolute path to your image in a template with {{ object.mug_shot. url }}.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.3.5 How do I make a variable available to all my templates?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Sometimes your templates all need the same thing. A common example would be dynamically generated menus. At first glance, it seems logical to add a common dictionary to the template context.</p> <p>The best way to do this in Django is to use a RequestContext. Details on how to do this are here: <a href="index.html#page_2042">Using</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_2042">RequestContext</a>.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_912"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.4 FAQ: Getting Help</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.4.1 How do I do X? Why doesn’t Y work? Where can I go to get help?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>First, please check if your question is answered on the <a href="index.html#page_905">FAQ. </a>Also, search for answers using your favorite</p> <p>search engine, and in <a href="https://forum.djangoproject.com/">the forum.</a></p> <p>If you can’t find an answer, please take a few minutes to formulate your question well. Explaining the prob-</p> <p>lems you are facing clearly will help others help you. See the StackOverflow guide on <a href="https://stackoverflow.com/help/how-to-ask">asking good questions</a>.</p> <p>Then, please post it in one of the following channels:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The Django Forum section <a href="https://forum.djangoproject.com/c/users/6">“Using Django”</a>. This is for web-based discussions.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The <a href="index.html#page_2820">django-users</a> mailing list. This is for email-based discussions.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The <a href="https://discord.gg/xcRH6mN4fa">Django Discord server</a> for chat-based discussions.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The <a href="https://web.libera.chat/#django">#django IRC channel</a> on the Libera.Chat IRC network. This is for chat-based discussions. If you’re</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">new to IRC, see the <a href="https://libera.chat/guides/connect">Libera.Chat documentation</a> for different ways to connect.</p> <p>In all these channels please abide by the <a href="https://www.djangoproject.com/conduct/">Django Code of Conduct. </a>In summary, being friendly and patient, considerate, respectful, and careful in your choice of words.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.4.2 Why hasn’t my message appeared on</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><i><b>django-users</b></i></span><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_2820">django-users</a> has a lot of subscribers. This is good for the community, as it means many people are available</p> <p>to contribute answers to questions. Unfortunately, it also means that <a href="index.html#page_2820">django-users</a> is an attractive target for spammers.</p> <p>In order to combat the spam problem, when you join the <a href="index.html#page_2820">django-users</a> mailing list, we manually moderate the first message you send to the list. This means that spammers get caught, but it also means that your first question to the list might take a little longer to get answered. We apologize for any inconvenience that this policy may cause.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.4.3 Nobody answered my question! What should I do?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Try making your question more specific, or provide a better example of your problem.</p> <p>As with most open-source projects, the folks on these channels are volunteers. If nobody has answered your question, it may be because nobody knows the answer, it may be because nobody can understand the ques-tion, or it may be that everybody that can help is busy.</p> <p>You can also try asking on a different channel. But please don’t post your question in all three channels in quick succession.</p> <p id="page_913" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You might notice we have a second mailing list, called <a href="index.html#page_2821">django-developers</a>. This list is for discussion of the development of Django itself. Please don’t email support questions to this mailing list. Asking a tech support</p> <p>question there is considered impolite, and you will likely be directed to ask on <a href="index.html#page_2820">django-users</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.4.4 I think I’ve found a bug! What should I do?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Detailed instructions on how to handle a potential bug can be found in our <a href="index.html#page_2808">Guide to contributing to Django</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.4.5 I think I’ve found a security problem! What should I do?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you think you’ve found a security problem with Django, please send a message to <a href="mailto:security@djangoproject.com">secu-</a></p> <p><a href="mailto:security@djangoproject.com">rity@djangoproject.com. </a>This is a private list only open to long-time, highly trusted Django developers, and its archives are not publicly readable.</p> <p>Due to the sensitive nature of security issues, we ask that if you think you have found a security problem, please don’t post a message on the forum, the Discord server, IRC, or one of the public mailing lists. Django</p> <p>has a <a href="index.html#page_2827">policy for handling security issues</a>; while a defect is outstanding, we would like to minimize any damage that could be inflicted through public knowledge of that defect.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.5 FAQ: Databases and models</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.1 How can I see the raw SQL queries Django is running?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Make sure your Django <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting is set to True. Then do this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">queries</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[{'sql': 'SELECT polls_polls.id, polls_polls.question, polls_polls.pub_date FROM polls_polls',</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'time': '0.002'}]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>connection.queries is only available if <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> is True. It’s a list of dictionaries in order of query execution. Each dictionary has the following:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sql- The raw SQL statement</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• time- How long the statement took to execute, in seconds.</p> <p>connection.queries includes all SQL statements – INSERTs, UPDATES, SELECTs, etc. Each time your app hits the database, the query will be recorded.</p> <p>If you are using <a href="index.html#page_220">multiple databases, </a>you can use the same interface on each member of the connections dictionary:</p> <p id="page_914"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connections</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connections[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_db_alias"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">queries</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to clear the query list manually at any point in your functions, call reset_queries(), like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">reset_queries</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">reset_queries()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.2 Can I use Django with a preexisting database?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Yes. See <a href="index.html#page_775">Integrating with a legacy database</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.3 If I make changes to a model, how do I update the database?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Take a look at Django’s support for <a href="index.html#page_446"><i>schema migrations</i>.</a></p> <p>If you don’t mind clearing data, your project’s manage.py utility has a <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>flush</i></a> option to reset the database to</p> <p>the state it was in immediately after <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> was executed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.4 Do Django models support multiple-column primary keys?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>No. Only single-column primary keys are supported.</p> <p>But this isn’t an issue in practice, because there’s nothing stopping you from adding other constraints (using the unique_together model option or creating the constraint directly in your database), and enforcing the uniqueness at that level. Single-column primary keys are needed for things such as the admin interface to work; e.g., you need a single value to specify an object to edit or delete.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.5 Does Django support NoSQL databases?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>NoSQL databases are not officially supported by Django itself.
