There are, however, a number of side projects and forks which allow NoSQL functionality in Django.</p> <p>You can take a look on <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/wiki/NoSqlSupport">the wiki page</a> which discusses some projects.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_915" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.5.6 How do I add database-specific options to my CREATE TABLE statements, such</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>as specifying MyISAM as the table type?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We try to avoid adding special cases in the Django code to accommodate all the database-specific options</p> <p>such as table type, etc. If you’d like to use any of these options, create a migration with a <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>RunSQL</i></a> operation that contains ALTER TABLE statements that do what you want to do.</p> <p>For example, if you’re using MySQL and want your tables to use the MyISAM table type, use the following SQL:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ALTER TABLE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp_mytable ENGINE</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">MyISAM;</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.6 FAQ: The admin</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.1 I can’t log in. When I enter a valid username and password, it just brings up the</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>login page again, with no error messages.</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The login cookie isn’t being set correctly, because the domain of the cookie sent out by Django doesn’t match</p> <p>the domain in your browser. Try setting the <a href="index.html#page_1942"><i>SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN</i></a> setting to match your domain. For ex-</p> <p>ample, if you’re going to <a href="https://www.example.com/admin/">“https://www.example.com/admin/</a>” in your browser, set SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN = 'www.example.com'.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.2 I can’t log in. When I enter a valid username and password, it brings up the</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>login page again, with a “Please enter a correct username and password” error.</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re sure your username and password are correct, make sure your user account has <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_staff</i></a> set to True. The admin site only allows access to users with those two fields both set to True.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.3 How do I automatically set a field’s value to the user who last edited the object</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>in the admin?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1038"><i>ModelAdmin</i></a> class provides customization hooks that allow you to transform an object as it saved, using</p> <p>details from the request. By extracting the current user from the request, and customizing the <a href="index.html#page_1063"><i>save_model()</i></a></p> <p>hook, you can update an object to reflect the user that edited it. See <a href="index.html#page_1063">the documentation on ModelAdmin</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1063">methods</a> for an example.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_916"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.4 How do I limit admin access so that objects can only be edited by the users who</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>created them?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1038"><i>ModelAdmin</i></a> class also provides customization hooks that allow you to control the visibility and editabil-</p> <p>ity of objects in the admin. Using the same trick of extracting the user from the request, the <a href="index.html#page_1073"><i>get_queryset()</i></a></p> <p>and <a href="index.html#page_1072"><i>has_change_permission()</i></a> can be used to control the visibility and editability of objects in the admin.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.5 My admin-site CSS and images showed up fine using the development server,</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>but they’re not displaying when using mod_wsgi.</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_871">serving the admin files</a> in the “How to use Django with mod_wsgi” documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.6 My “list_filter” contains a ManyToManyField, but the filter doesn’t display.</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django won’t bother displaying the filter for a ManyToManyField if there are no related objects.</p> <p>For example, if your <a href="index.html#page_1055"><i>list_filter</i></a> includes <a href="index.html#page_1360">sites</a><a href="index.html#page_1360">, </a>and there are no sites in your database, it won’t display a “Site” filter. In that case, filtering by site would be meaningless.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.7 Some objects aren’t appearing in the admin.</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Inconsistent row counts may be caused by missing foreign key values or a foreign key field incorrectly set to</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1615"><i>null=False</i></a> . If you have a record with a <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> pointing to a nonexistent object and that foreign key</p> <p>is included is <a href="index.html#page_1048"><i>list_display</i>, </a>the record will not be shown in the admin changelist because the Django model is declaring an integrity constraint that is not implemented at the database level.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.8 How can I customize the functionality of the admin interface?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You’ve got several options. If you want to piggyback on top of an add/change form that Django automat-</p> <p>ically generates, you can attach arbitrary JavaScript modules to the page via the model’s class Admin <a href="index.html#page_1076">js</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1076">parameter</a>. That parameter is a list of URLs, as strings, pointing to JavaScript modules that will be included within the admin form via a <script> tag.</p> <p>If you want more flexibility than is feasible by tweaking the auto-generated forms, feel free to write custom views for the admin. The admin is powered by Django itself, and you can write custom views that hook into the authentication system, check permissions and do whatever else they need to do.</p> <p>If you want to customize the look-and-feel of the admin interface, read the next question.</p> <p id="page_917" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.9 The dynamically-generated admin site is ugly! How can I change it?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>We like it, but if you don’t agree, you can modify the admin site’s presentation by editing the CSS stylesheet and/or associated image files. The site is built using semantic HTML and plenty of CSS hooks, so any changes you’d like to make should be possible by editing the stylesheet.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.10 What browsers are supported for using the admin?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The admin provides a fully-functional experience to the recent versions of modern, web standards compliant browsers. On desktop this means Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Safari, and others.</p> <p>On mobile and tablet devices, the admin provides a responsive experience for web standards compliant browsers. This includes the major browsers on both Android and iOS.</p> <p>Depending on feature support, there may be minor stylistic differences between browsers. These are consid-ered acceptable variations in rendering.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.6.11 What assistive technologies are supported for using the admin?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The admin is intended to be compatible with a wide range of assistive technologies, but there are currently many blockers. The support target is all latest versions of major assistive technologies, including Dragon, JAWS, NVDA, Orca, TalkBack, Voice Control, VoiceOver iOS, VoiceOver macOS, Windows Contrast Themes, ZoomText, and screen magnifiers.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.7 FAQ: Contributing code</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.7.1 How can I get started contributing code to Django?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Thanks for asking! We’ve written an entire document devoted to this question. It’s titled <a href="index.html#page_2751">Contributing to</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_2751">Django.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.7.2 I submitted a bug fix several weeks ago. Why are you ignoring my contribution?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Don’t worry: We’re not ignoring you!</p> <p>It’s important to understand there is a difference between “a ticket is being ignored” and “a ticket has not been attended to yet.” Django’s ticket system contains hundreds of open tickets, of various degrees of impact on end-user functionality, and Django’s developers have to review and prioritize.</p> <p>On top of that: the people who work on Django are all volunteers. As a result, the amount of time that we have to work on the framework is limited and will vary from week to week depending on our spare time. If we’re busy, we may not be able to spend as much time on Django as we might want.</p> <p id="page_918"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The best way to make sure tickets do not get hung up on the way to checkin is to make it dead easy, even for someone who may not be intimately familiar with that area of the code, to understand the problem and verify the fix:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Are there clear instructions on how to reproduce the bug? If this touches a dependency (such as Pillow),</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a contrib module, or a specific database, are those instructions clear enough even for someone not familiar with it?</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If there are several branches linked to the ticket, is it clear what each one does, which ones can be</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ignored and which matter?</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Does the change include a unit test? If not, is there a very clear explanation why not? A test expresses</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">succinctly what the problem is, and shows that the branch actually fixes it.</p> <p>If your contribution is not suitable for inclusion in Django, we won’t ignore it – we’ll close the ticket. So if your ticket is still open, it doesn’t mean we’re ignoring you; it just means we haven’t had time to look at it yet.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.7.3 When and how might I remind the team of a change I care about?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A polite, well-timed message in the forum/branch is one way to get attention. To determine the right time, you need to keep an eye on the schedule. If you post your message right before a release deadline, you’re not likely to get the sort of attention you require.</p> <p>Gentle reminders in the #contributing-getting-started channel in the <a href="https://discord.gg/xcRH6mN4fa">Django Discord server</a> can work.</p> <p>Another way to get traction is to pull several related tickets together. When someone sits down to review a bug in an area they haven’t touched for a while, it can take a few minutes to remember all the fine details of how that area of code works. If you collect several minor bug fixes together into a similarly themed group, you make an attractive target, as the cost of coming up to speed on an area of code can be spread over multiple tickets.</p> <p>Please refrain from emailing anyone personally or repeatedly raising the same issue over and over again. This sort of behavior will not gain you any additional attention – certainly not the attention that you need in order to get your issue addressed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.7.4 But I’ve reminded you several times and you keep ignoring my contribution!</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Seriously - we’re not ignoring you. If your contribution is not suitable for inclusion in Django, we will close the ticket. For all the other tickets, we need to prioritize our efforts, which means that some tickets will be addressed before others.</p> <p>One of the criteria that is used to prioritize bug fixes is the number of people that will likely be affected by a given bug. Bugs that have the potential to affect many people will generally get priority over those that are edge cases.</p> <p id="page_919" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another reason that a bug might be ignored for a while is if the bug is a symptom of a larger problem. While we can spend time writing, testing and applying lots of little changes, sometimes the right solution is to rebuild. If a rebuild or refactor of a particular component has been proposed or is underway, you may find that bugs affecting that component will not get as much attention. Again, this is a matter of prioritizing scarce resources. By concentrating on the rebuild, we can close all the little bugs at once, and hopefully prevent other little bugs from appearing in the future.</p> <p>Whatever the reason, please keep in mind that while you may hit a particular bug regularly, it doesn’t neces-sarily follow that every single Django user will hit the same bug. Different users use Django in different ways, stressing different parts of the code under different conditions. When we evaluate the relative priorities, we are generally trying to consider the needs of the entire community, instead of prioritizing the impact on one particular user. This doesn’t mean that we think your problem is unimportant – just that in the limited time we have available, we will always err on the side of making 10 people happy rather than making a single person happy.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.7.5 I’m sure my ticket is absolutely 100% perfect, can I mark it as “Ready For</b></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>Checkin” myself?</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Sorry, no. It’s always better to get another set of eyes on a ticket. If you’re having trouble getting that second set of eyes, see questions above.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>5.8 Troubleshooting</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This page contains some advice about errors and problems commonly encountered during the development of Django applications.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.8.1 Problems running</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>django-admin</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>command not found: django-admin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1433">django-admin</a> should be on your system path if you installed Django via pip. If it’s not in your path, ensure you have your virtual environment activated and you can try running the equivalent command python -m django.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_920"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>macOS permissions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using macOS, you may see the message “permission denied” when you try to run django-admin. This is because, on Unix-based systems like macOS, a file must be marked as “executable” before it can be run as a program. To do this, open Terminal.app and navigate (using the cd command) to the directory where</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1433">django-admin</a> is installed, then run the command sudo chmod +x django-admin.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>5.8.2 Miscellaneous</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>I’m getting a UnicodeDecodeError. What am I doing wrong?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This class of errors happen when a bytestring containing non-ASCII sequences is transformed into a Unicode string and the specified encoding is incorrect. The output generally looks like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0x?? in position ?:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ordinal not in range(128)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The resolution mostly depends on the context, however here are two common pitfalls producing this error:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Your system locale may be a default ASCII locale, like the “C” locale on UNIX-like systems (can be</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">checked by the locale command). If it’s the case, please refer to your system documentation to learn how you can change this to a UTF-8 locale.</p> <p>Related resources:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_2057">Unicode in Django</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://wiki.python.org/moin/UnicodeDecodeError">https://wiki.python.org/moin/UnicodeDecodeError</a></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <h2 id="page_921" style="text-align:right"><b>CHAPTER</b></h2> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>SIX</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>API REFERENCE</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.1 Applications</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django contains a registry of installed applications that stores configuration and provides introspection. It</p> <p>also maintains a list of available <a href="index.html#page_115">models</a>.</p> <p>This registry is called <a href="index.html#page_927"><i>apps</i></a> and it’s available in <a href="index.html#page_921"><i>django.apps</i></a><a href="index.html#page_921">:</a></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_app_config(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"admin"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">verbose_name</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'Administration'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.1.1 Projects and applications</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The term project describes a Django web application. The project Python package is defined primarily by a settings module, but it usually contains other things. For example, when you run django-admin startproject mysite you’ll get a mysite project directory that contains a mysite Python package with settings.py, urls.py, asgi.py and wsgi.py. The project package is often extended to include things like fixtures, CSS, and templates which aren’t tied to a particular application.</p> <p>A project’s root directory (the one that contains manage.py) is usually the container for all of a project’s applications which aren’t installed separately.</p> <p>The term application describes a Python package that provides some set of features. Applications <a href="index.html#page_88">may be</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_88">reused</a> in various projects.</p> <p>Applications include some combination of models, views, templates, template tags, static files, URLs, middle-</p> <p>ware, etc. They’re generally wired into projects with the <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting and optionally with other</p> <p>mechanisms such as URLconfs, the <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> setting, or template inheritance.</p> <p>It is important to understand that a Django application is a set of code that interacts with various parts of the framework. There’s no such thing as an Application object. However, there’s a few places where Django needs to interact with installed applications, mainly for configuration and also for introspection. That’s why</p> <p>the application registry maintains metadata in an <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> instance for each installed application.</p> <p id="page_922"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There’s no restriction that a project package can’t also be considered an application and have models, etc.</p> <p>(which would require adding it to <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.1.2 Configuring applications</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To configure an application, create an apps.py module inside the application, then define a subclass of</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> there.</p> <p>When <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> contains the dotted path to an application module, by default, if Django finds ex-</p> <p>actly one <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass in the apps.py submodule, it uses that configuration for the application. This</p> <p>behavior may be disabled by setting <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig.default</i></a> to False.</p> <p>If the apps.py module contains more than one <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass, Django will look for a single one where</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig.default</i></a> is True.</p> <p>If no <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass is found, the base <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> class will be used.</p> <p>Alternatively, <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> may contain the dotted path to a configuration class to specify it explicitly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INSTALLED_APPS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"polls.apps.PollsAppConfig"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>For application authors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re creating a pluggable app called “Rock ’n’ roll”, here’s how you would provide a proper name for the admin:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># rock_n_roll/apps.py</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AppConfig</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>RockNRollConfig</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AppConfig):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"rock_n_roll"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">verbose_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Rock ’n’ roll"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>RockNRollConfig will be loaded automatically when <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> contains 'rock_n_roll'. If you need</p> <p>to prevent this, set <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>default</i></a> to False in the class definition.</p> <p>You can provide several <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclasses with different behaviors. To tell Django which one to use by</p> <p>default, set <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>default</i></a> to True in its definition. If your users want to pick a non-default configuration, they</p> <p>must replace 'rock_n_roll' with the dotted path to that specific class in their <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting.</p> <p id="page_923" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig.name</i></a> attribute tells Django which application this configuration applies to. You can define</p> <p>any other attribute documented in the <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> API reference.</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclasses may be defined anywhere. The apps.py convention merely allows Django to load them</p> <p>automatically when <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> contains the path to an application module rather than the path to a configuration class.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If your code imports the application registry in an application’s __init__.py, the name apps will clash with the apps submodule. The best practice is to move that code to a submodule and import it. A workaround is to import the registry under a different name:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django_apps</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>For application users</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using “Rock ’n’ roll” in a project called anthology, but you want it to show up as “Jazz Manouche” instead, you can provide your own configuration:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># anthology/apps.py</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rock_n_roll.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">RockNRollConfig</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>JazzManoucheConfig</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(RockNRollConfig):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">verbose_name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Jazz Manouche"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># anthology/settings.py</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INSTALLED_APPS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"anthology.apps.JazzManoucheConfig"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This example shows project-specific configuration classes located in a submodule called apps.py. This is a</p> <p>convention, not a requirement. <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclasses may be defined anywhere.</p> <p>In this situation, <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> must contain the dotted path to the configuration class because it lives outside of an application and thus cannot be automatically detected.</p> <p id="page_924"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.1.3 Application configuration</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class AppConfig</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Application configuration objects store metadata for an application. Some attributes can be configured</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">in <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclasses. Others are set by Django and read-only.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configurable attributes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>AppConfig.<b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Full Python path to the application, e.g. 'django.contrib.admin'.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This attribute defines which application the configuration applies to. It must be set in all <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclasses.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It must be unique across a Django project.</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>label</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Short name for the application, e.g. 'admin'</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This attribute allows relabeling an application when two applications have conflicting labels. It defaults to the last component of name. It should be a valid Python identifier.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It must be unique across a Django project.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Warning: Changing this attribute after migrations have been applied for an application will result in breaking changes to a project or, in the case of a reusable app, any existing installs of that app. This is because AppConfig.label is used in database tables and migration files when referencing an app in the dependencies list.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>AppConfig.<b>verbose_name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Human-readable name for the application, e.g. “Administration”.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This attribute defaults to label.title().</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>path</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Filesystem path to the application directory, e.g. '/usr/lib/pythonX.Y/dist-packages/django/ contrib/admin'.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In most cases, Django can automatically detect and set this, but you can also provide an explicit override</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">as a class attribute on your <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass. In a few situations this is required; for instance if the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">app package is a <a href="index.html#page_927">namespace package</a> with multiple paths.</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>default</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set this attribute to False to prevent Django from selecting a configuration class automatically. This</p> <p id="page_925" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">is useful when apps.py defines only one <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass but you don’t want Django to use it by default.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set this attribute to True to tell Django to select a configuration class automatically. This is useful</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">when apps.py defines more than one <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> subclass and you want Django to use one of them by default.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">By default, this attribute isn’t set.</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>default_auto_field</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The implicit primary key type to add to models within this app. You can use this to keep <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>AutoField</i></a> as the primary key type for third party applications.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">By default, this is the value of <a href="index.html#page_1909"><i>DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Read-only attributes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>AppConfig.<b>module</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Root module for the application, e.g. <module 'django.contrib.admin' from 'django/contrib/ admin/__init__.py'>.</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>models_module</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Module containing the models, e.g. <span style="float:right"><module 'django.contrib.admin.models' from 'django/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">contrib/admin/models.py'>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It may be None if the application doesn’t contain a models module. Note that the database related</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">signals such as <a href="index.html#page_1960"><i>pre_migrate</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1961"><i>post_migrate</i></a> are only emitted for applications that have a models module.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>AppConfig.<b>get_models</b>(include_auto_created=False, include_swapped=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an iterable of <a href="index.html#page_1688"><i>Model</i></a> classes for this application.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Requires the app registry to be fully populated.</p> <p>AppConfig.<b>get_model</b>(model_name, require_ready=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the <a href="index.html#page_1688"><i>Model</i></a> with the given model_name. model_name is case-insensitive.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Raises <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#LookupError">LookupError</a> if no such model exists in this application.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Requires the app registry to be fully populated unless the require_ready argument is set to False.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">require_ready behaves exactly as in <a href="index.html#page_927"><i>apps.get_model()</i>.</a></p> <p>AppConfig.<b>ready</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Subclasses can override this method to perform initialization tasks such as registering signals. It is called as soon as the registry is fully populated.</p> <p id="page_926"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Although you can’t import models at the module-level where <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> classes are defined, you can</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">import them in ready(), using either an import statement or <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>get_model()</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you’re registering <a href="index.html#page_1953"><i>model signals</i>, </a>you can refer to the sender by its string label instead of using the model class itself.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.apps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">AppConfig</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models.signals</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pre_save</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>RockNRollConfig</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(AppConfig):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ready</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># importing model classes</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyModel</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># or...</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">MyModel</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_model(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"MyModel"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># registering signals with the model's string label</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">pre_save</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">connect(receiver, sender</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"app_label.MyModel"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Warning: Although you can access model classes as described above, avoid interacting with the</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">database in your <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> implementation. This includes model methods that execute queries</p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><a href="index.html#page_1696">(<i>save()</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1700"><i>delete()</i></a>, manager methods etc.), and also raw SQL queries via django.db.connection.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Your <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> method will run during startup of every management command. For example, even though the test database configuration is separate from the production settings, manage.py test would still execute some queries against your production database!</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: In the usual initialization process, the ready method is only called once by Django. But in some corner cases, particularly in tests which are fiddling with installed applications, ready might be called more than once. In that case, either write idempotent methods, or put a flag on your AppConfig classes to prevent rerunning code which should be executed exactly one time.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_927" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Namespace packages as apps</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Python packages without an __init__.py file are known as “namespace packages” and may be spread across</p> <p>multiple directories at different locations on sys.path (see <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0420/">PEP 420</a>).</p> <p>Django applications require a single base filesystem path where Django (depending on configuration) will search for templates, static assets, etc. Thus, namespace packages may only be Django applications if one of the following is true:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. The namespace package actually has only a single location (i.e. is not spread across more than one</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">directory.)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. The <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> class used to configure the application has a <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>path</i></a> class attribute, which is the absolute</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">directory path Django will use as the single base path for the application.</p> <p>If neither of these conditions is met, Django will raise <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>ImproperlyConfigured</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.1.4 Application registry</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>apps</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The application registry provides the following public API. Methods that aren’t listed below are con-sidered private and may change without notice.</p> <p>apps.<b>ready</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Boolean attribute that is set to True after the registry is fully populated and all <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>AppConfig.ready()</i></a> methods are called.</p> <p>apps.<b>get_app_configs</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an iterable of <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> instances.</p> <p>apps.<b>get_app_config</b>(app_label)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>AppConfig</i></a> for the application with the given app_label. Raises <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#LookupError">LookupError</a> if no such application exists.</p> <p>apps.<b>is_installed</b>(app_name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Checks whether an application with the given name exists in the registry. app_name is the full name of the app, e.g. 'django.contrib.admin'.</p> <p>apps.<b>get_model</b>(app_label, model_name, require_ready=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the <a href="index.html#page_1688"><i>Model</i></a> with the given app_label and model_name. As a shortcut, this method also accepts a single argument in the form app_label.model_name. model_name is case-insensitive.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Raises <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#LookupError">LookupError</a> if no such application or model exists. Raises <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#ValueError">ValueError</a> when called with a single argument that doesn’t contain exactly one dot.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Requires the app registry to be fully populated unless the require_ready argument is set to False.</p> <p id="page_928"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Setting require_ready to False allows looking up models <a href="index.html#page_928">while the app registry is being populated</a>, specifically during the second phase where it imports models. Then get_model() has the same ef-fect as importing the model. The main use case is to configure model classes with settings, such as</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTH_USER_MODEL</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When require_ready is False, get_model() returns a model class that may not be fully functional (reverse accessors may be missing, for example) until the app registry is fully populated. For this reason, it’s best to leave require_ready to the default value of True whenever possible.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.1.5 Initialization process</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How applications are loaded</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Django starts, <a href="index.html#page_928"><i>django.setup()</i></a> is responsible for populating the application registry.</p> <p><b>setup</b>(set_prefix=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Configures Django by:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Loading the settings.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Setting up logging.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• If set_prefix is True, setting the URL resolver script prefix to <a href="index.html#page_1915"><i>FORCE_SCRIPT_NAME</i></a> if defined, or</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">/ otherwise.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Initializing the application registry.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This function is called automatically:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• When running an HTTP server via Django’s ASGI or WSGI support.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• When invoking a management command.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It must be called explicitly in other cases, for instance in plain Python scripts.</p> <p>The application registry is initialized in three stages. At each stage, Django processes all applications in the</p> <p>order of <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. First Django imports each item in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If it’s an application configuration class, Django imports the root package of the application, defined by</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">its <a href="index.html#page_924"><i>name</i></a> attribute. If it’s a Python package, Django looks for an application configuration in an apps.py submodule, or else creates a default application configuration.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">At this stage, your code shouldn’t import any models!</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In other words, your applications’ root packages and the modules that define your application config-uration classes shouldn’t import any models, even indirectly.</p> <p id="page_929" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Strictly speaking, Django allows importing models once their application configuration is loaded. How-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ever, in order to avoid needless constraints on the order of <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>, it’s strongly recommended not import any models at this stage.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Once this stage completes, APIs that operate on application configurations such as <a href="index.html#page_927"><i>get_app_config()</i></a> become usable.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Then Django attempts to import the models submodule of each application, if there is one.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You must define or import all models in your application’s models.py or models/__init__.py. Oth-erwise, the application registry may not be fully populated at this point, which could cause the ORM to malfunction.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Once this stage completes, APIs that operate on models such as <a href="index.html#page_927"><i>get_model()</i></a> become usable.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Finally Django runs the <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>ready()</i></a> method of each application configuration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Troubleshooting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here are some common problems that you may encounter during initialization:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1470"><i>AppRegistryNotReady</i></a>: This happens when importing an application configuration or a models module</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">triggers code that depends on the app registry.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For example, <a href="index.html#page_2089"><i>gettext()</i></a> uses the app registry to look up translation catalogs in applications. To trans-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">late at import time, you need <a href="index.html#page_2089"><i>gettext_lazy()</i></a> instead. (Using <a href="index.html#page_2089"><i>gettext()</i></a> would be a bug, because the translation would happen at import time, rather than at each request depending on the active lan-guage.)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Executing database queries with the ORM at import time in models modules will also trigger this ex-ception. The ORM cannot function properly until all models are available.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This exception also happens if you forget to call <a href="index.html#page_928"><i>django.setup()</i></a> in a standalone Python script.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• ImportError: cannot import name ... This happens if the import sequence ends up in a loop.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To eliminate such problems, you should minimize dependencies between your models modules and do as little work as possible at import time. To avoid executing code at import time, you can move it into a function and cache its results. The code will be executed when you first need its results. This concept is known as “lazy evaluation”.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django.contrib.admin automatically performs autodiscovery of admin modules in installed appli-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">cations. To prevent it, change your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> to contain 'django.contrib.admin.apps. SimpleAdminConfig' instead of 'django.contrib.admin'.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• RuntimeWarning: Accessing the database during app initialization is discouraged. This</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">warning is triggered for database queries executed before apps are ready, such as during module im-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ports or in the <a href="index.html#page_925"><i>AppConfig.ready()</i></a> method. Such premature database queries are discouraged because <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_930" style="margin-left:2em">they will run during the startup of every management command, which will slow down your project startup, potentially cache stale data, and can even fail if migrations are pending.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For example, a common mistake is making a database query to populate form field choices:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>LocationForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">country</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ChoiceField(choices</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[c</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Country</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In the example above, the query from Country.objects.all() is executed during module import,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">because the QuerySet is iterated over. To avoid the warning, the form could use a <a href="index.html#page_1543"><i>ModelChoiceField</i></a> instead:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>LocationForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">country</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ModelChoiceField(queryset</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Country</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all())</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To make it easier to find the code that triggered this warning, you can make Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#warning-filter">treat warnings as</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#warning-filter">errors</a> to reveal the stack trace, for example with python -Werror manage.py shell.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.2 System check framework</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The system check framework is a set of static checks for validating Django projects. It detects common problems and provides hints for how to fix them. The framework is extensible so you can easily add your own checks.</p> <p>For details on how to add your own checks and integrate them with Django’s system checks, see the <a href="index.html#page_757">System</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_757">check topic guide</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.2.1 API reference</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CheckMessage</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CheckMessage</b>(level, msg, hint=None, obj=None, id=None)</p> <p>The warnings and errors raised by system checks must be instances of CheckMessage. An instance encapsu-lates a single reportable error or warning. It also provides context and hints applicable to the message, and a unique identifier that is used for filtering purposes.</p> <p>Constructor arguments are:</p> <p><b>level</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The severity of the message. Use one of the predefined values: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. If the level is greater or equal to ERROR, then Django will prevent management commands from exe-cuting. Messages with level lower than ERROR (i.e. warnings) are reported to the console, but can be silenced.</p> <p id="page_931" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>msg</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A short (less than 80 characters) string describing the problem. The string should not contain newlines.</p> <p><b>hint</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A single-line string providing a hint for fixing the problem. If no hint can be provided, or the hint is self-evident from the error message, the hint can be omitted, or a value of None can be used.</p> <p><b>obj</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Optional. An object providing context for the message (for example, the model where the problem was discovered). The object should be a model, field, or manager or any other object that defines a __str__() method. The method is used while reporting all messages and its result precedes the message.</p> <p><b>id</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">Optional string. A unique identifier for the issue. Identifiers should follow the pattern applabel.X001, where X is one of the letters CEWID, indicating the message severity (C for criticals, E for errors and so). The number can be allocated by the application, but should be unique within that application.</p> <p>There are subclasses to make creating messages with common levels easier. When using them you can omit the level argument because it is implied by the class name.</p> <p><b>class Debug</b>(msg, hint=None, obj=None, id=None)</p> <p><b>class Info</b>(msg, hint=None, obj=None, id=None)</p> <p><b>class Warning</b>(msg, hint=None obj=None, id=None)</p> <p><b>class Error</b>(msg, hint=None, obj=None, id=None)</p> <p><b>class Critical</b>(msg, hint=None, obj=None, id=None)</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.2.2 Builtin tags</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s system checks are organized using the following tags:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• admin: Checks of any admin site declarations.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• async_support: Checks asynchronous-related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• caches: Checks cache related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• compatibility: Flags potential problems with version upgrades.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• commands: Checks custom management commands related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• database: Checks database-related configuration issues. Database checks are not run by default be-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">cause they do more than static code analysis as regular checks do. They are only run by the <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> command or if you specify configured database aliases using the--database option when calling the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1434"><i>check</i></a> command.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• files: Checks files related configuration.</p> <p id="page_932"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• models: Checks of model, field, and manager definitions.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security: Checks security related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• signals: Checks on signal declarations and handler registrations.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sites: Checks <a href="index.html#page_1360"><i>django.contrib.sites</i></a> configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• staticfiles: Checks <a href="index.html#page_1369"><i>django.contrib.staticfiles</i></a> configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• templates: Checks template related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• translation: Checks translation related configuration.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• urls: Checks URL configuration.</p> <p>Some checks may be registered with multiple tags.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.2.3 Core system checks</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Asynchronous support</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following checks verify your setup for <a href="index.html#page_764">Asynchronous support:</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• async.E001: You should not set the <a href="index.html#page_768"><i>DJANGO_ALLOW_ASYNC_UNSAFE</i></a> environment variable in deploy-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ment. This disables <a href="index.html#page_768">async safety protection.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Backwards compatibility</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Compatibility checks warn of potential problems that might occur after upgrading Django.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 2_0.W001: Your URL pattern <pattern> has a route that contains (?P<, begins with a ^, or ends with</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a $. This was likely an oversight when migrating from url() to <a href="index.html#page_2068"><i>path()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 4_0.E001: As of Django 4.0, the values in the <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS</i></a> setting must start with a scheme</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">(usually http:// or https://) but found <hostname>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Caches</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following checks verify that your <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> setting is correctly configured:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• caches.E001: You must define a 'default' cache in your <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>CACHES</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• caches.W002: Your <cache> configuration might expose your cache or lead to corruption of your data</p> <p style="text-align:center">because its <a href="index.html#page_1891"><i>LOCATION</i></a> matches/is inside/contains <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> <a href="index.html#page_1945">/</a><a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> /<a href="index.html#page_1946"><i>STATICFILES_DIRS</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• caches.W003: Your <cache> cache <a href="index.html#page_1891"><i>LOCATION</i></a> is relative. Use an absolute path instead.</p> <p id="page_933" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MySQL and MariaDB</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’re using MySQL or MariaDB, the following checks will be performed:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• mysql.E001: MySQL/MariaDB does not allow unique CharFields to have a max_length > 255. This</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">check was changed to mysql.W003 in Django 3.1 as the real maximum size depends on many factors.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• mysql.W002: MySQL/MariaDB Strict Mode is not set for database connection <alias>. See also <a href="index.html#page_1421">Setting</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1421">sql_mode</a>.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• mysql.W003: MySQL/MariaDB may not allow unique CharFields to have a max_length > 255.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Managing files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following checks verify your setup for <a href="index.html#page_464">Managing files:</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• files.E001: The <a href="index.html#page_1914"><i>FILE_UPLOAD_TEMP_DIR</i></a> setting refers to the nonexistent directory <path>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Model fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E001: Field names must not end with an underscore.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E002: Field names must not contain "__".</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E003: pk is a reserved word that cannot be used as a field name.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E004: choices must be a mapping (e.g. a dictionary) or an iterable (e.g. a list or tuple).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E005: choices must be a mapping of actual values to human readable names or an iterable</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">containing (actual value, human readable name) tuples.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E006: db_index must be None, True or False.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E007: Primary keys must not have null=True.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E008: All validators must be callable.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E009: max_length is too small to fit the longest value in choices (<count> characters).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E010: <field> default should be a callable instead of an instance so that it’s not shared between</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">all field instances.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E011: <database> does not support default database values with expressions (db_default).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E012: <expression> cannot be used in db_default.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E100: AutoFields must set primary_key=True.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• fields.E110: BooleanFields do not accept null values. makemigrations commands must have the same autodetector.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Security</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The security checks do not make your site secure. They do not audit code, do intrusion detection, or do anything particularly complex. Rather, they help perform an automated, low-hanging-fruit checklist, that can help you to improve your site’s security.</p> <p>Some of these checks may not be appropriate for your particular deployment configuration. For instance, if you do your HTTP to HTTPS redirection in a load balancer, it’d be irritating to be constantly warned about</p> <p>not having enabled <a href="index.html#page_1929"><i>SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT</i></a> . Use <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>SILENCED_SYSTEM_CHECKS</i></a> to silence unneeded checks.</p> <p>The following checks are run if you use the <a href="index.html#page_1435"><i>check --deploy</i></a> option:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W001: You do not have <a href="index.html#page_1594"><i>django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">in your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> so the <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF</i></a>,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1929"><i>SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY</i></a> , <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY</i></a> , and <a href="index.html#page_1929"><i>SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT</i></a> settings will have no effect.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W002: You do not have <a href="index.html#page_1601"><i>django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware</i></a> in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> , so your pages will not be served with an 'x-frame-options' header. Unless there is a good reason for your site to be served in a frame, you should consider enabling this header to help prevent clickjacking attacks.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W003: You don’t appear to be using Django’s built-in cross-site request forgery protection</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">via the middleware <a href="index.html#page_1601">(<i>django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware</i></a> is not in your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> ). En-abling the middleware is the safest approach to ensure you don’t leave any holes.</p> <p id="page_940"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W004: You have not set a value for the <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS</i></a> setting. If your entire site is</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">served only over SSL, you may want to consider setting a value and enabling <a href="index.html#page_1595">HTTP Strict Transport Se-</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1595">curity. </a>Be sure to read the documentation first; enabling HSTS carelessly can cause serious, irreversible problems.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W005: You have not set the <a href="index.html#page_1927"><i>SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS</i></a> setting to True. Without this,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">your site is potentially vulnerable to attack via an insecure connection to a subdomain. Only set this to True if you are certain that all subdomains of your domain should be served exclusively via SSL.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W006: Your <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF</i></a> setting is not set to True, so your pages will not</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">be served with an 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' header. You should consider enabling this header to prevent the browser from identifying content types incorrectly.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W007: Your SECURE_BROWSER_XSS_FILTER setting is not set to True, so your pages will not</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">be served with an 'X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block' header. You should consider enabling this header to activate the browser’s XSS filtering and help prevent XSS attacks. This check is removed in Django 3.0 as the X-XSS-Protection header is no longer honored by modern browsers.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W008: Your <a href="index.html#page_1929"><i>SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT</i></a> setting is not set to True. Unless your site should be avail-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">able over both SSL and non-SSL connections, you may want to either set this setting to True or configure a load balancer or reverse-proxy server to redirect all connections to HTTPS.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W009: Your <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> has less than 50 characters, less than 5 unique characters, or it’s</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">prefixed with 'django-insecure-' indicating that it was generated automatically by Django. Please generate a long and random value, otherwise many of Django’s security-critical features will be vul-nerable to attack.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• security.W010: You have <a href="index.html#page_311"><i>django.contrib.sessions</i></a> in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> but you have not set</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1944"><i>SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE</i></a> to True. <p>Class-based views API reference. For introductory material, see the <a href="index.html#page_410">Class-based views</a> topic guide.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.3.1 Base views</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following three classes provide much of the functionality needed to create Django views. You may think of them as parent views, which can be used by themselves or inherited from. They may not provide all the capabilities required for projects, in which case there are Mixins and Generic class-based views.</p> <p>Many of Django’s built-in class-based views inherit from other class-based views or various mixins. Because this inheritance chain is very important, the ancestor classes are documented under the section title of An-cestors (MRO). MRO is an acronym for Method Resolution Order.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_950"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>View</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class</b> django.views.generic.base.<b>View</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The base view class. All other class-based views inherit from this base class. It isn’t strictly a generic view and thus can also be imported from django.views.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Method Flowchart</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">1. <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>setup()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:3em">2. <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>dispatch()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:3em">3. <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>http_method_not_allowed()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:3em">4. <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>options()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Example views.py:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">View</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyView</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(View):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">args,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>**</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">kwargs):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Hello, World!"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Example urls.py:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">myapp.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyView</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"mine/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, MyView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view(), name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"my-view"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Attributes</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>http_method_names</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The list of HTTP method names that this view will accept.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Default:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"get"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"put"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"patch"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"delete"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"head"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"options"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"trace"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Methods</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod as_view</b>(**initkwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a callable view that takes a request and returns a response:</p> <p id="page_951" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">response</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">MyView</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">as_view()(request)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The returned view has view_class and view_initkwargs attributes.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">When the view is called during the request/response cycle, the <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>setup()</i></a> method assigns the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a> to the view’s request attribute, and any positional and/or keyword arguments <a href="index.html#page_266">cap-</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_266">tured from the URL pattern</a> to the args and kwargs attributes, respectively. Then <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>dispatch()</i></a> is called.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If a View subclass defines asynchronous (async def) method handlers, as_view() will mark the returned callable as a coroutine function. An ImproperlyConfigured exception will be raised if both asynchronous (async def) and synchronous (def) handlers are defined on a single view-class.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>setup</b> ( request, *args, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Performs key view initialization prior to <a href="index.html#page_951"><i>dispatch()</i>.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If overriding this method, you must call super().</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>dispatch</b>(request, *args, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The view part of the view – the method that accepts a request argument plus arguments, and returns an HTTP response.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The default implementation will inspect the HTTP method and attempt to delegate to a method that matches the HTTP method; a GET will be delegated to get(), a POST to post(), and so on.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">By default, a HEAD request will be delegated to get(). If you need to handle HEAD requests in a</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">different way than GET, you can override the head() method. See <a href="index.html#page_445">Supporting other HTTP methods</a> for an example.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>http_method_not_allowed</b>(request, *args, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If the view was called with an HTTP method it doesn’t support, this method is called instead.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The default implementation returns HttpResponseNotAllowed with a list of allowed methods in plain text.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>options</b>(request, *args, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Handles responding to requests for the OPTIONS HTTP verb. Returns a response with the Allow header containing a list of the view’s allowed HTTP method names.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If the other HTTP methods handlers on the class are asynchronous (async def) then the response will be wrapped in a coroutine function for use with await.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_952"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TemplateView</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class</b> django.views.generic.base.<b>TemplateView</b></p> <p
