Returns the user object. When fetching or creating an user is called from a synchronous context, configure_user is called, aconfigure_user is called from async contexts.</p> <p id="page_1114"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The setup can be performed either once when the user is created (created is True) or on existing users (created is False) as a way of synchronizing attributes between the remote and the local systems.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">request is an <a href="index.html#page_1859"><i>HttpRequest</i></a> and may be None if it wasn’t provided to <a href="index.html#page_532"><i>authenticate()</i></a> (which passes it on to the backend).</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">aconfigure_user() function was added.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>user_can_authenticate</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns whether the user is allowed to authenticate. This method returns False for users with</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>is_active=False</i>. </a>Custom user models that don’t have an <a href="index.html#page_587"><i>is_active</i></a> field are allowed.</p> <p><b>class AllowAllUsersRemoteUserBackend</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Same as <a href="index.html#page_1113"><i>RemoteUserBackend</i></a> <span style="float:right">except that it doesn’t reject inactive users because</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>user_can_authenticate</i></a> always returns True.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Utility functions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>get_user</b>(request)</p> <p><b>aget_user</b>( request)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Asynchronous version: aget_user()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the user model instance associated with the given request’s session.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It checks if the authentication backend stored in the session is present in <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a>. If so, it uses the backend’s get_user() method to retrieve the user model instance and then ver-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ifies the session by calling the user model’s <a href="index.html#page_589"><i>get_session_auth_hash()</i></a> method. If the verification</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">fails and <a href="index.html#page_1926"><i>SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS</i></a> are provided, it verifies the session against each fallback key using</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_589"><i>get_session_auth_fallback_hash()</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an instance of <a href="index.html#page_1107"><i>AnonymousUser</i></a> if the authentication backend stored in the session is no longer</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">in <a href="index.html#page_1938"><i>AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS</i></a> , if a user isn’t returned by the backend’s get_user() method, or if the session auth hash doesn’t validate.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.5.3 The contenttypes framework</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django includes a <a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>contenttypes</i></a> application that can track all of the models installed in your Django-powered project, providing a high-level, generic interface for working with your models.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1115" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overview</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>At the heart of the contenttypes application is the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> model, which lives at django.contrib.</p> <p>contenttypes.models.ContentType. Instances of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> represent and store information about the</p> <p>models installed in your project, and new instances of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> are automatically created whenever new models are installed.</p> <p>Instances of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> have methods for returning the model classes they represent and for querying</p> <p>objects from those models. <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> also has a <a href="index.html#page_192">custom manager</a> that adds methods for working with</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> and for obtaining instances of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> for a particular model.</p> <p>Relations between your models and <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> can also be used to enable “generic” relationships between an instance of one of your models and instances of any model you have installed.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing the contenttypes framework</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The contenttypes framework is included in the default <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> list created by django-admin</p> <p>startproject, but if you’ve removed it or if you manually set up your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> list, you can en-</p> <p>able it by adding 'django.contrib.contenttypes' to your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>It’s generally a good idea to have the contenttypes framework installed; several of Django’s other bundled applications require it:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The admin application uses it to log the history of each object added or changed through the admin</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">interface.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Django’s <a href="index.html#page_598"><i>authentication framework</i></a> uses it to tie user permissions to specific models.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The ContentType model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class ContentType</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Each instance of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> has two fields which, taken together, uniquely describe an installed model:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>app_label</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The name of the application the model is part of. This is taken from the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>app_label</i></a> attribute of the model, and includes only the last part of the application’s Python import path; django.contrib.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">contenttypes, for example, becomes an <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>app_label</i></a> of contenttypes.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>model</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The name of the model class.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Additionally, the following property is available:</p> <p id="page_1116"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The human-readable name of the content type. This is taken from the <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>verbose_name</i></a> attribute of the model.</p> <p>Let’s look at an example to see how this works. If you already have the <a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>contenttypes</i></a> application installed,</p> <p>and then add <a href="index.html#page_1360"><i>the sites application</i></a> to your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting and run manage.py migrate to in-</p> <p>stall it, the model <a href="index.html#page_1360"><i>django.contrib.sites.models.Site</i></a> will be installed into your database. Along with it</p> <p>a new instance of <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> will be created with the following values:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>app_label</i></a> will be set to 'sites' (the last part of the Python path django.contrib.sites).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>model</i></a> will be set to 'site'.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Methods on ContentType instances</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Each <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instance has methods that allow you to get from a <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instance to the model it represents, or to retrieve objects from that model:</p> <p>ContentType.<b>get_object_for_this_type</b>(using=None, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Takes a set of valid <a href="index.html#page_150">lookup arguments</a> for the model the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> represents, and does <a href="index.html#page_1744"><i>a get()</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1744"><i>lookup</i></a> on that model, returning the corresponding object. The using argument can be used to specify a different database than the default one.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The using argument was added.</p> <p>ContentType.<b>model_class</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the model class represented by this <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instance.</p> <p>For example, we could look up the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> for the <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a> model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.contenttypes.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user_type</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(app_label</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, model</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user_type</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><ContentType: user></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>And then use it to query for a particular <a href="index.html#page_1102"><i>User</i></a>, or to get access to the User model class:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">model_class()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><class 'django.contrib.auth.models.User'></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">user_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_object_for_this_type(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Guido"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><User: Guido></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Together, <a href="index.html#page_1116"><i>get_object_for_this_type()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1116"><i>model_class()</i></a> enable two extremely important use cases:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Using these methods, you can write high-level generic code that performs queries on any installed model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">– instead of importing and using a single specific model class, you can pass an app_label and model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">into a <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> lookup at runtime, and then work with the model class or retrieve objects from it.</p> <p id="page_1117" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. You can relate another model to <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> as a way of tying instances of it to particular model</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">classes, and use these methods to get access to those model classes.</p> <p>Several of Django’s bundled applications make use of the latter technique. For example, <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>the permissions</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>system</i></a> in Django’s authentication framework uses a <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Permission</i></a> model with a foreign key to <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a>;</p> <p>this lets <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Permission</i></a> represent concepts like “can add blog entry” or “can delete news story”.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The ContentTypeManager</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class ContentTypeManager</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> also has a custom manager, <a href="index.html#page_1117"><i>ContentTypeManager</i></a>, which adds the following methods:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>clear_cache</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Clears an internal cache used by <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> to keep track of models for which it has created</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instances. You probably won’t ever need to call this method yourself; Django will call it automatically when it’s needed.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_for_id</b>(id)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Lookup a <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> by ID. Since this method uses the same shared cache as <a href="index.html#page_1117"><i>get_for_model()</i></a>, it’s preferred to use this method over the usual ContentType.objects.get(pk=id)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_for_model</b>(model, for_concrete_model=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Takes either a model class or an instance of a model, and returns the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instance rep-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">resenting that model. for_concrete_model=False allows fetching the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> of a proxy model.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_for_models</b>(*models, for_concrete_models=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Takes a variadic number of model classes, and returns a dictionary mapping the model classes to</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instances representing them. for_concrete_models=False allows fetching the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> of proxy models.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_by_natural_key</b>( app_label, model)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> instance uniquely identified by the given application label and model</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">name. The primary purpose of this method is to allow <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> objects to be referenced via a</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_740">natural key</a> during deserialization.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1117"><i>get_for_model()</i></a> method is especially useful when you know you need to work with a <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> but don’t want to go to the trouble of obtaining the model’s metadata to perform a manual lookup:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get_for_model(User)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><ContentType: user></span></p> <p id="page_1118"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Generic relations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Adding a foreign key from one of your own models to <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> allows your model to effectively tie itself</p> <p>to another model class, as in the example of the <a href="index.html#page_1108"><i>Permission</i></a> model above. But it’s possible to go one step</p> <p>further and use <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> to enable truly generic (sometimes called “polymorphic”) relationships between models.</p> <p>For example, it could be used for a tagging system like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.contenttypes.fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GenericForeignKey</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.contenttypes.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentType</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TaggedItem</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">tag</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SlugField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ForeignKey(ContentType, on_delete</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CASCADE)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">object_id</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">PositiveIntegerField()</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_object</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GenericForeignKey(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"content_type"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"object_id"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__str__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">tag</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">indexes</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Index(fields</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"content_type"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"object_id"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A normal <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> can only “point to” one other model, which means that if the TaggedItem model used</p> <p>a <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> it would have to choose one and only one model to store tags for. The contenttypes application provides a special field type (GenericForeignKey) which works around this and allows the relationship to be with any model:</p> <p><b>class GenericForeignKey</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">There are three parts to setting up a <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a>:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">1. Give your model a <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a> to <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1115">. </a>The usual name for this field is “content_type”.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">2. Give your model a field that can store primary key values from the models you’ll be relating to. For</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">most models, this means a <a href="index.html#page_1640"><i>PositiveIntegerField</i></a>. The usual name for this field is “object_id”.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">3. Give your model a <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a>, and pass it the names of the two fields described above.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If these fields are named “content_type” and “object_id”, you can omit this – those are the default</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">field names <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a> will look for.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Unlike for the <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i>, </a>a database index is not automatically created on the <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a>,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">so it’s recommended that you use <a href="index.html#page_1686"><i>Meta.indexes</i></a> to add your own multiple column index. This behavior</p> <p id="page_1119" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/23435">may change</a> in the future.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>for_concrete_model</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If False, the field will be able to reference proxy models. Default is True. This mirrors the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">for_concrete_model argument to <a href="index.html#page_1117"><i>get_for_model()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Primary key type compatibility</p> <p>The “object_id” field doesn’t have to be the same type as the primary key fields on the related models, but their</p> <p>primary key values must be coercible to the same type as the “object_id” field by its <a href="index.html#page_1657"><i>get_db_prep_value()</i></a> method.</p> <p>For example, if you want to allow generic relations to models with either <a href="index.html#page_1639"><i>IntegerField</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> pri-</p> <p>mary key fields, you can use <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> for the “object_id” field on your model since integers can be coerced</p> <p>to strings by <a href="index.html#page_1657"><i>get_db_prep_value()</i></a>.</p> <p>For maximum flexibility you can use a <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a> which doesn’t have a maximum length defined, however this may incur significant performance penalties depending on your database backend.</p> <p>There is no one-size-fits-all solution for which field type is best. You should evaluate the models you expect to be pointing to and determine which solution will be most effective for your use case.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Serializing references to <b>ContentType</b> objects</p> <p>If you’re serializing data (for example, when generating <a href="index.html#page_497"><i>fixtures</i>) </a>from a model that implements generic</p> <p>relations, you should probably be using a natural key to uniquely identify related <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> objects. See</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_740">natural keys</a> and <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>dumpdata --natural-foreign</i></a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will enable an API similar to the one used for a normal <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i>; </a>each TaggedItem will have a content_object field that returns the object it’s related to, and you can also assign to that field or use it when creating a TaggedItem:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">guido</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Just as <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a> accepts the names of the content-type and object-ID fields as arguments, so too</p> <p>does <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a>; if the model which has the generic foreign key is using non-default names for those <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_1122">fields, you must pass the names of the fields when setting up a <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a> to it. For example, if the TaggedItem model referred to above used fields named content_type_fk and object_primary_key to create</p> <p>its generic foreign key, then a <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a> back to it would need to be defined like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">tags</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GenericRelation(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">TaggedItem,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">content_type_field</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"content_type_fk"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">object_id_field</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"object_primary_key"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note also, that if you delete an object that has a <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a>, any objects which have a</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a> pointing at it will be deleted as well. In the example above, this means that if a Bookmark object were deleted, any TaggedItem objects pointing at it would be deleted at the same time.</p> <p>Unlike <a href="index.html#page_1643"><i>ForeignKey</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a> does not accept an <a href="index.html#page_1644"><i>on_delete</i></a> argument to customize this behavior;</p> <p>if desired, you can avoid the cascade-deletion by not using <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a>, and alternate behavior can be</p> <p>provided via the <a href="index.html#page_1956"><i>pre_delete</i></a> signal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Generic relations and aggregation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_177">Django’s database aggregation API</a> works with a <a href="index.html#page_1120"><i>GenericRelation</i></a>. For example, you can find out how many tags all the bookmarks have:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Bookmark</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">aggregate(Count(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"tags"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">{'tags__count': 3}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Generic relation in forms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1122"><i>django.contrib.contenttypes.forms</i></a> module provides:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1122"><i>BaseGenericInlineFormSet</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• A formset factory, <a href="index.html#page_1122"><i>generic_inlineformset_factory()</i></a>, for use with <a href="index.html#page_1118"><i>GenericForeignKey</i></a>.</p> <p><b>class BaseGenericInlineFormSet</b></p> <p><b>generic_inlineformset_factory</b>( model, form=ModelForm, formset=BaseGenericInlineFormSet,</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">ct_field='content_type', fk_field='object_id', fields=None,</p> <p style="text-align:right">exclude=None, extra=3, can_order=False, can_delete=True,</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">max_num=None, formfield_callback=None, validate_max=False, for_concrete_model=True, min_num=None, validate_min=False, absolute_max=None, can_delete_extra=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a GenericInlineFormSet using <a href="index.html#page_1549"><i>modelformset_factory()</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_1123" different from the defaults, content_type and object_id respectively. <span style="float:right">Other parameters are similar to those documented in</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1549"><i>modelformset_factory()</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1550"><i>inlineformset_factory()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1550">.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The for_concrete_model argument corresponds to the <a href="index.html#page_1119"><i>for_concrete_model</i></a> argument on GenericForeignKey .</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Generic relations in admin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>django.contrib.contenttypes.admin</i></a> module provides <a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>GenericTabularInline</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>GenericStackedInline</i></a> (subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>GenericInlineModelAdmin</i></a>)</p> <p>These classes and functions enable the use of generic relations in forms and the admin. See the <a href="index.html#page_365">model formset</a></p> <p>and <a href="index.html#page_1086">admin</a> documentation for more information.</p> <p><b>class GenericInlineModelAdmin</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>GenericInlineModelAdmin</i></a> class inherits all properties from an <a href="index.html#page_1077"><i>InlineModelAdmin</i></a> class. How-ever, it adds a couple of its own for working with the generic relation:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>ct_field</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">The name of the <a href="index.html#page_1115"><i>ContentType</i></a> foreign key field on the model. Defaults to content_type.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>ct_fk_field</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The name of the integer field that represents the ID of the related object. Defaults to object_id.</p> <p><b>class GenericTabularInline</b></p> <p><b>class GenericStackedInline</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_1123"><i>GenericInlineModelAdmin</i></a> with stacked and tabular layouts, respectively.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GenericPrefetch()</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GenericPrefetch</b>(lookup, querysets, to_attr=None)</p> <p>This lookup is similar to Prefetch() and it should only be used on GenericForeignKey. The querysets argument accepts a list of querysets, each for a different ContentType. style="font-size:0.87em">"content_object"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, [Bookmark</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">only(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TaggedItem</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">prefetch_related(prefetch)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">all()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<TaggedItem: Great>, <TaggedItem: Awesome>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.5.4 The flatpages app</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django comes with an optional “flatpages” application. It lets you store “flat” HTML content in a database and handles the management for you via Django’s admin interface and a Python API.</p> <p>A flatpage is an object with a URL, title and content. Use it for one-off, special-case pages, such as “About” or “Privacy Policy” pages, that you want to store in a database but for which you don’t want to develop a custom Django application.</p> <p>A flatpage can use a custom template or a default, systemwide flatpage template. It can be associated with one, or multiple, sites.</p> <p>The content field may optionally be left blank if you prefer to put your content in a custom template.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To install the flatpages app, follow these steps:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Install the <a href="index.html#page_1360"><i>sites framework</i></a> by adding 'django.contrib.sites' to your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting, if</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">it’s not already in there.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Also make sure you’ve correctly set <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>SITE_ID</i></a> to the ID of the site the settings file represents. This will usually be 1 (i.e. SITE_ID = 1, but if you’re using the sites framework to manage multiple sites, it could be the ID of a different site.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Add 'django.contrib.flatpages' to your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>Then either:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Add an entry in your URLconf. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pages/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, include(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.flatpages.urls"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>or:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Add 'django.contrib.flatpages.middleware.FlatpageFallbackMiddleware' to your <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. Run the command <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>manage.py migrate</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_1125" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How it works</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>manage.py migrate creates two tables in your database: django_flatpage and django_flatpage_sites. django_flatpage is a lookup table that maps a URL to a title and bunch of text content. django_flatpage_sites associates a flatpage with a site.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using the URLconf</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are several ways to include the flat pages in your URLconf. You can dedicate a particular path to flat pages:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pages/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, include(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.flatpages.urls"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also set it up as a “catchall” pattern. In this case, it is important to place the pattern at the end of the other urlpatterns:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.flatpages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">views</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Your other patterns here</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">re_path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">r"^(?P<url>.*/)$"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, views</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpage),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: If you set <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>APPEND_SLASH</i></a> to False, you must remove the slash in the catchall pattern or</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">flatpages without a trailing slash will not be matched.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another common setup is to use flat pages for a limited set of known pages and to hard code the urls, so you</p> <p>can reference them with the <a href="index.html#page_2002"><i>url</i></a> template tag:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.flatpages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">views</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about-us/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, views</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpage, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"url"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/about-us/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"about"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"license/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpage, {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"url"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/license/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"license"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1126"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Using the middleware</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1126"><i>FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</i></a> can do all of the work.</p> <p><b>class FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Each time any Django application raises a 404 error, this middleware checks the flatpages database for the requested URL as a last resort. Specifically, it checks for a flatpage with the given URL with a site</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ID that corresponds to the <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>SITE_ID</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If it finds a match, it follows this algorithm:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• If the flatpage has a custom template, it loads that template. Otherwise, it loads the template</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">flatpages/default.html.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• It passes that template a single context variable, flatpage, which is the flatpage object. It uses</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_2042"><i>RequestContext</i></a> in rendering the template.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The middleware will only add a trailing slash and redirect (by looking at the <a href="index.html#page_1889"><i>APPEND_SLASH</i></a> setting) if the resulting URL refers to a valid flatpage. Redirects are permanent (301 status code).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If it doesn’t find a match, the request continues to be processed as usual.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The middleware only gets activated for 404s – not for 500s or responses of any other status code.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Flatpages will not apply view middleware</p> <p>Because the FlatpageFallbackMiddleware is applied only after URL resolution has failed and produced a</p> <p>404, the response it returns will not apply any <a href="index.html#page_306">view middleware</a> methods. Only requests which are success-fully routed to a view via normal URL resolution apply view middleware.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that the order of <a href="index.html#page_1923"><i>MIDDLEWARE</i></a> matters. Generally, you can put <a href="index.html#page_1126"><i>FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</i></a> at the end of the list. This means it will run first when processing the response, and ensures that any other response-processing middleware see the real flatpage response rather than the 404.</p> <p>For more on middleware, read the <a href="index.html#page_303">middleware docs.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Ensure that your 404 template works</p> <p>Note that the <a href="index.html#page_1126"><i>FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</i></a> only steps in once another view has successfully produced a 404 response. If another view or middleware class attempts to produce a 404 but ends up rais-ing an exception instead, the response will become an HTTP 500 (“Internal Server Error”) and the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1126"><i>FlatpageFallbackMiddleware</i></a> will not attempt to serve a flat page.</p> <p id="page_1127" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>How to add, change and delete flatpages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Permissions to add or edit flatpages should be restricted to trusted users. Flatpages are defined</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">by raw HTML and are not sanitized by Django. As a consequence, a malicious flatpage can lead to various</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">security vulnerabilities, including permission escalation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Via the admin interface</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you’ve activated the automatic Django admin interface, you should see a “Flatpages” section on the admin index page. Edit flatpages as you edit any other object in the system.</p> <p>The FlatPage model has an enable_comments field that isn’t used by contrib.flatpages, but that could be useful for your project or third-party apps. It doesn’t appear in the admin interface, but you can add it by registering a custom ModelAdmin for FlatPage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.flatpages.admin</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FlatPageAdmin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.flatpages.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FlatPage</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.utils.translation</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">gettext_lazy</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">_</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Define a new FlatPageAdmin</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>FlatPageAdmin</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(FlatPageAdmin):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">fieldsets</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">_(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Advanced options"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:8em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"registration_required"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:8em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"template_name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:6em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Re-register FlatPageAdmin</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unregister(FlatPage)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(FlatPage, FlatPageAdmin)</span></p> <p id="page_1128"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Via the Python API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class FlatPage</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Flatpages are represented by a standard <a href="index.html#page_115">Django model,</a> which lives in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/contrib/flatpages/models.py">django/contrib/flatpages/models.py</a>. You can access flatpage objects via the <a href="index.html#page_143">Django database</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_143">API</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Check for duplicate flatpage URLs.</p> <p>If you add or modify flatpages via your own code, you will likely want to check for duplicate flatpage URLs within the same site. The flatpage form used in the admin performs this validation check, and can be im-ported from django.contrib.flatpages.forms.FlatpageForm and used in your own views.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Flatpage templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, flatpages are rendered via the template flatpages/default.html, but you can override that for a particular flatpage: in the admin, a collapsed fieldset titled “Advanced options” (clicking will expand it) contains a field for specifying a template name. If you’re creating a flat page via the Python API you can set the template name as the field template_name on the FlatPage object.</p> <p>Creating the flatpages/default.html template is your responsibility; in your template directory, create a flatpages directory containing a file default.html.</p> <p>Flatpage templates are passed a single context variable, flatpage, which is the flatpage object.</p> <p>Here’s a sample flatpages/default.html template:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b><!DOCTYPE html></b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">html</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">lang</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"en"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">head</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">title</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpage.title</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">title</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">head</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">body</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpage.content</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">body</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">html</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Since you’re already entering raw HTML into the admin page for a flatpage, both flatpage.title and</p> <p>flatpage.content are marked as not requiring <a href="index.html#page_1973">automatic HTML escaping</a> in the template.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1129" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Getting a list of FlatPage objects in your templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The flatpages app provides a template tag that allows you to iterate over all of the available flatpages on the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1362">current site.</a></p> <p>Like all custom template tags, you’ll need to <a href="index.html#page_1978">load its custom tag library</a> before you can use it. After loading</p> <p>the library, you can retrieve all current flatpages via the <a href="index.html#page_1129"><i>get_flatpages</i></a> tag:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>load</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_flatpages as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">flatpages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">><</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">href</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page.url</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{{</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">page.title</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>}}</b></i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">li</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>endfor</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"></</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ul</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Displaying registration_required flatpages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, the <a href="index.html#page_1129"><i>get_flatpages</i></a> template tag will only show flatpages that are marked registration_required = False. If you want to display registration-protected flatpages, you need to specify an authenticated user using a for clause.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_flatpages</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">for someuser</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">about_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you provide an anonymous user, <a href="index.html#page_1129"><i>get_flatpages</i></a> will behave the same as if you hadn’t provided a user – i.e., it will only show you public flatpages.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Limiting flatpages by base URL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>An optional argument, starts_with, can be applied to limit the returned pages to those beginning with a particular base URL. This argument may be passed as a string, or as a variable to be resolved from the context.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_flatpages</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'/about/'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">about_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_flatpages</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">about_prefix</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">about_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>{%</b></i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>get_flatpages</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'/about/'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">for someuser</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">about_pages</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i><b>%}</b></i></span></p> <p id="page_1130"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Integrating with django.contrib.sitemaps</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class FlatPageSitemap</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1130"><i>sitemaps.FlatPageSitemap</i></a> class looks at all publicly visible <a href="index.html#page_1124"><i>flatpages</i></a> defined for the current</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>SITE_ID</i></a> (see the <a href="index.html#page_1360"><i>sites documentation</i></a>) and creates an entry in the sitemap. These entries include</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">only the <a href="index.html#page_1352"><i>location</i></a> attribute – not <a href="index.html#page_1352"><i>lastmod</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1353"><i>changefreq</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1353"><i>priority</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1353">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Example</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here’s an example of a URLconf using <a href="index.html#page_1130"><i>FlatPageSitemap</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.flatpages.sitemaps</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">FlatPageSitemap</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.sitemaps.views</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sitemap</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">path</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># the sitemap</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"sitemap.xml"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">sitemap,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"sitemaps"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"flatpages"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: FlatPageSitemap}},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.sitemaps.views.sitemap"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.5.5 GeoDjango</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango intends to be a world-class geographic web framework. Its goal is to make it as easy as possible to build GIS web applications and harness the power of spatially enabled data.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeoDjango Tutorial</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Introduction</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango is an included contrib module for Django that turns it into a world-class geographic web frame-work. GeoDjango strives to make it as simple as possible to create geographic web applications, like location-based services. Its features include:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Django model fields for <a href="https://www.ogc.org/">OGC</a> geometries and raster data.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Extensions to Django’s ORM for querying and manipulating spatial data.</p> <p id="page_1131" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Loosely-coupled, high-level Python interfaces for GIS geometry and raster operations and data manip-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ulation in different formats.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Editing geometry fields from the admin.</p> <p>This tutorial assumes familiarity with Django; thus, if you’re brand new to Django, please read through the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_21">regular tutorial</a> to familiarize yourself with Django first.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: GeoDjango has additional requirements beyond what Django requires – please consult the <a href="index.html#page_1145">installation</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1145">documentation</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This tutorial will guide you through the creation of a geographic web application for viewing the <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20240123190237/https://thematicmapping.org/downloads/world_borders.php">world</a></p> <p><a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20240123190237/https://thematicmapping.org/downloads/world_borders.php">borders</a> <span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1131">1</a></span> <a href="index.html#page_1131">.</a> Some of the code used in this tutorial is taken from and/or inspired by the <a href="https://code.google.com/archive/p/geodjango-basic-apps">GeoDjango basic apps</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1131">project.<span style="font-size:0.67em">2</span></a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Proceed through the tutorial sections sequentially for step-by-step instructions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting Up</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Create a Spatial Database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Typically no special setup is required, so you can create a database as you would for any other project. We provide some tips for selected databases:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1151">Installing PostGIS</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1152">Installing SpatiaLite</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Create a New Project</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use the standard django-admin script to create a project called geodjango:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin startproject geodjango</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This will initialize a new project. Now, create a world Django application within the geodjango project:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geodjango</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py startapp world</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Special thanks to Bjørn Sandvik of</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://mastermaps.net/">mastermaps.net</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">for providing and maintaining this dataset.</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">2</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">GeoDjango basic apps was written by Dane Springmeyer, Josh Livni, and Christopher Schmidt.</span></p> <p id="page_1132"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Configure settings.py</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The geodjango project settings are stored in the geodjango/settings.py file. Edit the database connection settings to match your setup:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.gis.db.backends.postgis"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"geodjango"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"USER"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"geo"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition, modify the <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> setting to include <a href="index.html#page_1017"><i>django.contrib.admin</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1017">,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1130"><i>django.contrib.gis</i></a>, and world (your newly created application):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INSTALLED_APPS</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.admin"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.auth"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.contenttypes"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.sessions"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.messages"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.staticfiles"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.contrib.gis"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"world"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geographic Data</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>World Borders</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The world borders data is available in this <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20231220150759/https://thematicmapping.org/downloads/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.zip">zip file. </a>Create a data directory in the world application, download the world borders data, and unzip. On GNU/Linux platforms, use the following commands:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">mkdir world/data</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">world/data</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wget https://web.archive.org/web/20231220150759/https://thematicmapping.org/downloads/TM_WORLD_</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">BORDERS-0.3.zip</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">unzip TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.zip</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">../..</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The world borders ZIP file contains a set of data files collectively known as an <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapefile">ESRI Shapefile, </a>one of the most popular geospatial data formats. When unzipped, the world borders dataset includes files with the following extensions:</p> <p id="page_1133" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• .shp: Holds the vector data for the world borders geometries.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• .shx: Spatial index file for geometries stored in the .shp.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• .dbf: Database file for holding non-geometric attribute data (e.g., integer and character fields).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• .prj: Contains the spatial reference information for the geographic data stored in the shapefile.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Use ogrinfo to examine spatial data</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The GDAL ogrinfo utility allows examining the metadata of shapefiles or other vector data sources:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ogrinfo world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">INFO: Open of `world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp'</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">using driver `ESRI Shapefile' successful.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1: TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3 (Polygon)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>ogrinfo tells us that the shapefile has one layer, and that this layer contains polygon data. To find out more, we’ll specify the layer name and use the-so option to get only the important summary information:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ogrinfo -so world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">INFO: Open of `world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp'</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">using driver `ESRI Shapefile' successful.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Layer name: TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Geometry: Polygon</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Feature Count: 246</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Extent: (-180.000000, -90.000000) - (180.000000, 83.623596)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Layer SRS WKT:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOGCS["GCS_WGS_1984",</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATUM["WGS_1984",</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">SPHEROID["WGS_1984",6378137.0,298.257223563]],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">PRIMEM["Greenwich",0.0],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">UNIT["Degree",0.0174532925199433]]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">FIPS: String (2.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">ISO2: String (2.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">ISO3: String (3.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">UN: Integer (3.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">NAME: String (50.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AREA: Integer (7.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">POP2005: Integer (10.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">REGION: Integer (3.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SUBREGION: Integer (3.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LON: Real (8.3)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">LAT: Real (7.3)</span></p> <p id="page_1134"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This detailed summary information tells us the number of features in the layer (246), the geographic bounds of the data, the spatial reference system (“SRS WKT”), as well as type information for each attribute field. For example, FIPS: String (2.0) indicates that the FIPS character field has a maximum length of 2. Similarly, LON: Real (8.3) is a floating-point field that holds a maximum of 8 digits up to three decimal places.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geographic Models</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Defining a Geographic Model</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now that you’ve examined your dataset using ogrinfo, create a GeoDjango model to imported from django.contrib.gis.db.</p> <p>The default spatial reference system for geometry fields is WGS84 (meaning the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRID">SRID</a> is 4326) – in other words, the field coordinates are in longitude, latitude pairs in units of degrees. To use a different coordinate system, set the SRID of the geometry field with the srid argument. Use an integer representing the coordinate system’s EPSG code.</p> <p id="page_1135" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Run migrate</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>After defining your model, you need to sync it with the database. OK</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Importing Spatial Data</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This section will show you how to import the world borders shapefile into the database via GeoDjango models</p> <p>using the <a href="index.html#page_1272">LayerMapping data import utility.</a></p> <p>There are many different ways to import data into a spatial database – besides the tools included within GeoDjango, you may also use the following:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://gdal.org/programs/ogr2ogr.html">ogr2ogr</a>: A command-line utility included with GDAL that can import many vector data formats into</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">PostGIS, MySQL, and Oracle databases.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#shp2pgsql_usage">shp2pgsql: </a>This utility included with PostGIS imports ESRI shapefiles into PostGIS.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GDAL Interface</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Earlier, you used ogrinfo to examine the contents of the world borders shapefile. GeoDjango also includes a Pythonic interface to GDAL’s powerful OGR library that can work with all the vector data sources that OGR supports.</p> <p>First, invoke the Django shell:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py shell</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you downloaded the <a href="index.html#page_1132">World Borders</a> data earlier in the tutorial, then you can determine its path using</p> <p>Python’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path">pathlib.Path</a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pathlib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">world</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">world_shp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Path(world</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__file__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">resolve()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">parent</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>/</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"data"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>/</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now, open the world borders shapefile using GeoDjango’s <a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a> interface:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">/ ... /geodjango/world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp (ESRI Shapefile)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Data source objects can have different layers of geospatial features; however, shapefiles are only allowed to have one layer:</p> <p id="page_1137" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(lyr</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">len</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(lyr))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">246</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Unfortunately, the shapefile data format does not allow for greater specificity with regards to geom-etry types. This shapefile, like many others, actually includes MultiPolygon geometries, not Polygons. It’s important to use a more general field type in models: a GeoDjango MultiPolygonField will accept a Polygon geometry, but a PolygonField will not accept a MultiPolygon type geometry. This is why the WorldBorder model defined above uses a MultiPolygonField.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>Layer</i></a> may also have a spatial reference system associated with it. If it does, the srs attribute will return</p> <p>a <a href="index.html#page_1249"><i>SpatialReference</i></a> object:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span 84",6378137,298.257223563,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTHORITY["EPSG","7030"]],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">AUTHORITY["EPSG","4326"]]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">srs</span><span data uses longitude, latitude pairs in units of degrees.</p> <p>In addition, shapefiles also support attribute fields that may contain additional data. Here are the fields on <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_1138">the World Borders layer:</p> <p><span <span style="font-size:0.87em">[fld</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__name__</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Jersey 26</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">South Georgia South Sandwich Islands 338</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Taiwan 363</span></p> <p
