individual features may be retrieved by their feature ID:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">feat</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">lyr[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">234</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span be exported as WKT and GeoJSON:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span [ [ [ 12.415798, 43.957954 ], [ 12.450554, 43.979721 ], ...</span></p> <p id="page_1139" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>LayerMapping</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To import the data, use a LayerMapping in a Python script. Create a file called load.py inside the world application, with the following code:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pathlib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Path</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.utils</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LayerMapping</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">world_mapping</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"fips"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"FIPS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"iso3"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"ISO3"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"un"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"UN"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"area"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"AREA"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pop2005"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"POP2005"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"region"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"REGION"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"subregion"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"SUBREGION"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"lon"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"LON"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"lat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"LAT"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"mpoly"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"MULTIPOLYGON"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">world_shp</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__file__</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">resolve()</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">parent</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>/</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"data"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>/</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>run</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(verbose</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">lm</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LayerMapping(WorldBorder, world_shp, world_mapping, transform</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">lm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save(strict</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, verbose</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">verbose)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A few notes about what’s going on:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Each key in the world_mapping dictionary corresponds to a field in the WorldBorder model. The value</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">is the name of the shapefile field that data will be loaded from.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The key mpoly for the geometry field is MULTIPOLYGON, the geometry type GeoDjango will import the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">field as. Even simple polygons in the shapefile will automatically be converted into collections prior to insertion into the database.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The path to the shapefile is not absolute – in other words, if you move the world application (with data</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">subdirectory) to a different location, the script will still work.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The transform keyword is set to False because the data in the shapefile does not need to be converted</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">– it’s already in WGS84 (SRID=4326).</p> <p>Afterward, invoke the Django shell from the geodjango project directory:</p> <p id="page_1140"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py shell</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, import the load module, call the run routine, and watch LayerMapping do the work:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">world</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">load</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">load</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">run()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Try ogrinspect</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now that you’ve seen how to define geographic models and import data with the <a href="index.html#page_1272">LayerMapping data import</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1272">utility, </a>it’s possible to further automate this process with use of the <a href="index.html#page_1278"><i>ogrinspect</i></a> management command. The</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1278"><i>ogrinspect</i></a> command introspects a GDAL-supported vector data source (e.g., a shapefile) and generates a model definition and LayerMapping dictionary automatically.</p> <p>The general usage of the command goes as follows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py ogrinspect</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><data_source> <model_name></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>data_source is the path to the GDAL-supported data source and model_name is the name to use for the model. Command-line options may be used to further define how the model is generated.</p> <p>For example, the following command nearly reproduces the WorldBorder model and mapping dictionary created above, automatically:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py ogrinspect world/data/TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3.shp WorldBorder</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">\</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">--srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">--mapping --multi</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A few notes about the command-line options given above:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The--srid=4326 option sets the SRID for the geographic field.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The--mapping option tells ogrinspect to also generate a mapping dictionary for use with</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1274"><i>LayerMapping</i> .</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• The--multi option is specified so that the geographic field is a <a href="index.html#page_1162"><i>MultiPolygonField</i></a> instead of just a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1161"><i>PolygonField</i> .</a></p> <p>The command produces the following output, which may be copied directly into the models.py of a GeoD-jango application:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># This is an auto-generated Django model module created by ogrinspect.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>WorldBorder</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"subregion"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"SUBREGION"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"MULTIPOLYGON"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Queries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango adds spatial lookups to the Django ORM. For example, you can find the country in the WorldBorder table that contains a particular point. First, fire up the management shell:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py shell</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Now, define a point of interest<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1141">3</a></span>:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">3</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">This point is the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://www.law.uh.edu/">University of Houston Law Center</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em">.</span></p> <p id="page_1142"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt_wkt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"POINT(-95.3385 29.7245)"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The pnt_wkt string represents the point at -95.3385 degrees longitude, 29.7245 degrees latitude. The geometry is in a format known as Well Known Text (WKT), a standard issued by the Open Geospatial Consortium</p> <p>(OGC).<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1142">4</a></span> WorldBorder Import the model, and perform a contains lookup using the pnt_wkt as the parameter:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">world.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(mpoly__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt_wkt)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<WorldBorder: United States>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here, you retrieved a QuerySet with only one model: the border of the United States (exactly what you would expect).</p> <p>Similarly, you may also use a <a href="index.html#page_1210">GEOS geometry object</a>. Here, you can combine the intersects spatial lookup with the get method to retrieve only the WorldBorder instance for San Marino instead of a queryset:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">12.4604</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">43.9420</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(mpoly__intersects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><WorldBorder: San Marino></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The contains and intersects lookups are just a subset of the available queries – the <a href="index.html#page_1165">GeoDjango Database</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1165">API</a> documentation has more.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Automatic Spatial Transformations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When doing spatial queries, GeoDjango automatically transforms geometries if they’re in a different coor-</p> <p>dinate system. In the following example, coordinates will be expressed in <a href="https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/32140/">EPSG SRID 32140</a>, a coordinate system specific to south Texas only and in units of meters, not degrees:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry, Point</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">954158.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">4215137.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">32140</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that pnt may also be constructed with EWKT, an “extended” form of WKT that includes the SRID:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"SRID=32140;POINT(954158.1 4215137.1)"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango’s ORM will automatically wrap geometry values in transformation SQL, allowing the developer to work at a higher level of abstraction:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(mpoly__intersects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(qs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">query)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Generating the SQL</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">4</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Open Geospatial Consortium, Inc.,</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://www.ogc.org/standards/sfs">OpenGIS Simple Feature Specification For SQL</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em">.</span></p> <p id="page_1143" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SELECT "world_worldborder"."id", "world_worldborder"."name", "world_worldborder"."area",</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"world_worldborder"."pop2005", "world_worldborder"."fips", "world_worldborder"."iso2",</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"world_worldborder"."iso3", "world_worldborder"."un", "world_worldborder"."region",</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"world_worldborder"."subregion", "world_worldborder"."lon", "world_worldborder"."lat",</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"world_worldborder"."mpoly" FROM "world_worldborder"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WHERE ST_Intersects("world_worldborder"."mpoly", ST_Transform(%s, 4326))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># printing evaluates the queryset</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<WorldBorder: United States>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Raw queries</p> <p>When using <a href="index.html#page_200">raw queries</a>, you must wrap your geometry fields so that the field value can be recognized by GEOS:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span querying a non-default database:</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connections</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connections[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"your_gis_db_alias"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">City</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span myapp_city"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(connection</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span <p>You should only use raw queries when you know exactly what you’re doing.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Lazy Geometries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango loads geometries in a standardized textual representation. When the geometry field is first ac-</p> <p>cessed, GeoDjango creates a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> object, exposing powerful functionality, such as serialization properties for popular geospatial formats:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sm</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mpoly</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">wkt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># WKT</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">MULTIPOLYGON (((12.4157980000000006 43.9579540000000009, 12.4505540000000003 style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mpoly</span><span Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This includes access to all of the advanced geometric operations provided by the GEOS library:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">12.4604</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">43.9420</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mpoly</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">contains(pnt)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">True</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">contains(sm</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mpoly)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">False</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geographic annotations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango also offers a set of geographic annotations to compute distances and several other operations</p> <p>(intersection, difference, etc.). See the <a href="index.html#page_1195">Geographic Database Functions</a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Putting your data on the map</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geographic Admin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1017">Django’s admin application</a> supports editing geometry fields.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Basics</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Django admin allows users to create and modify geometries on a JavaScript slippy map (powered by</p> <p><a href="https://openlayers.org/">OpenLayers</a>).</p> <p>Let’s dive right in. Create a file called admin.py inside the world application with the following code:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">WorldBorder</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(WorldBorder, admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">ModelAdmin)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, edit your urls.py in the geodjango application folder as follows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.urls</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">include, path</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">urlpatterns</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">path(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"admin/"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">urls),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Create an admin user:</p> <p id="page_1145" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py createsuperuser</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, start up the Django development server:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python manage.py runserver</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, browse to http://localhost:8000/admin/, and log in with the user you just created. Browse to any of the WorldBorder entries – the borders may be edited by clicking on a polygon and dragging the vertices to the desired position.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GISModelAdmin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>With the <a href="index.html#page_1279"><i>GISModelAdmin</i></a>, GeoDjango uses an <a href="https://www.openstreetmap.org/">OpenStreetMap</a> layer in the admin. This provides more context</p> <p>(including street and thoroughfare details) than available with the <a href="index.html#page_1038"><i>ModelAdmin</i></a> (which uses the <a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20201024202709/https://earth-info.nga.mil/publications/vmap0.html">Vector Map</a></p> <p><a href="http://web.archive.org/web/20201024202709/https://earth-info.nga.mil/publications/vmap0.html">Level 0</a> WMS dataset hosted at <a href="https://www.osgeo.org/">OSGeo</a>).</p> <p>The PROJ datum shifting files must be installed (see the <a href="index.html#page_1149">PROJ installation instructions</a> for more details).</p> <p>If you meet this requirement, then use the GISModelAdmin option class in your admin.py file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">site</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">register(WorldBorder, admin</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">GISModelAdmin)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeoDjango Installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overview</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In general, GeoDjango installation requires:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. <a href="index.html#page_1146">Python and Django</a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. <a href="index.html#page_1146">Spatial database</a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. <a href="index.html#page_1146">Installing Geospatial libraries</a></p> <p>Details for each of the requirements and installation instructions are provided in the sections below. In addition, platform-specific instructions are available for:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1156">macOS</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1158">Windows</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use the Source</p> <p>Because GeoDjango takes advantage of the latest in the open source geospatial software technology, recent versions of the libraries are necessary. If binary packages aren’t available for your platform, installation <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_1146">from source may be required. When compiling the libraries from source, please follow the directions closely, especially if you’re a beginner.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Requirements</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Python and Django</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because GeoDjango is included with Django, please refer to Django’s <a href="index.html#page_113">installation instructions</a> for details on how to install.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostgreSQL (with PostGIS), MySQL, Oracle, and SQLite (with SpatiaLite) are the spatial databases currently supported.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: PostGIS is recommended, because it is the most mature and feature-rich open source spatial database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The geospatial libraries required for a GeoDjango installation depends on the spatial database used. The following lists the library requirements, supported versions, and any notes for each of the supported database backends:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Database Library Requirements Supported Versions Notes</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">PostgreSQL GEOS, GDAL, PROJ, PostGIS 14+ Requires PostGIS.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">MySQL GEOS, GDAL 8.0.11+ <a href="index.html#page_1166">Limited functionality</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">Oracle GEOS, GDAL 19+ XE not supported.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">SQLite GEOS, GDAL, PROJ, SpatiaLite 3.31.0+ Requires SpatiaLite 4.3+</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also <a href="https://trac.osgeo.org/postgis/wiki/UsersWikiPostgreSQLPostGIS">this comparison matrix</a> on the OSGeo Wiki for PostgreSQL/PostGIS/GEOS/GDAL possible combina-tions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geospatial libraries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing Geospatial libraries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango uses and/or provides interfaces for the following open source geospatial libraries:</p> <p id="page_1147" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Program Description Required Supported Versions</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="index.html#page_1210">GEOS</a> Geometry Engine Open Source Yes 3.13, 3.12, 3.11, 3.10, 3.9, 3.8</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="https://proj.org/">PROJ</a> Cartographic Projections Yes (PostgreSQL and SQLite 9.x, 8.x, 7.x, 6.x</p> <p style="margin-left:5em">library only)</p> <p style="text-align:center"><a href="index.html#page_1231">GDAL</a> Geospatial Data Abstraction Yes 3.9, 3.8, 3.7, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3,</p> <p style="margin-left:5em">Library 3.2, 3.1</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="index.html#page_1268">GeoIP</a> IP-based geolocation library No 2</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="https://postgis.net/">PostGIS</a> Spatial extensions for Post- Yes (PostgreSQL only) 3.4, 3.3, 3.2, 3.1</p> <p style="margin-left:5em">greSQL</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="https://www.gaia-gis.it/gaia-sins/">Spa-</a> Spatial extensions for SQLite Yes (SQLite only) 5.1, 5.0, 4.3</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><a href="https://www.gaia-gis.it/gaia-sins/">tiaLite</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that older or more recent versions of these libraries may also work totally fine with GeoDjango. Your mileage may vary.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The GeoDjango interfaces to GEOS, GDAL, and GeoIP may be used independently of Django. In other</p> <p>words, no database or settings file required – import them as normal from <a href="index.html#page_1130"><i>django.contrib.gis</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On Debian/Ubuntu, you are advised to install the following packages which will install, directly or by depen-dency, the required geospatial libraries:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sudo apt-get install binutils libproj-dev gdal-bin</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Please also consult platform-specific instructions if you are on <a href="index.html#page_1156">macOS</a> or <a href="index.html#page_1158">Windows</a><a href="index.html#page_1158">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Building from source</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When installing from source on UNIX and GNU/Linux systems, please follow the installation instructions carefully, and install the libraries in the given order. If using MySQL or Oracle as the spatial database, only GEOS is required.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: On Linux platforms, it may be necessary to run the ldconfig command after installing each library. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo make install</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo ldconfig</span></p> <p id="page_1148"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: macOS users must install <a href="https://developer.apple.com/xcode/">Xcode</a> in order to compile software from source.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GEOS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOS is a C++ library for performing geometric operations, and is the default internal geometry represen-tation used by GeoDjango (it’s behind the “lazy” geometries). Specifically, the C API library is called (e.g., libgeos_c.so) directly from Python using ctypes.</p> <p>First, download GEOS from the GEOS website and untar the source archive:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://download.osgeo.org/geos/geos-X.Y.Z.tar.bz2</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ tar xjf geos-X.Y.Z.tar.bz2</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then step into the GEOS directory, create a build folder, and step into it:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geos-X.Y.Z</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ mkdir build</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">build</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then build and install the package:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Release ..</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake --build .</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo cmake --build . --target install</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Troubleshooting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Can’t find GEOS library</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When GeoDjango can’t find GEOS, this error is raised:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">ImportError: Could not find the GEOS library (tried "geos_c"). Try setting GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH in</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">␣</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">your settings.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The most common solution is to properly configure your <a href="index.html#page_1155">Library environment settings</a> or set</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1149">GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH</a> in your settings.</p> <p>If using a binary package of GEOS (e.g., on Ubuntu), you may need to <a href="index.html#page_1156">Install binutils</a>.</p> <p id="page_1149" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your GEOS library is in a non-standard location, or you don’t want to modify the system’s library path</p> <p>then the <a href="index.html#page_1231"><i>GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH</i></a> setting may be added to your Django settings file with the full path to the GEOS C library. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'/home/bob/local/lib/libgeos_c.so'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The setting must be the full path to the C shared library; in other words you want to use libgeos_c.so, not libgeos.so.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See also <a href="index.html#page_1212">My logs are filled with GEOS-related errors.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PROJ</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://proj.org/">PROJ</a> is a library for converting geospatial data to different coordinate reference systems.</p> <p>First, download the PROJ source code:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://download.osgeo.org/proj/proj-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i> <span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1149">1</a></span> and datum shifting files (download proj-datumgrid-X.Y.tar.gz for PROJ < 7.x):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://download.osgeo.org/proj/proj-data-X.Y.tar.gz</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, untar the source code archive, and extract the datum shifting files in the data subdirectory. This must be done prior to configuration:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ tar xzf proj-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">proj-X.Y.Z/data</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ tar xzf ../../proj-data-X.Y.tar.gz</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">../..</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For PROJ 9.x and greater, releases only support builds using CMake (see <a href="https://proj.org/community/rfc/rfc-7.html#rfc7">PROJ RFC-7).</a></p> <p>To build with CMake ensure your system meets the <a href="https://proj.org/install.html#build-requirements">build requirements</a>. Then create a build folder in the PROJ directory, and step into it:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">The datum shifting files are needed for converting data to and from certain projections. For example, the PROJ string for the</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/3857/">Google projection (900913 or 3857)</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">requires the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">null</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">grid file only included in the extra datum shifting files. It is easier to install the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">shifting files now, then to have debug a problem caused by their absence later.</span></p> <p id="page_1150"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">proj-X.Y.Z</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ mkdir build</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">build</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, configure, make and install PROJ:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake ..</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake --build .</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo cmake --build . --target install</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GDAL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://gdal.org/">GDAL</a> is an excellent open source geospatial library that has support for reading most vector and raster</p> <p>spatial data formats. Currently, GeoDjango only supports <span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1150">2</a></span> <a href="index.html#page_1231">GDAL’s vector data</a> capabilities. <a href="index.html#page_1148">GEOS</a> and <a href="index.html#page_1149">PROJ</a> should be installed prior to building GDAL.</p> <p>First download the latest GDAL release version and untar the archive:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://download.osgeo.org/gdal/X.Y.Z/gdal-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">$ tar xzf gdal-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For GDAL 3.6.x and greater, releases only support builds using CMake. To build with CMake create a build folder in the GDAL directory, and step into it:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">gdal-X.Y.Z</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ mkdir build</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">build</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, configure, make and install GDAL:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake ..</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ cmake --build .</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo cmake --build . --target install</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have any problems, please see the troubleshooting section below for suggestions and solutions.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">2</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Specifically, GeoDjango provides support for the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://gdal.org/user/vector_data_model.html">OGR</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">library, a component of GDAL.</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1151" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Troubleshooting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Can’t find GDAL library</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When GeoDjango can’t find the GDAL library, configure your <a href="index.html#page_1155">Library environment settings</a> or set</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1151">GDAL_LIBRARY_PATH</a> in your settings.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GDAL_LIBRARY_PATH</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If your GDAL library is in a non-standard location, or you don’t want to modify the system’s library path</p> <p>then the <a href="index.html#page_1268"><i>GDAL_LIBRARY_PATH</i></a> setting may be added to your Django settings file with the full path to the GDAL library. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">GDAL_LIBRARY_PATH</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'/home/sue/local/lib/libgdal.so'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing PostGIS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://postgis.net/">PostGIS</a> adds geographic object support to PostgreSQL, turning it into a spatial database. <a href="index.html#page_1148">GEOS</a><a href="index.html#page_1148">,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1149">PROJ</a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1150">GDAL</a> should be installed prior to building PostGIS. You might also need additional libraries, see <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/postgis_installation.html#install_requirements">PostGIS</a></p> <p><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/postgis_installation.html#install_requirements">requirements.</a></p> <p>The <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/">psycopg</a> or <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/">psycopg2</a> module is required for use as the database adapter when using GeoDjango with PostGIS.</p> <p>On Debian/Ubuntu, you are advised to install the following packages: postgresql-x, postgresql-x-postgis-3, postgresql-server-dev-x, and python3-psycopg3 (x matching the Post-</p> <p>greSQL version you want to install). Alternately, you can <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/postgis_installation.html#install_short_version">build from source</a>. Consult the platform-specific</p> <p>instructions if you are on <a href="index.html#page_1156">macOS</a> or <a href="index.html#page_1158">Windows</a><a href="index.html#page_1158">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Post-installation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating a spatial database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostGIS includes an extension for PostgreSQL that’s used to enable spatial functionality:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ createdb</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><db name></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ psql <db name></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">> CREATE EXTENSION postgis;</span></p> <p id="page_1152"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The database user must be a superuser in order to run CREATE EXTENSION postgis;. The command is run</p> <p>during the <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> process. An alternative is to use a migration operation in your project:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CreateExtension</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">migrations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[CreateExtension(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"postgis"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you plan to use PostGIS raster functionality, you should also activate the postgis_raster extension. You</p> <p>can install the extension using the <a href="index.html#page_1335"><i>CreateExtension</i></a> migration operation, or directly by running CREATE EXTENSION postgis_raster;.</p> <p>GeoDjango does not currently leverage any <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/Topology.html">PostGIS topology functionality</a>. If you plan to use those fea-tures at some point, you can also install the postgis_topology extension by issuing CREATE EXTENSION postgis_topology;.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Managing the database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To administer the database, you can either use the pgAdmin III program (Start ‣ PostgreSQL X ‣ pgAdmin III) or the SQL Shell (Start ‣ PostgreSQL X ‣ SQL Shell). For example, to create a geodjango spatial database and user, the following may be executed from the SQL Shell as the postgres user:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">postgres</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b># CREATE USER</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geodjango</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>PASSWORD</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'my_passwd'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">postgres# CREATE DATABASE geodjango OWNER geodjango;</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing SpatiaLite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://www.gaia-gis.it/fossil/libspatialite/index">SpatiaLite</a> adds spatial support to SQLite, turning it into a full-featured spatial database.</p> <p>First, check if you can install SpatiaLite from system packages or binaries.</p> <p>For example, on Debian-based distributions that package SpatiaLite 4.3+, try to install the libsqlite3-mod-spatialite package. For older releases install spatialite-bin.</p> <p>For macOS, follow the <a href="index.html#page_1154">instructions below</a>.</p> <p>For Windows, you may find binaries on the <a href="https://www.gaia-gis.it/gaia-sins/">Gaia-SINS</a> home page.</p> <p>In any case, you should always be able to <a href="index.html#page_1153">install from source</a>.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1153" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Installing from source</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1146">GEOS and PROJ</a> should be installed prior to building SpatiaLite.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SQLite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Check first if SQLite is compiled with the <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/rtree.html">R*Tree module. </a>Run the sqlite3 command line interface and enter the following query:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">sqlite></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CREATE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">VIRTUAL</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TABLE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">testrtree</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>USING</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rtree(id,minX,maxX,minY,maxY);</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you obtain an error, you will have to recompile SQLite from source. Otherwise, skip this section.</p> <p>To install from sources, download the latest amalgamation source archive from the <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/download.html">SQLite download page</a>, and extract:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://www.sqlite.org/YYYY/sqlite-amalgamation-XXX0000.zip</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">$ unzip sqlite-amalgamation-XXX0000.zip</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">sqlite-amalgamation-XXX0000</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Next, run the configure script – however the CFLAGS environment variable needs to be customized so that SQLite knows to build the R*Tree module:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CFLAGS</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"-DSQLITE_ENABLE_RTREE=1"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">./configure</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ make</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo make install</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">..</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SpatiaLite library (libspatialite)</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Get the latest SpatiaLite library source bundle from the <a href="https://www.gaia-gis.it/gaia-sins/libspatialite-sources/">download page</a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://www.gaia-gis.it/gaia-sins/libspatialite-sources/libspatialite-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">$ tar xaf libspatialite-X.Y.Z.tar.gz</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">cd</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">libspatialite-X.Y.Z</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./configure</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ make</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo make install</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: For macOS users building from source, the SpatiaLite library and tools need to have their target configured:</p> <p id="page_1154"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ ./configure --target</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">macosx</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>macOS-specific instructions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To install the SpatiaLite library and tools, macOS users can use <a href="https://brew.sh/">Homebrew</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Homebrew</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://brew.sh/">Homebrew</a> handles all the SpatiaLite related packages on your behalf, including SQLite, SpatiaLite, PROJ, and GEOS. Install them like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew update</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install spatialite-tools</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install gdal</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, for GeoDjango to be able to find the SpatiaLite library, set the SPATIALITE_LIBRARY_PATH setting to its path. This will be within your brew install path, which you can check with:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">brew --prefix</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">/opt/homebrew</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Using this brew install path, the full path can be constructed like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SPATIALITE_LIBRARY_PATH</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/opt/homebrew/lib/mod_spatialite.dylib"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DATABASES configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Set the <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>ENGINE</i></a> setting to one of the <a href="index.html#page_1165">spatial backends</a><a href="index.html#page_1165">.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Add django.contrib.gis to INSTALLED_APPS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Like other Django contrib applications, you will only need to add <a href="index.html#page_1130"><i>django.contrib.gis</i></a> to <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> in your settings. This is so that the gis templates can be located – if not done, then features such as the geographic admin or KML sitemaps will not function properly.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1155" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Troubleshooting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you can’t find the solution to your problem here then participate in the community! You can:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Ask your question on the <a href="https://forum.djangoproject.com/c/internals/geodjango/13">GeoDjango</a> forum.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• File a ticket on the <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/newticket">Django trac</a> if you think there’s a bug. Make sure to provide a complete description</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">of the problem, versions used, and specify the component as “GIS”.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Library environment settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By far, the most common problem when installing GeoDjango is that the external shared libraries (e.g., for</p> <p>GEOS and GDAL) cannot be <a href="index.html#page_1155">located.<span style="font-size:0.67em">1</span></a> Typically, the cause of this problem is that the operating system isn’t aware of the directory where the libraries built from source were installed.</p> <p>In general, the library path may be set on a per-user basis by setting an environment variable, or by config-uring the library path for the entire system.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A user may set this environment variable to customize the library paths they want to use. The typical library directory for software built from source is /usr/local/lib. Thus, /usr/local/lib needs to be included in the LD_LIBRARY_PATH variable. For example, the user could place the following in their bash profile:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LD_LIBRARY_PATH</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/usr/local/lib</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting system library path</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On GNU/Linux systems, there is typically a file in /etc/ld.so.conf, which may include additional paths from files in another directory, such as /etc/ld.so.conf.d. As the root user, add the custom library path (like /usr/local/lib) on a new line in ld.so.conf. This is one example of how to do so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">echo</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">/usr/local/lib >> /etc/ld.so.conf</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo ldconfig</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For OpenSolaris users, the system library path may be modified using the crle utility. Run crle with no options to see the current configuration and use crle -l to set with the new library path. Be very careful when modifying the system library path:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># crle -l $OLD_PATH:/usr/local/lib</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html#ctypes.util.find_library">find_library()</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">GeoDjango uses the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">routine from</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">ctypes.util</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">to locate shared libraries.</span></p> <p id="page_1156"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Install binutils</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango uses the find_library function (from the ctypes.util Python module) to discover libraries. The find_library routine uses a program called objdump (part of the binutils package) to verify a shared library on GNU/Linux systems. Thus, if binutils is not installed on your Linux system then Python’s ctypes may not be able to find your library even if your library path is set correctly and geospatial libraries were built perfectly.</p> <p>The binutils package may be installed on Debian and Ubuntu systems using the following command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo apt-get install binutils</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Similarly, on Red Hat and CentOS systems:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo yum install binutils</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Platform-specific instructions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>macOS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Because of the variety of packaging systems available for macOS, users have several different options for installing GeoDjango. These options are:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1157">Postgres.app</a> (easiest and recommended)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1157">Homebrew</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1157">Fink</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1158">MacPorts</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1147">Building from source</a></p> <p>This section also includes instructions for installing an upgraded version of <a href="index.html#page_1156">Python</a> from packages provided by the Python Software Foundation, however, this is not required.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Python</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Although macOS comes with Python installed, users can use <a href="https://www.python.org/ftp/python/">framework installers</a> provided by the Python Software Foundation. An advantage to using the installer is that macOS’s Python will remain “pristine” for internal operating system use.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: You will need to modify the PATH environment variable in your .profile file so that the new version of Python is used when python is entered at the command-line:</p> <p id="page_1157" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PATH</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/Current/bin:</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">$PATH</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Postgres.app</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://postgresapp.com/">Postgres.app</a> is a standalone PostgreSQL server that includes the PostGIS extension. You will also need to</p> <p>install gdal and libgeoip with <a href="index.html#page_1157">Homebrew</a>.</p> <p>After installing Postgres.app, add the following to your .bash_profile so you can run the package’s pro-grams from the command-line. Replace X.Y with the version of PostgreSQL in the Postgres.app you installed:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PATH</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">$PATH</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:/Applications/Postgres.app/Contents/Versions/X.Y/bin</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can check if the path is set up correctly by typing which psql at a terminal prompt.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Homebrew</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://brew.sh/">Homebrew</a> provides “recipes” for building binaries and packages from source. It provides recipes for the GeoDjango prerequisites on Macintosh computers running macOS. Because Homebrew still builds the soft-</p> <p>ware from source, <a href="https://developer.apple.com/xcode/">Xcode</a> is required.</p> <p>Summary:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install postgresql</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install postgis</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install gdal</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ brew install libgeoip</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Fink</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://schwehr.blogspot.com/">Kurt Schwehr</a> has been gracious enough to create GeoDjango packages for users of the <a href="https://www.finkproject.org/">Fink</a> package system.</p> <p><a href="https://pdb.finkproject.org/pdb/browse.php?summary=django-gis">Different packages are available</a> (starting with django-gis), depending on which version of Python you want to use.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1158"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MacPorts</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://www.macports.org/">MacPorts</a> may be used to install GeoDjango prerequisites on computers running macOS. Because MacPorts</p> <p>still builds the software from source, <a href="https://developer.apple.com/xcode/">Xcode</a> is required.</p> <p>Summary:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install postgresql14-server</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install geos</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install proj6</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install postgis3</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install gdal</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ sudo port install libgeoip</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: You will also have to modify the PATH in your .profile so that the MacPorts programs are accessible from the command-line:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PATH</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/opt/local/bin:/opt/local/lib/postgresql14/bin</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition, add the DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH setting so that the libraries can be found by Python:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">/opt/local/lib:/opt/local/lib/postgresql14</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Windows</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Proceed through the following sections sequentially in order to install GeoDjango on Windows. In this tutorial we will install 64 bit versions of each application.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Python</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Install a 64 bit version of Python. See <a href="index.html#page_862">Install Python</a> for further information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Download the latest <a href="https://www.enterprisedb.com/downloads/postgres-postgresql-downloads">PostgreSQL 15.x installer</a> from the <a href="https://www.enterprisedb.com">EnterpriseDB</a> website. <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span
