style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">RasterField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Field Types</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Spatial fields consist of a series of geometry field types and one raster field type. Each of the geometry field</p> <p>types correspond to the OpenGIS Simple Features specification<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1161">1</a></span>. There is no such standard for raster data.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeometryField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GeometryField</b></p> <p>The base class for geometry fields.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PointField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class PointField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>LineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class LineStringField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1223"><i>LineString</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class PolygonField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>Polygon</i>.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">OpenGIS Consortium, Inc.,</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://www.ogc.org/standard/sfs/">Simple Feature Specification For SQL</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://www.ogc.org/standard/sfs/">.</a></span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1162"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiPointField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiPointField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>MultiPoint</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiLineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiLineStringField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1225"><i>MultiLineString</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiPolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiPolygonField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1225"><i>MultiPolygon</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeometryCollectionField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GeometryCollectionField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1225"><i>GeometryCollection</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>RasterField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class RasterField</b></p> <p>Stores a <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a>.</p> <p>RasterField is currently only implemented for the PostGIS backend.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Field Options</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to the regular <a href="index.html#page_1615">Field options</a> available for Django model fields, spatial fields have the following additional options. All are optional.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1163" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>srid</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseSpatialField.<b>srid</b></p> <p>Sets the <a href="index.html#page_1163">SRID<span style="font-size:0.67em">2</span></a> (Spatial Reference System Identity) of the geometry field to the given value. Defaults to 4326</p> <p>(also known as <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WGS84">WGS84</a>, units are in degrees of longitude and latitude).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Selecting an SRID</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Choosing an appropriate SRID for your model is an important decision that the developer should consider carefully. The SRID is an integer specifier that corresponds to the projection system that will be used to</p> <p>interpret the data in the spatial database.<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1163">3</a></span> Projection systems give the context to the coordinates that specify</p> <p>a location. Although the details of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesy">geodesy</a> are beyond the scope of this documentation, the general problem is that the earth is spherical and representations of the earth (e.g., paper maps, web maps) are not.</p> <p>Most people are familiar with using latitude and longitude to reference a location on the earth’s surface. However, latitude and longitude are angles, not distances. In other words, while the shortest path between two points on a flat surface is a straight line, the shortest path between two points on a curved surface (such</p> <p>as the earth) is an arc of a <a href="index.html#page_1163"><span style="font-size:0.67em">4</a></span> <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_circle">great circle .</a> Thus, additional computation is required to obtain distances in planar units (e.g., kilometers and miles). Using a geographic coordinate system may introduce complications for the developer later on. For example, SpatiaLite does not have the capability to perform distance calculations between geometries using geographic coordinate systems, e.g. constructing a query to find all points within 5 miles of a county boundary stored as WGS84.<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1163">5</a></span></p> <p>Portions of the earth’s surface may projected onto a two-dimensional, or Cartesian, plane. Projected coordi-nate systems are especially convenient for region-specific applications, e.g., if you know that your database</p> <p>will only cover geometries in <a href="https://spatialreference.org/ref/epsg/2796/">North Kansas</a>, then you may consider using projection system specific to that region. Moreover, projected coordinate systems are defined in Cartesian units (such as meters or feet), easing distance calculations.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you wish to perform arbitrary distance queries using non-point geometries in WGS84 in PostGIS and</p> <p>you want decent performance, enable the <a href="index.html#page_1164"><i>GeometryField.geography</i></a> keyword so that <a href="index.html#page_1165">geography database</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1165">type</a> is used instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Additional Resources:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://spatialreference.org/">spatialreference.org</a>: A Django-powered database of spatial reference systems.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">2</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See id. at Ch. 2.3.8, p. 39 (Geometry Values and Spatial Reference Systems).</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">3</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Typically, SRID integer corresponds to an EPSG (</span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://epsg.org/">European Petroleum Survey Group</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em">) identifier. However, it may also be associated</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.8em">with custom projections defined in spatial database’s spatial reference systems table.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.6em">4</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Terry A. Slocum, Robert B. McMaster, Fritz C. Kessler, & Hugh H. Howard, Thematic Cartography and Geographic Visualization</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.8em">(Prentice Hall, 2nd edition), at Ch. 7.1.3.</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">5</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">This limitation does not apply to PostGIS.</span></p> <p id="page_1164"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20080302095452/http://welcome.warnercnr.colostate.edu/class_info/nr502/lg3/datums_coordinates/spcs.html">The State Plane Coordinate System</a>: A website covering the various projection systems used in the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">United States. Much of the U.S. spatial data encountered will be in one of these coordinate systems rather than in a geographic coordinate system such as WGS84.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>spatial_index</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseSpatialField.<b>spatial_index</b></p> <p>Defaults to True. Creates a spatial index for the given geometry field.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: This is different from the db_index field option because spatial indexes are created in a different manner than regular database indexes. Specifically, spatial indexes are typically created using a variant of the R-Tree, while regular database indexes typically use B-Trees.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geometry Field Options</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are additional options available for Geometry fields. All the following options are optional.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>dim</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeometryField.<b>dim</b></p> <p>This option may be used for customizing the coordinate dimension of the geometry field. By default, it is set to 2, for representing two-dimensional geometries. For spatial backends that support it, it may be set to 3 for three-dimensional support.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: At this time 3D support is limited to the PostGIS and SpatiaLite backends.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>geography</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeometryField.<b>geography</b></p> <p>If set to True, this option will create a database column of type geography, rather than geometry. Please</p> <p>refer to the <a href="index.html#page_1165">geography type</a> section below for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Geography support is limited to PostGIS and will force the SRID to be 4326.</p> <p id="page_1165" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geography Type</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The geography type provides native support for spatial features represented with geographic coordinates</p> <p>(e.g., WGS84 longitude/latitude).<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1165">6</a></span> Unlike the plane used by a geometry type, the geography type uses a spherical representation of its data. Distance and measurement operations performed on a geography column automatically employ great circle arc calculations and return linear units. In other words, when ST_Distance is called on two geographies, a value in meters is returned (as opposed to degrees if called on a geometry column in WGS84).</p> <p>Because geography calculations involve more mathematics, only a subset of the PostGIS spatial lookups are</p> <p>available for the geography type. Practically, this means that in addition to the <a href="index.html#page_1190">distance lookups</a> only the</p> <p>following additional <a href="index.html#page_1177">spatial lookups</a> are available for geography columns:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1179"><i>bboverlaps</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1180"><i>coveredby</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1181"><i>covers</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1183"><i>intersects</i></a></p> <p>If you need to use a spatial lookup or aggregate that doesn’t support the geography type as input, you can</p> <p>use the <a href="index.html#page_1816"><i>Cast</i></a> database function to convert the geography column to a geometry type in the query:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.db.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PointField</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models.functions</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Cast</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(geom</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Cast(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"geography_field"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, PointField()))</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom__within</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">poly</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For more information, the PostGIS documentation contains a helpful section on determining <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#PostGIS_GeographyVSGeometry">when to use</a></p> <p><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#PostGIS_GeographyVSGeometry">geography data type over geometry data type</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeoDjango Database API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Backends</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango currently provides the following spatial database backends:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django.contrib.gis.db.backends.postgis</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django.contrib.gis.db.backends.mysql</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django.contrib.gis.db.backends.oracle</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django.contrib.gis.db.backends.spatialite</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">6</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">Please refer to the</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#PostGIS_Geography">PostGIS Geography Type</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">documentation for more details.</span></p> <p id="page_1166"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MySQL Spatial Limitations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports spatial functions operating on real geometries available in modern MySQL versions. How-ever, the spatial functions are not as rich as other backends like PostGIS.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Raster Support</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>RasterField is currently only implemented for the PostGIS backend. Spatial lookups are available for raster fields, but spatial database functions and aggregates aren’t implemented for raster fields.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating and Saving Models with Geometry Fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Here is an example of how to create a geometry object (assuming the Zipcode model):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">zipcode.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode(code</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">77096</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, poly</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POLYGON(( 10 10, 10 20, 20 20, 20 15, 10 10))"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects may also be used to save geometric models:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">poly</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POLYGON(( 10 10, 10 20, 20 20, 20 15, 10 10))"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode(code</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">77096</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, poly</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">poly)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Moreover, if the GEOSGeometry is in a different coordinate system (has a different SRID value) than that of the field, then it will be implicitly transformed into the SRID of the model’s field, using the spatial database’s transform procedure:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">poly_3084</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"POLYGON(( 10 10, 10 20, 20 20, 20 15, 10 10))"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">3084</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># SRID 3084 is 'NAD83(HARN) / Texas Centric Lambert Conformal'</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode(code</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">78212</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, poly</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">poly_3084)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">z</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">connection</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">queries[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>-</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">][</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"sql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># printing the last SQL statement executed (requires DEBUG=True)</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">INSERT INTO "geoapp_zipcode" ("code", "poly") VALUES (78212, ST_Transform(ST_GeomFromWKB('\\001 ...</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">', 3084), 4326))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Thus, geometry parameters may be passed in using the GEOSGeometry <a href="index.html#page_1166"><span style="font-size:0.67em">1</span> object, WKT (Well Known Text</a></span>),</p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See Open Geospatial Consortium, Inc.,</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://portal.ogc.org/files/?artifact_id=829">OpenGIS Simple Feature Specification For SQL</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://portal.ogc.org/files/?artifact_id=829">, </a>Document 99-049 (May 5, 1999), at Ch. 3.2.5,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.8em">p. 3-11 (SQL Textual Representation of Geometry).</span></p> <p id="page_1167" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>HEXEWKB (PostGIS specific – a WKB geometry in <a href="index.html#page_1167">hexadecimal<span style="font-size:0.67em">2</span></a>), and GeoJSON (see <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946.html">RFC 7946</a>). Essentially, if the input is not a GEOSGeometry object, the geometry field will attempt to create a GEOSGeometry instance from the input.</p> <p>For more information creating <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects, refer to the <a href="index.html#page_1211">GEOS tutorial</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating and Saving Models with Raster Fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When creating raster models, the raster field will implicitly convert the input into a <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> using lazy-</p> <p>evaluation. The raster field will therefore accept any input that is accepted by the <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> constructor.</p> <p>Here is an example of how to create a raster object from a raster file volcano.tif (assuming the Elevation model):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">elevation.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dem</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Volcano"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, rast</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/raster/volcano.tif"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dem</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> objects may also be used to save raster models:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.gdal</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GDALRaster</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rast</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"width"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"height"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Canyon"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"srid"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"scale"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>-</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"bands"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"data"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">range</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)}],</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dem</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Canyon"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, rast</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">rast)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dem</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that this equivalent to:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dem</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Canyon"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rast</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"width"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"height"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">10</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"name"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Canyon"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"srid"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"scale"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>-</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0.1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">2</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#EWKB_EWKT">PostGIS EWKB, EWKT and Canonical Forms</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#EWKB_EWKT">, </a>PostGIS documentation at Ch. 4.1.2.</span></p> <p id="page_1168"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"bands"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: [{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"data"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">range</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)}],</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango’s lookup types may be used with any manager method like filter(), exclude(), etc. However, the lookup types unique to GeoDjango are only available on spatial fields.</p> <p>Filters on ‘normal’ fields (e.g. <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a>) may be chained with those on geographic fields. Geographic lookups accept geometry and raster input on both sides and input types can be mixed freely.</p> <p>The general structure of geographic lookups is described below. A complete reference can be found in the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1177">spatial lookup reference.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geometry Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Geographic queries with geometries take the following general form (assuming the Zipcode model used in</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1160">GeoDjango Model API</a>):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>> qs = Zipcode.objects.filter(<field>__<lookup_type>=<parameter>)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>> qs = Zipcode.objects.exclude(...)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">rst)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this case, poly is the geographic field, <a href="index.html#page_1179"><i>contains</i></a> is the spatial lookup type, pnt is the parameter (which may</p> <p>be a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> object or a string of GeoJSON , WKT, or HEXEWKB), and rst is a <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> object.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Raster Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The raster lookup syntax is similar to the syntax for geometries. The only difference is that a band index can be specified as additional input. If no band index is specified, the first band is used by default (index 0). In that case the syntax is identical to the syntax for geometry lookups.</p> <p>To specify the band index, an additional parameter can be specified on both sides of the lookup. On the left hand side, the double underscore syntax is used to pass a band index. On the right hand side, a tuple of the raster and band index can be specified.</p> <p>This results in the following general form for lookups involving rasters (assuming the Elevation model used</p> <p>in the <a href="index.html#page_1160">GeoDjango Model API):</a></p> <p id="page_1169" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>> qs = Elevation.objects.filter(<field>__<lookup_type>=<parameter>)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>> qs = Elevation.objects.filter(<field>__<band_index>__<lookup_type>=<parameter>)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>> qs = Elevation.objects.filter(<field>__<lookup_type>=(<raster_input, <band_index>)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">rst)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__1__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(rst,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Elevation</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__1__contains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(rst,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On the left hand side of the example, rast is the geographic raster field and <a href="index.html#page_1179"><i>contains</i></a> is the spatial lookup</p> <p>type. On the right hand side, geom is a geometry input and rst is a <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> object. The band index defaults to 0 in the first two queries and is set to 1 on the others.</p> <p>While all spatial lookups can be used with raster objects on both sides, not all underlying operators natively accept raster input. For cases where the operator expects geometry input, the raster is automatically con-verted to a geometry. It’s important to keep this in mind when interpreting the lookup results.</p> <p>The type of raster support is listed for all lookups in the <a href="index.html#page_1171">compatibility table. </a>Lookups involving rasters are currently only available for the PostGIS backend.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Distance Queries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Introduction</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Distance calculations with spatial data is tricky because, unfortunately, the Earth is not flat. Some distance queries with fields in a geographic coordinate system may have to be expressed differently because of limi-</p> <p>tations in PostGIS. Please see the <a href="index.html#page_1163">Selecting an SRID</a> section in the <a href="index.html#page_1160">GeoDjango Model API</a> documentation for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Distance Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Availability: PostGIS, MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, SpatiaLite, PGRaster (Native)</p> <p>The following distance lookups are available:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1191"><i>distance_lt</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1192"><i>distance_lte</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1190"><i>distance_gt</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1191"><i>distance_gte</i></a></p> <p id="page_1170"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1192"><i>dwithin</i></a> (except MariaDB and MySQL)</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: For measuring, rather than querying on distances, use the <a href="index.html#page_1200"><i>Distance</i></a> function.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Distance lookups take a tuple parameter comprising:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. A geometry or raster to base calculations from; and</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. A number or <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> object containing the distance.</p> <p>If a <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> object is used, it may be expressed in any units (the SQL generated will use units converted to those of the field); otherwise, numeric parameters are assumed to be in the units of the field.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: In PostGIS, ST_Distance_Sphere does not limit the geometry types geographic distance queries are</p> <p>performed with.<span style="font-size:0.67em"><a href="index.html#page_1170">3</a></span> However, these queries may take a long time, as great-circle distances must be calculated on the fly for every row in the query. This is because the spatial index on traditional geometry fields cannot be used.</p> <p>For much better performance on WGS84 distance queries, consider using <a href="index.html#page_1165">geography columns</a> in your database instead because they are able to use their spatial index in distance queries. You can tell GeoD-jango to use a geography column by setting geography=True in your field definition.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For example, let’s say we have a SouthTexasCity model (from the <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/tests/gis_tests/distapp/models.py">GeoDjango distance tests</a> ) on a projected coordinate system valid for cities in southern Texas:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SouthTexasCity</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">30</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># A projected coordinate system (only valid for South Texas!)</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># is used, units are in meters.</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">point</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">PointField(srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">32140</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Then distance queries may be performed as follows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.measure</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">D</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ``D`` is a shortcut for ``Distance``</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geoapp.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SouthTexasCity</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"># Distances will be calculated from this point, which does not have to be projected.</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POINT(-96.876369 29.905320)"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"># If numeric parameter, units of field (meters in this case) are assumed.</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">3</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DistanceSphere.html">PostGIS documentation</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">on</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">ST_DistanceSphere</span><span style="font-size:0.8em">.</span></p> <p id="page_1171" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SouthTexasCity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(point__distance_lte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(pnt,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">7000</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"># Find all Cities within 7 km, > 20 miles away, and > 100 chains away (an obscure unit)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(point__distance_lte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(pnt, D(km</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">7</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SouthTexasCity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SouthTexasCity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(point__distance_gte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(pnt, D(chain</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">100</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Raster queries work the same way by replacing the geometry field point with a raster field, or the pnt object with a raster object, or both. To specify the band index of a raster input on the right hand side, a 3-tuple can be passed to the lookup as follows:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">qs</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SouthTexasCity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(point__distance_gte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(rst,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, D(km</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">7</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Where the band with index 2 (the third band) of the raster rst would be used for the lookup.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Compatibility Tables</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following table provides a summary of what spatial lookups are available for each spatial database</p> <p>backend. href="index.html#page_1194"><i>Union</i></a> X X X</p> <p id="page_1174"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeoDjango Forms API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango provides some specialized form fields and widgets in order to visually display and edit geolocalized</p> <p>data on a map. By default, they use <a href="https://openlayers.org/">OpenLayers</a>-powered maps, with a base WMS layer provided by <a href="https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/">NASA</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Field arguments</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to the regular <a href="index.html#page_1518">form field arguments</a>, GeoDjango form fields take the following optional arguments.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>srid</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Field.<b>srid</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This is the SRID code that the field value should be transformed to. For example, if the map widget SRID is different from the SRID more generally used by your application or database, the field will automatically convert input values into that SRID.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>geom_type</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Field.<b>geom_type</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You generally shouldn’t have to set or change that attribute which should be set up depending on the field class. It matches the OpenGIS standard geometry name.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Form field classes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeometryField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GeometryField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PointField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class PointField</b></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1175" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>LineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class LineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class PolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiPointField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiPointField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiLineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiLineStringField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultiPolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class MultiPolygonField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GeometryCollectionField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GeometryCollectionField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Form widgets</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango form widgets allow you to display and edit geographic data on a visual map. Note that none of the currently available widgets supports 3D geometries, hence geometry fields will fallback using a Textarea widget for such data.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Widget attributes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango widgets are template-based, so their attributes are mostly different from other Django widget attributes.</p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget.<b>geom_type</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The OpenGIS geometry type, generally set by the form field.</p> <p id="page_1176"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget.<b>map_srid</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">SRID code used by the map (default is 4326).</p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget.<b>display_raw</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Boolean value specifying if a textarea input showing the serialized representation of the current geom-etry is visible, mainly for debugging purposes (default is False).</p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget.<b>supports_3d</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Indicates if the widget supports edition of 3D data (default is False).</p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget.<b>template_name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The template used to render the map widget.</p> <p>You can pass widget attributes in the same manner that for any other Django widget. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>MyGeoForm</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Form):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">point</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">PointField(widget</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">forms</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">OSMWidget(attrs</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"display_raw"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">}))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Widget classes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>BaseGeometryWidget</p> <p><b>class BaseGeometryWidget</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This is an abstract base widget containing the logic needed by subclasses. You cannot directly use this widget for a geometry field. Note that the rendering of GeoDjango widgets is based on a template,</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">identified by the <a href="index.html#page_1176"><i>template_name</i></a> class attribute.</p> <p>OpenLayersWidget</p> <p><b>class OpenLayersWidget</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This is the default widget used by all GeoDjango form fields. template_name is gis/openlayers.html.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">OpenLayersWidget and <a href="index.html#page_1176"><i>OSMWidget</i></a> use the ol.js file hosted on the cdn.jsdelivr.net content-delivery network. You can subclass these widgets in order to specify your own version of the ol.js file in the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">js property of the inner Media class (see <a href="index.html#page_391">Assets as a static definition</a>).</p> <p>OSMWidget</p> <p><b>class OSMWidget</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This widget uses an OpenStreetMap base layer to display geographic objects on. Attributes are:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>template_name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">gis/openlayers-osm.html</p> <p id="page_1177" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>default_lat</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>default_lon</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The default center latitude and longitude are 47 and 5, respectively, which is a location in eastern France.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>default_zoom</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The default map zoom is 12.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1176"><i>OpenLayersWidget</i></a> note about JavaScript file hosting above also applies here. See also this <a href="https://help.openstreetmap.org/questions/10920/how-to-embed-a-map-in-my-https-site">FAQ</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://help.openstreetmap.org/questions/10920/how-to-embed-a-map-in-my-https-site">answer</a> about https access to map tiles.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GIS QuerySet API Reference</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The spatial lookups in this section are available for <a href="index.html#page_1161"><i>GeometryField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1162"><i>RasterField</i></a>.</p> <p>For an introduction, see the <a href="index.html#page_1168">spatial lookups introduction. </a>For an overview of what lookups are compatible</p> <p>with a particular spatial backend, refer to the <a href="index.html#page_1171">spatial lookup compatibility table</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Lookups with rasters</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All examples in the reference below are given for geometry fields and inputs, but the lookups can be used the same way with rasters on both sides. Whenever a lookup doesn’t support raster input, the input is automat-</p> <p>ically converted to a geometry where necessary using the <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/RT_ST_Polygon.html">ST_Polygon</a> function. See also the <a href="index.html#page_1168">introduction to</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1168">raster lookups.</a></p> <p>The database operators used by the lookups can be divided into three categories:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Native raster support N: the operator accepts rasters natively on both sides of the lookup, and raster</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">input can be mixed with geometry inputs.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Bilateral raster support B: the operator supports rasters only if both sides of the lookup receive raster</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">inputs. Raster data is automatically converted to geometries for mixed lookups.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Geometry conversion support C. The lookup does not have native raster support, all raster data is au-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">tomatically converted to geometries.</p> <p>The examples below show the SQL equivalent for the lookups in the different types of raster support. The same pattern applies to all spatial lookups.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1178"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Case Lookup SQL Equivalent</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">N, B rast__contains=rst ST_Contains(rast, rst)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">N, B rast__1__contains=(rst, 2) ST_Contains(rast, 1, rst, 2)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">B, C rast__contains=geom ST_Contains(ST_Polygon(rast), geom)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">B, C rast__1__contains=geom ST_Contains(ST_Polygon(rast, 1), geom)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">B, C poly__contains=rst ST_Contains(poly, ST_Polygon(rst))</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">B, C poly__contains=(rst, 1) ST_Contains(poly, ST_Polygon(rst, 1))</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">C rast__crosses=rst ST_Crosses(ST_Polygon(rast), ST_Polygon(rst))</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">C rast__1__crosses=(rst, 2) ST_Crosses(ST_Polygon(rast, 1), ST_Polygon(rst, 2))</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">C rast__crosses=geom ST_Crosses(ST_Polygon(rast), geom)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">C poly__crosses=rst ST_Crosses(poly, ST_Polygon(rst))</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Spatial lookups with rasters are only supported for PostGIS backends (denominated as PGRaster in this sec-tion).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>bbcontains</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Availability: <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Geometry_Contain.html">PostGIS</a>, MariaDB, MySQL, SpatiaLite, PGRaster (Native)</p> <p>Tests if the geometry or raster field’s bounding box completely contains the lookup geometry’s bounding box.</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__bbcontains</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:11em">Backend SQL Equivalent</p> <p style="margin-left:11em">PostGIS poly ~ geom</p> <p style="margin-left:11em">MariaDB MBRContains(poly, geom)</p> <p style="margin-left:11em">MySQL MBRContains(poly, geom)</p> <p style="margin-left:11em">SpatiaLite MbrContains(poly, geom)</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1179" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>bboverlaps</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Availability: </p> <p><b>relate</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Availability: <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Relate.html">PostGIS</a>, MariaDB, Oracle, SpatiaLite, PGRaster (Conversion)</p> <p>Tests if the geometry field is spatially related to the lookup geometry by the values given in the given pattern. This lookup requires a tuple parameter, (geom, pattern); the form of pattern will depend on the spatial backend:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MariaDB, PostGIS, and SpatiaLite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On these spatial backends the intersection pattern is a string comprising nine characters, which define inter-sections between the interior, boundary, and exterior of the geometry field and the lookup geometry. The intersection pattern matrix may only use the following characters: 1, 2, T, F, or *. This lookup type allows</p> <p>users to “fine tune” a specific geometric relationship consistent with the DE-9IM <a href="index.html#page_1185">model.<span style="font-size:0.67em">1</span></a></p> <p>Geometry example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># A tuple lookup parameter is used to specify the geometry and</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># the intersection pattern (the pattern here is for 'contains').</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__relate</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(geom,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"T*T***FF*"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostGIS and MariaDB SQL equivalent:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SELECT</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>WHERE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ST_Relate(poly, geom,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'T*T***FF*'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SpatiaLite SQL equivalent:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SELECT</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>WHERE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Relate(poly, geom,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'T*T***FF*'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Raster example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__relate</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(rast,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"T*T***FF*"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(rast__2__relate</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(rast,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"T*T***FF*"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostGIS SQL equivalent:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SELECT</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>WHERE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ST_Relate(poly, ST_Polygon(rast,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'T*T***FF*'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SELECT</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>WHERE</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ST_Relate(ST_Polygon(rast,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), ST_Polygon(rast,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'T*T***FF*'</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://portal.ogc.org/files/?artifact_id=829">OpenGIS Simple Feature Specification For SQL</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://portal.ogc.org/files/?artifact_id=829">, </a>at Ch. 2.1.13.2, p. 2-13 (The Dimensionally Extended Nine-Intersection Model).</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1186"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Oracle</b></p> <p CONTAINS, COVERS, ON, and ANYINTERACT. Multiple strings</p> <p>may be combined with the logical Boolean operator OR, for example, 'inside+touch' <a href="index.html#page_1186"><span style="font-size:0.67em">2</span> .</a> The relation strings are case-insensitive.</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b><<|</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1190"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Distance Lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Availability: PostGIS, Oracle, MariaDB, MySQL, SpatiaLite, PGRaster (Native)</p> <p>For an overview on performing distance queries, please refer to the <a href="index.html#page_1169">distance queries introduction</a>.</p> <p>Distance lookups take the following form:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><field>__<distance lookup>=(<geometry/raster>, <distance value>[, "spheroid"])</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><field>__<distance lookup>=(<raster>, <band_index>, <distance value>[, "spheroid"])</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><field>__<band_index>__<distance lookup>=(<raster>, <band_index>, <distance value>[, "spheroid"])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The value passed into a distance lookup is a tuple; the first two values are mandatory, and are the geometry</p> <p>to calculate distances to, and a distance value (either a number in units of the field, a <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> object, or</p> <p>a <a href="index.html#page_1785">query expression). </a>To pass a band index to the lookup, use a 3-tuple where the second entry is the band index.</p> <p>On every distance lookup except <a href="index.html#page_1192"><i>dwithin</i></a>, an optional element, 'spheroid', may be included to use the more accurate spheroid distance calculation functions on fields with a geodetic coordinate system.</p> <p>On PostgreSQL, the 'spheroid' option uses <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Distance_Spheroid.html">ST_DistanceSpheroid</a> instead of <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DistanceSphere.html">ST_DistanceSphere</a><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DistanceSphere.html">. </a>The simpler</p> <p><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Distance.html">ST_Distance</a> function is used with projected coordinate systems. Rasters are converted to geometries for spheroid based lookups.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>distance_gt</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Returns models where the distance to the geometry field from the lookup geometry is greater than the given distance value.</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__distance_gt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(geom, D(m</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)))</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:7em">Backend SQL Equivalent</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">PostGIS ST_Distance/ST_Distance_Sphere(poly, geom) > 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">MariaDB ST_Distance(poly, geom) > 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">MySQL ST_Distance(poly, geom) > 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">Oracle SDO_GEOM.SDO_DISTANCE(poly, geom, 0.05) > 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">SpatiaLite Distance(poly, geom) > 5</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1191" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>distance_gte</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Returns models where the distance to the geometry field from the lookup geometry is greater than or equal to the given distance value.</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(poly__distance_gte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(geom, D(m</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span geom) >= 5 MariaDB ST_Distance(poly, geom) >= 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">MySQL ST_Distance(poly, geom) >= 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">Oracle SDO_GEOM.SDO_DISTANCE(poly, geom, 0.05) >= 5</p> <p style="margin-left:7em">SpatiaLite Distance(poly, geom) >= 5</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>distance_lt</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Returns models where the distance to the geometry field from the lookup geometry is less than the given distance value.</p> <p>Example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">Zipcode</span><span this method is too expensive, consider using <a href="index.html#page_1193"><i>Collect</i></a> instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Example:</p> <p id="page_1195" Azimuth</b>(point_a, point_b, **extra)</p> <p>Availability: <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Azimuth.html">PostGIS</a>, SpatiaLite (LWGEOM/RTTOPO)</p> <p>Returns the azimuth in radians of the The azimuth is angle referenced from north and is positive clockwise: north = 0; east = <i>π</i>/2; south = <i>π</i>; west = 3<i>π</i>/2.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Difference</b>( expr1, expr2, **extra)</p> <p>Availability: MariaDB, <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/spatial-operator-functions.html#function_st-difference">MySQL</a>, <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Difference.html">PostGIS</a><a that does not intersect with geometry B.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Distance</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Distance</b>(expr1, expr2, spheroid=None, **extra)</p> <p>Availability: MariaDB, <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/spatial-relation-functions-object-shapes.html#function_st-distance">MySQL</a>, <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Distance.html">PostGIS</a><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Distance.html">, </a>Oracle, SpatiaLite</p> <p>Accepts two geographic fields or expressions and returns the distance between them, as a <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> object. On MySQL, a raw float value is returned when the coordinates are geodetic.</p> <p>On backends that support distance calculation on geodetic coordinates, the proper backend function is au-</p> <p>tomatically chosen depending on the SRID value of the geometries (e.g. <a href="https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DistanceSphere.html">ST_DistanceSphere</a> on PostGIS).</p> <p>When distances are calculated with geodetic (angular) coordinates, as is the case with the default WGS84 (4326) SRID, you can set the spheroid keyword argument to decide if the calculation should be based on a simple sphere (less accurate, less resource-intensive) or on a spheroid (more accurate, more resource-intensive).</p> <p>In the following example, the distance from the city of Hobart to every other <a href="index.html#page_1161"><i>PointField</i></a> in the AustraliaCity queryset is calculated:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span </p> <p><b>Measurement Objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1206"><i>django.contrib.gis.measure</i></a> module contains objects that allow for convenient representation of dis-</p> <p>tance and area units of <a href="index.html#page_1206">measure.<span style="font-size:0.67em">1</a></span> <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> Specifically, it implements two objects, and <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Area</i></a> – both of which</p> <p>may be accessed via the <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>D</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1210"><i>A</i></a> convenience aliases, respectively.</p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://koordinates.com/">Robert Coup</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">is the initial author of the measure objects, and was inspired by Brian Beck’s work in</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://github.com/geopy/geopy/">geopy</a></span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">and Geoff Biggs’ PhD</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.8em">work on dimensioned units for robotics.</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1207" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Example</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> objects may be instantiated using a keyword argument indicating the context of the units. In the example below, two different distance objects are instantiated in units of kilometers (km) and miles (mi):</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.measure</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">D, Distance</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">d1</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Distance(km</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d1)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">5.0 km</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">d2</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">D(mi</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># `D` is an alias for `Distance`</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d2)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">5.0 mi</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For conversions, access the preferred unit attribute to get a converted distance quantity:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">mi)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Converting 5 kilometers to miles</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">3.10685596119</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">km)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Converting 5 miles to kilometers</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">8.04672</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Moreover, arithmetic operations may be performed between the distance objects:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d1</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">d2)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Adding 5 miles to 5 kilometers</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">13.04672 km</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(d2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>-</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">d1)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Subtracting 5 kilometers from 5 miles</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1.89314403881 mi</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Two <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> objects multiplied together will yield an <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Area</i></a> object, which uses squared units of measure:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">d1</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>*</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">d2</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Returns an Area object.</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(a)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">40.2336 sq_km</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To determine what the attribute abbreviation of a unit is, the unit_attname class method may be used:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Distance</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unit_attname(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"US Survey Foot"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">survey_ft</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Distance</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unit_attname(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"centimeter"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">cm</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1208"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p>
