prefixed with sq_ (area units are</p> <p>square in nature). For example, Area(sq_m=2) creates an <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Area</i></a> object representing two square meters.</p> <p id="page_1209" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to unit with the sq_ prefix, the following units are also supported on <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Area</i></a>:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:12em">Unit Attribute Full name or alias(es)</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">ha Hectare</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Support for the ha unit was added.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Measurement API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Distance</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Distance</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To initialize a distance object, pass in a keyword corresponding to the desired <a href="index.html#page_1208">unit attribute name</a> set with desired value. For example, the following creates a distance object representing 5 miles:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">dist</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Distance(mi</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__getattr__</b>(unit_att)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the distance value in units corresponding to the given unit attribute. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(dist</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">km)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">8.04672</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod unit_attname</b>( unit_name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the distance unit attribute name for the given full unit name. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Distance</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unit_attname(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Mile"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'mi'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class D</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Alias for <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Distance</i></a> class.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Area</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Area</b>(**kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To initialize an area object, pass in a keyword corresponding to the desired <a href="index.html#page_1208">unit attribute name</a> set with desired value. For example, the following creates an area object representing 5 square miles:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">a</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Area(sq_mi</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p id="page_1210"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__getattr__</b>(unit_att)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the area value in units corresponding to the given unit attribute. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(a</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">sq_km)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">12.949940551680001</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod unit_attname</b>( unit_name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the area unit attribute name for the given full unit name. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Area</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">unit_attname(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Kilometer"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'sq_km'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class A</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Alias for <a href="index.html#page_1209"><i>Area</i></a> class.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GEOS API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Background</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>What is GEOS?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://libgeos.org/">GEOS</a> stands for Geometry Engine - Open Source, and is a C++ library, ported from the <a href="https://sourceforge.net/projects/jts-topo-suite/">Java Topology Suite</a>.</p> <p>GEOS implements the OpenGIS <a href="https://www.ogc.org/standard/sfs/">Simple Features for SQL</a> spatial predicate functions and spatial operators.</p> <p>GEOS, now an OSGeo project, was initially developed and maintained by <a href="http://www.refractions.net/">Refractions Research</a> of Victoria, Canada.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Features</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GeoDjango implements a high-level Python wrapper for the GEOS library, its features include:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• A BSD-licensed interface to the GEOS geometry routines, implemented purely in Python using ctypes.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Loosely-coupled to GeoDjango. For example, <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects may be used outside of a Django</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">project/application. In other words, no need to have <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> set or use a database, etc.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Mutability: <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects may be modified.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Cross-platform tested.</p> <p id="page_1211" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Tutorial</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This section contains a brief introduction and tutorial to using <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating a Geometry</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects may be created in a few ways. The first is to simply instantiate the object on some spatial input – the following are examples of creating the same geometry from WKT, HEX, WKB, and Geo-JSON:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POINT(5 23)"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># WKT</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"010100000000000000000014400000000000003740"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># HEX</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">memoryview</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">b"\x01\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x14@\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x007@"</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># WKB</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'{ "type": "Point", "coordinates": [ 5.000000, 23.000000 ] }'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># GeoJSON</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Another option is to use the constructor for the specific geometry type that you wish to create. For example,</p> <p>a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i></a> object may be created by passing in the X and Y coordinates into its constructor:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">23</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All these constructors take the keyword argument srid. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GEOSGeometry, LineString, Point</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(GEOSGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POINT (0 0)"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SRID=4326;POINT (0 0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(LineString((</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), (</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SRID=4326;LINESTRING (0 0, 1 1)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, srid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">32140</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">SRID=32140;POINT (0 0)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, there is the <a href="index.html#page_1227"><i>fromfile()</i></a> factory method which returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> object from a file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">fromfile</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">fromfile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/pnt.wkt"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">fromfile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">open</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/pnt.wkt"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p id="page_1212"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>My logs are filled with GEOS-related errors</p> <p>You find many TypeError or AttributeError exceptions filling your web server’s log files. This generally means that you are creating GEOS objects at the top level of some of your Python modules. Then, due to a race condition in the garbage collector, your module is garbage collected before the GEOS object. To prevent</p> <p>this, create <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects inside the local scope of your functions/methods.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Geometries are Pythonic</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects are ‘Pythonic’, in other words components may be accessed, modified, and iterated</p> <p>over using standard Python conventions. For example, you can iterate over the coordinates in a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">23</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[coord</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">coord</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[5.0, 23.0]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>With any geometry object, the <a href="index.html#page_1215"><i>GEOSGeometry.coords</i></a> property may be used to get the geometry coordinates as a Python tuple:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">coords</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">(5.0, 23.0)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can get/set geometry components using standard Python indexing techniques. However, what is re-</p> <p>turned depends on the geometry type of the object. For example, indexing on a <a href="index.html#page_1223"><i>LineString</i></a> returns a coor-dinate tuple:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.geos</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LineString</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">line</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">LineString((</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), (</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">50</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), (</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">50</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">50</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), (</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">50</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), (</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">line[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">(0.0, 0.0)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">line[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>-</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">(50.0, 0.0)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Whereas indexing on a <a For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Point(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">5</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">23</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(pnt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">srid)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">None</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">srid</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">pnt</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">srid</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">4326</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Output Properties</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The properties in this section export the <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> object into a different. This output may be in the form of a string, buffer, or even another object.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>ewkt</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the “extended” Well-Known Text of the geometry. This representation is specific to PostGIS</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">and is a superset of the OGC WKT <a href="index.html#page_1216">standard.<span style="font-size:0.67em">1</span></a> Essentially the SRID is prepended to the WKT represen-tation, for example SRID=4326;POINT(5 23).</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><span style="font-size:0.6em">1</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em">See</span> <span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#EWKB_EWKT">PostGIS EWKB, EWKT and Canonical Forms</a></span><span style="font-size:0.8em"><a href="https://postgis.net/docs/using_postgis_dbmanagement.html#EWKB_EWKT">, </a>PostGIS documentation at Ch. 4.1.2.</span></p> <p id="page_1217" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: The output from this property does not include the 3dm, 3dz, and 4d information that PostGIS supports in its EWKT representations.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>hex</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the WKB of this Geometry in hexadecimal form. Please note that the SRID value is not in-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">cluded in this representation because it is not a part of the OGC specification (use the <a href="index.html#page_1217"><i>GEOSGeometry.</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1217"><i>hexewkb</i></a> property instead).</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>hexewkb</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the EWKB of this Geometry in hexadecimal form. This is an extension of the WKB specifica-tion that includes the SRID value that are a part of this geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>json</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the GeoJSON representation of the geometry. Note that the result is not a complete GeoJSON</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">structure but only the geometry key content of a GeoJSON structure. See also <a href="index.html#page_1276">GeoJSON Serializer</a>.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>geojson</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Alias for <a href="index.html#page_1217"><i>GEOSGeometry.json</i>.</a></p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>kml</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="https://developers.google.com/kml/documentation/">KML</a> (Keyhole Markup Language) representation of the geometry. This should only be used for geometries with an SRID of 4326 (WGS84), but this restriction is not enforced.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>ogr</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns an <a href="index.html#page_1240"><i>OGRGeometry</i></a> object corresponding to the GEOS geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>wkb</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the WKB (Well-Known Binary) representation of this Geometry as a Python buffer. SRID</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">value is not included, use the <a href="index.html#page_1217"><i>GEOSGeometry.ewkb</i></a> property instead.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>ewkb</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Return the EWKB representation of this Geometry as a Python buffer. This is an extension of the WKB specification that includes any SRID value that are a part of this geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>wkt</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the Well-Known Text of the geometry (an OGC standard).</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1218"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Spatial Predicate Methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All of the following spatial predicate methods take another <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> instance (other) as a parameter, and return a boolean.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>contains</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if <a href="index.html#page_1219"><i>other.within(this)</i></a> returns True.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>covers</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if this geometry covers the specified geometry.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The covers predicate has the following equivalent definitions:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Every point of the other geometry is a point of this geometry.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• The <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DE-9IM">DE-9IM</a> Intersection Matrix for the two geometries is T*****FF*, *T****FF*, ***T**FF*, or</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">****T*FF*.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If either geometry is empty, returns False.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This predicate is similar to <a href="index.html#page_1218"><i>GEOSGeometry.contains()</i>, </a>but is more inclusive (i.e. returns True for more</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">cases). In particular, unlike <a href="index.html#page_1218"><i>contains()</i></a> it does not distinguish between points in the boundary and in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the interior of geometries. For most situations, covers() should be preferred to <a href="index.html#page_1218"><i>contains()</i>. </a>As an</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">added benefit, covers() is more amenable to optimization and hence should outperform <a href="index.html#page_1218"><i>contains()</i></a>.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>crosses</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two Geometries is T*T****** (for a point and a curve,a point and an area or a line and an area) 0******** (for two curves).</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>disjoint</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two geometries is FF*FF****.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>equals</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two geometries is T*F**FFF*.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>equals_exact</b>(other, tolerance=0)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns true if the two geometries are exactly equal, up to a specified tolerance. The tolerance value should be a floating point number representing the error tolerance in the comparison, e.g., poly1. equals_exact(poly2, 0.001) will compare equality to within one thousandth of a unit.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>equals_identical</b>( other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the two geometries are point-wise equivalent by checking that the structure, ordering, and values of all vertices are identical in all dimensions. NaN values are considered to be equal to other NaN values. Requires GEOS 3.12.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>intersects</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if <a href="index.html#page_1218"><i>GEOSGeometry.disjoint()</i></a> is False.</p> <p id="page_1219" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>overlaps</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns true if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two geometries is T*T***T** (for two points or two surfaces) 1*T***T** (for two curves).</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>relate_pattern</b>(other, pattern)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the elements in the DE-9IM intersection matrix for this geometry and the other matches the given pattern – a string of nine characters from the alphabet: {T, F, *, 0}.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>touches</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two geometries is FT*******, F**T***** or F***T****.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>within</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the DE-9IM intersection matrix for the two geometries is T*F**F***.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Topological Methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>buffer</b>(width, quadsegs=8)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> that represents all points whose distance from this geometry is less than or equal to the given width. The optional quadsegs keyword sets the number of segments used to ap-proximate a quarter circle (defaults is 8).</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>buffer_with_style</b>(width, quadsegs=8, end_cap_style=1, join_style=1, mitre_limit=5.0)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Same as <a href="index.html#page_1219"><i>buffer()</i></a>, but allows customizing the style of the buffer.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• end_cap_style can be round (1), flat (2), or square (3).</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• join_style can be round (1), mitre (2), or bevel (3).</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Mitre ratio limit (mitre_limit) only affects mitered join style.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>difference</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> representing the points making up this geometry that do not make up other.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>interpolate</b>(distance)</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>interpolate_normalized</b>( distance)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Given a distance (float), returns the point (or closest point) within the geometry <a href="index.html#page_1223">(<i>LineString</i></a> or</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1225"><i>MultiLineString</i></a>) at that distance. The normalized version takes the distance as a float between 0 (origin) and 1 (endpoint).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Reverse of <a href="index.html#page_1219"><i>GEOSGeometry.project()</i>.</a></p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>intersection</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> representing the points shared by this geometry and other.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>project</b>(point)</p> <p id="page_1220"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>project_normalized</b>(point)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the distance (float) from the origin of the geometry <a href="index.html#page_1223">(<i>LineString</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1225"><i>MultiLineString</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1225">) </a>to the point projected on the geometry (that is to a point of the line the closest to the given point). The normalized version returns the distance as a float between 0 (origin) and 1 (endpoint).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Reverse of <a href="index.html#page_1219"><i>GEOSGeometry.interpolate()</i></a>.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>relate</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the DE-9IM intersection matrix (a string) representing the topological relationship between this geometry and the other.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>simplify</b>(tolerance=0.0, preserve_topology=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a new <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a>, simplified to the specified tolerance using the Douglas-Peucker algo-rithm. A higher tolerance value implies fewer points in the output. If no tolerance is provided, it defaults to 0.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">By default, this function does not preserve topology. For example, <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>Polygon</i></a> objects can be split, be</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">collapsed into lines, or disappear. <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>Polygon</i></a> holes can be created or disappear, and lines may cross. By specifying preserve_topology=True, the result will have the same dimension and number of compo-nents as the input; this is significantly slower, however.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>sym_difference</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> combining the points in this geometry not in other, and the points in other not in this geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>union</b>(other)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> representing all the points in this geometry and the other.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Topological Properties</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>boundary</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the boundary as a newly allocated Geometry object.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>centroid</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i></a> object representing the geometric center of the geometry. The point is not guaranteed to be on the interior of the geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>convex_hull</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the smallest <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>Polygon</i></a> that contains all the points in the geometry.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>envelope</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a <a href="index.html#page_1224"><i>Polygon</i></a> that represents the bounding envelope of this geometry. Note that it can also return</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i></a> if the input geometry is a point.</p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>point_on_surface</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Computes and returns a <a href="index.html#page_1222"><i>Point</i></a> guaranteed to be on the interior of this geometry.</p> <p id="page_1221" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>GEOSGeometry.<b>unary_union</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Computes the union of all the elements of this geometry.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The result obeys the following contract:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• Unioning a set of <a href="index.html#page_1221"><i>GEOSGeometry.prepared</i></a> property. Once you have a PreparedGeometry instance its spatial predicate methods, listed below, may be used with other GEOSGeometry objects. An operation with a prepared geometry can be orders of magnitude faster – the more complex the geometry that is prepared, the larger the speedup in the operation. For more information, please consult the <a href="https://trac.osgeo.org/geos/wiki/PreparedGeometry">GEOS wiki page on prepared geometries.</a></p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">wkt_w</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">write(pnt)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'POINT (1.4 1.7)'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GEOS_LIBRARY_PATH</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A string specifying the location of the GEOS C library. Typically, this setting is only used if the GEOS C library is in a non-standard location (e.g., /home/bob/lib/libgeos_c.so).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The setting must be the full path to the C shared library; in other words you want to use libgeos_c.so, not libgeos.so.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Exceptions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception GEOSException</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The base GEOS exception, indicates a GEOS-related error.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GDAL API</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://gdal.org/">GDAL</a> stands for Geospatial Data Abstraction Library, and is a veritable “Swiss army knife” of GIS data</p> <p>functionality. A subset of GDAL is the <a href="https://gdal.org/user/vector_data_model.html">OGR</a> Simple Features Library, which specializes in reading and writing vector geographic data in a variety of standard formats.</p> <p>GeoDjango provides a high-level Python interface for some of the capabilities of OGR, including the reading and coordinate transformation of vector spatial data and minimal support for GDAL’s features with respect to raster (image) data.</p> <p id="page_1232"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Although the module is named gdal, GeoDjango only supports some of the capabilities of OGR and GDAL’s raster features at this time.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Overview</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Sample Data</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The GDAL/OGR tools described here are designed to help you read in your geospatial data, in order for most of them to be useful you have to have some data to work with. If you’re starting out and don’t yet have any data of your own to use, GeoDjango tests contain a number of data sets that you can use for testing. You can download them here:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/django/django/main/tests/gis_tests/data/cities/cities.</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>{</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">shp,prj,shx,dbf</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>}</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$ wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/django/django/main/tests/gis_tests/data/rasters/raster.tif</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Vector Data Source Objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DataSource</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a> is a wrapper for the OGR data source object that supports reading data from a variety of OGR-supported geospatial file formats and data sources using a consistent interface. Each data source is repre-</p> <p>sented by a <a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a> object which contains one or more layers of data. Each layer, represented by a <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>Layer</i></a></p> <p>object, contains some number of geographic features <a href="index.html#page_1236">(<i>Feature</i></a>), information about the type of features con-</p> <p>tained in that layer (e.g. points, polygons, etc.), as well as the names and types of any additional fields <a href="index.html#page_1238">(<i>Field</i></a>) of data that may be associated with each feature in that layer.</p> <p><b>class DataSource</b>( ds_input, encoding='utf-8')</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The constructor for DataSource only requires one parameter: the path of the file you want to read. However, OGR also supports a variety of more complex data sources, including databases, that may</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">be accessed by passing a special name string instead of a path. For more information, see the <a href="https://gdal.org/drivers/vector/">OGR</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://gdal.org/drivers/vector/">Vector Formats</a> documentation. The <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>name</i></a> property of a DataSource instance gives the OGR name of the underlying data source that it is using.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The optional encoding parameter allows you to specify a non-standard encoding of the strings in the source. This is typically useful when you obtain DjangoUnicodeDecodeError exceptions while reading field values.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Once you’ve created your DataSource, you can find out how many layers of data it contains by ac-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">cessing the <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>layer_count</i></a> property, or (equivalently) by using the len() function. For information on accessing the layers of data themselves, see the next section:</p> <p id="page_1233" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.gdal</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DataSource</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ds</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DataSource(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/your/cities.shp"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ds</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'/path/to/your/cities.shp'</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ds</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">layer_count</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># This file only contains one layer</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>layer_count</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of layers in the data source.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the name of the data source.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Layer</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Layer</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Layer is a wrapper for a layer of data in a DataSource object. You never create a Layer object directly.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Instead, you retrieve them from a <a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a> object, which is essentially a standard Python container of Layer objects. For example, you can access a specific layer by its index (e.g. ds[0] to access the first layer), or you can iterate over all the layers in the container in a for loop. The Layer itself acts as a container for geometric features.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Typically, all the features in a given layer have the same geometry type. The <a href="index.html#page_1234"><i>geom_type</i></a> property</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">of a layer is an <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>OGRGeomType</i></a> that identifies the feature type. We can use it to print out some basic</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">information about each layer in a <a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a>:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ds:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">print</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">'Layer "%s": %i %ss'</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>%</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">(layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">len</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(layer), layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Layer "cities": 3 Points</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The example output is from the cities data source, loaded above, which evidently contains one layer, called "cities", which contains three point features. For simplicity, the examples below assume that you’ve stored that layer in the variable layer:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ds[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the name of this layer in the data source.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'cities'</span></p> <p id="page_1234"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>num_feat</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of features in the layer. Same as len(layer):</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the geometry type of the layer, as an <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>OGRGeomType</i></a> object:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>num_fields</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of fields in the layer, i.e the number of fields of data associated with each feature in the layer:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">num_fields</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">4</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>fields</b></p> <p 'Population', 'Density', 'Created']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a list of the data types of each of the fields in this layer. These are subclasses of Field, discussed below:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[ft</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">__name__</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ft</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">field_types]</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">['OFTString', 'OFTReal', 'OFTReal', 'OFTDate']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>field_widths</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a list of the maximum field widths for each of the fields in this layer:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">field_widths</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">[80, 11, 24, 10]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>field_precisions</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns a list of the numeric precisions for each of the fields in this layer. You never create a Feature object directly. Instead, you retrieve</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">them from a <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>Layer</i></a> object. Each feature consists of a geometry and a set of fields containing additional</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">properties. The geometry of a field is accessible via its geom property, which returns an <a href="index.html#page_1240"><i>OGRGeometry</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">object. A Feature behaves like a standard Python container for its fields, which it returns as <a href="index.html#page_1238"><i>Field</i></a> objects: you can access a field directly by its index or name, or you can iterate over a feature’s fields, e.g. in a for loop.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>geom</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the geometry for this feature, as an OGRGeometry object:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">city</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">tuple</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(-104.609252, 38.255001)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A method that returns the value of the given field (specified by name) for this feature, not a Field wrapper object:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">city</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">get(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Population"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">102121</span></p> <p id="page_1237" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>geom_type</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the type of geometry for this feature, as an <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>OGRGeomType</i></a> object. style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of OGR vector drivers currently registered.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>OGR Geometries</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>OGRGeometry</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1240"><i>OGRGeometry</i></a> objects share similar functionality with <a href="index.html#page_1214"><i>GEOSGeometry</i></a> objects and are thin wrappers around OGR’s internal geometry representation. Thus, they allow for more efficient access to data when using</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a> . Unlike its GEOS counterpart, <a href="index.html#page_1240"><i>OGRGeometry</i></a> supports spatial reference systems and coordinate transformation:</p> <p id="page_1240"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.gis.gdal</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">OGRGeometry</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">polygon</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">OGRGeometry(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"POLYGON((0 0, 5 0, 5 5, 0 5))"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class OGRGeometry</b>(geom_input, srs=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This object is a wrapper for the <a href="https://gdal.org/api/ogrgeometry_cpp.html#ogrgeometry-class">OGR Geometry</a> class. These objects are instantiated directly from the given geom_input parameter, which may be a string containing WKT, HEX, GeoJSON, a buffer</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">containing WKB data, or an <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>OGRGeomType</i></a> object. These objects are also returned from the <a href="index.html#page_1236"><i>Feature.</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1236"><i>geom</i></a> attribute, when reading vector data from <a href="index.html#page_1233"><i>Layer</i></a> (which is in turn a part of a <a href="index.html#page_1232"><i>DataSource</i></a>).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod from_gml</b>(gml_string)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Constructs an <a href="index.html#page_1240"><i>OGRGeometry</i></a> from the given GML string.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>classmethod from_bbox</b>(bbox)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Constructs a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>Polygon</i></a> from the given bounding-box (a 4-tuple).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__len__</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of points in a <a href="index.html#page_1246"><i>LineString</i></a>, the number of rings in a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>Polygon</i></a>, or the number of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">geometries in a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>GeometryCollection</i></a>. Not applicable to other geometry types.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__iter__</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Iterates over the points in a <a href="index.html#page_1246"><i>LineString</i></a>, the rings in a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>Polygon</i></a>, or the geometries in a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>GeometryCollection</i> . </a>Not applicable to other geometry types.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__getitem__</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the point at the specified index for a <a href="index.html#page_1246"><i>LineString</i>, </a>the interior ring at the specified index for</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>Polygon</i></a>, or the geometry at the specified index in a <a href="index.html#page_1247"><i>GeometryCollection</i></a>. Not applicable to other geometry types.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>dimension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the number of coordinated dimensions of the geometry, i.e. 0 for points, 1 for lines, and so forth:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">polygon</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dimension</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>coord_dim</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the coordinate dimension of this geometry. <p>Represents a coordinate system transform. It is initialized with two <a href="index.html#page_1249"><i>SpatialReference</i></a>, representing the source and target coordinate systems, respectively. These objects should be used when performing the same coordinate transformation repeatedly on different geometries:</p> <p id="page_1253" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ct</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CoordTransform(SpatialReference(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"WGS84"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), SpatialReference(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAD83"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">feat</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">layer:</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">feat</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># getting clone of feature geometry</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">geom</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">transform(ct)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># transforming</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Raster Data Objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GDALRaster</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> is a wrapper for the GDAL raster source object that supports reading data from a variety of GDAL-supported geospatial file formats and data sources using a consistent interface. Each data source is</p> <p>represented by a <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> object which contains one or more layers of data named bands. Each band,</p> <p>represented by a <a href="index.html#page_1260"><i>GDALBand</i></a> object, contains georeferenced image data. For example, an RGB image is repre-sented as three bands: one for red, one for green, and one for blue.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: For raster data there is no difference between a raster instance and its data source. Unlike for the</p> <p>Geometry objects, <a href="index.html#page_1253"><i>GDALRaster</i></a> objects are always a data source. Temporary rasters can be instantiated in memory using the corresponding driver, but they will be of the same class as file-based raster sources.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GDALRaster</b>( ds_input, write=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The constructor for GDALRaster accepts two parameters. The first parameter defines the raster source, and the second parameter defines if a raster should be opened in write mode. For newly-created rasters, the second parameter is ignored and the new raster is always created in write mode.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The first parameter can take three forms: a string or <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.Path">Path</a> representing a file path (filesystem or GDAL virtual filesystem), a dictionary with values defining a new raster, or a bytes object representing a raster file.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If the input is a file path, the raster is opened from there. If the input is raw data in a dictionary, the parameters width, height, and srid are required. If the input is a bytes object, it will be opened using a GDAL virtual filesystem.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For a detailed description of how to create rasters using dictionary input, see <a href="index.html#page_1263">Creating rasters from</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1263">data</a>. For a detailed description of how to create rasters in the virtual filesystem, see <a href="index.html#page_1266">Using GDAL’s</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1266">Virtual Filesystem.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The following example shows how rasters can be created from different input sources (using the sample</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">data from the GeoDjango tests; see also the <a href="index.html#page_1232">Sample Data</a> section).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span Allowed dictionary key values are width, height, SRID, origin, scale, skew, datatype, driver, and name (filename).</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">By default, the warp functions keeps most parameters equal to the values of the original source raster, so only parameters that should be changed need to be specified. Note that this includes the driver, so for file-based rasters the warp function will create a new raster on disk.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The only parameter that is set differently from the source raster is the name. The default value of the raster name is the name of the source raster appended with '_copy' + source_driver_name. For file-based rasters it is recommended to provide the file path of the target raster.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The resampling algorithm used for warping can be specified with the resampling argument. The default is NearestNeighbor, and the other allowed values are Bilinear, Cubic, CubicSpline, Lanczos, Average, and Mode.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The max_error argument can be used to specify the maximum error measured in input pixels that is allowed in approximating the transformation. The default is 0.0 for exact calculations.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">For users familiar with GDAL, this function has a similar functionality to the gdalwarp command-line utility.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">For example, the warp function can be used for aggregating a raster to the double of its original pixel scale:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span Is equal to width * height.</p> <p id="page_1261" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>statistics</b>(refresh=False, approximate=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Compute statistics on the pixel values of this band. The return value is a tuple with the following structure: (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation).</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If the approximate argument is set to True, the statistics may be computed based on overviews or a subset of image tiles.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If the refresh argument is set to True, the statistics will be computed from the data directly, and the cache will be updated with the result.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If a persistent cache value is found, that value is returned. For raster formats using Persistent Auxiliary Metadata (PAM) services, the statistics might be cached in an auxiliary file. In some cases this metadata might be out of sync with the pixel values or cause values from a previous call to be returned which don’t reflect the value of the approximate argument. In such cases, use the refresh argument to get updated values and store them in the cache.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">For empty bands (where all pixel values are “no data”), all statistics are returned as None.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The statistics can also be retrieved directly by accessing the <a href="index.html#page_1261"><i>min</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1261"><i>max</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1261"><i>mean</i></a>, and <a href="index.html#page_1261"><i>std</i></a> properties.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>min</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The minimum pixel value of the band (excluding the “no data” value).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>max</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The maximum pixel value of the band (excluding the “no data” value).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>mean</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The mean of all pixel values of the band (excluding the “no data” value).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>std</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">The standard deviation of all pixel values of the band (excluding the “no data” value).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>nodata_value</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The “no data” value for a band is generally a special marker value used to mark pixels that are not valid data. Such pixels should generally not be displayed, nor contribute to analysis operations.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">To delete an existing “no data” value, set this property to None.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>datatype</b>(as_string=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The data type contained in the band, as an integer constant between 0 (Unknown) and 14. If as_string is True, the data type is returned as a string. Check out the “GDAL Pixel Type” column</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">in the <a href="index.html#page_1264">datatype value table</a> for possible values.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>color_interp</b>( as_string=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The color interpretation for the band, as an integer between 0and 16. If as_string is True, the data type is returned as a string with the following possible values: GCI_Undefined, GCI_GrayIndex, GCI_PaletteIndex, GCI_RedBand, GCI_GreenBand, GCI_BlueBand, GCI_AlphaBand, GCI_HueBand, GCI_SaturationBand, GCI_LightnessBand, GCI_CyanBand, <b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p id="page_1262" style="margin-left:4em">GCI_MagentaBand, GCI_YellowBand, GCI_BlackBand, GCI_YCbCr_YBand, GCI_YCbCr_CbBand, and GCI_YCbCr_CrBand. GCI_YCbCr_CrBand also represents GCI_Max because both correspond to the integer 16, but only GCI_YCbCr_CrBand is returned as a string.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>data</b>(data=None, offset=None, size=None, shape=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The accessor to the pixel values of the GDALBand. Returns the complete data array if no parameters are provided. A subset of the pixel array can be requested by specifying an offset and block size as tuples.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If NumPy is available, the data is returned as NumPy array. For performance reasons, it is highly recommended to use NumPy.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Data is written to the GDALBand if the data parameter is provided. The input can be of one of the following types - packed string, buffer, list, array, and NumPy array. The number of items in the input should normally correspond to the total number of pixels in the band, or to the number of pixels for a specific block of pixel values if the offset and size parameters are provided.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If the number of items in the input is different from the target pixel block, the shape parameter must be specified. The shape is a tuple that specifies the width and height of the input data in pixels. The data is then replicated to update the pixel values of the selected block. This is useful to fill an entire band with a single value, for instance.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rst</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">GDALRaster(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span
