<p id="page_1313" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Index transforms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Index transforms index into the array. Any non-negative integer can be used. There are no errors if it</p> <p>exceeds the <a href="index.html#page_1310"><i>size</i></a> of the array. The lookups available after the transform are those from the <a href="index.html#page_1309"><i>base_field</i></a>. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Second post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"thoughts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(tags__0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"thoughts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<Post: First post>, <Post: Second post>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(tags__1__iexact</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(tags__276</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"javascript"</span><span writing raw SQL. However these indexes and</p> <p>those used in <a href="index.html#page_1313"><i>slices</i></a> use 0-based indexing to be consistent with Python.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Slice transforms</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Slice transforms take a slice of the array. Any two non-negative integers can be used, separated by a single underscore. The lookups available after the transform do not change. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"thoughts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Second post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"thoughts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Post</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Third post"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, tags</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"django"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"python"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"thoughts"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(tags__0_1</span><span 1-based indexing for array fields when writing raw SQL. However these slices and</p> <p>those used in <a href="index.html#page_1313"><i>indexes</i></a> use 0-based indexing to be consistent with Python.</p> <p id="page_1314"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Multidimensional arrays with indexes and slices</p> <p>PostgreSQL has some rather esoteric behavior when using indexes and slices on multidimensional arrays. It will always work to use indexes to reach down to the final underlying data, but most other slices behave strangely at the database level and cannot be supported in a logical, consistent fashion by Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>HStoreField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class HStoreField</b>(**options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A field for storing key-value pairs. The Python data type used is a dict. Keys must be strings, and values may be either strings or nulls (None in Python).</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To use this field, you’ll need to:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">1. Add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">2. <a href="index.html#page_1335">Set up the hstore extension</a> in PostgreSQL.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">You’ll see an error like can't adapt type 'dict' if you skip the first step, or type "hstore" does not exist if you skip the second.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: On occasions it may be useful to require or restrict the keys which are valid for a given field. This can</p> <p>be done using the <a href="index.html#page_1347"><i>KeysValidator</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Querying HStoreField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to the ability to query by key, there are a number of custom lookups available for HStoreField.</p> <p>We will use the following example model:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.fields</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HStoreField</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Dog</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">CharField(max_length</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">200</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">data</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HStoreField()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>__str__</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span></p> <p id="page_1315" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Key lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To query based on a given key, you can use that key as the lookup name:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Rufus"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"breed"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"labrador"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Meg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"breed"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"collie"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(data__breed</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"collie"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<Dog: Meg>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can chain other lookups after key lookups:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<Dog: Rufus>, <Dog: Meg>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>or use F() expressions to annotate a key value. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(breed</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">F(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"data__breed"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">))[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rufus</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">breed</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">'labrador'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If the key you wish to query by clashes with the name of another lookup, you need to use the <a href="index.html#page_1315"><i>hstorefield.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1315"><i>contains</i></a> lookup instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Key transforms can also be chained with: <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>contains</i>,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1764"><i>icontains</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1767"><i>endswith</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1767"><i>iendswith</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>iexact</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1774"><i>regex</i></a>,</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1775"><i>iregex</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1766"><i>startswith</i></a>, and <a href="index.html#page_1766"><i>istartswith</i></a> lookups.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Since any string could be a key in a hstore value, any lookup other than those listed below will</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">be interpreted as a key lookup. No errors are raised. Be extra careful for typing mistakes, and always</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">check your queries work as you intend.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>contains</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>contains</i></a> lookup is overridden on <a href="index.html#page_1314"><i>HStoreField</i></a>. The returned objects are those where the given dict of key-value pairs are all contained in the field. It uses the SQL operator @>. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"labrador"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"owner"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"Bob"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Dog</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Meg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, data</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"breed"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{})</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1316"><b>Django Documentation, Release style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<Dog: Meg>]></span></p> <p id="page_1318"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Range Fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are five range field types, corresponding to the built-in range types in PostgreSQL. These fields are used to store a range of values; for example the start and end timestamps of an event, or the range of ages an activity is suitable for.</p> <p>All of the range fields translate to <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/pgtypes.html#adapt-range">psycopg Range objects</a> in Python, but also accept tuples as input if no bounds information is necessary. The default is lower bound included, upper bound excluded, that is [)</p> <p>(see the PostgreSQL documentation for details about <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rangetypes.html#RANGETYPES-IO">different bounds). </a>The default bounds can be changed</p> <p>for non-discrete range fields <a href="index.html#page_1319">(<i>DateTimeRangeField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1318"><i>DecimalRangeField</i></a>) by using the default_bounds argument.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>IntegerRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class IntegerRangeField</b>(**options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Stores a range of integers. Based on an <a href="index.html#page_1639"><i>IntegerField</i></a>. Represented by an int4range in the database and a django.db.backends.postgresql.psycopg_any.NumericRange in Python.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Regardless of the bounds specified when saving the data, PostgreSQL always returns a range in a canon-ical form that includes the lower bound and excludes the upper bound, that is [).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BigIntegerRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BigIntegerRangeField</b>(**options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Stores a range of large integers. Based on a <a href="index.html#page_1627"><i>BigIntegerField</i></a>. Represented by an int8range in the database and a django.db.backends.postgresql.psycopg_any.NumericRange in Python.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Regardless of the bounds specified when saving the data, PostgreSQL always returns a range in a canon-ical form that includes the lower bound and excludes the upper bound, that is [).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DecimalRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class DecimalRangeField</b>(default_bounds='[)', **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Stores a range of floating point values. Based on a <a href="index.html#page_1630"><i>DecimalField</i></a>. Represented by a numrange in the database and a django.db.backends.postgresql.psycopg_any.NumericRange in Python.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>default_bounds</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Optional. The value of bounds for list and tuple inputs. Django’s model and form field implementations use</p> <p>base classes below, and psycopg provides a <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/pgtypes.html#psycopg.types.range.register_range">register_range()</a> to allow use of custom range types.</p> <p><b>class RangeField</b>( **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Base class for model range fields.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>base_field</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The model field class to use.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>range_type</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The range type to use.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>form_field</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The form field class to use. Should be a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_1324"><i>django.contrib.postgres.forms.</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1324"><i>BaseRangeField</i></a>.</p> <p><b>class</b> django.contrib.postgres.forms.<b>BaseRangeField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Base class for form range fields.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>base_field</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The form field to use.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>range_type</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The range type to use.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Range operators</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class RangeOperators</b></p> <p>PostgreSQL provides a set of SQL operators that can be used together with the range data types (see <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-range.html#RANGE-OPERATORS-TABLE">the</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-range.html#RANGE-OPERATORS-TABLE">PostgreSQL documentation for the full details of range operators). </a>This class is meant as a convenient method to avoid typos. The operator names overlap with the names of corresponding lookups.</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>RangeOperators</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">EQUAL</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span <p><b>RangeBoundary() expressions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class RangeBoundary</b>(inclusive_lower=True, inclusive_upper=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>inclusive_lower</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If True (default), the lower bound is inclusive '[', otherwise it’s exclusive '('.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>inclusive_upper</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If False (default), the upper bound is exclusive ')', otherwise it’s inclusive ']'.</p> <p>A RangeBoundary() expression represents the range boundaries. It can be used with a custom range functions</p> <p>that expected boundaries, for example to define <a href="index.html#page_1304"><i>ExclusionConstraint</i>. </a>See <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rangetypes.html#RANGETYPES-INCLUSIVITY">the PostgreSQL documentation</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rangetypes.html#RANGETYPES-INCLUSIVITY">for the full details.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL specific form fields and widgets</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All of these fields and widgets are available from the django.contrib.postgres.forms module.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SimpleArrayField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SimpleArrayField</b>( base_field, delimiter=',', max_length=None, min_length=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A field which maps to an array. style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>HStoreField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class HStoreField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A field which accepts JSON encoded data for an <a href="index.html#page_1314"><i>HStoreField</i></a>. It casts all values (except nulls) to strings. It is represented by an HTML <textarea>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">User friendly forms</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">HStoreField is not particularly user friendly in most cases, however it is a useful way to format data from a client-side widget for submission to the server.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: On occasions it may be useful to require or restrict the keys which are valid for a given field.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This can be done using the <a href="index.html#page_1347"><i>KeysValidator</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Range Fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This group of fields all share similar functionality for accepting range data. <span style="float:right">They are based on</span></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1540"><i>MultiValueField</i></a>. They treat one omitted value as an unbounded range. They also validate that the lower</p> <p>bound is not greater than the upper bound. All of these fields use <a href="index.html#page_1329"><i>RangeWidget</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>IntegerRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class IntegerRangeField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Based on <a href="index.html#page_1534"><i>IntegerField</i></a> and translates its input into django.db.backends.postgresql.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">psycopg_any.NumericRange . Default for <a href="index.html#page_1318"><i>IntegerRangeField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1318"><i>BigIntegerRangeField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DecimalRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class DecimalRangeField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Based on <a href="index.html#page_1528"><i>DecimalField</i></a> and translates its input into django.db.backends.postgresql.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">psycopg_any.NumericRange . Default for <a href="index.html#page_1318"><i>DecimalRangeField</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_1329" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DateTimeRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class DateTimeRangeField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Based on <a href="index.html#page_1527"><i>DateTimeField</i></a> and translates its input into django.db.backends.postgresql.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">psycopg_any.DateTimeTZRange. Default for <a href="index.html#page_1319"><i>DateTimeRangeField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DateRangeField</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class DateRangeField</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Based on <a href="index.html#page_1527"><i>DateField</i></a> and translates its input into django.db.backends.postgresql.psycopg_any.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">DateRange. Default for <a href="index.html#page_1319"><i>DateRangeField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Widgets</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>RangeWidget</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class RangeWidget</b>(base_widget, attrs=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Widget used by all of the range fields. Based on <a href="index.html#page_1561"><i>MultiWidget</i>.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1329"><i>RangeWidget</i></a> has one required argument:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>base_widget</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">A <a href="index.html#page_1329"><i>RangeWidget</i></a> comprises a 2-tuple of base_widget.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>decompress</b> (value)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Takes a single “compressed” value of a field, for example a <a href="index.html#page_1319"><i>DateRangeField</i></a>, and returns a tuple representing a lower and upper bound.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL specific database functions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All of these functions are available from the django.contrib.postgres.functions module.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>RandomUUID</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class RandomUUID</b></p> <p>Returns a version 4 UUID.</p> <p>Usage example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.functions</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">RandomUUID</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Article</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">update(uuid</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">RandomUUID())</span></p> <p id="page_1330"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TransactionNow</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class TransactionNow</b></p> <p>Returns the date and time on the database server that the current transaction started. If you are not in a</p> <p>transaction it will return the date and time of the current statement. This is a complement to <a href="index.html#page_1826"><i>django.db.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1826"><i>models.functions.Now</i></a> , which returns the date and time of the current statement.</p> <p>Note that only the outermost call to <a href="index.html#page_209"><i>atomic()</i></a> sets up a transaction and thus sets the time that TransactionNow() will return; nested calls create savepoints which do not affect the transaction time.</p> <p>Usage example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.functions</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">TransactionNow</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Article</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(published__lte</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">TransactionNow())</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><QuerySet [<Article: How to Django>]></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL specific model indexes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The following are PostgreSQL specific <a href="index.html#page_1660">indexes</a> available from the django.contrib.postgres.indexes mod-ule.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BloomIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BloomIndex</b>( *expressions, length=None, columns=(), **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/bloom.html">bloom</a> index.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To use this index access you need to activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/bloom.html">bloom</a> extension on PostgreSQL. You can install it</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>BloomExtension</i></a> migration operation.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer number of bits from 1 to 4096 to the length parameter to specify the length of each index entry. PostgreSQL’s default is 80.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The columns argument takes a tuple or list of up to 32 values that are integer number of bits from 1 to 4095.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BrinIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BrinIndex</b>(*expressions, autosummarize=None, pages_per_range=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/brin.html">BRIN index.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set the autosummarize parameter to True to enable <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/brin.html#BRIN-OPERATION">automatic summarization</a> to be performed by autovacuum.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The pages_per_range argument takes a positive integer.</p> <p id="page_1331" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BTreeIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BTreeIndex</b>( *expressions, fillfactor=None, deduplicate_items=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a B-Tree index.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer value from 10 to 100 to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-STORAGE-PARAMETERS">fillfactor</a> parameter to tune how packed the index pages will be. PostgreSQL’s default is 90.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide a boolean value to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-implementation.html#BTREE-DEDUPLICATION">deduplicate_items</a> parameter to control whether deduplication is en-abled. PostgreSQL enables deduplication by default.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The deduplicate_items parameter was added.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GinIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GinIndex</b>(*expressions, fastupdate=None, gin_pending_list_limit=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin.html">gin index</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To use this index on data types not in the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin-builtin-opclasses.html">built-in operator classes</a>, you need to activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-gin.html">btree_gin</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-gin.html">extension</a> on PostgreSQL. You can install it using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>BtreeGinExtension</i></a> migration operation.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set the fastupdate parameter to False to disable the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin-implementation.html#GIN-FAST-UPDATE">GIN Fast Update Technique</a> that’s enabled by default in PostgreSQL.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer number of kilobytes to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html#GUC-GIN-PENDING-LIST-LIMIT">gin_pending_list_limit</a> parameter to tune the maximum size of the GIN pending list which is used when fastupdate is enabled.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>GistIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class GistIndex</b>(*expressions, buffering=None, fillfactor=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gist.html">GiST index</a>. <span style="float:right">These indexes are automatically created on spatial fields with</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1164"><i>spatial_index=True</i> . </a>They’re also useful on other types, such as <a href="index.html#page_1314"><i>HStoreField</i></a> or the <a href="index.html#page_1318">range</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1318">fields</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">To use this index on data types not in the built-in <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gist-builtin-opclasses.html">gist operator classes, </a>you need to activate the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-gist.html">btree_gist extension</a> on PostgreSQL. You can install it using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>BtreeGistExtension</i></a> migration oper-ation.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set the buffering parameter to True or False to manually enable or disable <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gist-implementation.html#GIST-BUFFERING-BUILD">buffering build</a> of the index.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer value from 10 to 100 to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-STORAGE-PARAMETERS">fillfactor</a> parameter to tune how packed the index pages will be. PostgreSQL’s default is 90.</p> <p id="page_1332"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>HashIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class HashIndex</b>(*expressions, fillfactor=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a hash index.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer value from 10 to 100 to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-STORAGE-PARAMETERS">fillfactor</a> parameter to tune how packed the index pages will be. PostgreSQL’s default is 90.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SpGistIndex</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SpGistIndex</b>(*expressions, fillfactor=None, **options)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates an <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/spgist.html">SP-GiST index</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Provide an integer value from 10 to 100 to the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-STORAGE-PARAMETERS">fillfactor</a> parameter to tune how packed the index pages will be. PostgreSQL’s default is 90.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>OpClass() expressions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class OpClass</b>(expression, name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">An OpClass() expression represents the expression with a custom <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-opclass.html">operator class</a> that can be used to define functional indexes, functional unique constraints, or exclusion constraints. To use it, you need</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>. Set the name parameter to the name of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-opclass.html">operator class.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">Index(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">OpClass(Lower(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"lower_username_idx"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">creates an index on Lower('username') using varchar_pattern_ops.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">UniqueConstraint(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">OpClass(Upper(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"description"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"text_pattern_ops"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"upper_description_unique"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">creates a unique constraint on Upper('description') using text_pattern_ops.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">ExclusionConstraint(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"exclude_overlapping_ops"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">expressions</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1333" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">(OpClass(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"circle"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, name</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"circle_ops"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">), RangeOperators</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">OVERLAPS),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">],</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">creates an exclusion constraint on circle using circle_ops.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL specific lookups</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Trigram similarity</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>trigram_similar</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The trigram_similar lookup allows you to perform trigram lookups, measuring the number of trigrams (three consecutive characters) shared, using a dedicated PostgreSQL extension. A trigram lookup is given an expression and returns results that have a similarity measurement greater than the current similarity threshold.</p> <p>To use it, add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> and activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtrgm.html">pg_trgm extension</a></p> <p>on PostgreSQL. You can install the extension using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>TrigramExtension</i></a> migration operation.</p> <p>The trigram_similar lookup can be used on <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">City</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(name__trigram_similar</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Middlesborough"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">['<City: Middlesbrough>']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>trigram_word_similar</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The trigram_word_similar lookup allows you to perform trigram word similarity lookups using a dedicated PostgreSQL extension. It can be approximately understood as measuring the greatest number of trigrams shared between the parameter and any substring of the field. A trigram word lookup is given an expression and returns results that have a word similarity measurement greater than the current similarity threshold.</p> <p>To use it, add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> and activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtrgm.html">pg_trgm extension</a></p> <p>on PostgreSQL. You can install the extension using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>TrigramExtension</i></a> migration operation.</p> <p>The trigram_word_similar lookup can be used on <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Sentence</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(name__trigram_word_similar</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Middlesborough"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">['<Sentence: Gumby rides on the path of Middlesbrough>']</span></p> <p id="page_1334"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>trigram_strict_word_similar</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Similar to <a href="index.html#page_1333"><i>trigram_word_similar</i></a>, except that it forces extent boundaries to match word boundaries.</p> <p>To use it, add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> and activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtrgm.html">pg_trgm extension</a></p> <p>on PostgreSQL. You can install the extension using the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>TrigramExtension</i></a> migration operation.</p> <p>The trigram_strict_word_similar lookup can be used on <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Unaccent</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The unaccent lookup allows you to perform accent-insensitive lookups using a dedicated PostgreSQL exten-sion.</p> <p>This lookup is implemented using <a href="index.html#page_1784"><i>Transform</i></a>, so it can be chained with other lookup functions. To use it, you</p> <p>need to add 'django.contrib.postgres' in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> and activate the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/unaccent.html">unaccent extension on</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/unaccent.html">PostgreSQL</a>. The <a href="index.html#page_1337"><i>UnaccentExtension</i></a> migration operation is available if you want to perform this activation using migrations).</p> <p>The unaccent lookup can be used on <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">City</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(name__unaccent</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"México"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">['<City: Mexico>']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(first_name__unaccent__startswith</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Jerem"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">['<User: Jeremy>', '<User: Jérémy>', '<User: Jérémie>', '<User: Jeremie>']</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: unaccent lookups should perform fine in most use cases. However, queries using this filter</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">will generally perform full table scans, which can be slow on large tables. In those cases, using dedicated</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">full text indexing tools might be appropriate.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1335" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database migration operations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>All of these <a href="index.html#page_1602">operations</a> are available from the django.contrib.postgres.operations module.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating extension using migrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can create a PostgreSQL extension in your database using a migration file. This example creates an hstore extension, but the same principles apply for other extensions.</p> <p>Set up the hstore extension in PostgreSQL before the first CreateModel or AddField operation that involves</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1314"><i>HStoreField</i></a> by adding a migration with the <a href="index.html#page_1336"><i>HStoreExtension</i></a> operation. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HStoreExtension</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[HStoreExtension(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The operation skips adding the extension if it already exists.</p> <p>For most extensions, this requires a database user with superuser privileges. If the Django database user doesn’t have the appropriate privileges, you’ll have to create the extension outside of Django migrations with a user that has them. In that case, connect to your Django database and run the query CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS hstore;.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CreateExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CreateExtension</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">An Operation subclass which installs a PostgreSQL extension. For common extensions, use one of the more specific subclasses below.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">This is a required argument. The name of the extension to be installed.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1336"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BloomExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BloomExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the bloom extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BtreeGinExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BtreeGinExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the btree_gin extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BtreeGistExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class BtreeGistExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the btree_gist extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CITextExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CITextExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the citext extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>CryptoExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CryptoExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the pgcrypto extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>HStoreExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class HStoreExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the hstore extension and also sets up the connection to interpret hstore data for possible use in subsequent migrations.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TrigramExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class TrigramExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the pg_trgm extension.</p> <p id="page_1337" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>UnaccentExtension</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class UnaccentExtension</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Installs the unaccent extension.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Managing collations using migrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to filter or order a column using a particular collation that your operating system provides but PostgreSQL does not, you can manage collations in your database using a migration file. These collations can</p> <p>then be used with the db_collation parameter on <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>, and their subclasses.</p> <p>For example, to create a collation for German phone book ordering:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CreateCollation</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Migration</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(migrations</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Migration):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">operations</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">CreateCollation(</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"case_insensitive"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">provider</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"icu"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">locale</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"und-u-ks-level2"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">deterministic</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>...</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class CreateCollation</b>(name, locale, *, provider='libc', deterministic=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Creates a collation with the given name, locale and provider.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Set the deterministic parameter to False to create a non-deterministic collation, such as for case-insensitive filtering.</p> <p><b>class RemoveCollation</b>(name, locale, *, provider='libc', deterministic=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Removes the collations named name.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When reversed this is creating a collation with the provided locale, provider, and deterministic arguments. Therefore, locale is required to make this operation reversible.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1338"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Concurrent index operations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostgreSQL supports the CONCURRENTLY option to CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX statements to add and remove indexes without locking out writes. This option is useful for adding or removing an index in a live production database.</p> <p><b>class AddIndexConcurrently</b>(model_name, index)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Like <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>AddIndex</i></a>, but creates an index with the CONCURRENTLY option. This has a few caveats to be aware</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">of when using this option, see <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-CONCURRENTLY">the PostgreSQL documentation of building indexes concurrently</a>.</p> <p><b>class RemoveIndexConcurrently</b>( model_name, name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Like <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>RemoveIndex</i></a>, but removes the index with the CONCURRENTLY option. This has a few caveats to be</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">aware of when using this option, see <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-dropindex.html">the PostgreSQL documentation</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The CONCURRENTLY option is not supported inside a transaction (see <a href="index.html#page_794">non-atomic migration</a>).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Adding constraints without enforcing validation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>PostgreSQL supports the NOT VALID option with the ADD CONSTRAINT statement to add check constraints without enforcing validation on existing rows. This option is useful if you want to skip the potentially lengthy scan of the table to verify that all existing rows satisfy the constraint.</p> <p>To validate check constraints created with the NOT VALID option at a later point of time, use the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1338"><i>ValidateConstraint</i></a> operation.</p> <p>See <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html#SQL-ALTERTABLE-NOTES">the PostgreSQL documentation</a> for more details.</p> <p><b>class AddConstraintNotValid</b>(model_name, constraint)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Like <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>AddConstraint</i></a>, but avoids validating the constraint on existing rows.</p> <p><b>class ValidateConstraint</b>(model_name, name)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Scans through the table and validates the given check constraint on existing rows.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: AddConstraintNotValid and ValidateConstraint operations should be performed in two separate</p> <p>migrations. Performing both operations in the same atomic migration has the same effect as <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>AddConstraint</i></a>, whereas performing them in a single non-atomic migration, may leave your database in an inconsistent state if the ValidateConstraint operation fails.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1339" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Full text search</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The database functions in the django.contrib.postgres.search module ease the use of PostgreSQL’s <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html">full</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html">text search engine.</a></p> <p>For the examples in this document, we’ll use the models defined in <a href="index.html#page_143">Making queries</a>.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>For a high-level overview of searching, see the <a href="index.html#page_189">topic documentation.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The search lookup</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A common way to use full text search is to search a single term against a single column in the database. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(body_text__search</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[<Entry: Cheese on Toast recipes>, <Entry: Pizza Recipes>]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This creates a to_tsvector in the database from the body_text field and a plainto_tsquery from the search term 'Cheese', both using the default database search configuration. The results are obtained by matching the query and the vector.</p> <p>To use the search lookup, 'django.contrib.postgres' must be in your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SearchVector</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SearchVector</b>(*expressions, config=None, weight=None)</p> <p>Searching against a single field is great but rather limiting. The Entry instances we’re searching belong to a Blog, which has a tagline field. To query against both fields, use a SearchVector:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.search</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchVector</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">search</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchVector(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"body_text"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"blog__tagline"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(search</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[<Entry: Cheese on Toast recipes>, <Entry: Pizza Recipes>]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The arguments to SearchVector can be any <a href="index.html#page_1804"><i>Expression</i></a> or the name of a field. Multiple arguments will be concatenated together using a space so that the search document includes them all.</p> <p>SearchVector objects can be combined together, allowing you to reuse them. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">search</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchVector(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"body_text"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>+</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchVector(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"blog__tagline"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">),</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1340"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">filter(search</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[<Entry: Cheese on Toast recipes>, <Entry: Pizza Recipes>]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1342">Changing the search configuration</a> and <a href="index.html#page_1343">Weighting queries</a> for an explanation of the config and weight parameters.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SearchQuery</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SearchQuery</b>(value, config=None, search_type='plain')</p> <p>SearchQuery translates the terms the user provides into a search query object that the database compares to a search vector. By default, all the words the user provides are passed through the stemming algorithms, and then it looks for matches for all of the resulting terms.</p> <p>If search_type is 'plain', which is the default, the terms are treated as separate keywords. If search_type is 'phrase', the terms are treated as a single phrase. If search_type is 'raw', then you can provide a for-matted search query with terms and operators. If search_type is 'websearch', then you can provide a formatted search query, similar to the one used by web search engines. 'websearch' requires PostgreSQL <i>≥</i></p> <p>11. Read PostgreSQL’s <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-controls.html#TEXTSEARCH-PARSING-QUERIES">Full Text Search docs</a> to learn about differences and syntax. Examples:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.search</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"red tomato"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># two keywords</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"tomato red"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># same results as above</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"red tomato"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, search_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"phrase"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># a phrase</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"tomato red"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, search_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"phrase"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># a different phrase</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"'tomato' & ('red' | 'green')"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, search_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"raw"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># boolean operators</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"'tomato' ('red' OR 'green')"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, search_type</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"websearch"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># websearch operators</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SearchQuery terms can be combined logically to provide more flexibility:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.search</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"meat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>&</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># AND</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"meat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>|</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># OR</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>~</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"meat"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># NOT</i></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1342">Changing the search configuration</a> for an explanation of the config parameter.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1341" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SearchRank</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SearchRank</b>( vector, query, weights=None, normalization=None, cover_density=False)</p> <p>So far, we’ve returned the results for which any match between the vector and the query are possible. It’s likely you may wish to order the results by some sort of relevancy. PostgreSQL provides a ranking function which takes into account how often the query terms appear in the document, how close together the terms are in the document, and how important the part of the document is where they occur. The better the match, the higher the value of the rank. To order by relevancy:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.search</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery, SearchRank, SearchVector</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">vector</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchVector(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"body_text"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">query</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"cheese"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(rank</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchRank(vector, query))</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">order_by(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"-rank"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">[<Entry: Cheese on Toast recipes>, <Entry: Pizza recipes>]</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1343">Weighting queries</a> for an explanation of the weights parameter.</p> <p>Set the cover_density parameter to True to enable the cover density ranking, which means that the prox-imity of matching query terms is taken into account.</p> <p>Provide an integer to the normalization parameter to control rank normalization. This integer is a bit mask, so you can combine multiple behaviors:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Value</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">rank</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchRank(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">vector,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">query,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">normalization</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Value(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">2</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">bitor(Value(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">4</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)),</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The PostgreSQL documentation has more details about <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-controls.html#TEXTSEARCH-RANKING">different rank normalization options.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SearchHeadline</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class SearchHeadline</b>(expression, query, config=None, start_sel=None, stop_sel=None,</p> <p style="text-align:right">max_words=None, min_words=None, short_word=None, highlight_all=None, max_fragments=None, fragment_delimiter=None)</p> <p>Accepts a single text field or an expression, a query, a config, and a set of options. Returns highlighted search results.</p> <p>Set the start_sel and stop_sel parameters to the string values to be used to wrap highlighted query terms in the document. PostgreSQL’s defaults are <b> and </b>.</p> <p id="page_1342"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Provide integer values to the max_words and min_words parameters to determine the longest and shortest headlines. PostgreSQL’s defaults are 35 and 15.</p> <p>Provide an integer value to the short_word parameter to discard words of this length or less in each headline. PostgreSQL’s default is 3.</p> <p>Set the highlight_all parameter to True to use the whole document in place of a fragment and ignore max_words, min_words, and short_word parameters. That’s disabled by default in PostgreSQL.</p> <p>Provide a non-zero integer value to the max_fragments to set the maximum number of fragments to display. That’s disabled by default in PostgreSQL.</p> <p>Set the fragment_delimiter string parameter to configure the delimiter between fragments. PostgreSQL’s default is " ... ".</p> <p>The PostgreSQL documentation has more details on <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-controls.html#TEXTSEARCH-HEADLINE">highlighting search results</a>.</p> <p>Usage example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.postgres.search</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchHeadline, SearchQuery</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">query</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchQuery(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"red tomato"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">entry</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Entry</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">annotate(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">headline</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SearchHeadline(</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"body_text"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">query,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">start_sel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span <p><b>Changing the search configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can specify the config attribute to a <a href="index.html#page_1339"><i>SearchVector</i></a> and <a <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.models</span> <span
