Code it up, and post it to the <a href="index.html#page_2820">django-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_2820">users</a> mailing list.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.6 Cross Site Request Forgery protection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The CSRF middleware and template tag provides easy-to-use protection against <a href="https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/csrf#overview">Cross Site Request Forgeries</a>. This type of attack occurs when a malicious website contains a link, a form button or some JavaScript that is intended to perform some action on your website, using the credentials of a logged-in user who visits the malicious site in their browser. A related type of attack, ‘login CSRF’, where an attacking site tricks a user’s browser into logging into a site with someone else’s credentials, is also covered.</p> <p>The first defense against CSRF attacks is to ensure that GET requests (and other ‘safe’ methods, as defined</p> <p>by <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.1">RFC 9110#section-9.2.1) </a>are side effect free. Requests via ‘unsafe’ methods, such as POST, PUT, and</p> <p>DELETE, can then be protected by the steps outlined in <a href="index.html#page_889">How to use Django’s CSRF protection</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.6.1 How it works</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The CSRF protection is based on the following things:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. A CSRF cookie that is a random secret value, which other sites will not have access to.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">CsrfViewMiddleware sends this cookie with the response whenever django.middleware.csrf. get_token() is called. It can also send it in other cases. For security reasons, the value of the secret is changed each time a user logs in.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. A hidden form field with the name ‘csrfmiddlewaretoken’, present in all outgoing POST forms.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In order to protect against <a href="https://www.breachattack.com/">BREACH</a> attacks, the value of this field is not simply the secret. It is scram-bled differently with each response using a mask. The mask is generated randomly on every call to get_token() , so the form field value is different each time.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This part is done by the <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> template tag.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. For all incoming requests that are not using HTTP GET, HEAD, OPTIONS or TRACE, a CSRF cookie</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">must be present, and the ‘csrfmiddlewaretoken’ field must be present and correct. If it isn’t, the user will get a 403 error.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">When validating the ‘csrfmiddlewaretoken’ field value, only the secret, not the full token, is compared with the secret in the cookie value. This allows the use of ever-changing tokens. While each request may use its own token, the secret remains common to all.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This check is done by CsrfViewMiddleware.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">4. CsrfViewMiddleware verifies the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Origin">Origin header, </a>if provided by the browser, against the current host</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">and the <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS</i></a> setting. This provides protection against cross-subdomain attacks.</p> <p id="page_1407" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">5. In addition, for HTTPS requests, if the Origin header isn’t provided, CsrfViewMiddleware performs</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">strict referer checking. This means that even if a subdomain can set or modify cookies on your domain, it can’t force a user to post to your application since that request won’t come from your own exact domain.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This also addresses a man-in-the-middle attack that’s possible under HTTPS when using a session inde-pendent secret, due to the fact that HTTP Set-Cookie headers are (unfortunately) accepted by clients even when they are talking to a site under HTTPS. (Referer checking is not done for HTTP requests because the presence of the Referer header isn’t reliable enough under HTTP.)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If the <a href="index.html#page_1892"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_DOMAIN</i></a> setting is set, the referer is compared against it. You can allow cross-subdomain requests by including a leading dot. For example, CSRF_COOKIE_DOMAIN = '.example. com' will allow POST requests from www.example.com and api.example.com. If the setting is not set, then the referer must match the HTTP Host header.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Expanding the accepted referers beyond the current host or cookie domain can be done with the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS</i></a> setting.</p> <p>This ensures that only forms that have originated from trusted domains can be used to POST data back.</p> <p>It deliberately ignores GET requests (and other requests that are defined as ‘safe’ by <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.1">RFC 9110#section-9.2.1</a>). These requests ought never to have any potentially dangerous side effects, and so a CSRF attack with a GET</p> <p>request ought to be harmless. <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.1">RFC 9110#section-9.2.1</a> defines POST, PUT, and DELETE as ‘unsafe’, and all other methods are also assumed to be unsafe, for maximum protection.</p> <p>The CSRF protection cannot protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, so use <a href="index.html#page_720">HTTPS</a> with <a href="index.html#page_1595">HTTP Strict</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1595">Transport Security</a>. It also assumes <a href="index.html#page_721">validation of the HOST header</a> and that there aren’t any <a href="index.html#page_718">cross-site script-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_718">ing vulnerabilities</a> on your site (because XSS vulnerabilities already let an attacker do anything a CSRF vul-nerability allows and much worse).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Removing the <b>Referer</b> header</p> <p>To avoid disclosing the referrer URL to third-party sites, you might want to <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/referrer-policy/#referrer-policy-delivery">disable the referer</a> on your site’s <a> tags. For example, you might use the <meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer"> tag or include the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer header. Due to the CSRF protection’s strict referer checking on HTTPS requests, those techniques cause a CSRF failure on requests with ‘unsafe’ methods. Instead, use alternatives like <a rel="noreferrer" ...>" for links to third-party sites.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1408"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.6.2 Limitations</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Subdomains within a site will be able to set cookies on the client for the whole domain. By setting the cookie and using a corresponding token, subdomains will be able to circumvent the CSRF protection. The only way to avoid this is to ensure that subdomains are controlled by trusted users (or, are at least unable to set cookies). Note that even without CSRF, there are other vulnerabilities, such as session fixation, that make giving subdomains to untrusted parties a bad idea, and these vulnerabilities cannot easily be fixed with current browsers.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.6.3 Utilities</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The examples below assume you are using function-based views. If you are working with class-based views,</p> <p>you can refer to <a href="index.html#page_415">Decorating class-based views</a>.</p> <p><b>csrf_exempt</b>(view)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This decorator marks a view as being exempt from the protection ensured by the middleware. Example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.http</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.csrf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_exempt</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@csrf_exempt</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">HttpResponse(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"Hello world"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>csrf_protect</b>(view)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Decorator that provides the protection of <a href="index.html#page_1601"><i>CsrfViewMiddleware</i></a> to a view.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Usage:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.csrf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">csrf_protect</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@csrf_protect</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_template.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, c)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>requires_csrf_token</b>(view)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Normally the <a href="index.html#page_1980"><i>csrf_token</i></a> template tag will not work if CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view or an equivalent like csrf_protect has not run. The view decorator requires_csrf_token can be used to</p> <p id="page_1409" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ensure the template tag does work. This decorator works similarly to csrf_protect, but never rejects an incoming request.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.shortcuts</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.views.decorators.csrf</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">requires_csrf_token</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">@requires_csrf_token</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>my_view</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(request):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">render(request,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_template.html"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, c)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ensure_csrf_cookie</b>(view)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This decorator forces a view to send the CSRF cookie.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.6.4 Settings</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A number of settings can be used to control Django’s CSRF behavior:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1892"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_AGE</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1892"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_DOMAIN</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_NAME</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1893"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_PATH</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_SAMESITE</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_HEADER_NAME</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS</i></a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_USE_SESSIONS</i></a></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1410"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.6.5 Frequently Asked Questions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Is posting an arbitrary CSRF token pair (cookie and POST data) a vulnerability?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>No, this is by design. Without a man-in-the-middle attack, there is no way for an attacker to send a CSRF token cookie to a victim’s browser, so a successful attack would need to obtain the victim’s browser’s cookie via XSS or similar, in which case an attacker usually doesn’t need CSRF attacks.</p> <p>Some security audit tools flag this as a problem but as mentioned before, an attacker cannot steal a user’s browser’s CSRF cookie. “Stealing” or modifying your own token using Firebug, Chrome dev tools, etc. isn’t a vulnerability.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Is it a problem that Django’s CSRF protection isn’t linked to a session by default?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>No, this is by design. Not linking CSRF protection to a session allows using the protection on sites such as a pastebin that allow submissions from anonymous users which don’t have a session.</p> <p>If you wish to store the CSRF token in the user’s session, use the <a href="index.html#page_1894"><i>CSRF_USE_SESSIONS</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Why might a user encounter a CSRF validation failure after logging in?</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For security reasons, CSRF tokens are rotated each time a user logs in. Any page with a form generated before a login will have an old, invalid CSRF token and need to be reloaded. This might happen if a user uses the back button after a login or if they log in a different browser tab.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.7 Databases</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django officially supports the following databases:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1412">PostgreSQL</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1418">MariaDB</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1418">MySQL</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1427">Oracle</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="index.html#page_1424">SQLite</a></p> <p>There are also a number of <a href="index.html#page_1432">database backends provided by third parties</a>.</p> <p>Django attempts to support as many features as possible on all database backends. However, not all database backends are alike, and we’ve had to make design decisions on which features to support and which assump-tions we can make safely.</p> <p>This file describes some of the features that might be relevant to Django usage. It is not intended as a re-placement for server-specific documentation or reference manuals.</p> <p id="page_1411" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.1 General notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Persistent connections</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Persistent connections avoid the overhead of reestablishing a connection to the database in each HTTP re-</p> <p>quest. They’re controlled by the <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>CONN_MAX_AGE</i></a> parameter which defines the maximum lifetime of a connec-tion. It can be set independently for each database.</p> <p>The default value is 0, preserving the historical behavior of closing the database connection at the end of each</p> <p>request. To enable persistent connections, set <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>CONN_MAX_AGE</i></a> to a positive integer of seconds. For unlimited persistent connections, set it to None.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connection management</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django opens a connection to the database when it first makes a database query. It keeps this connection open and reuses it in subsequent requests. Django closes the connection once it exceeds the maximum age</p> <p>defined by <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>CONN_MAX_AGE</i></a> or when it isn’t usable any longer.</p> <p>In detail, Django automatically opens a connection to the database whenever it needs one and doesn’t have one already — either because this is the first connection, or because the previous connection was closed.</p> <p>At the beginning of each request, Django closes the connection if it has reached its maximum age. If your</p> <p>database terminates idle connections after some time, you should set <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>CONN_MAX_AGE</i></a> to a lower value, so that Django doesn’t attempt to use a connection that has been terminated by the database server. (This problem may only affect very low traffic sites.)</p> <p>At the end of each request, Django closes the connection if it has reached its maximum age or if it is in an unrecoverable error state. If any database errors have occurred while processing the requests, Django checks whether the connection still works, and closes it if it doesn’t. Thus, database errors affect at most one request per each application’s worker thread; if the connection becomes unusable, the next request gets a fresh connection.</p> <p>Setting <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>CONN_HEALTH_CHECKS</i></a> to True can be used to improve the robustness of connection reuse and prevent errors when a connection has been closed by the database server which is now ready to accept and serve new connections, e.g. after database server restart. The health check is performed only once per request and only if the database is being accessed during the handling of the request.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1412"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Caveats</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Since each thread maintains its own connection, your database must support at least as many simultaneous connections as you have worker threads.</p> <p>Sometimes a database won’t be accessed by the majority of your views, for example because it’s the database</p> <p>of an external system, or thanks to caching. In such cases, you should set <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>CONN_MAX_AGE</i></a> to a low value or even 0, because it doesn’t make sense to maintain a connection that’s unlikely to be reused. This will help keep the number of simultaneous connections to this database small.</p> <p>The development server creates a new thread for each request it handles, negating the effect of persistent connections. Don’t enable them during development.</p> <p>When Django establishes a connection to the database, it sets up appropriate parameters, depending on the backend being used. If you enable persistent connections, this setup is no longer repeated every request. If you modify parameters such as the connection’s isolation level or time zone, you should either restore Django’s defaults at the end of each request, force an appropriate value at the beginning of each request, or disable persistent connections.</p> <p>If a connection is created in a long-running process, outside of Django’s request-response cycle, the connection will remain open until explicitly closed, or timeout occurs. You can use django.db. close_old_connections() to close all old or unusable connections.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Encoding</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django assumes that all databases use UTF-8 encoding. Using other encodings may result in unexpected behavior such as “value too long” errors from your database for data that is valid in Django. See the database specific notes below for information on how to set up your database correctly.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.2 PostgreSQL notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports PostgreSQL 14 and higher. <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/">psycopg</a> 3.1.8+ or <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/">psycopg2</a> 2.8.4+ is required, though the latest</p> <p><a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/">psycopg</a> 3.1.8+ is recommended.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Support for psycopg2 is likely to be deprecated and removed at some point in the future.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1413" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL connection settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> for details.</p> <p>To connect using a service name from the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgservice.html">connection service file</a> and a password from the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgpass.html">password file</a>, you</p> <p>must specify them in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 7: settings.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.postgresql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="font-size:0.87em">"passfile"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">".my_pgpass"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 8: .pg_service.conf</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">[my_service]</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">host=localhost</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">user=USER</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">dbname=NAME</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">port=5432</span></p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1414"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 9: .my_pgpass</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">localhost:5432:NAME:USER:PASSWORD</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The PostgreSQL backend passes the content of <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> as keyword arguments to the connection constructor,</p> <p>allowing for more advanced control of driver behavior. All available <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-PARAMKEYWORDS">parameters</a> are described in detail in the PostgreSQL documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Warning: Using a service name for testing purposes is not supported. This <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/33685">may be implemented later</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Optimizing PostgreSQL’s configuration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django needs the following parameters for its database connections:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• client_encoding: 'UTF8',</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• default_transaction_isolation: 'read committed' by default, or the value set in the connection</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">options (see below),</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <b>timezone</b>:</p> <p style="margin-left:5em">– when <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ</i></a> is True, 'UTC' by default, or the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>TIME_ZONE</i></a> value set for the connection,</p> <p style="margin-left:5em">– when <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ</i></a> is False, the value of the global <a href="index.html#page_1935"><i>TIME_ZONE</i></a> setting.</p> <p>If these parameters already have the correct values, Django won’t set them for every new connection, which improves performance slightly. You can configure them directly in postgresql.conf or more conveniently</p> <p>per database user with <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-alterrole.html">ALTER ROLE.</a></p> <p>Django will work just fine without this optimization, but each new connection will do some additional queries to set these parameters.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Isolation level</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Like PostgreSQL itself, Django defaults to the READ COMMITTED <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html">isolation level</a>. If you need a higher isolation</p> <p>level such as REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, set it in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration</p> <p>in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.backends.postgresql.psycopg_any</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">IsolationLevel</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"isolation_level"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: IsolationLevel</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">SERIALIZABLE,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1415" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Under higher isolation levels, your application should be prepared to handle exceptions raised on serialization failures. This option is designed for advanced uses.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Role</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to use a different role for database connections than the role use to establish the connection, set</p> <p>it in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.postgresql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"assume_role"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"my_application_role"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connection pool</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To use a connection pool with <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/">psycopg, </a>you can either set "pool" in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database</p> <p>configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> to be a dict to be passed to <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/api/pool.html#psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool">ConnectionPool</a>, or to True to use the ConnectionPool defaults:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.postgresql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"pool"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This option requires psycopg[pool] or <a href="https://pypi.org/project/psycopg-pool/">psycopg-pool</a> to be installed and is ignored with psycopg2.</p> <p id="page_1416"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Server-side parameters binding</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>With <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/">psycopg</a> 3.1.8+, Django defaults to the <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/cursors.html#client-side-binding-cursors">client-side binding cursors</a><a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/cursors.html#client-side-binding-cursors">. </a>If you want to use the <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/from_pg2.html#server-side-binding">server-side</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/from_pg2.html#server-side-binding">binding</a> set it in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.postgresql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"server_side_binding"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This option is ignored with psycopg2.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Indexes for varchar and text columns</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When specifying db_index=True on your model fields, Django typically outputs a single CREATE INDEX statement. However, if the database type for the field is either varchar or text (e.g., used by CharField,</p> <p>FileField, and TextField), then Django will create an additional index that uses an appropriate <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-opclass.html">PostgreSQL</a></p> <p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-opclass.html">operator class</a> for the column. The extra index is necessary to correctly perform lookups that use the LIKE operator in their SQL, as is done with the contains and startswith lookup types.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Migration operation for adding extensions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to add a PostgreSQL extension (like hstore, postgis, etc.) using a migration, use the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1335"><i>CreateExtension</i></a> operation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Server-side cursors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When using <a href="index.html#page_1752"><i>QuerySet.iterator()</i>, </a>Django opens a <a href="https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/cursors.html#server-side-cursors">server-side cursor</a>. By default, PostgreSQL assumes that only the first 10% of the results of cursor queries will be fetched. The query planner spends less time plan-ning the query and starts returning results faster, but this could diminish performance if more than 10% of the results are retrieved. PostgreSQL’s assumptions on the number of rows retrieved for a cursor query is controlled with the <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html#GUC-CURSOR-TUPLE-FRACTION">cursor_tuple_fraction</a> option.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1417" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Transaction pooling and server-side cursors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Using a connection pooler in transaction pooling mode (e.g. <a href="https://www.pgbouncer.org/">PgBouncer) </a>requires disabling server-side cursors for that connection.</p> <p>Server-side cursors are local to a connection and remain open at the end of a transaction when <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>AUTOCOMMIT</i></a> is True. A subsequent transaction may attempt to fetch more results from a server-side cursor. In transaction pooling mode, there’s no guarantee that subsequent transactions will use the same connection. If a different connection is used, an error is raised when the transaction references the server-side cursor, because server-side cursors are only accessible in the connection in which they were created.</p> <p>One solution is to disable server-side cursors for a connection in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> <span style="float:right">by setting</span></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1899"><i>DISABLE_SERVER_SIDE_CURSORS</i></a> to True.</p> <p>To benefit from server-side cursors in transaction pooling mode, you could set up <a href="index.html#page_220">another connection to the</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_220">database</a> in order to perform queries that use server-side cursors. This connection needs to either be directly to the database or to a connection pooler in session pooling mode.</p> <p>Another option is to wrap each QuerySet using server-side cursors in an <a href="index.html#page_209"><i>atomic()</i></a> block, because it disables autocommit for the duration of the transaction. This way, the server-side cursor will only live for the duration of the transaction.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Manually-specifying values of auto-incrementing primary keys</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django uses PostgreSQL’s identity columns to store auto-incrementing primary keys. An identity column is</p> <p>populated with values from a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createsequence.html">sequence</a> that keeps track of the next available value. Manually assigning a value to an auto-incrementing field doesn’t update the field’s sequence, which might later cause a conflict. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.contrib.auth.models</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"alice"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, pk</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">1</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><User: alice></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># The sequence hasn't been updated; its next value is 1.</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">User</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">objects</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create(username</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"bob"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth_user_pkey" DETAIL:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">Key (id)=(1) already exists.</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you need to specify such values, reset the sequence afterward to avoid reusing a value that’s already in the</p> <p>table. The <a href="index.html#page_1453"><i>sqlsequencereset</i></a> management command generates the SQL statements to do that.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1418"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Test database templates</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can use the <a href="index.html#page_1901"><i>TEST['TEMPLATE']</i></a> setting to specify a <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createdatabase.html">template</a> (e.g. 'template0') from which to create a test database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Speeding up test execution with non-durable settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can speed up test execution times by <a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/non-durability.html">configuring PostgreSQL to be non-durable</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: This is dangerous: it will make your database more susceptible to data loss or corruption in</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">the case of a server crash or power loss. Only use this on a development machine where you can easily</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">restore the entire contents of all databases in the cluster.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.3 MariaDB notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports MariaDB 10.5 and higher.</p> <p>To use MariaDB, use the MySQL backend, which is shared between the two. See the <a href="index.html#page_1418">MySQL notes</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.4 MySQL notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Version support</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports MySQL 8.0.11 and higher.</p> <p>Django’s inspectdb feature uses the information_schema database, which contains detailed data on all database schemas.</p> <p>Django expects the database to support Unicode (UTF-8 encoding) and delegates to it the task of enforcing transactions and referential integrity. It is important to be aware of the fact that the two latter ones aren’t actually enforced by MySQL when using the MyISAM storage engine, see the next section.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Storage engines</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL has several <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/storage-engines.html">storage engines. </a>You can change the default storage engine in the server configuration.</p> <p>MySQL’s default storage engine is <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/innodb-storage-engine.html">InnoDB</a>. This engine is fully transactional and supports foreign key refer-ences. It’s the recommended choice. However, the InnoDB autoincrement counter is lost on a MySQL restart because it does not remember the AUTO_INCREMENT value, instead recreating it as “max(id)+1”. This may result in an inadvertent reuse of <a href="index.html#page_1626"><i>AutoField</i></a> values.</p> <p>The main drawbacks of <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/myisam-storage-engine.html">MyISAM</a> are that it doesn’t support transactions or enforce foreign-key constraints.</p> <p id="page_1419" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MySQL DB API Drivers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL has a couple drivers that implement the Python Database API described in <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/">PEP 249:</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/mysqlclient/">mysqlclient</a> is a native driver. It’s the recommended choice.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/connector/python/">MySQL Connector/Python</a> is a pure Python driver from Oracle that does not require the MySQL client</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">library or any Python modules outside the standard library.</p> <p>In addition to a DB API driver, Django needs an adapter to access the database drivers from its ORM. Django</p> <p>provides an adapter for mysqlclient while MySQL Connector/Python includes <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/connector-python/en/connector-python-django-backend.html">its own.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>mysqlclient</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django requires <a href="index.html#page_1419">mysqlclient</a> 1.4.3 or later.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MySQL Connector/Python</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL Connector/Python is available from the <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/connector/python/">download page</a>. The Django adapter is available in versions 1.1.X and later. It may not support the most recent releases of Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Time zone definitions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you plan on using Django’s <a href="index.html#page_693">timezone support, </a>use <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/mysql-tzinfo-to-sql.html">mysql_tzinfo_to_sql</a> to load time zone tables into the MySQL database. This needs to be done just once for your MySQL server, not per database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating your database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/create-database.html">create your database</a> using the command-line tools and this SQL:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>CREATE DATABASE <</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">dbname</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>></b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">CHARACTER</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>SET</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">utf8mb4;</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This ensures all tables and columns will use UTF-8 by default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Collation settings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The collation setting for a column controls the order in which data is sorted as well as what strings compare as</p> <p>equal. You can specify the db_collation parameter to set the collation name of the column for <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i></a></p> <p>and <a href="index.html#page_1642"><i>TextField</i></a>.</p> <p>The collation can also be set on a database-wide level and per-table. This is <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/charset.html">documented thoroughly</a> in the MySQL documentation. In such cases, you must set the collation by directly manipulating the database settings or tables. Django doesn’t provide an API to change them.</p> <p id="page_1420"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, with a UTF-8 database, MySQL will use the utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci collation. This results in all string equality comparisons being done in a case-insensitive manner. That is, "Fred" and "freD" are consid-ered equal at the database level. If you have a unique constraint on a field, it would be illegal to try to insert both "aa" and "AA" into the same column, since they compare as equal (and, hence, non-unique) with the default collation. If you want case-sensitive comparisons on a particular column or table, change the column or table to use the utf8mb4_0900_as_cs collation.</p> <p>Please note that according to <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/charset-unicode-sets.html">MySQL Unicode Character Sets, </a>comparisons for the utf8mb4_general_ci collation are faster, but slightly less correct, than comparisons for utf8mb4_unicode_ci. If this is acceptable for your application, you should use utf8mb4_general_ci because it is faster. If this is not acceptable (for example, if you require German dictionary order), use utf8mb4_unicode_ci because it is more accurate.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: Model formsets validate unique fields in a case-sensitive manner. Thus when using a case-</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">insensitive collation, a formset with unique field values that differ only by case will pass validation, but</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">upon calling save(), an IntegrityError will be raised.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connecting to the database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Refer to the <a href="index.html#page_1887">settings documentation.</a></p> <p>Connection settings are used in this order:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> , <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PASSWORD</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> , <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a></p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. MySQL option files.</p> <p>In other words, if you set the name of the database in <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a>, this will take precedence over <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> , which</p> <p>would override anything in a <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/option-files.html">MySQL option file</a>.</p> <p>Here’s a sample configuration which uses a MySQL option file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># settings.py</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.mysql"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"read_default_file"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/my.cnf"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># my.cnf</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[client]</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1421" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">database</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">NAME</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">user</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">USER</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">password</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">PASSWORD</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">default-character-set</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">utf8mb4</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Several other <a href="https://mysqlclient.readthedocs.io/user_guide.html#functions-and-attributes">MySQLdb connection options</a> may be useful, such as ssl, init_command, and sql_mode.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting sql_mode</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The default value of the sql_mode option contains STRICT_TRANS_TABLES. That option escalates warnings</p> <p>into errors when data are truncated upon insertion, so Django highly recommends activating a <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/sql-mode.html#sql-mode-strict">strict mode</a> for MySQL to prevent data loss (either STRICT_TRANS_TABLES or STRICT_ALL_TABLES).</p> <p>If you need to customize the SQL mode, you can set the sql_mode variable like other MySQL options: either in</p> <p>a config file or with the entry 'init_command': "SET sql_mode='STRICT_TRANS_TABLES'" in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a></p> <p>part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Isolation level</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When running concurrent loads, database transactions from different sessions (say, separate threads han-dling different requests) may interact with each other. These interactions are affected by each session’s</p> <p><a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html">transaction isolation level. </a>You can set a connection’s isolation level with an 'isolation_level' entry in</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>. Valid values for this entry are the four stan-dard isolation levels:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 'read uncommitted'</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 'read committed'</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 'repeatable read'</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 'serializable'</p> <p>or None to use the server’s configured isolation level. However, Django works best with and defaults to read committed rather than MySQL’s default, repeatable read. Data loss is possible with repeatable read. In</p> <p>particular, you may see cases where <a href="index.html#page_1745"><i>get_or_create()</i></a> will raise an <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>IntegrityError</i></a> but the object won’t</p> <p>appear in a subsequent <a href="index.html#page_1744"><i>get()</i></a> call.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1422"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Creating your tables</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When Django generates the schema, it doesn’t specify a storage engine, so tables will be created with whatever default storage engine your database server is configured for. The easiest solution is to set your database server’s default storage engine to the desired engine.</p> <p>If you’re using a hosting service and can’t change your server’s default storage engine, you have a couple of options.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• After the tables are created, execute an ALTER TABLE statement to convert a table to a new storage</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">engine (such as InnoDB):</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ALTER TABLE <</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">tablename</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>></b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ENGINE</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">INNODB;</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This can be tedious if you have a lot of tables.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Another option is to use the init_command option for MySQLdb prior to creating your tables:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"init_command"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"SET default_storage_engine=INNODB"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This sets the default storage engine upon connecting to the database. After your tables have been created, you should remove this option as it adds a query that is only needed during table creation to each database connection.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Table names</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are <a href="https://bugs.mysql.com/bug.php?id=48875">known issues</a> in even the latest versions of MySQL that can cause the case of a table name to be altered when certain SQL statements are executed under certain conditions. It is recommended that you use lowercase table names, if possible, to avoid any problems that might arise from this behavior. Django uses lowercase table names when it auto-generates table names from models, so this is mainly a consideration if you are overriding the table name via the <a href="index.html#page_1679"><i>db_table</i></a> parameter.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Savepoints</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Both the Django ORM and MySQL (when using the InnoDB <a href="index.html#page_1418">storage engine) </a>support database <a href="index.html#page_217">savepoints</a><a href="index.html#page_217">.</a></p> <p>If you use the MyISAM storage engine please be aware of the fact that you will receive database-generated</p> <p>errors if you try to use the <a href="index.html#page_217">savepoint-related methods of the transactions API. </a>The reason for this is that detecting the storage engine of a MySQL database/table is an expensive operation so it was decided it isn’t worth to dynamically convert these methods in no-op’s based in the results of such detection.</p> <p id="page_1423" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Notes on specific fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Character fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any fields that are stored with VARCHAR column types may have their max_length restricted to 255 characters</p> <p>if you are using unique=True for the field. This affects <a href="index.html#page_1628"><i>CharField</i>,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1641"><i>SlugField</i></a>. See <a href="https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/create-index.html#create-index-column-prefixes">the MySQL documentation</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TextField limitations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL can index only the first N chars of a BLOB or TEXT column. Since TextField doesn’t have a defined length, you can’t mark it as unique=True. MySQL will report: “BLOB/TEXT column ‘<db_column>’ used in key specification without a key length”.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Fractional seconds support for Time and DateTime fields</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL can store fractional seconds, provided that the column definition includes a fractional indication (e.g. DATETIME(6)).</p> <p>Django will not upgrade existing columns to include fractional seconds if the database server supports it. If you want to enable them on an existing database, it’s up to you to either manually update the column on the target database, by executing a command like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ALTER TABLE `</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">your_table</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>` MODIFY `</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">your_datetime_column</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>`</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DATETIME(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">6</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>or using a <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>RunSQL</i></a> operation in a <a href="index.html#page_457">data migration</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TIMESTAMP columns</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you are using a legacy database that contains TIMESTAMP columns, you must set <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ = False</i></a> to avoid</p> <p>data corruption. <a href="index.html#page_1440"><i>inspectdb</i></a> maps these columns to <a href="index.html#page_1630"><i>DateTimeField</i></a> and if you enable timezone support, both MySQL and Django will attempt to convert the values from UTC to local time.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Row locking with QuerySet.select_for_update()</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>MySQL and MariaDB do not support some options to the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE statement. <span style="float:right">If</span></p> <p>select_for_update() is used with an unsupported option, then a <a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>NotSupportedError</i></a> is raised.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1424"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:12em">Option MariaDB MySQL</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">SKIP LOCKED X (<i>≥</i>10.6) X</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">NOWAIT X X</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">OF X</p> <p style="margin-left:12em">NO KEY</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When using select_for_update() on MySQL, make sure you filter a queryset against at least a set of fields contained in unique constraints or only against fields covered by indexes. Otherwise, an exclusive write lock will be acquired over the full table for the duration of the transaction.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Automatic typecasting can cause unexpected results</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When performing a query on a string type, but with an integer value, MySQL will coerce the types of all values in the table to an integer before performing the comparison. If your table contains the values 'abc', 'def' and you query for WHERE mycolumn=0, both rows will match. Similarly, WHERE mycolumn=1 will match the value 'abc1'. Therefore, string type fields included in Django will always cast the value to a string before using it in a query.</p> <p>If you implement custom model fields that inherit from <a href="index.html#page_1656"><i>Field</i></a> directly, are overriding <a href="index.html#page_1657"><i>get_prep_value()</i></a>,</p> <p>or use <a href="index.html#page_1799"><i>RawSQL</i>,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1732"><i>extra()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1732">, </a>or <a href="index.html#page_201"><i>raw()</i></a>, you should ensure that you perform appropriate typecasting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.5 SQLite notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports SQLite 3.31.0 and later.</p> <p><a href="https://www.sqlite.org/">SQLite</a> provides an excellent development alternative for applications that are predominantly read-only or require a smaller installation footprint. As with all database servers, though, there are some differences that are specific to SQLite that you should be aware of.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Substring matching and case sensitivity</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For all SQLite versions, there is some slightly counterintuitive behavior when attempting to match some</p> <p>types of strings. These are triggered when using the <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>iexact</i></a> or <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>contains</i></a> filters in Querysets. The behavior splits into two cases:</p> <p>1. For substring matching, all matches are done case-insensitively. That is a filter such as filter(name__contains="aa") will match a name of "Aabb".</p> <p>2. For strings containing characters outside the ASCII range, all exact string matches are performed case-</p> <p>sensitively, even when the case-insensitive options are passed into the query. So the <a href="index.html#page_1763"><i>iexact</i></a> filter will behave</p> <p>exactly the same as the <a href="index.html#page_1762"><i>exact</i></a> filter in these cases.</p> <p id="page_1425" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some possible workarounds for this are <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/faq.html#q18">documented at sqlite.org</a>, but they aren’t utilized by the default SQLite backend in Django, as incorporating them would be fairly difficult to do robustly. Thus, Django exposes the default SQLite behavior and you should be aware of this when doing case-insensitive or substring filtering.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Decimal handling</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQLite has no real decimal internal type. Decimal values are internally converted to the REAL data type (8-</p> <p>byte IEEE floating point number), as explained in the <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html#storage_classes_and_datatypes">SQLite datatypes documentation, </a>so they don’t support correctly-rounded decimal floating point arithmetic.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>“Database is locked” errors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQLite is meant to be a lightweight database, and thus can’t support a high level of concurrency. OperationalError: database is locked errors indicate that your application is experiencing more con-currency than sqlite can handle in default configuration. This error means that one thread or process has an exclusive lock on the database connection and another thread timed out waiting for the lock the be released.</p> <p>Python’s SQLite wrapper has a default timeout value that determines how long the second thread is allowed to wait on the lock before it times out and raises the OperationalError: database is locked error.</p> <p>If you’re getting this error, you can solve it by:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Switching to another database backend. At a certain point SQLite becomes too “lite” for real-world</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">applications, and these sorts of concurrency errors indicate you’ve reached that point.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Rewriting your code to reduce concurrency and ensure that database transactions are short-lived.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Increase the default timeout value by setting the timeout database option:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"timeout"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">20</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This will make SQLite wait a bit longer before throwing “database is locked” errors; it won’t really do anything to solve them.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1426"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Transactions behavior</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQLite supports three transaction modes: DEFERRED, IMMEDIATE, and EXCLUSIVE.</p> <p>The default is DEFERRED. If you need to use a different mode, set it in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database</p> <p>configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>, for example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"transaction_mode"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"IMMEDIATE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To make sure your transactions wait until timeout before raising “Database is Locked”, change the transac-tion mode to IMMEDIATE.</p> <p>For the best performance with IMMEDIATE and EXCLUSIVE, transactions should be as short as possible. This</p> <p>might be hard to guarantee for all of your views so the usage of <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>ATOMIC_REQUESTS</i></a> is discouraged in this case.</p> <p>For more information see <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html#deferred_immediate_and_exclusive_transactions">Transactions in SQLite.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>QuerySet.select_for_update() not supported</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>SQLite does not support the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE syntax. Calling it will have no effect.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Isolation when using QuerySet.iterator()</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are special considerations described in <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/isolation.html">Isolation In SQLite</a> when modifying a table while iterating over</p> <p>it using <a href="index.html#page_1752"><i>QuerySet.iterator()</i>. </a>If a row is added, changed, or deleted within the loop, then that row may or may not appear, or may appear twice, in subsequent results fetched from the iterator. Your code must handle this.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Enabling JSON1 extension on SQLite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To use <a href="index.html#page_1639"><i>JSONField</i></a> on SQLite, you need to enable the <a href="https://www.sqlite.org/json1.html">JSON1 extension</a> on Python’s <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#module-sqlite3">sqlite3</a> library. If the extension is not enabled on your installation, a system error (fields.E180) will be raised.</p> <p>To enable the JSON1 extension you can follow the instruction on <a href="https://code.djangoproject.com/wiki/JSON1Extension">the wiki page</a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: The JSON1 extension is enabled by default on SQLite 3.38+.</p> <p id="page_1427" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Setting pragma options</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><a href="https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html">Pragma options</a> can be set upon connection by using the init_command in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database</p> <p>configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a>. The example below shows how to enable extra durability of synchronous writes and change the cache_size:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.sqlite3"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:5em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"init_command"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"PRAGMA synchronous=3; PRAGMA cache_size=2000;"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.6 Oracle notes</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django supports <a href="https://www.oracle.com/">Oracle Database Server</a> versions 19c and higher. Version 1.3.2 or higher of the <a href="https://oracle.github.io/python-oracledb/">oracledb</a> Python driver is required.</p> <p>Deprecated since version 5.0: Support for cx_Oracle is deprecated.</p> <p>In order for the python manage.py migrate command to work, your Oracle database user must have priv-ileges to run the following commands:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE TABLE</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE SEQUENCE</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE PROCEDURE</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE TRIGGER</p> <p>To run a project’s test suite, the user usually needs these additional privileges:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE USER</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• ALTER USER</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• DROP USER</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE TABLESPACE</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• DROP TABLESPACE</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE SESSION WITH ADMIN OPTION</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE TABLE WITH ADMIN OPTION</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE SEQUENCE WITH ADMIN OPTION</p> <p id="page_1428"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE PROCEDURE WITH ADMIN OPTION</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• CREATE TRIGGER WITH ADMIN OPTION</p> <p>While the RESOURCE role has the required CREATE TABLE, CREATE SEQUENCE, CREATE PROCEDURE, and CREATE TRIGGER privileges, and a user granted RESOURCE WITH ADMIN OPTION can grant RESOURCE, such a user can-not grant the individual privileges (e.g. CREATE TABLE), and thus RESOURCE WITH ADMIN OPTION is not usu-ally sufficient for running tests.</p> <p>Some test suites also create views or materialized views; to run these, the user also needs CREATE VIEW WITH ADMIN OPTION and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW WITH ADMIN OPTION privileges. In particular, this is needed for Django’s own test suite.</p> <p>All of these privileges are included in the DBA role, which is appropriate for use on a private developer’s database.</p> <p>The Oracle database backend uses the SYS.DBMS_LOB and SYS.DBMS_RANDOM packages, so your user will re-quire execute permissions on it. It’s normally accessible to all users by default, but in case it is not, you’ll need to grant permissions like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>GRANT EXECUTE ON</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SYS.DBMS_LOB</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TO user</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>GRANT EXECUTE ON</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">SYS.DBMS_RANDOM</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>TO user</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">;</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Connecting to the database</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To connect using the service name of your Oracle database, your settings.py file should look something like this:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.oracle"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"xe"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"USER"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"PASSWORD"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_password"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"HOST"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"PORT"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">""</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this case, you should leave both <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a> empty. However, if you don’t use a tnsnames.ora file or a</p> <p>similar naming method and want to connect using the SID (“xe” in this example), then fill in both <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a> like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"django.db.backends.oracle"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1429" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"xe"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"USER"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_user"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"PASSWORD"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"a_password"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"HOST"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"dbprod01ned.mycompany.com"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"PORT"</span><span
