style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"1540"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You should either supply both <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a> , or leave both as empty strings. Django will use a different connect descriptor depending on that choice.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Full DSN and Easy Connect</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>A Full DSN or Easy Connect string can be used in <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> if both <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>HOST</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PORT</i></a> are empty. This format is required when using RAC or pluggable databases without tnsnames.ora, for example.</p> <p>Example of an Easy Connect string:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"localhost:1521/orclpdb1"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Example of a full DSN string:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"NAME"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: (</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"(DESCRIPTION=(ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=localhost)(PORT=1521))"</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"(CONNECT_DATA=(SERVICE_NAME=orclpdb1)))"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Threaded option</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you plan to run Django in a multithreaded environment (e.g. Apache using the default MPM module on any modern operating system), then you must set the threaded option of your Oracle database configuration to True:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"threaded"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Failure to do this may result in crashes and other odd behavior.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1430"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>INSERT</b> <i>. . .</i> <b>RETURNING INTO</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, the Oracle backend uses a RETURNING INTO clause to efficiently retrieve the value of an AutoField when inserting new rows. This behavior may result in a DatabaseError in certain unusual setups, such as when inserting into a remote table, or into a view with an INSTEAD OF trigger. The RETURNING INTO clause can be disabled by setting the use_returning_into option of the database configuration to False:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">"OPTIONS"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"use_returning_into"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In this case, the Oracle backend will use a separate SELECT query to retrieve AutoField values.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Naming issues</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Oracle imposes a name length limit of 30 characters. To accommodate this, the backend truncates database identifiers to fit, replacing the final four characters of the truncated name with a repeatable MD5 hash value. Additionally, the backend turns database identifiers to all-uppercase.</p> <p>To prevent these transformations (this is usually required only when dealing with legacy databases or ac-cessing tables which belong to other users), use a quoted name as the value for db_table:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>LegacyModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">db_table</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'"name_left_in_lowercase"'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>ForeignModel</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(models</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>Meta</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">db_table</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'"OTHER_USER"."NAME_ONLY_SEEMS_OVER_30"'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Quoted names can also be used with Django’s other supported database backends; except for Oracle, however, the quotes have no effect.</p> <p>When running migrate, an ORA-06552 error may be encountered if certain Oracle keywords are used as the name of a model field or the value of a db_column option. Django quotes all identifiers used in queries to prevent most such problems, but this error can still occur when an Oracle datatype is used as a column name. In particular, take care to avoid using the names date, timestamp, number or float as a field name.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1431" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>NULL and empty strings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django generally prefers to use the empty string ('') rather than NULL, but Oracle treats both identically. To get around this, the Oracle backend ignores an explicit null option on fields that have the empty string as a possible value and generates DDL as if null=True. When fetching from the database, it is assumed that a NULL value in one of these fields really means the empty string, and the data is silently converted to reflect this assumption.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TextField limitations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Oracle backend stores TextFields as NCLOB columns. Oracle imposes some limitations on the usage of such LOB columns in general:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• LOB columns may not be used as primary keys.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• LOB columns may not be used in indexes.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• LOB columns may not be used in a SELECT DISTINCT list. This means that attempting to use the</p> <p style="text-align:center">QuerySet.distinct method on a model that includes TextField columns will result in an ORA-00932 error when run against Oracle. As a workaround, use the QuerySet.defer method in conjunction with distinct() to prevent TextField columns from being included in the SELECT DISTINCT list.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.7 Subclassing the built-in database backends</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django comes with built-in database backends. You may subclass an existing database backends to modify its behavior, features, or configuration.</p> <p>Consider, for example, that you need to change a single database feature. First, you have to create a new directory with a base module in it. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">mysite/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">...</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">mydbengine/</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">__init__.py</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">base.py</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The base.py module must contain a class named DatabaseWrapper that subclasses an existing engine from the django.db.backends module. Here’s an example of subclassing the PostgreSQL engine to change a fea-ture class allows_group_by_selected_pks_on_model:</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:center">Listing 10: mysite/mydbengine/base.py</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.db.backends.postgresql</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">base, features</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continues on next page)</span></p> <p id="page_1432"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-align:right"><span style="font-size:0.8em">(continued from previous page)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>DatabaseFeatures</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(features</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DatabaseFeatures):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>def</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>allows_group_by_selected_pks_on_model</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">self</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, model):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>return True</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>class</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>DatabaseWrapper</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(base</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">DatabaseWrapper):</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">features_class</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DatabaseFeatures</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Finally, you must specify a <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>DATABASE-ENGINE</i></a> in your settings.py file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">DATABASES</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">{</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"default"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">: {</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">"ENGINE"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"mydbengine"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span></p> <p style="margin-left:3em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># ...</i></span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">},</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">}</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can see the current list of database engines by looking in <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/db/backends">django/db/backends.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.7.8 Using a 3rd-party database backend</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In addition to the officially supported databases, there are backends provided by 3rd parties that allow you to use other databases with Django:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-cockroachdb/">CockroachDB</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-firebird/">Firebird</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-google-spanner/">Google Cloud Spanner</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/mssql-django/">Microsoft SQL Server</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-snowflake/">Snowflake</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-tidb/">TiDB</a></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <a href="https://pypi.org/project/django-yugabytedb/">YugabyteDB</a></p> <p>The Django versions and ORM features supported by these unofficial backends vary considerably. Queries regarding the specific capabilities of these unofficial backends, along with any support queries, should be directed to the support channels provided by each 3rd party project.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1433" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.8</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>django-admin</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>and</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>manage.py</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django-admin is Django’s command-line utility for administrative tasks. This document outlines all it can do.</p> <p>In addition, manage.py is automatically created in each Django project. It does the same thing as</p> <p>django-admin but also sets the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable so that it points to your project’s settings.py file.</p> <p>The django-admin script should be on your system path if you installed Django via pip. If it’s not in your path, ensure you have your virtual environment activated.</p> <p>Generally, when working on a single Django project, it’s easier to use manage.py than django-admin. If you</p> <p>need to switch between multiple Django settings files, use django-admin with <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> or</p> <p>the<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--settings</i></a> command line option.</p> <p>The command-line examples throughout this document use django-admin to be consistent, but any example can use manage.py or python -m django just as well.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.8.1 Usage</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin <command></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">manage.py <command></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m django <command></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>[</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">options</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>]</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>command should be one of the commands listed in this document. options, which is optional, should be zero or more of the options available for the given command.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Getting runtime help</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin help</b></p> <p>Run django-admin help to display usage information and a list of the commands provided by each appli-cation.</p> <p>Run django-admin help --commands to display a list of all available commands.</p> <p>Run django-admin help <command> to display a description of the given command and a list of its available options.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1434"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>App names</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Many commands take a list of “app names.” An “app name” is the basename of the package containing your</p> <p>models. For example, if your <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> contains the string 'mysite.blog', the app name is blog.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Determining the version</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin version</b></p> <p>Run django-admin version to display the current Django version.</p> <p>The output follows the schema described in <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/">PEP 440:</a></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1.4.dev17026</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1.4a1</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">1.4</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Displaying debug output</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Use<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--verbosity</i></a>, where it is supported, to specify the amount of notification and debug information that django-admin prints to the console.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.8.2 Available commands</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>check</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin check [app_label [app_label ...]]</b></p> <p>Uses the <a href="index.html#page_930">system check framework</a> to inspect the entire Django project for common problems.</p> <p>By default, all apps will be checked. You can check a subset of apps by providing a list of app labels as arguments:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin check auth admin myapp</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--tag</b> TAGS,<b>-t</b> TAGS</p> <p>The system check framework performs many different types of checks that are <a href="index.html#page_931">categorized with tags</a>. You can use these tags to restrict the checks performed to just those in a particular category. For example, to perform only models and compatibility checks, run:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin check --tag models --tag compatibility</span></p> <p id="page_1435" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to run checks requiring database access:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin check --database default --database other</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, these checks will not be run.</p> <p><b>--list-tags</b></p> <p>Lists all available tags.</p> <p><b>--deploy</b></p> <p>Activates some additional checks that are only relevant in a deployment setting.</p> <p>You can use this option in your local development environment, but since your local development settings module may not have many of your production settings, you will probably want to point the check command</p> <p>at a different settings module, either by setting the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable, or by passing the--settings option:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin check --deploy --settings=production_settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Or you could run it directly on a production or staging deployment to verify that the correct settings are in use (omitting--settings). You could even make it part of your integration test suite.</p> <p><b>--fail-level</b> {CRITICAL,ERROR,WARNING,INFO,DEBUG}</p> <p>Specifies the message level that will cause the command to exit with a non-zero status. Default is ERROR.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>compilemessages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin compilemessages</b></p> <p>Compiles .po files created by <a href="index.html#page_1442"><i>makemessages</i></a> to .mo files for use with the built-in gettext support. See <a href="index.html#page_649">Inter-</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_649">nationalization and localization.</a></p> <p><b>--locale</b> LOCALE,<b>-l</b> LOCALE</p> <p>Specifies the locale(s) to process. If not provided, all locales are processed.</p> <p><b>--exclude</b> EXCLUDE,<b>-x</b> EXCLUDE</p> <p>Specifies the locale(s) to exclude from processing. If not provided, no locales are excluded.</p> <p><b>--use-fuzzy</b>,<b>-f</b></p> <p>Includes <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/manual/html_node/Fuzzy-Entries.html">fuzzy translations</a> into compiled files.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p id="page_1436"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages --locale=pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages --locale=pt_BR --locale=fr -f</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages -l pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages -l pt_BR -l fr --use-fuzzy</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages --exclude=pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages --exclude=pt_BR --exclude=fr</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages -x pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages -x pt_BR -x fr</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--ignore</b> PATTERN,<b>-i</b> PATTERN</p> <p>Ignores directories matching the given <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/glob.html#module-glob">glob-style </a>pattern. Use multiple times to ignore more.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin compilemessages --ignore=cache --ignore=outdated/*/locale</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>createcachetable</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin createcachetable</b></p> <p>Creates the cache tables for use with the database cache backend using the information from your settings</p> <p>file. See <a href="index.html#page_599">Django’s cache framework</a> for more information.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database in which the cache table(s) will be created. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--dry-run</b></p> <p>Prints the SQL that would be run without actually running it, so you can customize it or use the migrations framework.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>dbshell</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin dbshell</b></p> <p>Runs the command-line client for the database engine specified in your <a href="index.html#page_1896"><i>ENGINE</i></a> setting, with the connection</p> <p>parameters specified in your <a href="index.html#page_1900"><i>USER</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>PASSWORD</i></a>, etc., settings.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• For PostgreSQL, this runs the psql command-line client.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• For MySQL, this runs the mysql command-line client.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• For SQLite, this runs the sqlite3 command-line client.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• For Oracle, this runs the sqlplus command-line client.</p> <p id="page_1437" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This command assumes the programs are on your PATH so that a call to the program name (psql, mysql, sqlite3, sqlplus) will find the program in the right place. There’s no way to specify the location of the program manually.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database onto which to open a shell. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--</b>ARGUMENTS</p> <p>Any arguments following a--divider will be passed on to the underlying command-line client. For example, with PostgreSQL you can use the psql command’s-c flag to execute a raw SQL query directly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin dbshell -- -c</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'select current_user'</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">current_user</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">--------------</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">postgres</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">(1 row)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On MySQL/MariaDB, you can do this with the mysql command’s-e flag:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin dbshell -- -e</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"select user()"</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">+----------------------+</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">| user()</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">|</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">+----------------------+</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">| djangonaut@localhost |</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">+----------------------+</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Be aware that not all options set in the <a href="index.html#page_1898"><i>OPTIONS</i></a> part of your database configuration in <a href="index.html#page_1895"><i>DATABASES</i></a> are passed to the command-line client, e.g. 'isolation_level'.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>diffsettings</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin diffsettings</b></p> <p>Displays differences between the current settings file and Django’s default settings (or another settings file</p> <p>specified by<a href="index.html#page_1437"><i>--default</i>).</a></p> <p>Settings that don’t appear in the defaults are followed by "###". For example, the default settings don’t</p> <p>define <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>ROOT_URLCONF</i></a> , so <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>ROOT_URLCONF</i></a> is followed by "###" in the output of diffsettings.</p> <p><b>--all</b></p> <p>Displays all settings, even if they have Django’s default value. Such settings are prefixed by "###".</p> <p id="page_1438"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--default</b> MODULE</p> <p>The settings module to compare the current settings against. Leave empty to compare against Django’s default settings.</p> <p><b>--output</b> {hash,unified}</p> <p>Specifies the output format. Available values are hash and unified. hash is the default mode that displays the output that’s described above. unified displays the output similar to diff -u. Default settings are prefixed with a minus sign, followed by the changed setting prefixed with a plus sign.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>dumpdata</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin dumpdata [app_label[.ModelName] [app_label[.ModelName] ...]]</b></p> <p>Outputs to standard output all data in the database associated with the named application(s).</p> <p>If no application name is provided, all installed applications will be dumped.</p> <p>The output of dumpdata can be used as input for <a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>loaddata</i>.</a></p> <p>When result of dumpdata is saved as a file, it can serve as a <a href="index.html#page_248">fixture</a> for <a href="index.html#page_497">tests</a> or as an <a href="index.html#page_773">initial data</a>.</p> <p>Note that dumpdata uses the default manager on the model for selecting the records to dump. If you’re using</p> <p>a <a href="index.html#page_192">custom manager</a> as the default manager and it filters some of the available records, not all of the objects will be dumped.</p> <p><b>--all</b>,<b>-a</b></p> <p>Uses Django’s base manager, dumping records which might otherwise be filtered or modified by a custom manager.</p> <p><b>--format</b> FORMAT</p> <p>Specifies the serialization format of the output. Defaults to JSON. Supported formats are listed in <a href="index.html#page_734">Serialization</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_734">formats.</a></p> <p><b>--indent</b> INDENT</p> <p>Specifies the number of indentation spaces to use in the output. Defaults to None which displays all data on single line.</p> <p><b>--exclude</b> EXCLUDE,<b>-e</b> EXCLUDE</p> <p>Prevents specific applications or models (specified in the form of app_label.ModelName) from being dumped. If you specify a model name, then only that model will be excluded, rather than the entire application. You can also mix application names and model names.</p> <p>If you want to exclude multiple applications, pass--exclude more than once:</p> <p id="page_1439" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin dumpdata --exclude=auth --exclude=contenttypes</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database from which data will be dumped. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--natural-foreign</b></p> <p>Uses the natural_key() model method to serialize any foreign key and many-to-many relationship to ob-jects of the type that defines the method. If you’re dumping contrib.auth Permission objects or contrib.</p> <p>contenttypes ContentType objects, you should probably use this flag. See the <a href="index.html#page_740">natural keys</a> documentation for more details on this and the next option.</p> <p><b>--natural-primary</b></p> <p>Omits the primary key in the serialized data of this object since it can be calculated during deserialization.</p> <p><b>--pks</b> PRIMARY_KEYS</p> <p>Outputs only the objects specified by a comma separated list of primary keys. This is only available when dumping one model. By default, all the records of the model are output.</p> <p><b>--output</b> OUTPUT,<b>-o</b> OUTPUT</p> <p>Specifies a file to write the serialized data to. By default, the data goes to standard output.</p> <p>When this option is set and--verbosity is greater than 0 (the default), a progress bar is shown in the termi-nal.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Fixtures compression</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The output file can be compressed with one of the bz2, gz, lzma, or xz formats by ending the filename with the corresponding extension. For example, to output the data as a compressed JSON file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin dumpdata -o mydata.json.gz</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>flush</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin flush</b></p> <p>Removes all data from the database and re-executes any post-synchronization handlers. The table of which migrations have been applied is not cleared.</p> <p>If you would rather start from an empty database and rerun all migrations, you should drop and recreate</p> <p>the database and then run <a href="index.html#page_1446"><i>migrate</i></a> instead.</p> <p id="page_1440"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to flush. Defaults to default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>inspectdb</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin inspectdb [table [table ...]]</b></p> <p>Introspects the database tables in the database pointed-to by the <a href="index.html#page_1897"><i>NAME</i></a> setting and outputs a Django model module (a models.py file) to standard output.</p> <p>You may choose what tables or views to inspect by passing their names as arguments. If no arguments are</p> <p>provided, models are created for views only if the<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--include-views</i></a> option is used. Models for partition</p> <p>tables are created on PostgreSQL if the<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--include-partitions</i></a> option is used.</p> <p>Use this if you have a legacy database with which you’d like to use Django. The script will inspect the database and create a model for each table within it.</p> <p>As you might expect, the created models will have an attribute for every field in the table. Note that inspectdb has a few special cases in its field-name output:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If inspectdb cannot map a column’s type to a model field type, it’ll use TextField and will insert the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Python comment 'This field type is a guess.' next to the field in the generated model. The rec-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">ognized fields may depend on apps listed in <a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a>. For example, <a href="index.html#page_1296"><i>django.contrib.postgres</i></a> adds recognition for several PostgreSQL-specific field types.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• If the database column name is a Python reserved word (such as 'pass', 'class' or 'for'), inspectdb</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">will append '_field' to the attribute name. For example, if a table has a column 'for', the gener-ated model will have a field 'for_field', with the db_column attribute set to 'for'. inspectdb will insert the Python comment 'Field renamed because it was a Python reserved word.' next to the field.</p> <p>This feature is meant as a shortcut, not as definitive model generation. After you run it, you’ll want to look over the generated models yourself to make customizations. In particular, you’ll need to rearrange models’ order, so that models that refer to other models are ordered properly.</p> <p>Django doesn’t create database defaults when a <a href="index.html#page_1623"><i>default</i></a> is specified on a model field. Similarly, database defaults aren’t translated to model field defaults or detected in any fashion by inspectdb.</p> <p>By default, inspectdb creates unmanaged models. That is, managed = False in the model’s Meta class tells Django not to manage each table’s creation, modification, and deletion. If you do want to allow Django to</p> <p>manage the table’s lifecycle, you’ll need to change the <a href="index.html#page_1681"><i>managed</i></a> option to True (or remove it because True is its default value).</p> <p id="page_1441" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Database-specific notes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Oracle</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Models are created for materialized views if<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--include-views</i></a> is used.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PostgreSQL</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Models are created for foreign tables.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Models are created for materialized views if<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--include-views</i></a> is used.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Models are created for partition tables if<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--include-partitions</i></a> is used.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to introspect. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--include-partitions</b></p> <p>If this option is provided, models are also created for partitions.</p> <p>Only support for PostgreSQL is implemented.</p> <p><b>--include-views</b></p> <p>If this option is provided, models are also created for database views.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>loaddata</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin loaddata fixture [fixture ...]</b></p> <p>Searches for and loads the contents of the named <a href="index.html#page_248">fixture</a> into the database.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database into which the data will be loaded. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--ignorenonexistent</b>,<b>-i</b></p> <p>Ignores fields and models that may have been removed since the fixture was originally generated.</p> <p><b>--app</b> APP_LABEL</p> <p>Specifies a single app to look for fixtures in rather than looking in all apps.</p> <p><b>--format</b> FORMAT</p> <p>Specifies the <a href="index.html#page_734">serialization format</a> (e.g., json or xml) for fixtures <a href="index.html#page_1442">read from stdin</a>.</p> <p id="page_1442"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--exclude</b> EXCLUDE,<b>-e</b> EXCLUDE</p> <p>Excludes loading the fixtures from the given applications and/or models (in the form of app_label or app_label.ModelName). Use the option multiple times to exclude more than one app or model.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Loading fixtures from stdin</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can use a dash as the fixture name to load input from sys.stdin. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin loaddata --format=json -</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When reading from stdin, the<a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>--format</i></a> option is required to specify the <a href="index.html#page_734">serialization format</a> of the input (e.g., json or xml).</p> <p>Loading from stdin is useful with standard input and output redirections. For example:</p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin dumpdata --format=json --database=test app_label.ModelName | django-admin loaddata --</span><span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">format=json --database=prod -</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata</i></a> command can be used to generate input for loaddata.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>For more detail about fixtures see the <a href="index.html#page_248">Fixtures</a> topic.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>makemessages</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin makemessages</b></p> <p>Runs over the entire source tree of the current directory and pulls out all strings marked for translation. It creates (or updates) a message file in the conf/locale (in the Django tree) or locale (for project and application)</p> <p>directory. After making changes to the messages files you need to compile them with <a href="index.html#page_1435"><i>compilemessages</i></a> for</p> <p>use with the builtin gettext support. See the <a href="index.html#page_677">i18n documentation</a> for details.</p> <p>This command doesn’t require configured settings. However, when settings aren’t configured, the command</p> <p>can’t ignore the <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1945"><i>STATIC_ROOT</i></a> directories or include <a href="index.html#page_1921"><i>LOCALE_PATHS</i></a>.</p> <p><b>--all</b>,<b>-a</b></p> <p>Updates the message files for all available languages.</p> <p><b>--extension</b> EXTENSIONS,<b>-e</b> EXTENSIONS</p> <p>Specifies a list of file extensions to examine (default: html, txt, py or js if<a href="index.html#page_1443"><i>--domain</i></a> is djangojs).</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p id="page_1443" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=de --extension xhtml</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Separate multiple extensions with commas or use-e or--extension multiple times:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=de --extension=html,txt --extension xml</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--locale</b> LOCALE,<b>-l</b> LOCALE</p> <p>Specifies the locale(s) to process.</p> <p><b>--exclude</b> EXCLUDE,<b>-x</b> EXCLUDE</p> <p>Specifies the locale(s) to exclude from processing. If not provided, no locales are excluded.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=pt_BR --locale=fr</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages -l pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages -l pt_BR -l fr</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --exclude=pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --exclude=pt_BR --exclude=fr</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages -x pt_BR</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages -x pt_BR -x fr</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--domain</b> DOMAIN,<b>-d</b> DOMAIN</p> <p>Specifies the domain of the messages files. Supported options are:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django for all *.py, *.html and *.txt files (default)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• djangojs for *.js files</p> <p><b>--symlinks</b>,<b>-s</b></p> <p>Follows symlinks to directories when looking for new translation strings.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=de --symlinks</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--ignore</b> PATTERN,<b>-i</b> PATTERN</p> <p>Ignores files or directories matching the given <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/glob.html#module-glob">glob</a>-style pattern. Use multiple times to ignore more.</p> <p>These patterns are used by default: 'CVS', '.*', '*~', '*.pyc'.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p id="page_1444"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin makemessages --locale=en_US --ignore=apps/* --ignore=secret/*.html</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--no-default-ignore</b></p> <p>Disables the default values of--ignore.</p> <p><b>--no-wrap</b></p> <p>Disables breaking long message lines into several lines in language files.</p> <p><b>--no-location</b></p> <p>Suppresses writing ‘#: filename:line’ comment lines in language files. Using this option makes it harder for technically skilled translators to understand each message’s context.</p> <p><b>--add-location</b> [{full,file,never}]</p> <p>Controls #: filename:line comment lines in language files. If the option is:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• full (the default if not given): the lines include both file name and line number.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• file: the line number is omitted.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• never: the lines are suppressed (same as<a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>--no-location</i></a>).</p> <p>Requires gettext 0.19 or newer.</p> <p><b>--no-obsolete</b></p> <p>Removes obsolete message strings from the .po files.</p> <p><b>--keep-pot</b></p> <p>Prevents deleting the temporary .pot files generated before creating the .po file. This is useful for debugging errors which may prevent the final language files from being created.</p> <p>See also:</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_682">Customizing the makemessages command</a> for instructions on how to customize the keywords that</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1442"><i>makemessages</i></a> passes to xgettext.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>makemigrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin makemigrations [app_label [app_label ...]]</b></p> <p>Creates new migrations based on the changes detected to your models. Migrations, their relationship with</p> <p>apps and more are covered in depth in <a href="index.html#page_446">the migrations documentation</a>.</p> <p>Providing one or more app names as arguments will limit the migrations created to the app(s) specified and any dependencies needed (the table at the other end of a ForeignKey, for example).</p> <p id="page_1445" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>To add migrations to an app that doesn’t have a migrations directory, run makemigrations with the app’s app_label.</p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts. If a suppressed prompt cannot be resolved automatically, the command will exit with error code 3.</p> <p><b>--empty</b></p> <p>Outputs an empty migration for the specified apps, for manual editing. This is for advanced users and should not be used unless you are familiar with the migration format, migration operations, and the dependencies between your migrations.</p> <p><b>--dry-run</b></p> <p>Shows what migrations would be made without actually writing any migrations files to disk. Using this option along with--verbosity 3 will also show the complete migrations files that would be written.</p> <p><b>--merge</b></p> <p>Enables fixing of migration conflicts.</p> <p><b>--name</b> NAME,<b>-n</b> NAME</p> <p>Allows naming the generated migration(s) instead of using a generated name. The name must be a valid</p> <p>Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#identifiers">identifier</a>.</p> <p><b>--no-header</b></p> <p>Generate migration files without Django version and timestamp header.</p> <p><b>--check</b></p> <p>Makes makemigrations exit with a non-zero status when model changes without migrations are detected. Implies--dry-run.</p> <p><b>--scriptable</b></p> <p>Diverts log output and input prompts to stderr, writing only paths of generated migration files to stdout.</p> <p><b>--update</b></p> <p>Merges model changes into the latest migration and optimize the resulting operations.</p> <p>The updated migration will have a generated name. In order to preserve the previous name, set it using--name.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1446"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>migrate</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin migrate [app_label] [migration_name]</b></p> <p>Synchronizes the database state with the current set of models and migrations. Migrations, their relationship</p> <p>with apps and more are covered in depth in <a href="index.html#page_446">the migrations documentation.</a></p> <p>The behavior of this command changes depending on the arguments provided:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• No arguments: All apps have all of their migrations run.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <app_label>: The specified app has its migrations run, up to the most recent migration. This may</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">involve running other apps’ migrations too, due to dependencies.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• <app_label> <migrationname>: Brings the database schema to a state where the named migration is</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">applied, but no later migrations in the same app are applied. This may involve unapplying migrations if you have previously migrated past the named migration. You can use a prefix of the migration name, e.g. 0001, as long as it’s unique for the given app name. Use the name zero to migrate all the way back i.e. to revert all applied migrations for an app.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: When unapplying migrations, all dependent migrations will also be unapplied, regardless of</p> <p style="margin-left:1em"><app_label>. You can use--plan to check which migrations will be unapplied.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to migrate. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--fake</b></p> <p>Marks the migrations up to the target one (following the rules above) as applied, but without actually running the SQL to change your database schema.</p> <p>This is intended for advanced users to manipulate the current migration state directly if they’re manually applying changes; be warned that using--fake runs the risk of putting the migration state table into a state where manual recovery will be needed to make migrations run correctly.</p> <p><b>--fake-initial</b></p> <p>Allows Django to skip an app’s initial migration if all database tables with the names of all models created by</p> <p>all <a href="index.html#page_1603"><i>CreateModel</i></a> operations in that migration already exist. This option is intended for use when first running migrations against a database that preexisted the use of migrations. This option does not, however, check for matching database schema beyond matching table names and so is only safe to use if you are confident that your existing schema matches what is recorded in your initial migration.</p> <p><b>--plan</b></p> <p>Shows the migration operations that will be performed for the given migrate command.</p> <p id="page_1447" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--run-syncdb</b></p> <p>Allows creating tables for apps without migrations. While this isn’t recommended, the migrations framework is sometimes too slow on large projects with hundreds of models.</p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts. An example prompt is asking about removing stale content types.</p> <p><b>--check</b></p> <p>Makes migrate exit with a non-zero status when unapplied migrations are detected.</p> <p><b>--prune</b></p> <p>Deletes nonexistent migrations from the django_migrations table. This is useful when migration files re-</p> <p>placed by a squashed migration have been removed. See <a href="index.html#page_459">Squashing migrations</a> for more details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>optimizemigration</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin optimizemigration app_label migration_name</b></p> <p>Optimizes the operations for the named migration and overrides the existing file. If the migration contains functions that must be manually copied, the command creates a new migration file suffixed with _optimized that is meant to replace the named migration.</p> <p><b>--check</b></p> <p>Makes optimizemigration exit with a non-zero status when a migration can be optimized.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>runserver</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin runserver [addrport]</b></p> <p>Starts a lightweight development web server on the local machine. By default, the server runs on port 8000 on the IP address 127.0.0.1. You can pass in an IP address and port number explicitly.</p> <p>If you run this script as a user with normal privileges (recommended), you might not have access to start a port on a low port number. Low port numbers are reserved for the superuser (root).</p> <p>This server uses the WSGI application object specified by the <a href="index.html#page_1937"><i>WSGI_APPLICATION</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: DO NOT USE THIS SERVER IN A PRODUCTION SETTING.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">This lightweight development server has not gone through security audits or performance tests, hence</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">is unsuitable for production. Making this server able to handle a production environment is outside the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">scope of Django.</p> <p id="page_1448"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The development server automatically reloads Python code for each request, as needed. You don’t need to restart the server for code changes to take effect. However, some actions like adding files don’t trigger a restart, so you’ll have to restart the server in these cases.</p> <p>If you’re using Linux or MacOS and install both <a href="https://pypi.org/project/pywatchman/">pywatchman</a> and the <a href="https://facebook.github.io/watchman/">Watchman</a> service, kernel signals will be used to autoreload the server (rather than polling file modification timestamps each second). This offers better performance on large projects, reduced response time after code changes, more robust change detection, and a reduction in power usage. Django supports pywatchman 1.2.0 and higher.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Large directories with many files may cause performance issues</p> <p>When using Watchman with a project that includes large non-Python directories like node_modules, it’s ad-</p> <p>visable to ignore this directory for optimal performance. See the <a href="https://facebook.github.io/watchman/docs/config#ignore_dirs">watchman documentation</a> for information on how to do this.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Watchman timeout</p> <p><b>DJANGO_WATCHMAN_TIMEOUT</b></p> <p>The default timeout of Watchman client is 5 seconds. <span style="float:right">You can change it by setting the</span></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1448"><i>DJANGO_WATCHMAN_TIMEOUT</i></a> environment variable.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>When you start the server, and each time you change Python code while the server is running, the system</p> <p>check framework will check your entire Django project for some common errors (see the <a href="index.html#page_1434"><i>check</i></a> command). If any errors are found, they will be printed to standard output. You can use the--skip-checks option to skip running system checks.</p> <p>You can run as many concurrent servers as you want, as long as they’re on separate ports by executing django-admin runserver more than once.</p> <p>Note that the default IP address, 127.0.0.1, is not accessible from other machines on your network. To make your development server viewable to other machines on the network, use its own IP address (e.g. 192. 168.2.1), 0 (shortcut for 0.0.0.0), 0.0.0.0, or :: (with IPv6 enabled).</p> <p>You can provide an IPv6 address surrounded by brackets (e.g. [200a::1]:8000). This will automatically enable IPv6 support.</p> <p>A hostname containing ASCII-only characters can also be used.</p> <p>If the <a href="index.html#page_1369">staticfiles</a> contrib app is enabled (default in new projects) the <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command will be overridden</p> <p>with its own <a href="index.html#page_1372">runserver</a> command.</p> <p>Logging of each request and response of the server is sent to the <a href="index.html#page_1585">django.server</a> logger.</p> <p><b>--noreload</b></p> <p id="page_1449" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Disables the auto-reloader. This means any Python code changes you make while the server is running will not take effect if the particular Python modules have already been loaded into memory.</p> <p><b>--nothreading</b></p> <p>Disables use of threading in the development server. The server is multithreaded by default.</p> <p><b>--ipv6</b>,<b>-6</b></p> <p>Uses IPv6 for the development server. This changes the default IP address from 127.0.0.1 to ::1.</p> <p><b>HIDE_PRODUCTION_WARNING</b></p> <p>By default, a warning is printed to the console that runserver is not suitable for production:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production setting. Use a production</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">␣</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">WSGI or ASGI server instead.</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">For more information on production servers see: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/|version|/howto/</span> <span variable to "true" to hide this warning.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Examples of using different ports and addresses</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Port 8000 on IP runserver 7000</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Port 7000 on IP address 1.2.3.4:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin runserver 1.2.3.4:7000</span></p> <p <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving static files with the development server</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>By default, the development server doesn’t serve any static files for your site (such as CSS files, images, things</p> <p>under <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> and so forth). If you want to configure Django to serve static media, read <a href="index.html#page_843">How to manage</a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_843">static files (e.g. images, JavaScript, CSS).</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Serving with ASGI in development</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django’s runserver command provides a WSGI server. In order to run under ASGI you will need to use an</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_875">ASGI server. </a>The Django Daphne project provides <a href="index.html#page_876">Integration with runserver</a> that you can use.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sendtestemail</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin sendtestemail [email [email ...]]</b></p> <p>Sends a test email (to confirm email sending through Django is working) to the recipient(s) specified. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin sendtestemail foo@example.com bar@example.com</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>There are a couple of options, and you may use any combination of them together:</p> <p><b>--managers</b></p> <p>Mails the email addresses specified in <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MANAGERS</i></a> using <a href="index.html#page_638"><i>mail_managers()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_638">.</a></p> <p><b>--admins</b></p> <p>Mails the email addresses specified in <a href="index.html#page_1888"><i>ADMINS</i></a> using <a href="index.html#page_637"><i>mail_admins()</i></a><a href="index.html#page_637">.</a></p> <p id="page_1451" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>shell</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin shell</b></p> <p>Starts the Python interactive interpreter.</p> <p><b>--interface</b> {ipython,bpython,python},<b>-i</b> {ipython,bpython,python}</p> <p>Specifies the shell to use. By default, Django will use <a href="https://ipython.org/">IPython</a> or <a href="https://bpython-interpreter.org/">bpython</a> if either is installed. If both are installed, specify which one you want like so:</p> <p>IPython:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin shell -i ipython</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>bpython:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin shell -i bpython</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you have a “rich” shell installed but want to force use of the “plain” Python interpreter, use python as the interface name, like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin shell -i python</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--no-startup</b></p> <p>Disables reading the startup script for the “plain” Python interpreter. By default, the script pointed to by</p> <p>the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONSTARTUP">PYTHONSTARTUP</a> environment variable or the ~/.pythonrc.py script is read.</p> <p><b>--command</b> COMMAND,<b>-c</b> COMMAND</p> <p>Lets you pass a command as a string to execute it as Django, like so:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin shell --command="import django; print(django.__version__)"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also pass code in on standard input to execute it. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin shell <<EOF</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">> import django</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">> print(django.__version__)</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">> EOF</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On Windows, the REPL is output due to implementation limits of <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/select.html#select.select">select.select()</a> on that platform.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1452"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>showmigrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin showmigrations [app_label [app_label ...]]</b></p> <p>Shows all migrations in a project. You can choose from one of two formats:</p> <p><b>--list</b>,<b>-l</b></p> <p>Lists all of the apps Django knows about, the migrations available for each app, and whether or not each migration is applied (marked by an [X] next to the migration name). For a--verbosity of 2 and above, the applied datetimes are also shown.</p> <p>Apps without migrations are also listed, but have (no migrations) printed under them.</p> <p>This is the default output format.</p> <p><b>--plan</b>,<b>-p</b></p> <p>Shows the migration plan Django will follow to apply migrations. Like--list, applied migrations are marked by an [X]. For a--verbosity of 2 and above, all dependencies of a migration will also be shown.</p> <p>app_labels arguments limit the output, however, dependencies of provided apps may also be included.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to examine. Defaults to default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sqlflush</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin sqlflush</b></p> <p>Prints the SQL statements that would be executed for the <a href="index.html#page_1439"><i>flush</i></a> command.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database for which to print the SQL. Defaults to default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sqlmigrate</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin sqlmigrate app_label migration_name</b></p> <p>Prints the SQL for the named migration. This requires an active database connection, which it will use to resolve constraint names; this means you must generate the SQL against a copy of the database you wish to later apply it on.</p> <p>Note that sqlmigrate doesn’t colorize its output.</p> <p><b>--backwards</b></p> <p>Generates the SQL for unapplying the migration. By default, the SQL created is for running the migration in the forwards direction.</p> <p id="page_1453" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database for which to generate the SQL. Defaults to default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>sqlsequencereset</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin sqlsequencereset app_label [app_label ...]</b></p> <p>Prints the SQL statements for resetting sequences for the given app name(s).</p> <p>Sequences are indexes used by some database engines to track the next available number for automatically incremented fields.</p> <p>Use this command to generate SQL which will fix cases where a sequence is out of sync with its automatically incremented field data.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database for which to print the SQL. Defaults to default.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>squashmigrations</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin squashmigrations app_label [start_migration_name] migration_name</b></p> <p>Squashes the migrations for app_label up to and including migration_name down into fewer migrations, if possible. The resulting squashed migrations can live alongside the unsquashed ones safely. For more</p> <p>information, please read <a href="index.html#page_459">Squashing migrations.</a></p> <p>When start_migration_name is given, Django will only include migrations starting from and including</p> <p>this migration. This helps to mitigate the squashing limitation of <a href="index.html#page_1609"><i>RunPython</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>django.db.migrations.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1607"><i>operations.RunSQL</i></a> migration operations.</p> <p><b>--no-optimize</b></p> <p>Disables the optimizer when generating a squashed migration. By default, Django will try to optimize the operations in your migrations to reduce the size of the resulting file. Use this option if this process is failing or creating incorrect migrations, though please also file a Django bug report about the behavior, as optimization is meant to be safe.</p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts.</p> <p><b>--squashed-name</b> SQUASHED_NAME</p> <p>Sets the name of the squashed migration. When omitted, the name is based on the first and last migration, with _squashed_ in between.</p> <p id="page_1454"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--no-header</b></p> <p>Generate squashed migration file without Django version and timestamp header.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>startapp</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin startapp name [directory]</b></p> <p>Creates a Django app directory structure for the given app name in the current directory or the given desti-nation.</p> <p>By default, <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/conf/app_template">the new directory</a> contains a models.py file and other app template files. If only the app name is given, the app directory will be created in the current working directory.</p> <p>If the optional destination is provided, Django will use that existing directory rather than creating a new one. You can use ‘.’ to denote the current working directory.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin startapp myapp /Users/jezdez/Code/myapp</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--template</b> TEMPLATE</p> <p>Provides the path to a directory with a custom app template file, or a path to an uncompressed archive (.tar) or a compressed archive (.tar.gz, .tar.bz2, .tar.xz, .tar.lzma, .tgz, .tbz2, .txz, .tlz, .zip) containing the app template files.</p> <p>For example, this would look for an app template in the given directory when creating the myapp app:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin startapp --template=/Users/jezdez/Code/my_app_template myapp</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django will also accept URLs (http, https, ftp) to compressed archives with the app template files, down-loading and extracting them on the fly.</p> <p>For example, taking advantage of GitHub’s feature to expose repositories as zip files, you can use a URL like:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin startapp --template=https://github.com/githubuser/django-app-template/archive/main.</span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>,</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.47em"><i>→</i></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">zip myapp</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--extension</b> EXTENSIONS,<b>-e</b> EXTENSIONS</p> <p>Specifies which file extensions in the app template should be rendered with the template engine. Defaults to py.</p> <p><b>--name</b> FILES,<b>-n</b> FILES</p> <p>Specifies which files in the app template (in addition to those matching--extension) should be rendered with the template engine. Defaults to an empty list.</p> <p id="page_1455" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--exclude</b> DIRECTORIES,<b>-x</b> DIRECTORIES</p> <p>Specifies which directories in the app template should be excluded, in addition to .git and __pycache__. If this option is not provided, directories named __pycache__ or starting with . will be excluded.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_2034"><i>template context</i></a> used for all matching files is:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Any option passed to the startapp command (among the command’s supported options)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• app_name – the app name as passed to the command</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• app_directory – the full path of the newly created app</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• camel_case_app_name – the app name in camel case format</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• docs_version – the version of the documentation: 'dev' or '1.x'</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django_version – the version of Django, e.g. '2.0.3'</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: When the app template files are rendered with the Django template engine (by default all</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">*.py files), Django will also replace all stray template variables contained. For example, if one of the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Python files contains a docstring explaining a particular feature related to template rendering, it might</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">result in an incorrect example.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">To work around this problem, you can use the <a href="index.html#page_2001"><i>templatetag</i></a> template tag to “escape” the various parts</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">of the template syntax.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">In addition, to allow Python template files that contain Django template language syntax while also</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">preventing packaging systems from trying to byte-compile invalid *.py files, template files ending with</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">.py-tpl will be renamed to .py.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: The contents of custom app (or project) templates should always be audited before use:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Such templates define code that will become part of your project, and this means that such code will</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">be trusted as much as any app you install, or code you write yourself. Further, even rendering the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">templates is, effectively, executing code that was provided as input to the management command. The</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Django template language may provide wide access into the system, so make sure any custom template</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">you use is worthy of your trust.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1456"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>startproject</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin startproject name [directory]</b></p> <p>Creates a Django project directory structure for the given project name in the current directory or the given destination.</p> <p>By default, <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/conf/project_template">the new directory</a> contains manage.py and a project package (containing a settings.py and other files).</p> <p>If only the project name is given, both the project directory and project package will be named <projectname> and the project directory will be created in the current working directory.</p> <p>If the optional destination is provided, Django will use that existing directory as the project directory, and create manage.py and the project package within it. Use ‘.’ to denote the current working directory.</p> <p>For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin startproject myproject /Users/jezdez/Code/myproject_repo</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--template</b> TEMPLATE</p> <p>Specifies a directory, file path, or URL of a custom project template. See the <a href="index.html#page_1454"><i>startapp --template</i></a> docu-mentation for examples and usage.</p> <p><b>--extension</b> EXTENSIONS,<b>-e</b> EXTENSIONS</p> <p>Specifies which file extensions in the project template should be rendered with the template engine. Defaults to py.</p> <p><b>--name</b> FILES,<b>-n</b> FILES</p> <p>Specifies which files in the project template (in addition to those matching--extension) should be rendered with the template engine. Defaults to an empty list.</p> <p><b>--exclude</b> DIRECTORIES,<b>-x</b> DIRECTORIES</p> <p>Specifies which directories in the project template should be excluded, in addition to .git and __pycache__. If this option is not provided, directories named __pycache__ or starting with . will be excluded.</p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_2034"><i>template context</i></a> used is:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Any option passed to the startproject command (among the command’s supported options)</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• project_name – the project name as passed to the command</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• project_directory – the full path of the newly created project</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• secret_key – a random key for the <a href="index.html#page_1925"><i>SECRET_KEY</i></a> setting</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• docs_version – the version of the documentation: 'dev' or '1.x'</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• django_version – the version of Django, e.g. '2.0.3'</p> <p id="page_1457" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Please also see the <a href="index.html#page_1455">rendering warning</a> and <a href="index.html#page_1455">trusted code warning</a> as mentioned for <a href="index.html#page_1454"><i>startapp</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>test</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin test [test_label [test_label ...]]</b></p> <p>Runs tests for all installed apps. See <a href="index.html#page_469">Testing in Django</a> for more information.</p> <p><b>--failfast</b></p> <p>Stops running tests and reports the failure immediately after a test fails.</p> <p><b>--testrunner</b> TESTRUNNER</p> <p>Controls the test runner class that is used to execute tests. This value overrides the value provided by the</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1934"><i>TEST_RUNNER</i></a> setting.</p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts. A typical prompt is a warning about deleting an existing test database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Test runner options</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The test command receives options on behalf of the specified<a href="index.html#page_1457"><i>--testrunner</i></a>. These are the options of the</p> <p>default test runner: <a href="index.html#page_525"><i>DiscoverRunner</i></a>.</p> <p><b>--keepdb</b></p> <p>Preserves the test database between test runs. This has the advantage of skipping both the create and destroy actions which can greatly decrease the time to run tests, especially those in a large test suite. If the test database does not exist, it will be created on the first run and then preserved for each subsequent run. Unless</p> <p>the <a href="index.html#page_1901"><i>MIGRATE</i></a> test setting is False, any unapplied migrations will also be applied to the test database before running the test suite.</p> <p><b>--shuffle</b> [SEED]</p> <p>Randomizes the order of tests before running them. This can help detect tests that aren’t properly isolated. The test order generated by this option is a deterministic function of the integer seed given. When no seed is passed, a seed is chosen randomly and printed to the console. To repeat a particular test order, pass a seed.</p> <p>The test orders generated by this option preserve Django’s <a href="index.html#page_473">guarantees on test order. </a>They also keep tests grouped by test case class.</p> <p>The shuffled orderings also have a special consistency property useful when narrowing down isolation issues. Namely, for a given seed and when running a subset of tests, the new order will be the original shuffling restricted to the smaller set. Similarly, when adding tests while keeping the seed the same, the order of the original tests will be the same in the new order.</p> <p id="page_1458"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--reverse</b>,<b>-r</b></p> <p>Sorts test cases in the opposite execution order. This may help in debugging the side effects of tests that aren’t</p> <p>properly isolated. <a href="index.html#page_473">Grouping by test class</a> is preserved when using this option. This can be used in conjunction with--shuffle to reverse the order for a particular seed.</p> <p><b>--debug-mode</b></p> <p>Sets the <a href="index.html#page_1907"><i>DEBUG</i></a> setting to True prior to running tests. This may help troubleshoot test failures.</p> <p><b>--debug-sql</b>,<b>-d</b></p> <p>Enables <a href="index.html#page_1586">SQL logging</a> for failing tests. If--verbosity is 2, then queries in passing tests are also output.</p> <p><b>--parallel</b> [N]</p> <p><b>DJANGO_TEST_PROCESSES</b></p> <p>Runs tests in separate parallel processes. Since modern processors have multiple cores, this allows running tests significantly faster.</p> <p>Using--parallel without a value, or with the value auto, runs one test process per core according to</p> <p><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html#multiprocessing.cpu_count">multiprocessing.cpu_count(). </a>You can override this by passing the desired number of processes, e.g.</p> <p>--parallel 4, or by setting the <a href="index.html#page_1458"><i>DJANGO_TEST_PROCESSES</i></a> environment variable.</p> <p>Django distributes test cases — <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#unittest.TestCase">unittest.TestCase</a> subclasses — to subprocesses. If there are fewer test case classes than configured processes, Django will reduce the number of processes accordingly.</p> <p>Each process gets its own database. You must ensure that different test case classes don’t access the same resources. For instance, test case classes that touch the filesystem should create a temporary directory for their own use.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: If you have test classes that cannot be run in parallel, you can use SerializeMixin to run them</p> <p>sequentially. See <a href="index.html#page_521">Enforce running test classes sequentially.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This option requires the third-party tblib package to display tracebacks correctly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">$</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">python -m pip install tblib</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This feature isn’t available on Windows. It doesn’t work with the Oracle database backend either.</p> <p>If you want to use <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pdb.html#module-pdb">pdb</a> while debugging tests, you must disable parallel execution (--parallel=1). You’ll see something like bdb.BdbQuit if you don’t.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">Warning: When test parallelization is enabled and a test fails, Django may be unable to display the</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">exception traceback. This can make debugging difficult. If you encounter this problem, run the affected</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">test without parallelization to see the traceback of the failure.</p> <p id="page_1459" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:1em">This is a known limitation. It arises from the need to serialize objects in order to exchange them between</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">processes.
