See <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html#pickle-picklable">What can be pickled and unpickled?</a> for details.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--tag</b> TAGS</p> <p>Runs only tests <a href="index.html#page_510">marked with the specified tags. </a>May be specified multiple times and combined with <a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>test</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>--exclude-tag</i></a>.</p> <p>Tests that fail to load are always considered matching.</p> <p><b>--exclude-tag</b> EXCLUDE_TAGS</p> <p>Excludes tests <a href="index.html#page_510">marked with the specified tags</a>. May be specified multiple times and combined with <a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>test</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1459"><i>--tag</i></a>.</p> <p><b>-k</b> TEST_NAME_PATTERNS</p> <p>Runs test methods and classes matching test name patterns, in the same way as <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#cmdoption-unittest-k">unittest's -k option</a>. Can be specified multiple times.</p> <p><b>--pdb</b></p> <p>Spawns a pdb debugger at each test error or failure. If you have it installed, ipdb is used instead.</p> <p><b>--buffer</b>,<b>-b</b></p> <p>Discards output (stdout and stderr) for passing tests, in the same way as <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#cmdoption-unittest-b">unittest's --buffer option</a>.</p> <p><b>--no-faulthandler</b></p> <p>Django automatically calls <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/faulthandler.html#faulthandler.enable">faulthandler.enable()</a> when starting the tests, which allows it to print a trace-back if the interpreter crashes. Pass--no-faulthandler to disable this behavior.</p> <p><b>--timing</b></p> <p>Outputs timings, including database setup and total run time.</p> <p><b>--durations</b> N</p> <p>Shows the N slowest test cases (N=0 for all).</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Python 3.12 and later</p> <p>This feature is only available for Python 3.12 and later.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1460"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>testserver</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin testserver [fixture [fixture ...]]</b></p> <p>Runs a Django development server (as in <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a>) using data from the given fixture(s).</p> <p>For example, this command:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin testserver mydata.json</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><i>. . .</i>would perform the following steps:</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">1. Create a test database, as described in <a href="index.html#page_472">The test database</a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">2. Populate the test database with fixture data from the given fixtures. (For more on fixtures, see the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">documentation for <a href="index.html#page_1441"><i>loaddata</i></a> above.)</p> <p style="margin-left:1em">3. Runs the Django development server (as in <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a>), pointed at this newly created test database</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">instead of your production database.</p> <p>This is useful in a number of ways:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• When you’re writing <a href="index.html#page_469">unit tests</a> of how your views act with certain fixture data, you can use testserver</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to interact with the views in a web browser, manually.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Let’s say you’re developing your Django application and have a “pristine” copy of a database that</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">you’d like to interact with. You can dump your database to a <a href="index.html#page_248">fixture</a> (using the <a href="index.html#page_1438"><i>dumpdata</i></a> command, explained above), then use testserver to run your web application with that data. With this arrange-ment, you have the flexibility of messing up your data in any way, knowing that whatever data changes you’re making are only being made to a test database.</p> <p>Note that this server does not automatically detect changes to your Python source code (as <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> does). It does, however, detect changes to templates.</p> <p><b>--addrport</b> ADDRPORT</p> <p>Specifies a different port, or IP address and port, from the default of 127.0.0.1:8000. This value follows</p> <p>exactly the same format and serves exactly the same function as the argument to the <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a> command.</p> <p>Examples:</p> <p>To run the test server on port 7000 with fixture1 and fixture2:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin testserver --addrport 7000 fixture1 fixture2</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin testserver fixture1 fixture2 --addrport 7000</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>(The above statements are equivalent. We include both of them to demonstrate that it doesn’t matter whether the options come before or after the fixture arguments.)</p> <p>To run on 1.2.3.4:7000 with a test fixture:</p> <p id="page_1461" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin testserver --addrport 1.2.3.4:7000 test</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts. A typical prompt is a warning about deleting an existing test database.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.8.3 Commands provided by applications</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some commands are only available when the django.contrib application that <a href="index.html#page_894">implements</a> them has been</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>enabled</i></a>. This section describes them grouped by their application.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.contrib.auth</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>changepassword</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin changepassword [<username>]</b></p> <p>This command is only available if Django’s <a href="index.html#page_530">authentication system</a> (django.contrib.auth) is installed.</p> <p>Allows changing a user’s password. It prompts you to enter a new password twice for the given user. If the entries are identical, this immediately becomes the new password. If you do not supply a user, the command will attempt to change the password whose username matches the current user.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to query for the user. Defaults to default.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin changepassword ringo</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>createsuperuser</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin createsuperuser</b></p> <p><b>DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD</b></p> <p>This command is only available if Django’s <a href="index.html#page_530">authentication system</a> (django.contrib.auth) is installed.</p> <p>Creates a superuser account (a user who has all permissions). This is useful if you need to create an initial superuser account or if you need to programmatically generate superuser accounts for your site(s).</p> <p>When run interactively, this command will prompt for a password for the new superuser account. When run</p> <p>non-interactively, you can provide a password by setting the <a href="index.html#page_1461"><i>DJANGO_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD</i></a> environment variable. Otherwise, no password will be set, and the superuser account will not be able to log in until a password has been manually set for it.</p> <p id="page_1462"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>In non-interactive mode, the <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>USERNAME_FIELD</i></a> and required fields (listed in <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>REQUIRED_FIELDS</i></a>) fall back to DJANGO_SUPERUSER_<uppercase_field_name> environment variables, unless they are overridden by a com-mand line argument. For example, to provide an email field, you can use DJANGO_SUPERUSER_EMAIL envi-ronment variable.</p> <p><b>--noinput</b>,<b>--no-input</b></p> <p>Suppresses all user prompts. If a suppressed prompt cannot be resolved automatically, the command will exit with error code 1.</p> <p><b>--username</b> USERNAME</p> <p><b>--email</b> EMAIL</p> <p>The username and email address for the new account can be supplied by using the--username and--email arguments on the command line. If either of those is not supplied, createsuperuser will prompt for it when running interactively.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database into which the superuser object will be saved.</p> <p>You can subclass the management command and override get_input_data() if you want to customize data input and validation. Consult the source code for details on the existing implementation and the method’s</p> <p>parameters. For example, it could be useful if you have a ForeignKey in <a href="index.html#page_586"><i>REQUIRED_FIELDS</i></a> and want to allow creating an instance instead of entering the primary key of an existing instance.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.contrib.contenttypes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>remove_stale_contenttypes</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin remove_stale_contenttypes</b></p> <p>This command is only available if Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1114">contenttypes app</a> (<a href="index.html#page_1114"><i>django.contrib.contenttypes</i></a>) is installed.</p> <p>Deletes stale content types (from deleted models) in your database. Any objects that depend on the deleted content types will also be deleted. A list of deleted objects will be displayed before you confirm it’s okay to proceed with the deletion.</p> <p><b>--database</b> DATABASE</p> <p>Specifies the database to use. Defaults to default.</p> <p><b>--include-stale-apps</b></p> <p>Deletes stale content types including ones from previously installed apps that have been removed from</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1917"><i>INSTALLED_APPS</i></a> . Defaults to False.</p> <p id="page_1463" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.contrib.gis</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ogrinspect</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This command is only available if <a href="index.html#page_1130">GeoDjango</a> (django.contrib.gis) is installed.</p> <p>Please refer to its <a href="index.html#page_1278"><i>description</i></a> in the GeoDjango documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.contrib.sessions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>clearsessions</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django-admin clearsessions</b></p> <p>Can be run as a cron job or directly to clean out expired sessions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>django.contrib.staticfiles</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>collectstatic</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This command is only available if the <a href="index.html#page_843">static files application</a> (django.contrib.staticfiles) is installed.</p> <p>Please refer to its <a href="index.html#page_1370"><i>description</i></a> in the <a href="index.html#page_1369">staticfiles</a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>findstatic</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>This command is only available if the <a href="index.html#page_843">static files application</a> (django.contrib.staticfiles) is installed.</p> <p>Please refer to its <a href="index.html#page_1371"><i>description</i></a> in the <a href="index.html#page_1369">staticfiles</a> documentation.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.8.4 Default options</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Although some commands may allow their own custom options, every command allows for the following options by default:</p> <p><b>--pythonpath</b> PYTHONPATH</p> <p>Adds the given filesystem path to the Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.path">sys.path</a> module attribute. <span style="float:right">If this isn’t provided,</span></p> <p>django-admin will use the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONPATH">PYTHONPATH</a> environment variable.</p> <p>This option is unnecessary in manage.py, because it takes care of setting the Python path for you.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p id="page_1464"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin migrate --pythonpath='/home/djangoprojects/myproject'</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--settings</b> SETTINGS</p> <p>Specifies the settings module to use. The settings module should be in Python package syntax, e.g. mysite.</p> <p>settings. If this isn’t provided, django-admin will use the <a href="index.html#page_746"><i>DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE</i></a> environment variable.</p> <p>This option is unnecessary in manage.py, because it uses settings.py from the current project by default.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin migrate --settings=mysite.settings</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--traceback</b></p> <p>Displays a full stack trace when a <a href="index.html#page_900"><i>CommandError</i></a> is raised. By default, django-admin will show an error message when a CommandError occurs and a full stack trace for any other exception.</p> <p>This option is ignored by <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a>.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin migrate --traceback</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--verbosity</b> {0,1,2,3},<b>-v</b> {0,1,2,3}</p> <p>Specifies the amount of notification and debug information that a command should print to the console.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 0 means no output.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 1 means normal output (default).</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 2 means verbose output.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• 3 means very verbose output.</p> <p>This option is ignored by <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>runserver</i></a>.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin migrate --verbosity 2</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--no-color</b></p> <p>Disables colorized command output. Some commands format their output to be colorized. For example, errors will be printed to the console in red and SQL statements will be syntax highlighted.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin runserver --no-color</span></p> <p id="page_1465" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>--force-color</b></p> <p>Forces colorization of the command output if it would otherwise be disabled as discussed in <a href="index.html#page_1465">Syntax coloring</a>. For example, you may want to pipe colored output to another command.</p> <p><b>--skip-checks</b></p> <p>Skips running system checks prior to running the command. <span style="float:right">This option is only available if the</span></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_898"><i>requires_system_checks</i></a> command attribute is not an empty list or tuple.</p> <p>Example usage:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin migrate --skip-checks</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.8.5 Extra niceties</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Syntax coloring</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>DJANGO_COLORS</b></p> <p>The django-admin / manage.py commands will use pretty color-coded output if your terminal supports ANSI-colored output. It won’t use the color codes if you’re piping the command’s output to another program unless</p> <p>the<a href="index.html#page_1464"><i>--force-color</i></a> option is used.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Windows support</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>On Windows 10, the <a href="https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/p/windows-terminal-preview/9n0dx20hk701">Windows Terminal</a> application, <a href="https://code.visualstudio.com">VS Code</a>, and PowerShell (where virtual terminal pro-cessing is enabled) allow colored output, and are supported by default.</p> <p>Under Windows, the legacy cmd.exe native console doesn’t support ANSI escape sequences so by default there is no color output. In this case either of two third-party libraries are needed:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Install <a href="https://pypi.org/project/colorama/">colorama</a>, a Python package that translates ANSI color codes into Windows API calls. Django</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">commands will detect its presence and will make use of its services to color output just like on Unix-based platforms. colorama can be installed via pip:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">...\></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">py -m pip install</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"colorama >= 0.4.6"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Install <a href="http://adoxa.altervista.org/ansicon/">ANSICON</a>, a third-party tool that allows cmd.exe to process ANSI color codes. Django commands</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">will detect its presence and will make use of its services to color output just like on Unix-based platforms.</p> <p>Other modern terminal environments on Windows, that support terminal colors, but which are not automat-ically detected as supported by Django, may “fake” the installation of ANSICON by setting the appropriate environmental variable, ANSICON="on".</p> <p id="page_1466"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Custom colors</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The colors used for syntax highlighting can be customized. Django ships with three color palettes:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• dark, suited to terminals that show white text on a black background. This is the default palette.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• light, suited to terminals that show black text on a white background.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• nocolor, which disables syntax highlighting.</p> <p>You select a palette by setting a <a href="index.html#page_1465"><i>DJANGO_COLORS</i></a> environment variable to specify the palette you want to use. For example, to specify the light palette under a Unix or OS/X BASH shell, you would run the following at a command prompt:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DJANGO_COLORS</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"light"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>You can also customize the colors that are used. Django specifies a number of roles in which color is used:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• error- A major error.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• notice- A minor error.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• success- A success.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• warning- A warning.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sql_field- The name of a model field in SQL.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sql_coltype- The type of a model field in SQL.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sql_keyword- An SQL keyword.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• sql_table- The name of a model in SQL.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_info- A 1XX HTTP Informational server response.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_success- A 2XX HTTP Success server response.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_not_modified- A 304 HTTP Not Modified server response.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_redirect- A 3XX HTTP Redirect server response other than 304.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_not_found- A 404 HTTP Not Found server response.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_bad_request- A 4XX HTTP Bad Request server response other than 404.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• http_server_error- A 5XX HTTP Server Error response.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• migrate_heading- A heading in a migrations management command.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• migrate_label- A migration name.</p> <p>Each of these roles can be assigned a specific foreground and background color, from the following list:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• black</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• red</p> <p id="page_1467" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• green</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• yellow</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• blue</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• magenta</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• cyan</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• white</p> <p>Each of these colors can then be modified by using the following display options:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• bold</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• underscore</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• blink</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• reverse</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• conceal</p> <p>A color specification follows one of the following patterns:</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• role=fg</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• role=fg/bg</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• role=fg,option,option</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• role=fg/bg,option,option</p> <p>where role is the name of a valid color role, fg is the foreground color, bg is the background color and each option is one of the color modifying options. Multiple color specifications are then separated by a semicolon. For example:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DJANGO_COLORS</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"error=yellow/blue,blink;notice=magenta"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>would specify that errors be displayed using blinking yellow on blue, and notices displayed using magenta. All other color roles would be left uncolored.</p> <p>Colors can also be specified by extending a base palette. If you put a palette name in a color specification, all the colors implied by that palette will be loaded. So:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">export</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">DJANGO_COLORS</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"light;error=yellow/blue,blink;notice=magenta"</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>would specify the use of all the colors in the light color palette, except for the colors for errors and notices which would be overridden as specified.</p> <p id="page_1468"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Bash completion</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>If you use the Bash shell, consider installing the Django bash completion script, which lives in <a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/extras/django_bash_completion">ex-</a></p> <p><a href="https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/extras/django_bash_completion">tras/django_bash_completion</a> in the Django source distribution. It enables tab-completion of django-admin and manage.py commands, so you can, for instance<i>. . .</i></p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Type django-admin.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Press [TAB] to see all available options.</p> <p style="text-indent:1em">• Type sql, then [TAB], to see all available options whose names start with sql.</p> <p>See <a href="index.html#page_894">How to create custom django-admin commands</a> for how to add customized actions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Black formatting</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The Python files created by <a href="index.html#page_1456"><i>startproject</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1454"><i>startapp</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1447"><i>optimizemigration</i></a>, <a href="index.html#page_1444"><i>makemigrations</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1444">, </a>and</p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1453"><i>squashmigrations</i></a> are formatted using the black command if it is present on your PATH.</p> <p>If you have black globally installed, but do not wish it used for the current project, you can set the PATH explicitly:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">PATH</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">path/to/venv/bin django-admin makemigrations</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>For commands using stdout you can pipe the output to black if needed:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">django-admin inspectdb | black -</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.9 Running management commands from your code</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>django.core.management.<b>call_command</b>( name, *args, **options)</p> <p>To call a management command from code use call_command().</p> <p><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">the name of the command to call or a command object. Passing the name is preferred unless the object is required for testing.</p> <p><b>*args</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">a list of arguments accepted by the command. Arguments are passed to the argument parser, so you can use the same style as you would on the command line. For example, call_command('flush', '--verbosity=0').</p> <p><b>**options</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">named options accepted on the command-line. Options are passed to the command without trig-</p> <p id="page_1469" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">gering the argument parser, which means you’ll need to pass the correct type. For example, call_command('flush', verbosity=0) (zero must be an integer rather than a string).</p> <p>Examples:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.management.commands</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">loaddata</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"flush"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, verbosity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, interactive</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"loaddata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"test_data"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, verbosity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(loaddata</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">Command(),</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"test_data"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, verbosity</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">0</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that command options that take no arguments are passed as keywords with True or False, as you can see with the interactive option above.</p> <p>Named arguments can be passed by using either one of the following syntaxes:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Similar to the command line</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dumpdata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"--natural-foreign"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># Named argument similar to the command line minus the initial dashes and</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># with internal dashes replaced by underscores</i></span></p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dumpdata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, natural_foreign</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><i># `use_natural_foreign_keys` is the option destination variable</i></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dumpdata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, use_natural_foreign_keys</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Some command options have different names when using call_command() instead of django-admin or manage.py. For example, django-admin createsuperuser --no-input translates to call_command('createsuperuser', interactive=False). <span style="float:right">To find what keyword argument name</span></p> <p>to use for call_command(), check the command’s source code for the dest argument passed to parser. add_argument().</p> <p>Command options which take multiple options are passed a list:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dumpdata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, exclude</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">[</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"contenttypes"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"auth"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">])</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The return value of the call_command() function is the same as the return value of the handle() method of the command.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1470"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.9.1 Output redirection</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note that you can redirect standard output and error streams as all commands support the stdout and stderr options. For example, you could write:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>with</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">open</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"/path/to/command_output"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">,</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"w"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>as</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">f:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">management</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">call_command(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"dumpdata"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, stdout</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">f)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.10 Django Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django raises some of its own exceptions as well as standard Python exceptions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.1 Django Core Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django core exception classes are defined in django.core.exceptions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>AppRegistryNotReady</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception AppRegistryNotReady</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">This exception is raised when attempting to use models before the <a href="index.html#page_928">app loading process, </a>which initializes the ORM, is complete.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ObjectDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception ObjectDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The base class for <a href="index.html#page_1677"><i>Model.DoesNotExist</i></a> exceptions. A try/except for ObjectDoesNotExist will catch</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1677"><i>DoesNotExist</i></a> exceptions for all models.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">See <a href="index.html#page_1744"><i>get()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>EmptyResultSet</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception EmptyResultSet</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">EmptyResultSet may be raised during query generation if a query won’t return any results. Most Django projects won’t encounter this exception, but it might be useful for implementing custom lookups and expressions.</p> <p id="page_1471" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>FullResultSet</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception FullResultSet</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">FullResultSet may be raised during query generation if a query will match everything. Most Django projects won’t encounter this exception, but it might be useful for implementing custom lookups and expressions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>FieldDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception FieldDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The FieldDoesNotExist exception is raised by a model’s _meta.get_field() method when the re-quested field does not exist on the model or on the model’s parents.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MultipleObjectsReturned</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception MultipleObjectsReturned</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The base class for <a href="index.html#page_1677"><i>Model.MultipleObjectsReturned</i></a> exceptions. A try/except for</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">MultipleObjectsReturned will catch <a href="index.html#page_1677"><i>MultipleObjectsReturned</i></a> exceptions for all models.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">See <a href="index.html#page_1744"><i>get()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SuspiciousOperation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception SuspiciousOperation</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1471"><i>SuspiciousOperation</i></a> exception is raised when a user has performed an operation that should be considered suspicious from a security perspective, such as tampering with a session cookie. Subclasses of SuspiciousOperation include:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• DisallowedHost</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• DisallowedModelAdminLookup</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• DisallowedModelAdminToField</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• DisallowedRedirect</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• InvalidSessionKey</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• RequestDataTooBig</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• SuspiciousFileOperation</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• SuspiciousMultipartForm</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• SuspiciousSession</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• TooManyFieldsSent</p> <p id="page_1472"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• TooManyFilesSent</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If a SuspiciousOperation exception reaches the ASGI/WSGI handler level it is logged at the Error</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">level and results in a <a href="index.html#page_1877"><i>HttpResponseBadRequest</i>. </a>See the <a href="index.html#page_707">logging documentation</a> for more information.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>PermissionDenied</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception PermissionDenied</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>PermissionDenied</i></a> exception is raised when a user does not have permission to perform the action requested.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ViewDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception ViewDoesNotExist</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">The <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>ViewDoesNotExist</i></a> exception is raised by <a href="index.html#page_2063"><i>django.urls</i></a> when a requested view does not exist.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>MiddlewareNotUsed</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception MiddlewareNotUsed</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>MiddlewareNotUsed</i></a> exception is raised when a middleware is not used in the server configuration.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ImproperlyConfigured</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception ImproperlyConfigured</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>ImproperlyConfigured</i></a> exception is raised when Django is somehow improperly configured – for example, if a value in settings.py is incorrect or unparseable.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>FieldError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception FieldError</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1472"><i>FieldError</i></a> exception is raised when there is a problem with a model field. This can happen for several reasons:</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A field in a model clashes with a field of the same name from an abstract base class</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• An infinite loop is caused by ordering</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A keyword cannot be parsed from the filter parameters</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A field cannot be determined from a keyword in the query parameters</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A join is not permitted on the specified field</p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A field name is invalid</p> <p id="page_1473" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:3em">• A query contains invalid order_by arguments</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>ValidationError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception ValidationError</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>ValidationError</i></a> exception is raised when data fails form or model field validation. For more</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">information about validation, see <a href="index.html#page_1574">Form and Field Validation,</a> <a href="index.html#page_1692">Model Field Validation</a> and the <a href="index.html#page_2091">Validator</a></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_2091">Reference.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>NON_FIELD_ERRORS</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>NON_FIELD_ERRORS</b></p> <p>ValidationErrors that don’t belong to a particular field in a form or model are classified as NON_FIELD_ERRORS. This constant is used as a key in dictionaries that otherwise map fields to their respective list of errors.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>BadRequest</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception BadRequest</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>BadRequest</i></a> exception is raised when the request cannot be processed due to a client error. If a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">BadRequest exception reaches the ASGI/WSGI handler level it results in a <a href="index.html#page_1877"><i>HttpResponseBadRequest</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>RequestAborted</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception RequestAborted</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>RequestAborted</i></a> exception is raised when an HTTP body being read in by the handler is cut off midstream and the client connection closes, or when the client does not send data and hits a timeout where the server closes the connection.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">It is internal to the HTTP handler modules and you are unlikely to see it elsewhere. If you are modifying HTTP handling code, you should raise this when you encounter an aborted request to make sure the socket is closed cleanly.</p> <div style="page-break-after:always"></div> <p id="page_1474"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SynchronousOnlyOperation</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception SynchronousOnlyOperation</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>SynchronousOnlyOperation</i></a> exception is raised when code that is only allowed in synchronous Python code is called from an asynchronous context (a thread with a running asynchronous event loop). These parts of Django are generally heavily reliant on thread-safety to function and don’t work correctly under coroutines sharing the same thread.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you are trying to call code that is synchronous-only from an asynchronous thread, then create a syn-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">chronous thread and call it in that. You can accomplish this is with <a href="index.html#page_770"><i>asgiref.sync.sync_to_async()</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.2 URL Resolver exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>URL Resolver exceptions are defined in django.urls.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Resolver404</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception Resolver404</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>Resolver404</i></a> exception is raised by <a href="index.html#page_2065"><i>resolve()</i></a> if the path passed to resolve() doesn’t map to a</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">view. It’s a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_285"><i>django.http.Http404</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>NoReverseMatch</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception NoReverseMatch</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>NoReverseMatch</i></a> exception is raised by <a href="index.html#page_2063"><i>django.urls</i></a> when a matching URL in your URLconf can-not be identified based on the parameters supplied.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.3 Database Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Database exceptions may be imported from django.db.</p> <p>Django wraps the standard database exceptions so that your Django code has a guaranteed common imple-mentation of these classes.</p> <p><b>exception Error</b></p> <p><b>exception InterfaceError</b></p> <p><b>exception DatabaseError</b></p> <p><b>exception DataError</b></p> <p><b>exception OperationalError</b></p> <p id="page_1475" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception IntegrityError</b></p> <p><b>exception InternalError</b></p> <p><b>exception ProgrammingError</b></p> <p><b>exception NotSupportedError</b></p> <p>The Django wrappers for database exceptions behave exactly the same as the underlying database excep-</p> <p>tions. See <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/">PEP 249</a>, the Python Database API Specification v2.0, for further information.</p> <p>As per <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-3134/">PEP 3134, </a>a __cause__ attribute is set with the original (underlying) database exception, allowing access to any additional information provided.</p> <p><b>exception</b> models.<b>ProtectedError</b></p> <p>Raised to prevent deletion of referenced objects when using <a href="index.html#page_1645"><i>django.db.models.PROTECT</i></a> . <a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>models.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>ProtectedError</i></a> is a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>IntegrityError</i></a>.</p> <p><b>exception</b> models.<b>RestrictedError</b></p> <p>Raised to prevent deletion of referenced objects when using <a href="index.html#page_1645"><i>django.db.models.RESTRICT</i></a> . <a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>models.</i></a></p> <p><a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>RestrictedError</i></a> is a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_1474"><i>IntegrityError</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.4 HTTP Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>HTTP exceptions may be imported from django.http.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>UnreadablePostError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception UnreadablePostError</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>UnreadablePostError</i></a> is raised when a user cancels an upload.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.5 Sessions Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Sessions exceptions are defined in django.contrib.sessions.exceptions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>SessionInterrupted</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception SessionInterrupted</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1475"><i>SessionInterrupted</i></a> is raised when a session is destroyed in a concurrent request. It’s a subclass of</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1473"><i>BadRequest</i> .</a></p> <p id="page_1476"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.6 Transaction Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Transaction exceptions are defined in django.db.transaction.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>TransactionManagementError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception TransactionManagementError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"><a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>TransactionManagementError</i></a> is raised for any and all problems related to database transactions.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.7 Testing Framework Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Exceptions provided by the django.test package.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>RedirectCycleError</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>exception</b> client.<b>RedirectCycleError</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>RedirectCycleError</i></a> is raised when the test client detects a loop or an overly long chain of redirects.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.10.8 Python Exceptions</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django raises built-in Python exceptions when appropriate as well. See the Python documentation for further</p> <p>information on the <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#bltin-exceptions">Built-in Exceptions.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.47em"><b>6.11 File handling</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.11.1 The</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>File</b></span> <span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>object</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>The <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>django.core.files</i></a> module and its submodules contain built-in classes for basic file handling in Django.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The File class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class File</b>(file_object, name=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> class is a thin wrapper around a Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-file-object">file object</a> with some Django-specific additions. In-ternally, Django uses this class when it needs to represent a file.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> objects have the following attributes and methods:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The name of the file including the relative path from <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> .</p> <p id="page_1477" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>size</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The size of the file in bytes.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>file</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The underlying <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-file-object">file object</a> that this class wraps.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Be careful with this attribute in subclasses.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Some subclasses of <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i>, </a>including <a href="index.html#page_1478"><i>ContentFile</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1633"><i>FieldFile</i></a>, may replace this attribute with</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">an object other than a Python <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-file-object">file object</a>. In these cases, this attribute may itself be a <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> subclass (and not necessarily the same subclass). Whenever possible, use the attributes and methods of the subclass itself rather than the those of the subclass’s file attribute.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>mode</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The read/write mode for the file.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>open</b>(mode=None, *args, **kwargs)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Open or reopen the file (which also does File.seek(0)). The mode argument allows the same</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">values as Python’s built-in <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open">open().</a> *args and **kwargs are passed after mode to Python’s built-</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">in <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open">open().</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">When reopening a file, mode will override whatever mode the file was originally opened with; None means to reopen with the original mode.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">It can be used as a context manager, e.g. with file.open() as f:.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>__iter__</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Iterate over the file yielding one line at a time.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>chunks</b>(chunk_size=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Iterate over the file yielding “chunks” of a given size. chunk_size defaults to 64 KB.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">This is especially useful with very large files since it allows them to be streamed off disk and avoids storing the whole file in memory.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>multiple_chunks</b>(chunk_size=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns True if the file is large enough to require multiple chunks to access all of its content give some chunk_size.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>close</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Close the file.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In addition to the listed methods, <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> exposes the following attributes and methods of its file ob-ject: encoding, fileno, flush, isatty, newlines, read, readinto, readline, readlines, seek, tell, truncate, write, writelines, readable(), writable(), and seekable().</p> <p id="page_1478"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The ContentFile class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class ContentFile</b>(content, name=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The ContentFile class inherits from <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a>, but unlike <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> it operates on string content (bytes also supported), rather than an actual file. For example:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.base</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentFile</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">f1</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentFile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"esta frase está en español"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">f2</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">ContentFile(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">b"these are bytes"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The ImageFile class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class ImageFile</b>(file_object, name=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Django provides a built-in class specifically for images. <a href="index.html#page_1478"><i>django.core.files.images.ImageFile</i></a> in-</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">herits all the attributes and methods of <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a>, and additionally provides the following:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>width</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Width of the image in pixels.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>height</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Height of the image in pixels.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Additional methods on files attached to objects</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Any <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> that is associated with an object (as with Car.photo, below) will also have a couple of extra meth-ods:</p> <p>File.<b>save</b>( name, content, save=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Saves a new file with the file name and contents provided. This will not replace the existing file, but will create a new file and update the object to point to it. If save is True, the model’s save() method will be called once the file is saved. That is, these two lines:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">car</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">photo</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"myphoto.jpg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, content, save</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=False</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">car</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save()</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">are equivalent to:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">car</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">photo</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">save(</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"myphoto.jpg"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">, content, save</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=True</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note that the content argument must be an instance of either <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i></a> or of a subclass of <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>File</i>, </a>such as</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1478"><i>ContentFile</i> .</a></p> <p id="page_1479" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>File.<b>delete</b>(save=True)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Removes the file from the model instance and deletes the underlying file. If save is True, the model’s save() method will be called once the file is deleted.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.11.2 File storage API</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Getting the default storage class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Django provides convenient ways to access the default storage class:</p> <p><b>storages</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A dictionary-like object that allows retrieving a storage instance using its alias as defined by <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">storages has an attribute backends, which defaults to the raw value provided in <a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Additionally, storages provides a create_storage() method that accepts the dictionary used in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> for a backend, and returns a storage instance based on that backend definition. This may be useful for third-party packages needing to instantiate storages in tests:</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>from</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">django.core.files.storage</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>import</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">backends</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">{'default': {'BACKEND': 'django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage'},</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"><span style="font-size:0.87em">'staticfiles': {'BACKEND': 'django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.StaticFilesStorage'},</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">'custom': {'BACKEND': 'package.storage.CustomStorage'}}</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">>>></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storage_instance</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>=</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">storages</span><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>.</b></span><span style="font-size:0.87em">create_storage({</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">"BACKEND"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">:</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">"package.storage.CustomStorage"</span><span style="font-size:0.87em">})</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class DefaultStorage</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>DefaultStorage</i></a> provides lazy access to the default storage system as defined by default key in</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1931"><i>STORAGES</i></a> . <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>DefaultStorage</i></a> uses <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>storages</i></a> internally.</p> <p><b>default_storage</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>default_storage</i></a> is an instance of the <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>DefaultStorage</i>.</a></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The FileSystemStorage class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class FileSystemStorage</b>(location=None, base_url=None, file_permissions_mode=None,</p> <p style="margin-left:10em">directory_permissions_mode=None, allow_overwrite=False)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1479"><i>FileSystemStorage</i></a> class implements basic file storage on a local filesystem. It inherits from</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1481"><i>Storage</i></a> and provides implementations for all the public methods thereof.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: The FileSystemStorage.delete() method will not raise an exception if the given file name does not exist.</p> <p id="page_1480"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>location</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Absolute path to the directory that will hold the files. Defaults to the value of your <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>base_url</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">URL that serves the files stored at this location. Defaults to the value of your <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>file_permissions_mode</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The file system permissions that the file will receive when it is saved. <span style="float:right">Defaults to</span></p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1914"><i>FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS</i></a> .</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>directory_permissions_mode</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The file system permissions that the directory will receive when it is saved. Defaults to</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1914"><i>FILE_UPLOAD_DIRECTORY_PERMISSIONS</i></a> .</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>allow_overwrite</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">Flag to control allowing saving a new file over an existing one. Defaults to False.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_created_time</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> of the system’s ctime, i.e. <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.path.html#os.path.getctime">os.path.getctime()</a><a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.path.html#os.path.getctime">. </a>On some systems (like Unix), this is the time of the last metadata change, and on others (like Windows), it’s the creation time of the file.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The InMemoryStorage class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class InMemoryStorage</b>(location=None, base_url=None, file_permissions_mode=None,</p> <p style="margin-left:9em">directory_permissions_mode=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1480"><i>InMemoryStorage</i></a> class implements a memory-based file storage. It has no persistence, but can be useful for speeding up tests by avoiding disk access.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>location</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Absolute path to the directory name assigned to files. Defaults to the value of your <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_ROOT</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>base_url</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">URL that serves the files stored at this location. Defaults to the value of your <a href="index.html#page_1922"><i>MEDIA_URL</i></a> setting.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>file_permissions_mode</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The file system permissions assigned to files, provided for compatibility with FileSystemStorage.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Defaults to <a href="index.html#page_1914"><i>FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS</i></a>.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>directory_permissions_mode</b></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The file system permissions assigned to directories, provided for compatibility with</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">FileSystemStorage . Defaults to <a href="index.html#page_1914"><i>FILE_UPLOAD_DIRECTORY_PERMISSIONS</i></a>.</p> <p id="page_1481" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>The Storage class</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class Storage</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The <a href="index.html#page_1481"><i>Storage</i></a> class provides a standardized API for storing files, along with a set of default behaviors that all other storage systems can inherit or override as necessary.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Note: When methods return naive datetime objects, the effective timezone used will be the current</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">value of os.environ['TZ']; note that this is usually set from Django’s <a href="index.html#page_1935"><i>TIME_ZONE</i></a>.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>delete</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Deletes the file referenced by name. If deletion is not supported on the target storage system this will raise NotImplementedError instead.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>exists</b>(name)</p> <p style="text-align:center">Returns True if a file referenced by the given name already exists in the storage system.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_accessed_time</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> of the last accessed time of the file. For storage systems unable to return the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">last accessed time this will raise <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#NotImplementedError">NotImplementedError.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ</i></a> is True, returns an aware datetime, otherwise returns a naive datetime in the local timezone.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_alternative_name</b>(file_root, file_ext)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns an alternative filename based on the file_root and file_ext parameters, an underscore plus a random 7 character alphanumeric string is appended to the filename before the extension.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_available_name</b> ( name, max_length=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a filename based on the name parameter that’s free and available for new content to be written to on the target storage system.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The length of the filename will not exceed max_length, if provided. If a free unique filename</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">cannot be found, a <a href="index.html#page_1471"><i>SuspiciousFileOperation</i></a> exception will be raised.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If a file with name already exists, <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>get_alternative_name()</i></a> is called to obtain an alternative name.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_created_time</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> of the creation time of the file. For storage systems unable to return the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">creation time this will raise <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#NotImplementedError">NotImplementedError.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ</i></a> is True, returns an aware datetime, otherwise returns a naive datetime in the local timezone.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_modified_time</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime">datetime</a> of the last modified time of the file. For storage systems unable to return the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">last modified time this will raise <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#NotImplementedError">NotImplementedError.</a></p> <p id="page_1482"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:4em">If <a href="index.html#page_1936"><i>USE_TZ</i></a> is True, returns an aware datetime, otherwise returns a naive datetime in the local timezone.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>get_valid_name</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns a filename based on the name parameter that’s suitable for use on the target storage sys-tem.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>generate_filename</b>(filename)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Validates the filename by calling <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>get_valid_name()</i></a> and returns a filename to be passed to the</p> <p style="margin-left:4em"><a href="index.html#page_1482"><i>save()</i></a> method.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The filename argument may include a path as returned by <a href="index.html#page_1631"><i>FileField.upload_to</i>. </a>In that case,</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">the path won’t be passed to <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>get_valid_name()</i></a> but will be prepended back to the resulting name.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The default implementation uses <a href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.path.html#module-os.path">os.path</a> operations. Override this method if that’s not appro-priate for your storage.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>listdir</b>(path)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Lists the contents of the specified path, returning a 2-tuple of lists; the first item being directories, the second item being files. For storage systems that aren’t able to provide such a listing, this will raise a NotImplementedError instead.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>open</b> (name, mode='rb')</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Opens the file given by name. Note that although the returned file is guaranteed to be a File object, it might actually be some subclass. In the case of remote file storage this means that read-ing/writing could be quite slow, so be warned.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>path</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The local filesystem path where the file can be opened using Python’s standard open(). For stor-age systems that aren’t accessible from the local filesystem, this will raise NotImplementedError instead.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>save</b>(name, content, max_length=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Saves a new file using the storage system, preferably with the name specified. If there already exists a file with this name name, the storage system may modify the filename as necessary to get a unique name. The actual name of the stored file will be returned.</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The max_length argument is passed along to <a href="index.html#page_902"><i>get_available_name()</i>.</a></p> <p style="margin-left:4em">The content argument must be an instance of <a href="index.html#page_1476"><i>django.core.files.File</i></a> or a file-like object that can be wrapped in File.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>size</b> (name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the total size, in bytes, of the file referenced by name. For storage systems that aren’t able to return the file size this will raise NotImplementedError instead.</p> <p id="page_1483" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><b>url</b>(name)</p> <p style="margin-left:4em">Returns the URL where the contents of the file referenced by name can be accessed. For storage systems that don’t support access by URL this will raise NotImplementedError instead.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><span style="font-size:1.2em"><b>6.11.3 Uploaded Files and Upload Handlers</b></span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Uploaded files</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class UploadedFile</b></p> <p>During file uploads, the actual file data is stored in <a href="index.html#page_1861"><i>request.FILES</i></a>. Each entry in this dictionary is an UploadedFile object (or a subclass) – a wrapper around an uploaded file. You’ll usually use one of these methods to access the uploaded content:</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>read</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Read the entire uploaded data from the file. Be careful with this method: if the uploaded file is huge it can overwhelm your system if you try to read it into memory. You’ll probably want to use chunks() instead; see below.</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>multiple_chunks</b>(chunk_size=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns True if the uploaded file is big enough to require reading in multiple chunks. By default this will be any file larger than 2.5 megabytes, but that’s configurable; see below.</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>chunks</b>(chunk_size=None)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A generator returning chunks of the file. If multiple_chunks() is True, you should use this method in a loop instead of read().</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">In practice, it’s often easiest to use chunks() all the time. Looping over chunks() instead of using read() ensures that large files don’t overwhelm your system’s memory.</p> <p>Here are some useful attributes of UploadedFile:</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>name</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The name of the uploaded file (e.g. my_file.txt).</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>size</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The size, in bytes, of the uploaded file.</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>content_type</b></p> <p style="text-align:center">The content-type header uploaded with the file (e.g. <i>text/plain</i> or <i>application/pdf</i>). Like any data supplied by the user, you shouldn’t trust that the uploaded file is actually this type. You’ll still need to validate that the file contains the content that the content-type header claims – “trust but verify.”</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>content_type_extra</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A dictionary containing extra parameters passed to the content-type header. This is typically pro-vided by services, such as Google App Engine, that intercept and handle file uploads on your behalf.</p> <p id="page_1484"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p style="margin-left:2em">As a result your handler may not receive the uploaded file content, but instead a URL or other pointer</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">to the file (see <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2388.html#section-5.3">RFC 2388</a>).</p> <p>UploadedFile.<b>charset</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">For <i>text/*</i> content-types, the character set (i.e. utf8) supplied by the browser. Again, “trust but verify” is the best policy here.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Note: Like regular Python files, you can read the file line-by-line by iterating over the uploaded file:</p> <p><span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>for</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">line</span> <span style="font-size:0.87em"><b>in</b></span> <span style="font-size:0.87em">uploadedfile:</span></p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><span style="font-size:0.87em">do_something_with(line)</span></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Lines are split using <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0278/">universal newlines. </a>The following are recognized as ending a line: the Unix end-of-line convention '\n', the Windows convention '\r\n', and the old Macintosh convention '\r'.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Subclasses of UploadedFile include:</p> <p><b>class TemporaryUploadedFile</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A file uploaded to a temporary location (i.e. stream-to-disk). This class is used by the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1484"><i>TemporaryFileUploadHandler</i></a> . In addition to the methods from <a href="index.html#page_1483"><i>UploadedFile</i></a><a href="index.html#page_1483">, </a>it has one additional method:</p> <p>TemporaryUploadedFile.<b>temporary_file_path</b>()</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Returns the full path to the temporary uploaded file.</p> <p><b>class InMemoryUploadedFile</b></p> <p style="margin-left:2em">A file uploaded into memory (i.e. stream-to-memory). This class is used by the</p> <p style="margin-left:2em"><a href="index.html#page_1484"><i>MemoryFileUploadHandler</i></a> .</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Built-in upload handlers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Together the <a href="index.html#page_1484"><i>MemoryFileUploadHandler</i></a> and <a href="index.html#page_1484"><i>TemporaryFileUploadHandler</i></a> provide Django’s default file upload behavior of reading small files into memory and large ones onto disk. They are located in django. core.files.uploadhandler.</p> <p><b>class MemoryFileUploadHandler</b></p> <p>File upload handler to stream uploads into memory (used for small files).</p> <p><b>class TemporaryFileUploadHandler</b></p> <p>Upload handler that streams data into a temporary file using <a href="index.html#page_1484"><i>TemporaryUploadedFile</i>.</a></p> <p id="page_1485" style="text-align:right"><b>Django Documentation, Release 5.2.dev20241127161328</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Writing custom upload handlers</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>class FileUploadHandler</b></p> <p>All file upload handlers should be subclasses of django.core.files.uploadhandler.FileUploadHandler. You can define upload handlers wherever you wish.</p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p><b>Required methods</b></p> <p style="text-align:center"> </p> <p>Custom file upload handlers must define the following methods:</p> <p>FileUploadHandler.<b>receive_data_chunk</b>(raw_data, start)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Receives a “chunk” of data from the file upload.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">raw_data is a bytestring containing the uploaded data.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">start is the position in the file where this raw_data chunk begins.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The data you return will get fed into the subsequent upload handlers’ receive_data_chunk methods. In this way, one handler can be a “filter” for other handlers.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Return None from receive_data_chunk to short-circuit remaining upload handlers from getting this chunk. This is useful if you’re storing the uploaded data yourself and don’t want future handlers to store a copy of the data.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">If you raise a StopUpload or a SkipFile exception, the upload will abort or the file will be completely skipped.</p> <p>FileUploadHandler.<b>file_complete</b>(file_size)</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">Called when a file has finished uploading.</p> <p style="margin-left:2em">The handler should return an UploadedFile object that will be stored in request.FILES.
